Name: concept_language_binding_ledger
Title: Where Does the Concept Meet the Language? A Causal Audit of Language Re-binding Failures in Multilingual Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual reasoning errors in non-dominant languages are not caused by faulty language-agnostic concept computation, but by a localized failure to *re-bind* the correct language identity onto correctly-computed concepts in late layers. We hypothesize that (a) concept computation and language re-binding are causally separable stages, (b) most cross-lingual reasoning failures occur at the re-binding stage rather than the concept stage, and (c) re-binding failure rate grows monotonically with script/typological distance while concept-stage accuracy stays roughly constant.
Related Work: Prior work established that LLMs form shared semantic/concept spaces in middle layers with language-specific decoding in late layers (Semantic Hub Hypothesis 2024; Separating Tongue from Thought 2024; Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025), that grammatical concepts are shared (Brinkmann et al. 2025), and that shared geometry extends to meta-cognitive difficulty (Civelli et al. 2026). Beneath the Surface of Consistency (2024) shows script similarity dominates knowledge sharing, and Tracing the Roots of Facts (2024) categorizes facts as independent/shared/transferred. However, all these works either (i) study single-token word translation or static concept probes, or (ii) demonstrate the two-stage structure descriptively. None decomposes *multi-step reasoning* errors in a language into a concept-stage vs. binding-stage causal attribution, nor quantifies what fraction of downstream task failures are attributable to each stage. Our contribution is a causal error-attribution framework ('binding ledger') applied to reasoning chains, distinguishing 'the model got the reasoning right but spoke the wrong language / degraded fluency' from 'the model genuinely reasoned wrong in this language.'
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs answer factual and reasoning questions far more reliably in their dominant pretraining language than in low-resource languages. Interpretability work suggests models compute in a shared, language-agnostic concept space in middle layers and then decode into a target language in late layers. We ask a sharper causal question: when a model fails a reasoning task in language X, does it fail because the concept-stage computation was wrong, or because the late-stage re-binding of the target language onto a correctly-computed concept failed? We introduce the Binding Ledger, a causal attribution procedure that, for each reasoning failure, uses activation patching to swap late-layer language-identity features and mid-layer concept representations between a correct dominant-language run and the failing target-language run, classifying each failure as concept-stage or binding-stage. We evaluate on multi-step arithmetic, multilingual factual QA (mLAMA/BMLAMA), and short chain-of-thought tasks across 20+ languages spanning several scripts and families in Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2. We predict that (1) a large fraction of failures in typologically-close, different-script languages are binding-stage, recoverable by a lightweight late-layer language-vector correction with no retraining; (2) concept-stage accuracy is far more uniform across languages than end-task accuracy, quantifying an upper bound on gains from fixing binding alone; and (3) binding failure scales with script/typological distance while concept accuracy does not. The framework yields both mechanistic insight and a cheap, training-free intervention for narrowing the multilingual gap.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Tasks: (i) multilingual factual QA from BMLAMA (existing; 6,792 balanced cloze QA pairs) and mLAMA (existing; ~44k templated facts over 53 languages), subsampled to 2,000 facts; (ii) a constructed multi-step arithmetic set of 1,000 items with operands verbalized as number words per language (built from scratch, ground truth exact by construction); (iii) short chain-of-thought word problems from MGSM (existing; 250 parallel problems). Languages: 20 spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families; English is the dominant anchor. Factual and arithmetic items exist in all 20; MGSM CoT is limited to its native languages plus machine-translation extensions with native-speaker spot-checks on 10% (this asymmetry is reported, not hidden). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, all weights frozen; greedy decoding, temperature 0. Stage localisation (run once per model, reused below): layer-wise language-identity linear probes (L2-regularised logistic regression, 3 seeds) and logit-lens locate the concept mid-layers and language-identity late-layers; per-language "language vectors" are the mean late-layer activation difference between that language and English. The concept/language layer split and probe accuracy are reported before any attribution.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- causal separability of the concept and re-binding stages): tests whether mid-layer concept computation and late-layer language re-binding can be moved independently, i.e. a double dissociation. Data: 500 parallel items answered correctly in English (from the sets above). Model: frozen, activation patching. Method: (a) patch the mid-layer concept representation from a DIFFERENT-content English item into the run and measure change in answer content and change in output language; (b) steer the late-layer language vector toward another language and measure change in output language and change in answer content. Decisive metric: the double-dissociation contrast -- (fraction of items whose answer CONTENT changes under the concept patch) versus (fraction whose OUTPUT LANGUAGE changes under the language steer), each paired with its off-target effect. Convincing result: the concept patch changes answer content in >=60% of items while changing output language in <=10%, AND the language steer changes output language in >=60% while changing answer content in <=10%. Indecision band: an off-target effect of 10-30% on either manipulation = stages only partially separable (attribution downstream is reported as noisier); off-target >30% on both = the stages are entangled and H1 is refuted. Negative result (moving one stage always drags the other) means the two-stage decomposition does not hold, invalidating the ledger.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the Binding Ledger: what fraction of failures are re-binding failures): tests claim (b), that most cross-lingual reasoning failures are binding-stage. Data: every target-language failure that has a corresponding correct English run (expected thousands of failure items pooled across tasks, models, and 20 languages; all used). Model: frozen, patching. Method, per failure: CONCEPT-STAGE test -- patch the mid-layer concept representation from the correct English run into the failing target run; if the answer becomes correct in the target language, label the failure concept-stage. BINDING-STAGE test -- keep the target-language concept representation and apply the late-layer language-vector correction (the training-free re-binding fix); if the answer recovers, label it binding-stage. Cases recovered by neither or both are reported separately. Decisive metric: fraction of failures classified binding-stage, pooled across the 20 languages (and reported per language). Convincing result: binding-stage fraction >60% pooled. Indecision band: 45-55% cannot support the word "most" and is reported as "substantial but not a majority"; <45% means concept-stage failures dominate and (b) is refuted. Negative result (majority concept-stage) means the cross-lingual gap is largely genuine reasoning failure, not re-binding.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- binding failure scales with distance while concept accuracy stays flat): tests claim (c) in both halves. Data: the per-language binding-stage fractions from Experiment 2, plus concept-stage accuracy = task accuracy achievable when the concept stage is forced correct (English concept patched in), measured per language. Predictors: lang2vec typological distance to English and a binary same-script indicator. Decisive metric: Spearman(binding-stage fraction, typological distance) with bootstrap CIs, AND the across-language spread (max-minus-min) of concept-stage accuracy versus the spread of end-task accuracy. Convincing result: Spearman >=0.5 with its 95% CI lower bound above 0.2, different-script languages showing higher binding fractions than same-script ones, AND concept-stage accuracy spread <=10 percentage points (pp) while end-task accuracy spread >=30 pp (concept computation roughly uniform, end-task not). Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.5 = weak monotonic scaling (reported as suggestive); <0.2 = no scaling, refuting the first half of (c). Concept-accuracy spread 10-20 pp = partially uniform; >20 pp = concept accuracy varies nearly as much as end-task accuracy, refuting the second half of (c). Negative result (no distance relationship, or concept accuracy as variable as end-task accuracy) refutes H3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. The clean two-stage (concept then binding) decomposition may not hold for all models or deeper reasoning, making attribution noisy; we mitigate by validating the split with probes before attribution. 2. Activation patching across languages can produce degenerate outputs (as noted by When Meanings Meet 2024, some 'gains' are behavioral shifts like copying vs translating); we include manual/automatic error analysis to avoid mislabeling. 3. Tokenizer differences across scripts complicate representation alignment for concept patching; we restrict concept swaps to items with matched answer-token structure or use last-token-of-answer representations. 4. The training-free intervention may trade fluency for correctness; we report both. 5. Findings may be model-specific; using three model families addresses generality but not exhaustively. 6. Low-resource-language ground truth translations may contain noise, affecting labels; we use human-verified benchmark subsets where possible.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty is not the two-stage shared-concept/late-decoding story, which is already in the prior work family, but the causal attribution of multilingual reasoning failures into concept-stage vs re-binding-stage and quantifying the fraction of failures explained by each. The closest prior work already supports the mechanism descriptively; the delta is the move to multi-step reasoning, failure-level causal accounting, and an intervention-friendly ledger. That is non-trivial, but still an incremental extension of an active line rather than a wholly new mechanism or task.

impact.reasoning: The underlying phenomenon is important: why multilingual LLMs underperform in non-dominant languages, and whether the gap is a fixable late-decoding problem or a genuine reasoning deficit. That matters to multilingual NLP, interpretability, and inference-time repair work. If the result holds, it could shift attention from retraining toward cheap late-layer interventions; if it fails, it still tells researchers that the gap is deeper than re-binding. Serious researchers would likely care either way.

As written, it is plausible for a serious venue if executed well, but not yet airtight.

Name: latent_language_suppression
Title: The Ghost in the Machine Translation: Automatic Co-activation and Active Suppression of Non-target Languages in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Like the bilingual brain, multilingual LLMs automatically co-activate the non-target language's answer as a latent competitor during monolingual generation, and must *actively suppress* it in late layers. We hypothesize that (a) the non-target (typically English) answer is linearly decodable from internal states even during purely target-language generation, (b) a specific, identifiable late-layer suppression mechanism damps this competitor, and (c) both the strength of co-activation and the failure of suppression (causing code-switching / wrong-language leakage errors) scale with typological/script distance between the target language and the model's dominant language.
Related Work: Interpretability work frames LLMs as computing in a language-agnostic concept space (Semantic Hub 2024) and 'transitioning' to the target language in final layers, with failures at this transition causing inconsistency (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Paths Not Taken 2025). These works model the dominant language as an intermediate *pivot* that is translated away, and non-target languages as simply absent. Cross-lingual knowledge-conflict work (CLEAR 2026) studies conflict between explicit external evidence, not internal automatic co-activation. In contrast, decades of cognitive neuroscience (Language Conflict in the Bilingual Brain 2008; RLD & Bilingual Control 2019) show non-target languages are *automatically and involuntarily co-activated* and must be *actively inhibited*, with cost scaling with relative language distance. No ML paper tests whether LLMs implement an analogous automatic-activation-plus-inhibition control mechanism, nor operationalizes 'suppression cost' as a measurable, causally-manipulable circuit. We reframe cross-lingual leakage errors not as a passive translation failure but as an active *interference-control* failure, and provide the first causal characterization of a suppression mechanism in LLMs.
Abstract: Multilingual language models answer questions in many languages, and interpretability work describes an English-centric internal pipeline that is 'translated away' before output. We propose a fundamentally different, cognitively-inspired lens: drawing on bilingualism neuroscience, we hypothesize that the non-target language is not passively absent but *automatically co-activated* as a latent competitor, which the model must *actively suppress* to produce fluent monolingual text. We test three claims. First, during purely target-language generation, the correct answer token in the model's dominant language remains linearly decodable from hidden states well into late layers (co-activation). Second, there exists an identifiable suppression mechanism (specific late-layer attention heads / directions) that damps the competitor; ablating it induces code-switching and wrong-language leakage. Third, both co-activation strength and suppression failure scale with typological and script distance from the dominant language, mirroring the neuroscience 'relative language distance' effect. We operationalize a per-item Suppression Cost (logit-space distance the competitor is pushed down over late layers) and a Leakage Rate (wrong-language output). Experiments span multilingual factual QA (mLAMA/BMLAMA) and translation-free generation across 20+ languages and Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2. We predict a clean dose-response between lang2vec distance and suppression cost, causal identification of a suppression circuit, and that steering along the recovered suppression direction reduces code-switching in low-resource languages at inference with no retraining. This bridges cognitive theories of bilingual control with mechanistic interpretability and yields a training-free fix for language leakage.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Tasks: multilingual factual QA (mLAMA + BMLAMA, existing) subsampled to 2,000 short-answer items, plus 1,000 open-ended target-language generation prompts (constructed), each with a known dominant-language (English) reference answer token. Languages: 20+ spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families; English is the dominant language. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, all weights frozen; greedy decoding, temperature 0, 3 paraphrase seeds. Every output is passed through an automatic language-identifier (with human spot-checks on 5%) so co-activation is measured only while the surface output is verified to be in the target language. Two quantities recur: Suppression Cost = the drop in the dominant-language competitor answer's logit RANK from its peak-activation layer to the output layer; Leakage Rate = fraction of outputs that switch wholly or partly (code-switch) into the dominant language.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- automatic co-activation of the dominant-language answer): tests claim (a), that the dominant-language answer is decodable during purely target-language generation. Data/model as Setup. Method: at each layer apply logit-lens and trained linear probes (L2 logistic regression, 3 seeds, held-out items) to detect the dominant-language (English) answer token while the output is confirmed target-language. Decisive metric: layer-wise decodability of the English answer (probe accuracy and logit-lens rank), contrasted against two baselines -- decodability of an UNRELATED third-language answer and of a random token (chance). Convincing result: English-answer decodability exceeds the unrelated-language baseline by >=15 percentage points (pp) in mid-to-late layers across most languages -- co-activation is specific to the dominant language, not a generic shared-concept effect. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above the unrelated-language baseline = weak co-activation (reported as such); <5 pp = no dominant-specific co-activation and claim (a) is refuted. Negative result (English answer no more decodable than an unrelated language) means apparent co-activation is just the shared concept space, refuting (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- an identifiable late-layer suppression mechanism): tests claim (b), that a specific late-layer mechanism actively damps the competitor. Data/model as Setup, frozen, activation patching and attention-head attribution. Method: (1) track the competitor logit rank across late layers to compute Suppression Cost and verify the competitor is actively pushed DOWN after a peak (not merely never boosted); (2) localise the suppressing components via head/MLP attribution and patching, ablate them, and measure the rise in competitor logit and the change in Leakage Rate; (3) recover a suppression direction (mean activation difference between clean and leakage-prone runs) and AMPLIFY it, testing the reverse effect. Decisive metric: increase in Leakage Rate when the identified suppression components are ablated, relative to ablating a size-matched RANDOM set of components. Convincing result: ablating the identified components raises Leakage Rate by >=20 pp over random-component ablation and raises the competitor logit, a small set (<=5% of heads or a single direction) accounts for the majority of the effect, AND amplifying the recovered direction reduces baseline Leakage Rate -- a bidirectionally functional suppression mechanism. Indecision band: leakage increase of 8-20 pp over random = diffuse/partial suppression (reported as a direction-based, not head-based, account); <8 pp, or a competitor that never actively drops (Suppression Cost approximately 0), = no identifiable active suppression and (b) is refuted. Negative result (ablation matches random, or no active push-down) refutes the suppression-mechanism claim.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- co-activation and suppression failure scale with distance): tests claim (c). Data: per-language co-activation strength (Experiment 1), Suppression Cost, and Leakage Rate (Experiment 2). Predictors: lang2vec typological distance to English and a binary same-script indicator. Decisive metric: Spearman(co-activation strength, distance) and Spearman(Leakage Rate, distance), with bootstrap CIs. Convincing result: Spearman >=0.5 with 95% CI lower bound above 0.2 for BOTH co-activation and Leakage Rate, distant/different-script languages showing higher co-activation and higher leakage. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.5 = weak monotonic scaling (suggestive only); <0.2 for either = no scaling and that half of (c) is refuted. Negative result (no distance relationship) refutes the dose-response claim.

Experiment 4 (H1/H2 -- is the competitor the DOMINANT or the typologically NEAREST high-resource language): tests the "typically English" qualifier in (a) and the identity of the suppression target, so distance in Experiment 3 is not confounded. Data: target languages each paired with the dominant language (English) AND their typologically nearest high-resource language (e.g. Spanish for Catalan, Hindi for Marathi). Model as Setup. Method: repeat the Experiment 1 co-activation probe and the Experiment 2 Suppression Cost for both candidate competitors. Decisive metric: per target language, dominant-competitor co-activation/Suppression Cost minus nearest-competitor co-activation/Suppression Cost. Convincing result: the dominant language (English) shows higher co-activation and Suppression Cost than the nearest high-resource language by >=10 pp for the majority of target languages, supporting "typically English". Indecision band: the two competitors within 5-10 pp = dual competitor (reported as co-activation of both); nearest > dominant = the competitor is the nearest high-resource language, qualifying (a). Negative result (nearest dominates) replaces the English-centric reading with a nearest-language account -- an informative correction rather than a null.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. The 'competitor' might be decodable simply because the concept space is shared, not because of genuine co-activation of a specific language's token; we control by comparing dominant-language decodability against unrelated languages and by testing whether it is actively suppressed (dynamic drop) rather than merely present. 2. Logit-lens/probe decodability can reflect the readout basis rather than a used representation; we require the causal ablation (leakage induction) to confirm functional relevance. 3. Suppression may be diffuse rather than localized to identifiable heads, weakening the circuit story; we report degree of localization honestly and fall back on a direction-based (not head-based) account. 4. Leakage may be rare in strong models, limiting statistical power; we include low-resource languages and adversarial prompts to elicit it. 5. Distinguishing 'dominant language' from 'typologically nearest high-resource language' as the suppression target requires careful language selection; Experiment 4 is designed for this. 6. Findings may vary across model families; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty is in the *active suppression* framing plus the measurable Suppression Cost / distance-dose-response claim. However, the co-activation and steering/localization parts are heavily pre-empted by recent multilingual steering and language-control work, and the competitor-decoding claim is close to shared-concept-space findings. The main delta over prior work is the dynamic causal story (boost then push-down) and the bilingual-inhibition analogy, not a wholly new mechanism or task.

Name: storage_topology_via_edit_propagation
Title: Shared or Duplicated? Using Knowledge Edits to Map the Cross-Lingual Storage Topology of Facts, and Predicting Transfer Before Editing
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs store facts along a spectrum from language-shared (single parameter locus serving all languages) to language-duplicated (redundant per-language copies). Which regime a given fact occupies determines whether an edit in one language propagates to others, and this regime is measurable by an intrinsic PRE-edit mechanistic signature (overlap of causally-important components across languages). Consequently, cross-lingual edit propagation is predictable per-fact and per-language-pair from this signature alone, without performing the edit.
Related Work: A large body of work shows factual edits fail to propagate across languages, especially across script families (Cross-Lingual Knowledge Editing 2024, Bi-ZsRE; XME 2024; MLaKE 2024), and proposes better editing methods (MEMLA, LU-LAFNs via language-agnostic factual neurons, LangEdit null-space, MEMAT attention editing, ReMaKE retrieval). ECLeKTic (2025) shows SOTA models fail to share knowledge across languages behaviorally. These works either (i) measure propagation post-hoc as a benchmark, or (ii) propose fixes; LU-LAFNs identifies shared neurons but uses them only to improve editing. None treats editing as a causal probe to reverse-engineer a per-fact storage topology, nor establishes that an intrinsic PRE-edit mechanistic signature predicts which facts/language-pairs will transfer. Our contribution is diagnostic and predictive: a taxonomy (shared vs. duplicated vs. hybrid) grounded in causal tracing, a demonstration that edit-propagation patterns causally validate this taxonomy, and a cheap pre-edit predictor of transferability that generalizes across facts, languages, and models.
Abstract: Editing a fact in one language of a multilingual LLM often fails to update the same fact when queried in another language, particularly across different scripts. Prior work treats this as a benchmark failure and proposes better editing algorithms. We instead use knowledge editing as a causal probe to reverse-engineer how facts are stored across languages. We hypothesize a storage spectrum: some facts live at a single, language-shared parameter locus that serves all languages, while others are redundantly duplicated into language-specific copies; a fact's position on this spectrum dictates whether an edit propagates. We first derive, for each fact, an intrinsic PRE-edit signature by causal tracing (activation patching) the components most responsible for recalling the fact independently in each language, and computing their cross-language overlap (a sharedness score). We then perform locate-and-edit updates in a single source language and measure recovery in every other language, building a propagation matrix. Our central claim is that the pre-edit sharedness score predicts post-edit propagation per fact and per language-pair, with high overlap yielding transfer and low overlap yielding language-locked edits. We test on mLAMA and Bi-ZsRE across 12+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. We further show sharedness correlates with typological/script distance, that many facts are hybrid (shared for near languages, duplicated for far ones), and that editing at the causally-shared locus (rather than the default) improves propagation. This yields a mechanistic map of cross-lingual knowledge and a training-free predictor of transferability.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Data: parallel factual triples from mLAMA (existing; ~44k templated facts over 53 languages) and Bi-ZsRE (existing bilingual edit benchmark), subsampled to 1,500 subject-relation-object facts with clean single-token or short objects. Languages: 12 spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels; English is the reference. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen except during edits; greedy, temperature 0. Locate-and-edit uses ROME and MEMIT with the authors' default hyperparameters; causal tracing uses activation patching and causal mediation (ROME-style corrupted-restored runs). Editing 1,500 facts x 12 source languages with per-fact tracing is heavy but each ROME edit and trace is seconds-scale, keeping the whole suite within a single-GPU-week budget per model.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- a measurable, reproducible pre-edit cross-lingual sharedness signature): tests that facts occupy a real, non-degenerate storage spectrum readable before any edit. Data/model as Setup. Method: for each fact, causal-trace independently in each language to find the top-k components (MLP/attention) whose restoration recovers the object token; define per-language-pair sharedness = Jaccard overlap (and rank correlation) of those causally-important components; aggregate to a per-fact sharedness profile. Decisive metric: the across-fact distribution of sharedness AND its stability across the two tracing methods (patching vs causal mediation), measured as Spearman between the two methods' sharedness scores. Convincing result: sharedness spans a wide, non-degenerate range (interquartile range >0.3 on the 0-1 Jaccard scale) and the two tracing methods agree at Spearman >=0.5 -- the signature reflects storage structure, not tracing noise. Secondary: sharedness correlates negatively with lang2vec distance and is lower across scripts (the hybrid pattern: shared for near languages, duplicated for far). Indecision band: method agreement 0.3-0.5 = usable but noisy (downstream claims carry the caveat); <0.3 = the signature is a tracing artifact, undermining H1; a near-constant distribution (IQR <0.1) = no topology variation, refuting the spectrum. Negative result (no reproducible variation) means there is no measurable storage topology.

Experiment 2 (H3 -- predicting edit propagation from the pre-edit signature, core test): tests that cross-lingual propagation is predictable per fact and per language-pair from the pre-edit signature ALONE, without editing. Data/model as Setup. Method: apply ROME/MEMIT to change each fact in a single source language and query every target language, recording edit success (source), cross-lingual propagation (target reliability), and locality (unrelated facts unchanged); condition all analyses on successful source-language edits. Train a predictor mapping the Experiment 1 pre-edit sharedness signature to per-pair propagation, on a fact split, and test on held-out facts AND held-out language pairs. Decisive metric: AUC for predicting transfer vs no-transfer on held-out facts/pairs from the pre-edit signature alone (with Spearman(sharedness, propagation reliability) reported alongside). Convincing result: held-out AUC >=0.75 and Spearman >=0.5, generalising to held-out language pairs. Indecision band: AUC 0.6-0.75 = weak predictor (reported as partial); AUC <0.6 (near chance 0.5) = the signature does not predict propagation, refuting H3. Negative result (chance-level prediction) refutes the pre-edit predictability claim.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- edit locus causally governs propagation, validating the topology): tests that the regime is causally real -- editing at the shared locus propagates, editing a single-language locus of a duplicated fact stays language-locked. Data: high-sharedness (shared) vs low-sharedness (duplicated) facts from Experiment 1, matched on source-edit success. Model as Setup. Method: for each fact edit at (i) a single language's own causal locus, (ii) the union / most-shared locus, and (iii) the default ROME locus; measure cross-lingual propagation and locality. Decisive metric: propagation reliability from editing the shared/union locus versus a single-language locus, contrasted between shared and duplicated facts (the interaction is the evidence). Convincing result: for shared facts, editing the shared locus yields >=20 pp higher cross-lingual propagation than a single-language locus, while duplicated facts require multi-locus editing and single-locus edits stay language-locked, with locality preserved (unrelated facts change <5%). Indecision band: shared-locus advantage 8-20 pp = partial causal support; <8 pp = edit locus does not matter and the topology is not the causal propagation mechanism, refuting H2. Negative result (propagation independent of edit locus) refutes the causal reality of the storage topology.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Causal tracing localization is noisy and can be diffuse, weakening the sharedness signal; we mitigate with multiple tracing methods (patching + causal mediation) and report stability. 2. Tokenization differences across scripts complicate identifying comparable causal components and matching object tokens; we restrict to facts with clean object tokenization and use last-token-of-object representations. 3. Locate-and-edit methods have their own artifacts (may fail to edit at all in low-resource languages), confounding propagation with edit success; we condition analyses on successful source-language edits. 4. Sharedness and propagation could both simply track resource level rather than a genuine storage topology; we control by matching facts across resource levels and testing predictor generalization to held-out language pairs. 5. The shared/duplicated dichotomy may be a continuum with no clean clusters; we present it as a spectrum and report continuous predictive power rather than forcing discrete classes. 6. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims requiring novelty are: (1) multilingual facts occupy a shared/duplicated/hybrid storage spectrum; (2) a pre-edit mechanistic signature from cross-language causal-component overlap can measure that spectrum; (3) this signature predicts cross-lingual edit propagation per fact and language pair without editing; (4) editing at the shared locus improves propagation; and (5) typological/script distance relates to sharedness. From the proposal plus search summary, the taxonomy itself is not new: prior work already categorizes multilingual factual storage into similar shared/independent/transferred regimes, and language-agnostic factual neurons have already been used for cross-lingual editing. The main non-trivial delta is the predictive framing: using pre-edit causal overlap as an intrinsic predictor of transfer, with held-out fact/pair generalization, and treating edits as a causal probe rather than only a benchmark/fix. That is meaningfully different, but it sits close to existing multilingual editing and mechanistic-localization work. Novelty will hinge on clearly beating simple baselines such as subject-token similarity and on showing the predictor is not just rediscovering prior shared-neuron effects.

impact.reasoning: The underlying problem is predicting when an update made in one language of a multilingual LLM will or will not transfer to other languages. People who care include multilingual knowledge-editing researchers, interpretability researchers, and model maintainers deploying global systems. The strongest case is: if transferability can be predicted before editing, practitioners can avoid wasted edits and researchers gain a mechanistic handle on multilingual knowledge sharing. This is a real problem, not a curiosity, because multilingual consistency matters for maintenance and safety. Name: reasoning_language_mismatch
Title: Thinking in One Language, Writing in Another: Measuring the Cost of Surface-Latent Reasoning-Language Mismatch in Multilingual CoT
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs have a per-item 'latent reasoning language' (the language whose token representations dominate hidden states during the reasoning steps), which is often but not always English. Reasoning accuracy is governed less by the surface language of the prompt and more by the *mismatch* between the surface CoT language the model is forced to write in and its latent reasoning language: the larger this mismatch (measured in the model's own representation space and by typological distance), the greater the 'reasoning drag' (accuracy loss). Consequently, per-item alignment of the surface CoT language to the model's latent language should improve multilingual reasoning more than uniformly forcing English or the prompt language.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs route reasoning through an English-centric latent space (Do Llamas Work in English? 2024; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English? 2025; Transfer Neurons Hypothesis 2025), that latent multilingual reasoning is English-aligned but uneven (Large Reasoning Models Are Not Yet Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026), that language mixing in traces reflects internal preferences and constrained decoding to Latin/Han helps (Language Mixing in Reasoning Models 2025), and that ablating language-specific components boosts reasoning (When Less Language is More 2025). All of these characterize the latent language as a global, largely fixed English-centric pivot, and treat improvements as either removing language (ablation) or forcing a single reasoning script for everyone. None (i) measures a *per-item* latent reasoning language that varies across items and languages, (ii) causally quantifies a 'mismatch cost' between the forced surface CoT language and the model's own per-item latent language, or (iii) proposes per-item surface-language selection aligned to the latent language rather than one global choice. We reframe multilingual CoT failure as a surface-latent language *alignment* problem and provide a causal, item-level account plus a training-free per-item intervention.
Abstract: Multilingual language models are widely believed to 'think in English' internally while writing chain-of-thought (CoT) in the prompt's language. We challenge the assumption that this latent reasoning language is a fixed, global, English-centric pivot. Instead, we hypothesize that each reasoning problem induces a *latent reasoning language*—the language whose token representations dominate hidden states during the reasoning steps—that varies across items, and that multilingual reasoning accuracy is driven by the *mismatch* between the surface language the model is forced to verbalize CoT in and this per-item latent language. We introduce two measurements: (1) a per-item Latent Language Profile, obtained by applying logit-lens/probing to hidden states at reasoning-step token positions to identify which language's tokens are most decodable; and (2) a Mismatch Cost, the accuracy change when the model is constrained (via constrained decoding / instruction) to reason in a surface language that agrees vs. disagrees with its latent profile. We predict Mismatch Cost grows with the representational and typological distance between surface and latent languages. We validate on multilingual math (MGSM), commonsense (XCOPA), and multi-hop QA across 15+ languages and Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, and a distilled reasoning model. Finally we test a training-free per-item intervention that selects the surface CoT language matching the model's measured latent language, comparing against uniform-English, prompt-language, and forced-Latin/Han baselines. The framework yields a mechanistic, item-level view of where language helps or hurts reasoning and a cheap, self-selected multilingual reasoning strategy.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Tasks: MGSM multilingual grade-school math (existing; 250 parallel problems), XCOPA commonsense (existing; ~500 items/language), and a translated 2-hop QA subset (300 items). Languages: 15 spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families; items are parallel translations so true difficulty is fixed across languages (MT plus native-speaker spot-checks on 10%). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (a reasoning-distilled model where language mixing is documented). All weights frozen; chain-of-thought at temperature 0, 3 prompt seeds. Language-ID probes are L2 logistic regressions trained on held-out data, validated by cross-language transfer accuracy before use.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- a per-item latent reasoning language that varies across items): tests that the latent reasoning language is item-dependent, not a single globally fixed pivot. Data/model as Setup. Method: for each item run CoT and, at the token positions of reasoning steps, apply logit-lens and the trained language-ID probes at mid-to-late layers to get a per-item distribution over which language's step/answer tokens are most decodable; take the dominant latent language per item. Decisive metric: the fraction of items whose latent language differs from the model's own MODAL latent language (across-item variability), tested against a globally-fixed null. Convincing result: >=20% of items have a latent language different from the modal one and the variation is systematic (e.g. shifts with task or target language), rejecting the globally-fixed null. Indecision band: 8-20% non-modal = weak variability, mostly a global pivot (reported as such, with the non-English fraction and its predictive value still a contribution); <8% = the latent language is effectively globally fixed and H1's per-item-variation claim collapses to the known global-pivot picture. Negative result (latent language essentially always English) refutes per-item variation; the reasoning-distilled model, with more documented language mixing, is the decisive test case.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- Mismatch Cost, causal and distance-scaled): tests that accuracy is driven by the surface-latent language mismatch, growing with distance, and that the effect is internal rather than a surface artifact. Data/model as Setup. Method: for each item elicit CoT under surface languages that (a) match the measured latent language, (b) equal the prompt language, (c) equal English, (d) are maximally distant, enforcing the reasoning-step language via constrained decoding; Mismatch Cost = accuracy(matched) - accuracy(mismatched). Causal control: steer late-layer language vectors to align/misalign the INTERNAL language while holding the surface language fixed, isolating internal alignment from surface tokens. Decisive metric: Mismatch Cost in exact-match accuracy points, and Spearman(Mismatch Cost, distance) where distance is both representational (cosine of mean reasoning-step activations) and lang2vec typological. Convincing result: matched exceeds mismatched by >=3 accuracy points on average, Spearman(Mismatch Cost, distance) >=0.4 with 95% CI lower bound above 0.15, AND the steering control reproduces the accuracy change when only the internal language is altered -- the latent language is functional, not merely decodable. Indecision band: matched advantage 1-3 points = weak (reported as suggestive); <1 point = no mismatch cost, refuting H2; a null steering control (internal alignment has no accuracy effect) means decodability is epiphenomenal and the causal claim is refuted even if the behavioral gap holds. Negative result (no accuracy difference by match) refutes the mismatch account.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- per-item alignment beats uniform language choices): tests that selecting the surface CoT language per item to match the measured latent language improves reasoning more than any single global choice. Data/model as Setup. Method: at inference measure the latent language from a short forced CoT prefix, then generate the full CoT in that language. Systems compared: per-item alignment vs uniform-English, prompt-language, forced-Latin/Han, and an oracle (best language per item, upper bound). Decisive metric: exact-match accuracy averaged over the 15 languages (with extra compute and output-language fidelity reported). Convincing result: per-item alignment beats the best fixed baseline (English or prompt-language) by >=2 accuracy points and closes >=50% of the gap to the oracle, at <2x inference compute. Indecision band: 0.5-2 point gain over the best fixed baseline = marginal (the full comparison and oracle gap are reported); <0.5 point = no benefit over a fixed choice, refuting H3. Negative result (a fixed choice matches or beats per-item alignment) refutes the actionable per-item-alignment claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Logit-lens/probe decodability at reasoning-step positions may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally-used latent language; we require the causal steering control (in Exp. 2) to confirm functional relevance rather than relying on decodability alone. 2. The per-item latent language may in practice be almost always English for some models, collapsing the hypothesis to a global-pivot story; even so, quantifying the small non-English fraction and its predictive value for accuracy is a contribution, and we include a reasoning-distilled model where language mixing (hence latent variability) is documented to be larger. 3. Constrained decoding can degrade fluency and confound accuracy with generation difficulty; we report output-language fidelity and use steering as a fluency-preserving alternative. 4. Tokenization/script differences complicate cross-language logit-lens comparison; we restrict probes to answer/step tokens with clean tokenization and validate probes with held-out data. 5. The per-item intervention adds a short extra forward pass; we report its compute overhead and compare to the oracle to bound achievable gains. 6. Findings may be model-specific; four models across families and one reasoning model address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims requiring novelty are: (1) multilingual LLMs have a per-item latent reasoning language rather than a fixed global English pivot; (2) accuracy is governed by mismatch between forced surface CoT language and that latent language; (3) mismatch cost scales with representational/typological distance; (4) causal steering can isolate internal-language effects from mere output-language effects; and (5) per-item surface-language selection improves reasoning over uniform language choices. From the proposal plus search summary, the most defensible novelty is the item-level latent-language measurement and the causal mismatch-cost framing. However, prior language-mixing work already shows item/step-level variation and probe-guided language-switch interventions, so the intervention itself is close to existing work. The actual delta over closest prior work is whole-item latent-language profiling plus causal quantification of surface-latent mismatch, not the broader claim that language alignment matters.

Name: cultural_frame_register
Title: Which Answer Is True Here? A Mechanistic Study of How Multilingual LLMs Select Among Culturally-Relative Truths
Short Hypothesis: For claims whose truth value is genuinely relative to a cultural/geographic frame (e.g., 'people drive on the left', 'the head of state is a monarch', 'the school year starts in spring'), multilingual LLMs store multiple mutually-contradictory candidate answers simultaneously and select among them via an internal 'frame register' set in mid layers. We hypothesize that (a) the query language acts as an implicit, weak frame selector that competes with explicit textual frame cues, (b) this selection is mediated by a small, causally-identifiable set of directions/components separable from the answer-content computation, and (c) selection failures (giving the answer correct for the wrong frame) scale with typological/script distance between the query language and the language canonically associated with the intended frame.
Related Work: Recent interpretability work localizes 'culture neurons' separable from language neurons (Isolating Culture Neurons 2025), finds cultural localization in middle layers steerable by cultural vectors (Localized Cultural Knowledge is Conserved 2025), documents a Cultural-Linguistic Synergy where in-language cultural queries activate more specialized neurons (Disentangling Language and Culture 2025), shows cross-lingual alignment causes cultural erasure fixable by layer-specific Surgical Steering (Rethinking Cross-lingual Alignment 2025), and finds internal paths are more language- than content-driven (Language over Content 2025). Factual-storage work (Tracing the Roots of Facts 2024; Lost in Multilinguality 2025) categorizes facts as shared/independent and finds a language-agnostic concept space with late-layer decoding. All of this treats cultural knowledge as static localized content or measures bias toward one canonical (often Western) answer. None studies claims with NO single correct answer—where multiple contradictory answers are simultaneously true under different frames—nor characterizes the mechanism that *selects* among stored competing answers as a function of an explicit-vs-implicit (language) frame cue. We reframe cultural knowledge as a frame-conditioned selection problem and provide the first causal account of a 'frame register' plus a diagnostic of when language overrides explicit context.
Abstract: Many claims about the world have no universal truth value: whether people drive on the left, whether the head of state is a monarch, or when the school year begins depends on the cultural or geographic frame in which the question is asked. Multilingual LLMs must therefore not merely recall facts but *select* which stored, frame-dependent answer applies. We investigate this selection mechanism. We construct FRAME-REL, a controlled dataset of culturally-relative claims for which several countries have known, mutually-contradictory ground-truth answers, and probe models under two orthogonal frame cues: an explicit textual cue (naming the country) and an implicit cue (the query language). We first show that multiple contradictory candidate answers are simultaneously linearly decodable from mid-layer hidden states before selection collapses to one output, evidencing parallel storage rather than a single canonical answer. Using activation patching, we localize a compact 'frame register'—mid-layer components that, when swapped between a same-question run under frame A and under frame B, flip the selected answer without altering answer content. We then quantify a competition between explicit and implicit (language) cues: how often does asking in language L override an explicit country cue, and does this override scale with typological/script distance between L and the frame's canonical language? Experiments span 15+ languages and Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. We further test a training-free intervention that steers the frame register to fix mismatched selections without harming fluency, and compare against explicit-prompting baselines. The work recasts multilingual cultural knowledge as frame-conditioned selection and delivers a causal, controllable account.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Dataset FRAME-REL (constructed): culturally-relative claim templates with verifiable per-country ground truth that differs across countries -- driving side, monarchy vs republic, currency, primary-school start season, calendar/new-year timing, measurement units, and plug voltage. Each claim type has >=6 countries with mutually-contradictory answers and their canonical languages; ~40 claim types x countries give ~2,500 base items, each rendered in 15 query languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families, crossed with the explicit country cue present vs absent (all items used; per-country answers native-speaker validated). A matched set of ordinary single-answer factual claims serves as a control that should show NO parallel storage and NO flippable register. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen; greedy, temperature 0, 3 paraphrase seeds; short answer tokens, last-token-of-answer representations (tokenisation statistics reported).

Experiment 1 (H1 -- parallel storage of contradictory answers and a compact, separable frame register): tests that several frame-dependent answers are stored simultaneously and that a small, causally-identifiable mid-layer register selects among them, separable from answer content. Data/model as Setup. Method: (A) parallel-storage probe -- logit-lens and per-layer linear probes test whether multiple countries' answers are simultaneously decodable in mid layers before the output emerges, contrasted with the single-answer factual control; (B) locate the register -- run the identical question under explicit frame A (country A) vs frame B (country B), producing different answers, then activation-patch mid-layer components from the A-run into the B-run and find the minimal set whose patching flips the selected answer to A's while the set of candidate answers is preserved; (C) separability/steering -- measure overlap of the register with previously reported language-specific and culture-specific neurons, and test that a per-country frame direction (mean activation difference at the register) steers selection when injected. Decisive metric: the patching flip rate (selection changes to the donor frame with content preserved), reported with the size/location of the patched set, alongside mid-layer co-decodability of contradictory answers. Convincing result: >=2 contradictory answers are co-decodable in mid layers well above the single-answer control; patching a compact set (a few components, <5% of the layer's units) flips selection in >=50% of A/B pairs while the candidate set is preserved; and the register overlaps little (<30% Jaccard) with pure language/culture neurons. Indecision band: co-decodability only marginally above the control, or flip rate 25-50% = a diffuse register (reported as a direction-based, not compact-component, account); flip <25% or no parallel co-decodability = no frame-register selection mechanism and H1 is refuted. Negative result (a single answer stored, patching cannot flip selection) refutes parallel storage and the register.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the query language competes with the explicit frame cue): tests claim (a), that the query language is an implicit frame selector competing with explicit textual cues. Data: items with the explicit country cue set to country C but posed in language L (the canonical language of a DIFFERENT country D). Model as Setup. Decisive metric: language-override rate = fraction of outputs matching D (language wins) rather than C (explicit wins), with a neither bucket reported. Convincing result: language-override rate >=15% -- the query language measurably shifts selection even against an explicit country cue. Indecision band: 5-15% = weak implicit selection (reported as such); <5% = the query language does not compete with explicit cues and (a) is refuted. Negative result (the explicit cue always wins) means language is not a frame selector.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- selection failure scales with distance): tests claim (c). Data: per-language language-override rate (Experiment 2) and frame-selection error rate. Predictors: lang2vec typological distance and a binary same-script indicator between the query language L and the intended frame's canonical language. Decisive metric: Spearman(language-override / selection-error, distance) with bootstrap CIs. Convincing result: Spearman >=0.5 with 95% CI lower bound above 0.2, distant/different-script languages showing more wrong-frame selection. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.5 = weak scaling (suggestive); <0.2 = no scaling and (c) is refuted. Negative result (no distance relationship) refutes the dose-response claim. As an applied check tied to H1, steering the frame register to the intended frame on mismatched items is compared against an explicit-country-prompt and a translate-to-English baseline, reporting selection-correction rate, fluency (perplexity), and answer-content preservation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Ground truth for culturally-relative claims can be ambiguous or change over time; we restrict to unambiguous, stable, verifiable claims (driving side, monarchy status, plug voltage) and have annotators validate per-country answers. 2. Logit-lens/probe decodability of multiple candidates may reflect the readout basis rather than functional parallel storage; we require the causal patching flip (in Exp. 1) to confirm functional relevance. 3. The frame register may be diffuse rather than compact, weakening the localization story; we report degree of localization honestly and fall back to a direction-based account. 4. Some models may simply always default to the canonical/Western answer regardless of frame, collapsing selection; even so, quantifying the near-absence of frame sensitivity and its language dependence is a contribution, and multiple models mitigate this. 5. Tokenization differences across scripts complicate cross-language probing and answer matching; we restrict to claims with clean, short answer tokens and use last-token-of-answer representations. 6. Steering may trade content preservation for correct selection; we report both. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty: (1) culturally-relative claims should be modeled as frame-conditioned truth selection rather than ordinary factual recall; (2) multilingual LLMs simultaneously represent multiple contradictory but frame-valid answers before generation; (3) a compact mid-layer 'frame register' causally selects among those answers and is separable from answer-content computation; (4) query language functions as an implicit frame cue that can compete with explicit frame text; (5) failures increase with language/frame distance. From the proposal plus search summary, the strongest novelty is the problem definition and mechanistic selection account. Prior work already localizes culture/language neurons and behaviorally shows prompt language and explicit framing affect outputs, so H2 alone is not novel. The actual delta over closest prior work is: moving from static cultural knowledge localization and behavioral framing effects to a causal mechanism for selecting among multiple simultaneously valid contradictory answers, tested on a controlled dataset of no-single-truth claims. That is non-trivial, though the 'compact register' claim is ambitious and only moderately separated from existing culture-neuron work unless the selector/content distinction is convincingly shown.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether multilingual LLMs can choose the correct culturally/geographically framed answer when multiple contradictory answers are all valid under different frames. Stakeholders are multilingual fairness/alignment researchers, interpretability researchers, and builders of global assistants/search/chat systems. The strongest one-line case is: globally deployed assistants must answer frame-relative questions according to the user's intended cultural context, not a hidden language prior. Name: numeral_morphology_magnitude_leak
Title: Four-Twenty-Ten Is Not Ninety: How Numeral-System Morphology Distorts the Shared Magnitude Representation in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a number is written as words, multilingual LLMs are supposed to recover a language-agnostic magnitude, but the surface *morphology* of a language's numeral system leaks into the internal representation. Specifically, for languages with opaque/non-decimal numeral construction (e.g., French vigesimal 'quatre-vingt-dix' = 90, Danish 'halvfems', Georgian, Basque), the model's internal magnitude estimate is systematically pulled toward the values of the literal component morphemes, and this compositional-leakage grows with the typological distance of the numeral system from a transparent base-10 system. This predicts (a) a measurable, direction-consistent magnitude distortion, (b) that distortion tracks numeral-system opacity rather than general language resource level, and (c) that a training-free steering correction along the recovered magnitude direction can repair the leak.
Related Work: A rich interpretability literature shows LLMs encode numbers as digit-wise base-10 (Zhu et al. 2024), sinusoidally (2025), as log-magnitude linear directions (LLMs Know More About Numbers 2026), and in low-dimensional monotonic subspaces (Heinzerling & Inui 2024). Multilingual numeracy work shows accuracy drops across scripts/formats (The Effect of Scripts and Formats on LLM Numeracy 2026), that models fail cross-linguistic numeral puzzles because they lack implicit compositional numeral structure (Investigating linguistic-mathematical reasoning 2025), and that embeddings support grammaticality but not value comparison across languages (Probing for Multilingual Numerical Understanding 2020). All of these either study digits/notation in a single language, or study behavioral failure on cross-linguistic puzzles. None asks the sharp mechanistic question: when a value is expressed as *number words* in different natural languages, is the recovered internal magnitude language-agnostic, and does the *morphological transparency* of the numeral system causally distort that internal magnitude? We uniquely use cross-linguistic numeral morphology as a controlled probe of the shared-vs-language-specific magnitude representation, introduce a 'compositional-leakage' distortion metric grounded in numeral-system typology, and provide a causal steering fix.
Abstract: Multilingual language models must map number words in any language onto a shared notion of magnitude: French 'quatre-vingt-dix', literally 'four-twenty-ten', and English 'ninety' should both point to 90. But numeral systems differ dramatically in morphological transparency—some are cleanly decimal (Chinese, English), others vigesimal or idiosyncratic (French, Danish, Georgian, Basque). We ask whether the model recovers a language-agnostic magnitude regardless of surface morphology, or whether the literal values of a numeral's component morphemes leak into the internal representation. Using established magnitude-probing tools (linear log-magnitude probes, monotonic subspaces), we decode the model's internal magnitude for numbers spelled out as words across 12+ languages spanning transparent-decimal, additive, vigesimal, and irregular numeral systems. We define a compositional-leakage score: the systematic bias of the decoded magnitude toward the summed/producted values of the literal component morphemes. We predict (1) that leakage is measurable and direction-consistent, pulling estimates of opaque numerals (e.g., 90) toward morpheme-implied values; (2) that leakage magnitude correlates with a numeral-system opacity index and is dissociable from language resource level (a transparent low-resource language leaks less than an opaque high-resource one); and (3) that steering activations along the recovered clean magnitude direction repairs downstream comparison and arithmetic errors on opaque numerals without retraining. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. The study turns numeral-system typology into a precise instrument for measuring where the multilingual magnitude representation is shared versus contaminated by language-specific surface form.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Stimuli (constructed): parallel numbers 0-1000, oversampling ranges where morphology diverges (70-99, teens, round hundreds), spelled out as words in 12 languages chosen to span numeral-system typology -- transparent-decimal (English, Chinese, Turkish, Japanese), additive/subtractive (Welsh, a Latin-style set), vigesimal (French, Danish, Basque, Georgian), and irregular teens/inversion (German, Dutch). Each numeral is annotated with its component morphemes and their literal values, and each language gets a numeral-system Opacity Index (mean absolute difference between morpheme-implied composition and true decimal value, plus a non-decimal-base indicator). English digit-format numbers are the language-agnostic anchor. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen; last-token-of-numeral representations; probes are ridge/linear log-magnitude regressions, 3 seeds, validated on held-out numbers. Tokenisation statistics for number words are reported and stimuli are curated for clean morpheme boundaries.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- measurable, direction-consistent compositional leakage, causally due to morphology): tests claims (a) and the causal core. Data/model as Setup. Method: train linear log-magnitude probes / identify monotonic magnitude subspaces on English digit numbers, then apply the SAME probe to hidden states of word-form numerals in every language; define the compositional-leakage score by regressing decoded-magnitude error on (true value) and (morpheme-implied value), the coefficient on morpheme-implied value being the leakage. Causal test: patch/ablate the component-morpheme token representations and measure whether decoded magnitude shifts toward vs away from morpheme-implied values. Decisive metric: the leakage coefficient (fraction of the morpheme-implied deviation reflected in decoded magnitude) for opaque numerals, plus the causal shift in decoded magnitude under morpheme patching. Convincing result: probe transfer is valid (held-out digit numbers decoded within 5% relative error), the leakage coefficient is significantly positive and direction-consistent (opaque numerals pulled toward morpheme-implied values) at >=0.15, AND morpheme patching causally moves decoded magnitude toward the morpheme-implied value. Indecision band: leakage coefficient 0.05-0.15 = weak leakage (reported as such); <0.05 or CI including 0 = no measurable leakage; a null morpheme-patch means any leakage is not morphology-driven. Negative result (no leakage, or probe fails to transfer) means the magnitude representation is genuinely shared -- an informative refutation of the leakage claim.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- leakage tracks numeral-system opacity, not resource level): tests claim (b). Data/model as Setup. Predictors: per-language leakage coefficient (Experiment 1) against the Opacity Index vs a resource-level proxy (pretraining token share / mLAMA accuracy). Decisive metric: Spearman(leakage, Opacity Index) vs Spearman(leakage, resource proxy), with bootstrap CIs, and the crucial contrast of a transparent LOW-resource language (Turkish or Swahili) vs an opaque HIGH-resource one (French). Convincing result: |Spearman with Opacity Index| >=0.5 and exceeds |Spearman with resource| by >=0.2, with the contrast pair ordered by opacity (French leaks more than Turkish) not resource. Indecision band: the two correlations within 0.05-0.2 of each other = a mixed account; opacity not stronger, or gap <0.05 = the opacity claim is refuted. Negative result (leakage tracks resource, not opacity) reassigns the effect to resource scarcity.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- training-free steering repairs the leak): tests claim (c). Data: magnitude-comparison ("which is larger, [word-form A] or [word-form B]?") and simple word-form arithmetic over opaque numerals, plus non-numeric prompts for a fluency control. Model: extract the clean magnitude direction from digit/transparent anchors; at inference, project out the morpheme-leakage component (or steer the activation toward the correct-magnitude location) for opaque numerals. Systems compared: steering vs a translate-numeral-to-digits prompting baseline vs no intervention. Decisive metric: reduction in decoded-magnitude relative error on opaque numerals, then comparison/arithmetic accuracy gain, with a specificity check that non-numeric fluency (perplexity) is unharmed; the pre-intervention link that high-leakage items have higher error (beyond true value) is reported first. Convincing result: steering cuts decoded-magnitude error by >=50% and raises comparison/arithmetic accuracy by >=4 points on opaque numerals while fluency is unharmed and matches or beats the translate-to-digits baseline. Indecision band: 20-50% error reduction or a 1.5-4 point accuracy gain = partial repair (reported as such); <20% error reduction or <1.5 point gain = steering does not repair the leak and H3 is refuted. Negative result (no repair, or repair only by harming fluency) refutes the steering claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used magnitude; we require the causal morpheme-patching (in Exp. 1) and the steering-repair behavioral effect (in Exp. 3) to establish functional relevance. 2. Tokenization of number words differs across languages and may split morphemes unevenly, confounding morpheme-value attribution; we curate stimuli with clean morpheme boundaries and use last-token representations, and report tokenization statistics. 3. Leakage might be confounded with frequency (opaque numerals may be rarer strings); we control by matching frequency ranges and including the resource-level dissociation. 4. The Opacity Index is a hand-constructed metric; we report robustness to alternative operationalizations and validate with multiple annotators. 5. Some models may resolve morphology so well that leakage is negligible—still a positive finding (magnitude is genuinely shared) and multiple models/languages give statistical power to detect small effects. 6. Steering may trade repair for fluency; we report both. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty: (1) multilingual LLMs may not recover a fully language-agnostic magnitude from number words; (2) numeral morphology causes systematic internal magnitude distortion toward literal component values; (3) this distortion scales with typological opacity rather than resource level; (4) a typology-grounded compositional-leakage metric can measure the effect; (5) training-free steering along a recovered magnitude direction can repair it. Relative to the cited work, the closest family is numeric-representation probing/geometry plus multilingual numeracy behavior studies. The actual delta is a new mechanistic question and measurement setup at the representation level, not just another benchmark. It is more than an obvious extension because it links numeral typology to internal magnitude geometry and proposes causal patching plus steering. The main caveat is that it still heavily reuses existing probe machinery and may look like a targeted application of known tools unless the typology and causal evidence are especially clean.

If the result holds, it would support language-aware evaluation and mitigation of numeracy failures; if null, it would strengthen the claim that magnitude representations abstract away morphology. The strongest case is that numeral wording could systematically bias quantitative reasoning in multilingual deployment.
