Name: tense_grammaticalization_gap
Title: When the Grammar Is Silent: How Multilingual LLMs Represent Time in Tenseless vs. Tensed Languages
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs build a shared, language-agnostic 'reference-time' representation (the abstract past/present/future ordering a sentence describes) that is distinct from the surface tense-morphology representation. We hypothesize that (a) for morphologically tensed languages the model can lazily read reference time off surface tense features, while for tenseless/aspect-only languages (Chinese, Indonesian, Yoruba) it must infer reference time from lexical/pragmatic context using a slower, later-layer, more error-prone circuit; (b) this creates a measurable 'grammaticalization gap' in the robustness and localization of the abstract time representation that tracks whether a language grammatically marks tense, NOT its resource level; and (c) the abstract reference-time direction transfers across languages, so it can be causally read from a tensed language and injected to repair temporal inference in a tenseless one.
Related Work: Prior probing work shows tense is easy to decode in morphologically-marked languages (French) but hard in Chinese, attributing the drop to memorization vs. abstraction (Multilingual Probe for Tense 2021), and that transformers encode aspect features like telicity/duration (About Time 2022; Verbal Aspect 2024). Recent interpretability shows grammatical concepts (number, gender, tense) share cross-lingual feature directions (Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025) and that tense/aspect are steerable orthogonal directions (Steering Tense and Aspect 2025). LLMs also encode linear time and 'temporal heads' for factual dates (Language Models Represent Space and Time 2023; Temporal Heads 2025). Cross-linguistic NLI work shows LLMs struggle with perfect-aspect temporal inference in Chinese/Japanese (2025). However, ALL prior work either (i) probes surface tense morphology, or (ii) studies factual event dates, and treats the tenseless-language decoding drop as a probing artifact. None distinguishes the abstract SENTENCE-INTERNAL reference-time representation (the situation's temporal location, present regardless of whether grammar marks it) from surface tense morphology, nor tests whether tenseless languages recruit a distinct, later, error-prone inference circuit, nor uses a tensed language as a causal donor to repair temporal inference in a tenseless one. We reframe the classic French-vs-Chinese gap as a mechanistic grammaticalization-gap phenomenon with a causal cross-lingual fix.
Abstract: Some languages grammatically mark when an event happened (English 'walked' vs 'walks'); others, like Chinese, Indonesian, and Yoruba, are largely tenseless and leave temporal location to be inferred from adverbs, aspect markers, and pragmatics. Yet any comprehending model must recover the same abstract reference time. We ask how multilingual LLMs represent this abstract sentence-internal time, and whether the mechanism differs when grammar is silent. We distinguish two representations: surface tense morphology (which verb form appears) and abstract reference time (past/present/future location of the described situation). Using parallel sentences whose reference time is fixed by context across tensed and tenseless languages, we train linear probes and locate the layers and components that encode reference time in each. We predict a 'grammaticalization gap': in tensed languages reference time is decodable early and localizes with surface-tense features, whereas in tenseless languages it emerges only in later layers via a distinct, more error-prone circuit, and this gap tracks whether a language marks tense rather than its resource level (e.g., low-resource tensed Swahili patterns with English, high-resource tenseless Chinese with Indonesian). We causally test whether the abstract reference-time direction is shared: extracting it from a tensed language and steering it into a tenseless-language forward pass should repair temporal-inference errors without harming fluency. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B and 12+ languages of both types. This recasts the classic tense-probing gap as a controllable, cross-lingually transferable mechanistic phenomenon.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Stimuli (constructed): ~600 parallel minimal-pair sentences whose abstract reference time (past/present/future) is fixed either by an explicit temporal adverbial ("yesterday"/"now"/"tomorrow") or in a BARE-CONTEXT version (no adverbial, inferable only from lexical/pragmatic cues). Rendered in 12 languages split into TENSED (English, Spanish, Russian, Swahili [low-resource but tensed], Hindi) and TENSELESS/aspect-only (Chinese, Indonesian, Yoruba, Thai, Vietnamese). Each item carries two separate labels: surface tense-morphology and abstract reference time. Bare-context items are kept only where native-speaker annotators agree with high inter-annotator agreement. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen; linear probes (3 seeds, held-out validation); verb-token or clause-final representations; tokenisation statistics reported. Emergence layer = first layer at which a probe exceeds 90% accuracy (or its peak), reported as a fraction of model depth.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- a distinct, later, error-prone reference-time circuit when grammar is silent): tests that abstract reference time is separable from surface tense and, in tenseless languages, emerges later via a distinct circuit whose weakness predicts errors. Data/model as Setup. Method: (a) two-target probing -- train separate per-layer probes for surface tense morphology and for abstract reference time, per language, and record emergence layers; (b) circuit localisation -- activation patching / attention-head attribution find the components carrying reference time in tensed vs tenseless languages, with Jaccard overlap of the two circuits and whether tenseless languages recruit additional later components tied to adverbial/context tokens; (c) behavioural link -- on a temporal-inference task (order two events / answer a when-question), test that low reference-time probe confidence in tenseless bare-context items predicts errors beyond the true label. Decisive metric: the reference-time emergence-layer difference (tenseless minus tensed) and the tensed-vs-tenseless circuit Jaccard overlap, with the behavioural link reported alongside. Convincing result: in tensed languages reference time is decodable early and its probe tracks the surface-tense probe; in tenseless languages it emerges >=15% of model depth LATER, dissociates from surface tense, its circuit overlaps the tensed circuit at Jaccard <=0.4 while recruiting later adverbial-tied components, and low probe confidence predicts behavioural error at Spearman >=0.3. Indecision band: an emergence delay of 5-15% of depth or Jaccard 0.4-0.6 = a weak/partial distinct-circuit effect (reported as such); a delay <5% of depth with Jaccard >0.6 = no distinct circuit and H1 is refuted. Negative result (reference time decoded identically and via the same circuit in both language types) refutes the grammaticalisation-gap mechanism.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the gap tracks whether a language marks tense, not its resource level): tests claim (b). Data/model as Setup. Method: define the grammaticalisation gap per language = reference-time emergence delay plus the bare-context robustness drop (fall in probe accuracy from adverbial to bare context). Predictors: a binary "grammatically marks tense" typology indicator vs a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / mLAMA accuracy). Decisive metric: Spearman(gap, typology indicator) vs Spearman(gap, resource proxy), bootstrap CIs, with the crucial contrast of low-resource tensed Swahili vs high-resource tenseless Chinese. Convincing result: |Spearman with typology| >=0.5 and exceeds |Spearman with resource| by >=0.2, with Swahili patterning with the tensed languages and Chinese with the tenseless ones. Indecision band: the two correlations within 0.05-0.2 of each other = a mixed account; typology not stronger, or gap <0.05 = the typology claim is refuted. Negative result (the gap tracks resource) reassigns it to resource scarcity.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- a shared reference-time direction that transfers and repairs by injection): tests claim (c). Data: bare-context temporal-inference items where the model errs in tenseless languages, plus perfect-aspect temporal-NLI items (Chinese/Japanese style). Model: extract the abstract reference-time direction (mean activation difference past vs future) from a TENSED donor language; (a) test cross-lingual decodability by applying the donor probe to a tenseless language; (b) steer the donor-derived direction into the tenseless-language forward pass on erring items. Systems compared: donor-direction steering vs a same-language steering baseline vs a translate-to-English baseline. Decisive metric: temporal-inference/NLI accuracy gain in the tenseless language, then output fluency (perplexity) and specificity (unrelated features unchanged), with donor-probe cross-lingual transfer accuracy reported first. Convincing result: the donor probe transfers well above chance (within 10 pp of in-language accuracy) AND steering the donor direction raises tenseless temporal-inference accuracy by >=5 points without harming fluency (<5% perplexity increase), matching or beating same-language steering. Indecision band: cross-lingual transfer 10-25 pp below in-language, or a 2-5 point accuracy gain = partial sharing/repair (reported as such); transfer near chance or <2 point gain = the direction is not shared/transferable and H3 is refuted. Negative result (no transfer, steering fails) refutes the shared-direction and causal-repair claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability may reflect the readout basis rather than a used representation; we require the causal steering-repair (in Exp. 3) and the behavioral link (in Exp. 1) to establish functional relevance. 2. Separating 'abstract reference time' from 'surface tense' is hard in tensed languages where they nearly coincide; the tenseless languages and the bare-context condition are the crucial dissociating cases and are designed for exactly this. 3. Ground-truth reference time in bare-context tenseless sentences can be genuinely ambiguous; we restrict to items validated by native-speaker annotators with high agreement. 4. Tokenization/script differences complicate cross-language probing; we use clean sentence-final or verb-token representations and report tokenization statistics. 5. Some models may simply route everything through English tense, collapsing the tenseless circuit into a translation step; even so, showing this (via the shared-direction transfer) is a positive, informative result. 6. The typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen languages (Swahili tensed low-resource, Chinese tenseless high-resource); we report robustness to alternative language choices. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty are: (1) multilingual LLMs encode abstract sentence-internal reference time separately from surface tense morphology; (2) tenseless languages induce a distinct later, less robust, more error-prone circuit for recovering reference time; (3) the tensed-vs-tenseless gap tracks grammatical tense marking rather than language resource level; (4) abstract reference-time directions transfer across languages and can causally repair temporal inference in tenseless inputs. From the proposal plus search summary, the main genuinely new piece is the reference-time-vs-surface-tense distinction and the grammaticalization-gap mechanism. However, localization, shared cross-lingual grammatical directions, and steering are already heavily pre-empted by TenseLoC, Latent Grammatical Concepts, and related steering work. So the closest prior family is multilingual tense localization/steering and temporal probing; the actual delta is narrowing the target from surface tense to abstract reference time and arguing for a distinct inference circuit in tenseless languages. That is non-trivial, but only if the paper cleanly demonstrates the dissociation rather than rebranding known tense effects.

impact.reasoning: The behavior under study is how multilingual LLMs recover event time when grammar does or does not overtly mark tense, and whether failures in tenseless languages reflect representational and mechanistic gaps. Audiences include multilingual NLP, interpretability researchers, temporal reasoning/NLI, and typology/cognitive-science-adjacent communities. review.reasoning: Interesting and fairly well structured, but there are significant technical vulnerabilities. The core hypothesis is partly precise and falsifiable, with thresholds and predicted directions, but the central construct 'abstract reference time' remains hard to operationalize and may collapse into lexical cue detection or dataset artifacts. Related work is decent but must be more specific about what exactly is pre-empted. The experiments are plausible but not yet strong enough to isolate mechanism: ~600 items across 12 languages is likely underpowered for layerwise, per-language, per-condition probing and circuit claims; emergence-layer thresholds and Jaccard overlap feel somewhat arbitrary; and causal steering from tensed donors may simply inject an English-like tense bias rather than repair abstract temporal reasoning. Key missing controls include adversarial lexical-cue controls, translationese controls, same-semantics paraphrases, stronger baselines than translate-to-English, and tests separating adverbial detection from reference-time abstraction. Narrative-wise, the proposal occasionally overclaims from probe decodability to representation. If executed extremely carefully it could be workshop/solid conference material, but for a serious ML venue it needs a tighter construct definition, stronger controls, and a more credible experimental design for causal claims.

Name: grammatical_gender_concept_leak
Title: The Gender You Didn't Ask For: Causal Leakage of Query-Language Grammatical Gender into the Shared Concept Space and Cross-Lingual Semantic Judgments
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM represents an inanimate concept, the grammatical gender that concept happens to carry in the query language covertly enters the model's language-agnostic concept representation and causally biases downstream *semantic* judgments (e.g., attribute association, pronoun choice, adjective selection), even when the answer is produced in a gender-neutral language like English or Chinese. We hypothesize (a) a covert 'concept-gender' direction, distinct from surface agreement features, that inherits the query language's grammatical gender; (b) that this leakage is causally responsible for cross-lingual semantic-gender inconsistencies; and (c) that leakage strength scales with how strongly the query language grammaticalizes gender, and can be removed by a training-free projection along a shared concept-gender direction.
Related Work: Prior work shows grammatical gender contaminates static/contextual word embeddings of inanimate nouns (Gonen et al. 2019; embedding-disentangling methods 2020-2022), that gender subspaces are partly shared across languages so classification transfers but removal does not (Analyzing Gender Representation 2022), that grammatical concepts including gender share cross-lingual feature directions in LLMs (Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025), and that grammatical gender biases text-to-image outputs (Beyond Content 2025). Distributional accounts test whether opposite-gender noun pairs shift embedding semantics (Testing a Distributional Account 2024). All of this is either (i) about static/contextual embeddings and their geometry, or (ii) about behavioral bias in image generation. None asks the sharp causal, generation-time question inside a decoder LLM: does the *query language's* grammatical gender leak into the *shared concept representation* used during reasoning and thereby causally alter *semantic* judgments produced in a gender-neutral output language? We use opposite-gender cross-lingual noun pairs (key: feminine ES / masculine DE) as a controlled natural experiment, provide activation-patching causal evidence for a 'concept-gender' direction separate from surface agreement, quantify leakage vs. degree of grammaticalization, and deliver a training-free debiasing projection whose effect is validated behaviorally in a neutral output language.
Abstract: Many languages grammatically gender inanimate nouns, and these assignments are largely arbitrary and disagree across languages: a bridge is feminine in German but masculine in Spanish. We investigate whether multilingual LLMs, which are widely believed to compute in a shared language-agnostic concept space, keep this concept space free of the query language's grammatical gender, or whether that gender covertly leaks in and biases genuinely semantic judgments. Using cross-lingual noun pairs with opposite grammatical genders as a natural experiment, we ask the model to make semantic-gender judgments (which attribute/adjective/pronoun best fits a concept) in a gender-neutral output language (English or Chinese) while varying the gendered language in which the concept is introduced. We first show that a covert 'concept-gender' direction is linearly decodable from mid-layer representations and inherits the query language's grammatical gender, distinct from surface agreement features. Using activation patching, we causally test whether swapping this direction between a masculine-language run and a feminine-language run flips the model's semantic judgment without changing the concept's identity, establishing that grammatical gender leakage is causally responsible for cross-lingual semantic inconsistency. We predict leakage strength scales with how strongly the query language grammaticalizes gender (Slavic/Germanic/Romance vs. English/Chinese controls) and not with resource level. Finally, we recover a shared concept-gender direction and apply a training-free projection that removes leakage, measuring restored cross-lingual consistency without harming fluency. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across 8+ languages. The work reveals a subtle language-specific contaminant of the supposedly shared concept space and provides a mechanistic, controllable account.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Stimuli (constructed from existing lexica): ~300 inanimate concrete nouns with attested grammatical gender across 6 gendered languages spanning gender-marking strength -- Romance (Spanish, French, Italian), Germanic (German, 3-gender), Slavic (Russian, Polish) -- plus 2 gender-neutral controls (English, Chinese). A key subset has OPPOSITE grammatical gender across >=2 languages (e.g. key, bridge, sun, moon), giving matched minimal pairs that dissociate grammatical from any semantic gender. Per-language grammatical gender is annotated. A separate semantically-gendered control set (man/woman/king/queen) is included, which SHOULD retain gender. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen; greedy, temperature 0, multiple paraphrases; last-token-of-concept or neutral-prompt final-token representations; linear probes (3 seeds, held-out nouns); tokenisation statistics reported.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- a covert concept-gender direction, distinct from surface agreement, with behavioural leakage): tests claim (a). Data/model as Setup. Method: (a) concept-gender probe -- linear probes at each layer decode the grammatical gender of the concept from mid-layer hidden states, using held-out nouns; test that the decoded concept-gender inherits the QUERY language's assignment, that a control probe on the gender-neutral languages is near chance, and that it is distinct from surface agreement features; (b) behavioural leakage -- pose semantic-gender judgments with the answer forced into a gender-NEUTRAL output language (English/Chinese): masculine- vs feminine-associated adjective choice, personification pronoun ("he or she?"), and adjective-fit ranking. Decisive metric: cross-lingual inconsistency = fraction of opposite-gender pairs whose neutral-language judgment flips with the query language, plus the concept-gender probe accuracy above the neutral-language chance baseline. Convincing result: the probe decodes concept-gender well above the neutral-language baseline and inherits the query-language assignment, AND the behavioural flip rate on opposite-gender pairs is >=15 percentage points (pp) above the neutral-query baseline. Indecision band: a flip rate 5-15 pp above baseline = weak leakage (reported as such); <5 pp, or a probe at neutral-language chance = no covert concept-gender and (a) is refuted. Negative result (no decodable concept-gender, judgments invariant to query language) refutes the leakage claim.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- grammatical gender causally drives the semantic judgment): tests claim (b). Data: opposite-gender pair concepts. Model: frozen, activation patching. Method: run two forward passes introducing the concept in a masculine-marking vs a feminine-marking language, both answering in English; activation-patch the mid-layer concept representation (or the isolated concept-gender direction) from the masculine run into the feminine run and measure whether the English semantic judgment flips to match the donor's grammatical gender while concept identity (topic/answer content) is preserved. Decisive metric: causal flip rate versus number/location of patched components, with an identity-preservation check. Convincing result: patching flips the semantic judgment in >=50% of pairs with identity preserved (>=95%), and the isolated concept-gender direction alone suffices to flip it. Indecision band: flip rate 25-50% = partial causal role (reported as such); <25% = grammatical gender is not causally responsible and (b) is refuted. Negative result (patching does not flip judgments, or only by destroying concept identity) refutes the causal claim.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- leakage scales with grammaticalisation and is selectively removable): tests claim (c). Data/model as Setup, including the semantically-gendered control set. Method: (a) dose-response -- correlate per-language leakage (behavioural flip rate + probe decodability) with a gender-marking-strength index (number of genders, agreement pervasiveness) vs a resource-level proxy; (b) training-free debiasing -- extract a shared concept-gender direction (mean activation difference masculine vs feminine, pooled across gendered languages) and project it out of the concept representation at inference; (c) selectivity -- verify the semantically-gendered control set retains gender. Systems compared: projection vs embedding-debiasing-style baselines vs translate-to-English-first. Decisive metric: reduction in cross-lingual inconsistency after projection, together with Spearman(leakage, grammaticalisation strength) vs Spearman(leakage, resource proxy). Convincing result: |Spearman with grammaticalisation| >=0.5 and exceeds |Spearman with resource| by >=0.2 with English/Chinese controls near zero, AND projection cuts cross-lingual inconsistency by >=50% while the semantically-gendered controls retain gender (specificity: <10% change) and fluency (perplexity) is unharmed. Indecision band: the two correlations within 0.05-0.2 of each other = a mixed account; an inconsistency reduction of 20-50% = partial debiasing; a reduction <20%, or controls also stripped of gender, = the debiasing fails or is non-selective and H3 is refuted. Negative result (leakage tracks resource, or projection cannot remove it selectively) refutes the scaling and debiasing claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of concept-gender may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; we require the causal patching flip (in Exp. 2) and behavioral debiasing (in Exp. 3) to establish functional relevance. 2. Some 'semantic gender' judgments may reflect genuine cultural stereotypes rather than grammatical leakage; the opposite-gender minimal pairs and gender-neutral control languages are designed to isolate the grammatical contribution, and we control for stereotype associations of the target concepts. 3. Leakage may be small in strong models that fully abstract away grammar—still an informative positive result (concept space is genuinely clean), and multiple languages/models give statistical power. 4. Tokenization differences across languages/scripts complicate concept-token localization; we use last-token-of-concept or neutral-prompt final-token representations and report tokenization statistics. 5. Debiasing may over-remove and harm legitimately gendered concepts; the semantically-gendered control set (in Exp. 3) tests selectivity, and we report specificity/fluency. 6. Behavioral tasks (pronoun/adjective choice) may be prompt-sensitive; we average over multiple paraphrases and report robustness. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty is not the existence of grammatical-gender bias or decodability, but the claim that query-language gender leaks into a shared concept representation in decoder LLMs and causally changes semantic judgments in a neutral output language. That is meaningfully beyond the prior embedding-geometry and behavioral-bias literature, especially with activation patching and a neutral-language design. However, much of the scaffolding—cross-lingual gender directions, decodability, disentangling, and behavioral bias—is already known, so the novelty is mainly in the causal generation-time mechanism and the specific setting.

Name: false_friend_meaning_leak
Title: Gift Means Poison: Causally Tracing How Interlingual Homographs Leak the Wrong-Language Meaning Into Multilingual LLM Computation
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM processes an interlingual homograph (a false friend, e.g. German 'Gift' = poison vs English 'gift' = present), the wrong-language meaning is automatically co-activated as a latent competitor in mid layers, and semantic errors occur when the model fails to disambiguate using context. We hypothesize (a) both meanings are simultaneously linearly decodable before disambiguation collapses to one, (b) a causally-identifiable mid-layer 'meaning-selection' step resolves the competition, (c) selection failure scales with the frequency balance between the two meanings and with the mismatch between the query-context language and the model's dominant language, and (d) steering along a recovered meaning direction can causally repair or induce the wrong reading.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs perform below random on interlingual-homograph disambiguation and rely on orthography over semantics (Multilingual LLMs Struggle to Link Orthography and Semantics 2025). Small bilingual-model studies show shared embeddings produce facilitation for BOTH friends and false friends, driven by frequency, failing to reproduce human interference (Skrjanec et al. 2026; Cumulative Frequency 2021). Tokenizer-level work maps false friends to shared subwords and proposes language cues at tokenization (Tokenizing Crosslingual Homographs 2026; False Friends Are Not Foes 2025). Embedding-geometry work characterizes shared vs language-partitioned spaces (Hyperpolyglot LLMs 2023; BERT is Not an Interlingua 2019). All of this is either (i) behavioral, (ii) about static embeddings/tokenization, or (iii) in tiny controlled bilingual models. None gives a causal, generation-time mechanistic account inside a large decoder LLM of HOW the wrong-language meaning is co-activated and selected against, WHERE disambiguation happens, and WHAT modulates failure. We use false friends as a controlled natural experiment to probe the shared-vs-specific meaning representation, provide activation-patching causal evidence for a mid-layer meaning-selection step, quantify failure drivers (frequency balance, language dominance, context strength), and deliver a causal steering intervention.
Abstract: Interlingual homographs, or false friends, are words with identical surface form but different meanings across languages: German 'Gift' means poison, but English 'gift' means present. Such words are a natural stress test for the shared subword vocabularies of multilingual LLMs. Behavioral studies show models resolve them poorly, but how the wrong meaning enters computation, where it is (or is not) suppressed, and what governs failure remain unknown mechanistically. We treat false friends as a controlled probe of whether the model computes a single, context-appropriate meaning or covertly co-activates both. Using a curated cross-lingual false-friend set with matched cognate and monosemous controls, we first show via logit-lens and linear probes that in mid layers both meanings of a false friend are simultaneously decodable before selection collapses to one, unlike controls. Using activation patching, we localize a compact mid-layer meaning-selection step: swapping its activation between a context that forces meaning A and one that forces meaning B flips the model's downstream semantic judgment while preserving that the word is a false friend. We then quantify what drives selection failure: the frequency balance between the two meanings, the mismatch between the surrounding-context language and the model's dominant language, and context strength. Finally, we extract a meaning direction and steer it to causally repair mis-selections in disambiguating context, and to induce the wrong reading in weak context, validated behaviorally. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across English-German, English-Spanish, English-French, English-Dutch, and English-Russian false-friend pairs. The work provides the first causal, generation-time account of cross-lingual meaning interference in large LLMs and a controllable fix.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Stimuli (constructed from validated databases): a cross-lingual false-friend set from the Dutch-English homograph database (existing) plus curated English-German/Spanish/French/Russian pairs, ~200 false friends, each with its two meanings and canonical languages, matched COGNATE controls (same form, same meaning) and MONOSEMOUS single-language controls. For each false friend: paired disambiguating contexts (one forcing meaning A, one forcing meaning B) and a weak/neutral context, each rendered with the surrounding context in language A vs language B; per-meaning corpus frequency gives a frequency-balance score; intended meaning is native-speaker validated. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen; greedy, temperature 0; homograph-token representations; linear probes (3 seeds, held-out items); tokenisation reported and shared-token vs split-token cases tracked.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- parallel activation of both meanings): tests claim (a), that both meanings are simultaneously decodable before selection collapses to one. Data/model as Setup. Method: at the homograph token position apply logit-lens and per-layer linear probes to test whether BOTH meaning answer tokens (e.g. "poison" and "present") are decodable in mid layers before one dominates, contrasted with monosemous controls (which should show a single meaning). Decisive metric: mid-layer co-decodability rank of the two meanings for false friends versus the secondary-meaning decodability of monosemous controls. Convincing result: both meanings are decodable above chance in mid layers for false friends, with the secondary-meaning decodability >=15 percentage points (pp) above the monosemous-control baseline -- genuine parallel activation, not a readout artefact. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above the control baseline = weak co-activation (reported as such); <5 pp = no parallel activation and (a) is refuted. Negative result (only the context-appropriate meaning decodable, as for controls) refutes co-activation.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- a causally-identifiable mid-layer meaning-selection step): tests claim (b). Data: identical false friends under context A vs context B, yielding different downstream answers. Model: frozen, activation patching. Method: patch mid-layer components from the A-run into the B-run and find the minimal set whose patching flips the model's semantic judgment to A's meaning while lexical identity (that it is this word) is preserved. Decisive metric: flip rate versus number/location of patched components, with an identity-preservation check. Convincing result: a compact mid-layer set flips the semantic judgment in >=50% of pairs while preserving lexical identity (>=95%). Indecision band: flip rate 25-50% = a diffuse selection step (reported as a direction-based account); <25% = no localisable meaning-selection step and (b) is refuted. Negative result (patching cannot flip the judgment) refutes the selection-step claim.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- what drives selection failure): tests claim (c). Data/model as Setup. Method: regress selection-failure rate on (i) the frequency-balance score, (ii) context-language vs dominant-language mismatch (lang2vec typological distance), and (iii) context strength. Decisive metric: standardised regression coefficients and Spearman correlations with bootstrap CIs for each driver. Convincing result: failure rises with a balanced or dominant-favouring frequency and with language mismatch, each with |Spearman| >=0.3 and a 95% CI excluding 0. Indecision band: |Spearman| 0.15-0.3 for a driver = weak (reported as such); <0.15, or CI including 0 = that driver does not modulate failure and the corresponding part of (c) is refuted. Negative result (failure unrelated to frequency balance or mismatch) refutes the failure-driver claim.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- causal steering repairs and induces the reading): tests claim (d). Data: disambiguating-context items where the model errs (for repair) and weak-context items (for induction). Model: extract a meaning direction (mean activation difference between meaning-A and meaning-B runs) at the selection layer; (a) in disambiguating context, steer toward the correct meaning and measure repair rate; (b) in weak context, steer to induce the wrong reading. Systems compared: steering vs a translate-to-context-language baseline vs a tokenizer-language-cue prompt baseline. Decisive metric: repair rate and induction rate, then downstream-task accuracy, output fluency (perplexity), and specificity (unrelated items unchanged). Convincing result: steering repairs >=40% of mis-selections and induces the wrong reading in >=40% of weak-context items, with fluency unharmed and specificity preserved -- a bidirectionally functional meaning direction. Indecision band: repair/induction of 20-40% = partial (reported as such); <20%, or effects only obtained by harming fluency, = the direction is not causally functional and (d) is refuted. Negative result (steering neither repairs nor induces) refutes the causal-steering claim. Ablations reported here: layer sweep, shared-token vs split-token homographs, whether the competitor is the dominant-language meaning or the higher-frequency meaning, and probe transfer across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe co-decodability may reflect the readout basis rather than functional co-activation; we require the causal patching flip (in Exp. 2) and steering repair/induction (in Exp. 4) to establish functional relevance. 2. False-friend meanings often differ in frequency, confounding co-activation with mere frequency; we explicitly model frequency balance (in Exp. 3) and include frequency-matched subsets. 3. Tokenization varies: some homographs split into different subwords across contexts, breaking the 'shared surface form' premise; we report per-item tokenization and analyze shared-token vs split-token cases separately (in the Exp. 4 ablations). 4. Strong models may resolve context so well that interference is rare in disambiguating contexts; the weak-context and induction experiments (in Exp. 4) still yield informative causal results, and multiple languages/models give statistical power. 5. Ground-truth intended meaning in weak contexts can be genuinely ambiguous; we restrict to native-speaker-validated items with high agreement. 6. Steering may trade correctness for fluency; we report both. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that need to be novel are: (1) interlingual homographs in multilingual decoder LLMs trigger simultaneous latent co-activation of both language-specific meanings before disambiguation; (2) there exists a causally localizable mid-layer meaning-selection step that resolves this competition; (3) failure rates are modulated by frequency balance, context-language/model-dominant-language mismatch, and context strength; (4) a recovered meaning direction can bidirectionally repair or induce the selected reading. Relative to the cited prior work, the phenomenon that models fail on false-friend disambiguation and often prefer higher-resource/higher-frequency senses is already known, and tokenizer/shared-embedding explanations are also partly explored. The real delta is the generation-time mechanistic and causal account inside large decoder LLMs, especially the localized selection step and steering intervention. Studying false friends in large multilingual decoder models is a meaningfully different setting from prior tiny bilingual models and purely behavioral studies. The proposal is therefore non-trivial and moderately-to-strongly novel, though some subclaims—especially co-activation and frequency effects—look like mechanistic follow-ons to already observed behavioral biases rather than wholly new findings.
revision_notes: State explicitly which claim is the primary novelty: e.g., 'first causal localization of a meaning-selection circuit for cross-lingual homographs in large decoder LLMs,' rather than spreading novelty across four partially overlapping claims.
Differentiate more sharply from existing mechanistic interpretability work on polysemy/ambiguity in monolingual LMs, not just multilingual false-friend papers.
Clarify whether the novelty is a new phenomenon, a new mechanism, a new task/dataset, or a new intervention; right now it is mostly mechanism plus intervention, with dataset/task as support.
Add one stronger non-obvious prediction that distinguishes the proposed mechanism from simpler baselines such as token-frequency bias or shallow language-ID gating.
If possible, expand beyond a curated benchmark to a reusable public dataset/tooling resource; this would increase novelty via artifact contribution as well.

impact.reasoning: The underlying problem is cross-lingual semantic interference in multilingual LLMs: models may silently activate the wrong-language meaning of a shared surface form, causing misinterpretation in multilingual, code-switched, translation, and semantic reasoning settings. Relevant audiences include multilingual NLP researchers, interpretability researchers, model builders, tokenizer designers, and practitioners deploying multilingual assistants. The strongest case for importance is that if multilingual LLMs systematically leak wrong-language senses, then current evaluations understate a real semantic reliability failure in multilingual applications. If the result holds, it could shift follow-up work toward internal-mechanism diagnostics and targeted fixes rather than only tokenizer or prompt-level mitigations. Still, the practical scope is somewhat bounded: false-friend disambiguation is important but narrower than broader multilingual robustness, and the proposal does not yet show how often this failure materially affects high-value downstream tasks. On the 'so what?' test: a strong positive result would likely change how multilingual interpretability and robustness are studied; a null result would also matter by suggesting behavioral failures do not reflect persistent internal co-activation. So there is meaningful phenomenon value, but real-world reach is not yet maximized in the writeup.

Quantify expected prevalence: how common are false-friend-like collisions in deployed multilingual usage or common benchmarks?
Explain what practitioners would do differently if the result is positive versus negative.
Position the work as a broader probe of multilingual semantic binding, with false friends as the minimal test case, to widen the perceived audience.

review.reasoning: The proposal is unusually concrete and testable, with explicit hypotheses, thresholds, controls, and negative-result criteria. That is a major strength. However, there are several technical gaps a strict reviewer would press on. First, 'both meanings are linearly decodable' does not by itself establish functional co-activation, and the current bridge from probe evidence to computation remains vulnerable even with patching. Second, the notion of a compact 'meaning-selection step' may be too discretized; selection could be distributed across layers/heads, and the proposed >=50% patch-flip threshold is somewhat arbitrary. Third, the regression claims in H3 risk confounding frequency, resource imbalance, tokenization, script effects, and language-family differences; the current design may be underpowered with ~200 items across many languages. Fourth, steering via mean-difference directions may succeed for reasons unrelated to a true semantic competitor representation. Fifth, several important baselines are missing: monolingual lexical ambiguity/polysemy controls, language-ID interventions beyond tokenization, and causal scrubbing-style alternatives to activation patching. Related work is reasonably specific for the multilingual false-friend niche, but broader interpretability positioning is still thin. If executed carefully, this could be a solid workshop/Findings/interpretability paper and possibly stronger, but for a serious ML venue it needs tighter causal argumentation, stronger controls, and more principled analysis of alternative explanations.

Name: honorific_register_binding
Title: Who Am I Talking To? A Causal Study of How Multilingual LLMs Represent Social Register and Bind It to Honorific Grammar
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs build a shared, language-agnostic representation of the social relationship between speaker and addressee (relative status/formality), stored separately from surface honorific morphology. When generating in a language that grammatically forces an honorific/register choice (Japanese/Korean honorifics, T-V distinction), the model reads register off this shared 'social-register' variable via a late-layer binding step. We hypothesize (a) an abstract social-register direction that is decodable across languages including register-lax ones like English; (b) that honorific errors in obligatory-honorific languages arise from a binding failure that lazily inherits the register implied by the input/query language rather than re-inferring it from context; and (c) that this inheritance bias scales with how strongly a language grammaticalizes register, not with its resource level, and can be causally repaired by steering the shared register direction.
Related Work: Prior work studies politeness behaviorally and stylistically (TyDiP 2022; Comparing Styles across Languages 2023; Should We Respect LLMs? 2024) and probes negation/passivization/function words in monolingual BERT-era models (Negation Scope 2020; Controlling the Imprint 2020; Function Words 2022). Interpretability work shows LLMs share cross-lingual concept and grammatical-concept directions (Semantic Hub 2024; Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025) and decode into the target language in late layers. However, all politeness work is behavioral/stylistic and treats register as an output style, while all mechanistic multilingual work targets semantic content or morphological features like gender/number/tense. None isolates the abstract social-relationship variable (relative speaker-addressee status) as a distinct, causally-manipulable representation, none studies the late-layer binding of this variable onto obligatory honorific grammar, and none tests whether register is lazily inherited from the input language. We uniquely treat honorification/T-V typology as a controlled probe of the shared-vs-specific pragmatic representation, give causal (patching + steering) evidence for a register-binding step, and dissociate grammaticalization strength from resource level.
Abstract: Languages encode the social relationship between speaker and addressee very differently: Japanese and Korean obligatorily mark honorification through verb morphology, Romance/Slavic/German languages force a T-V (informal/formal 'you') choice, and English leaves register largely to lexical and pragmatic cues. Any competent multilingual model must nonetheless recover the same abstract social relationship and, when the target language demands it, commit to a grammatical register. We ask how multilingual LLMs represent this social-register variable and how they bind it onto honorific grammar. We distinguish two representations: an abstract, language-agnostic social-register variable (the relative status/formality of the interlocutors, present regardless of grammatical marking) and the surface honorific/T-V morphology that realizes it. Using parallel dialogues whose social relationship is fixed by context across register-marking and register-lax languages, we train linear probes and localize where register is encoded and where it is bound to grammar. We predict (1) the abstract register direction is decodable across languages, including English; (2) honorific errors in obligatory-honorific languages stem from a late-layer binding failure that lazily inherits the register implied by the query/input language; and (3) this inheritance bias tracks grammaticalization strength, not resource level (e.g., high-resource register-lax English vs. lower-resource register-heavy Korean). We causally test binding via activation patching and repair errors by steering the shared register direction, measuring restored register correctness without harming fluency. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across 10+ languages. The work provides the first mechanistic, controllable account of pragmatic social register in multilingual LLMs.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Stimuli (constructed): parallel dialogue/instruction items whose speaker-addressee social relationship is unambiguously fixed by context (e.g. a student writing to a professor = high formality vs texting a close friend = low formality; power, status, and intimacy dimensions varied), ~500 base items each with a bare-context variant (relationship inferable only from lexical cues) and an explicit-context variant. Rendered in 10+ languages spanning three register-grammar types: OBLIGATORY-HONORIFIC (Japanese, Korean), T-V DISTINCTION (Spanish, French, German, Russian, Hindi), and REGISTER-LAX (English, Chinese, Indonesian). The correct target register per item is native-speaker validated, and each language gets a register-grammaticalisation-strength index (obligatory verb morphology > T-V pronoun > lexical-only). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen; greedy, temperature 0, 3 paraphrase seeds; verb-final or reply-final token representations; linear probes (3 seeds, held-out items); obligatory-honorific, T-V, and lexical cases analysed separately; tokenisation reported.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- an abstract, cross-lingual social-register direction distinct from surface morphology): tests claim (a). Data/model as Setup. Method: train per-layer linear probes to decode the intended social register (formal/informal, or ordinal level) from mid-layer hidden states on held-out items; test that it is decodable in register-lax languages (English/Chinese) too and that a probe trained on one language transfers to others (cross-lingual sharing); contrast with a surface-morphology probe (which honorific/T-V form appears) to establish the abstract-vs-surface dissociation. Decisive metric: cross-lingual register-probe transfer accuracy, plus register decodability in register-lax languages. Convincing result: register is decodable above chance in register-lax languages and the register probe transfers cross-lingually within 10 percentage points (pp) of in-language accuracy, while the surface-morphology probe does NOT transfer (a clear abstract-vs-surface dissociation). Indecision band: cross-lingual transfer 10-25 pp below in-language = partially shared (reported as such); transfer >25 pp below in-language, or register-lax decodability at chance = the register variable is not abstract/shared and (a) is refuted. Negative result (register decodable only where grammatically marked, no transfer) refutes the shared-representation claim.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- honorific errors are a late-layer binding failure that lazily inherits the input-language register): tests claim (b). Data/model as Setup, activation patching. Method: (a) lazy-inheritance test -- hold the target generation language fixed (e.g. Japanese) but vary the language/framing of the context (English formal framing vs Japanese informal context, etc.) and measure how often the output register matches the INPUT-language-implied register rather than the context-mandated register; (b) localise the binding step -- run the identical item under context forcing FORMAL vs INFORMAL (different honorific outputs in an obligatory-honorific language) and activation-patch late-layer components from the formal run into the informal run to find the minimal set whose patching flips the produced register while message content is preserved. Decisive metric: the late-layer register-flip rate under patching (with content preserved), and the lazy-inheritance rate. Convincing result: a compact late-layer set flips the produced register in >=50% of items with content preserved (>=95%), AND the inheritance rate is >=20 pp higher when generating an obligatory-honorific language from a register-lax input than in matched controls -- a locatable binding step that lazily inherits input-language register. Indecision band: a flip rate 25-50% = a diffuse binding step; an inheritance excess of 8-20 pp = weak lazy inheritance (both reported as partial); a flip rate <25% or an inheritance excess <8 pp = no binding-failure mechanism and (b) is refuted. Negative result (register recomputed from context regardless of input language, no locatable binding step) refutes the lazy-inheritance account.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- inheritance scales with grammaticalisation and is causally repairable): tests claim (c). Data/model as Setup. Method: (a) dose-response -- correlate register-error and inheritance rate with the grammaticalisation-strength index vs a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / benchmark accuracy), with the crucial contrast of register-lax high-resource English vs register-heavy lower-resource Korean; (b) steering repair -- extract a shared social-register direction (mean activation difference formal vs informal, pooled across languages) at the binding layer, steer mis-registered items toward the correct register, and in bare context steer to INDUCE the wrong register. Systems compared: steering vs an explicit register-instruction prompting baseline vs a translate-context-first baseline. Decisive metric: Spearman(inheritance/error, grammaticalisation strength) vs Spearman(., resource proxy), then repair rate and induction rate, with content preservation, fluency (perplexity), and specificity. Convincing result: |Spearman with grammaticalisation| >=0.5 and exceeds |Spearman with resource| by >=0.2 (English patterning as register-lax despite high resource, Korean as register-heavy despite lower resource), AND steering repairs >=40% of mis-registered items and induces the wrong register in >=40% of bare-context items with content preserved and fluency unharmed. Indecision band: the two correlations within 0.05-0.2 of each other = a mixed account; repair/induction of 20-40% = partial (reported as such); correlations not stronger for grammaticalisation, or repair/induction <20%, = H3 is refuted. Negative result (inheritance tracks resource, or steering neither repairs nor induces register) refutes the scaling and causal-repair claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of abstract register may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used variable; we require the causal patching flip (in Exp. 2) and steering repair/induction (in Exp. 3) to establish functional relevance. 2. Ground-truth register in bare-context items can be genuinely ambiguous; we restrict to native-speaker-validated items with high inter-annotator agreement. 3. Separating abstract register from surface morphology is hard in obligatory-honorific languages where they nearly coincide; the register-lax languages and bare-context condition are the crucial dissociating cases. 4. Some models may produce degenerate or under-marked register in low-resource honorific languages (e.g., always default polite), collapsing the effect; quantifying such near-absence of register sensitivity is itself informative, and multiple models/languages give statistical power. 5. Tokenization of honorific verb endings varies across languages; we use verb-final or reply-final token representations and report tokenization statistics; obligatory-honorific vs T-V vs lexical cases are analyzed separately. 6. The grammaticalization-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen languages; we report robustness to alternative language choices. 7. Steering may trade register correctness for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: The core abstract-register representation and cross-lingual decodability are substantially pre-empted by the cited SAE/register work in the search summary. The most novel remaining claim is the mechanism: a late-layer binding step that maps a shared social-register variable onto obligatory honorific grammar, plus the lazy-inheritance failure hypothesis and grammaticalization-vs-resource dissociation. That is a real delta, but much of the paper’s headline novelty is already occupied.

If the result holds, researchers working on multilingual pragmatics and control would care; broader ML practice may care only modestly unless the mechanism generalizes widely.

Name: implicit_comparative_method
Title: Does the Model Know the Comparative Method? Causally Isolating an Implicit Sound-Correspondence Engine in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs can predict cognate forms across related languages by internally applying REGULAR sound-correspondence rules (an implicit 'comparative method') rather than only memorizing attested cognate pairs, and this rule-application is driven by an identifiable, causally-manipulable internal mechanism that generalizes to held-out language pairs and even nonce (invented) words.
Related Work: Historical-linguistics NLP shows specialized character-based models learn sound correspondences and latent diachronic information (Probing Multilingual Cognate Prediction, Fournier 2022; List 2018 automatic correspondence inference), and that mBERT/NMT representations cluster by phylogenetic/typological relatedness (Probing mBERT for Genetic/Typological Signals 2020; Language Embeddings Sometimes Contain Typological Generalizations 2023; Investigating Multilingual NMT Representations 2019). Transfer work exploits cognates and phonetic alignment for low-resource languages (PhoneXL 2023; Transliteration for Morphological Inflection 2020; Hamshentsnag 2025). ALL of this either (i) uses task-specialized character-level cognate/NMT models, or (ii) probes STATIC encoder representations for typology, treating relatedness as a similarity signal. None asks whether a modern GENERATIVE multilingual LLM, prompted in-context, applies REGULAR sound-correspondence rules productively (to nonce/unseen forms), nor gives CAUSAL mechanistic evidence that a specific internal component implements this rule-application distinct from lexical memorization. We reframe cognate prediction as a test of an implicit, causally-real comparative-method engine and provide the first location+intervention account.
Abstract: Historical linguistics reconstructs language history via the comparative method: identifying REGULAR sound correspondences (e.g., Latin 'p' -> English 'f' in pater/father, pisces/fish) and applying them productively. We ask whether multilingual LLMs have implicitly acquired such an engine. The sharp question is whether a model predicts cognates by APPLYING a regular rule that generalizes to words it has never seen paired (including invented nonce forms), or merely RETRIEVES memorized cognate pairs. We first establish the behavior: given a few in-context correspondence exemplars from a language pair, can the model transform a held-out real word, and crucially a NONCE word (which cannot be memorized), into its cognate form obeying the correspondence? We test across language families (Romance, Germanic, Slavic, Indo-Aryan, Turkic) using established cognate resources (NorthEuraLex, CogNet, IELex) and nonce stimuli constructed to obey known correspondences. We predict above-chance productive rule application that degrades gracefully with the number/regularity of correspondences and with typological distance. We then locate the mechanism: probing and vocabulary-projection to find where correspondence rules are represented, and activation patching / steering to test causality. Our central mechanistic claim is that SOME internal component (a small set of mid-layer features/heads) carries the active correspondence rule: patching it from a Latin->English run into a Latin->German run should switch the applied correspondence, and steering along a recovered 'correspondence direction' should induce or repair rule application on nonce words. Experiments use Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. This bridges the comparative method with mechanistic interpretability and dissociates rule-based generalization from lexical memorization in multilingual LLMs.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters); base weights are frozen throughout. Probes are L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers trained on cached hidden states with a 60/20/20 train/validation/test split by item and 3 seeds {0,1,2} for probe initialization and split; behavioral generation is greedy decoding with 3 prompt-sampling seeds (exemplar choice and order); activation patching and steering add or replace activations at inference with no weight updates. "pp" = percentage points; "correspondence-obedience rate" = fraction of rule-relevant segments transformed exactly as the annotated sound-correspondence rule dictates.

Experiment 1 (H1 - productive rule application vs lexical memorization): Tests whether the model applies a regular sound-correspondence rule to forms it cannot have memorized, rather than only retrieving attested cognate pairs. Data: real cognate pairs used as-is from NorthEuraLex (~1,016 concepts x 100+ languages), CogNet (~8M pairs, 338 languages), and IELex (~200 Indo-European concepts); we sample 120 pairs per family for Romance, Germanic, Slavic, Indo-Aryan, and Turkic (600 real items), keeping only pairs with clean single-word tokenization and an annotated regular correspondence. We also construct 60 nonce source words per family (300 total) that obey source-language phonotactics and to which an annotated correspondence set applies deterministically, so the correct target cannot have been seen. Fewer than the full resource because each item requires per-segment correspondence annotation and clean tokenization. In-context prompt gives k=5 correspondence exemplars, then asks for the cognate of a held-out real word and of a nonce word. Systems compared: model output vs (i) copy-source baseline, (ii) random-correspondence baseline, (iii) memorization ceiling (obedience on already-seen real pairs). Decisive metric: nonce-word correspondence-obedience rate (exact-match and normalized edit distance secondary). Convincing result: nonce obedience exceeds both the copy-source and random-correspondence baselines by >=15 pp averaged over the three models AND is within 20 pp of real-word obedience. Indecision band: a nonce-vs-baseline gap of 5-15 pp is inconclusive (weak/partial rule use); we then report per-family results and withhold the global productive-rule claim. Negative result: nonce obedience within 5 pp of baseline means the model does not apply the rule productively, and the central claim of the hypothesis fails.

Experiment 2 (H2 - a locatable internal representation of the active correspondence): Tests whether a compact set of mid-layer components carries the identity of the correspondence being applied and is decodable before output. Data: the Exp. 1 items; hidden states cached at every layer at the source word's last token and at exemplar-pair positions. A per-layer linear probe decodes (i) the target segment corresponding to the source segment and (ii) the active correspondence-set identity (e.g. Latin->English vs Latin->German); logit-lens vocabulary projection and attention attribution rank the heads that read exemplar pairs. Systems compared: trained probe vs label-shuffled-control probe vs random-direction baseline. Decisive metric: peak-layer probe accuracy for correspondence-set identity minus shuffled-control accuracy; secondary: number of heads accounting for 80% of attribution mass. Convincing result: identity decodable at a mid-layer >=15 pp above the shuffled control with <=10 heads carrying most attribution, yielding ranked candidate components for Exp. 3. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control means a weak/diffuse signal; we still pass candidates to the causal test but flag low localization. Negative result: <=5 pp above control means no decodable correspondence representation, and we rely solely on the causal search in Exp. 3. Decodability alone is not evidence of use; Exp. 3 is required.

Experiment 3 (H2/H3 - the representation is causally manipulable): Tests whether intervening on the located component switches the applied correspondence and induces or repairs rule application, dissociating rule from retrieval. Data: the five families plus a held-out language pair per family not used in Exp. 2 probe training, and the nonce items. (a) Activation patching: run one source word under correspondence set A (Latin->English) vs B (Latin->German), patch the candidate mid-layer component from the A-run into the B-run. (b) Steering: a "correspondence direction" = mean activation difference between correct-rule and wrong-rule runs, computed on training items and applied to held-out/nonce items. Systems compared: patch/steer at the candidate component vs random-component and random-direction controls; effect on nonce items (pure rule) vs high-frequency memorized cognates (retrieval control). Decisive metric: correspondence-switch rate (fraction where the applied correspondence flips A->B under patching), and steering repair/induction rate, each minus its control; lexical-identity preservation (edit distance to intended stem unchanged within noise) reported alongside. Convincing result: switch and repair/induction rates >=15 pp above control with specificity (unrelated segments unchanged) AND larger on nonce than on memorized cognates. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control is inconclusive - consistent with a distributed rather than localized mechanism; we then report degree of localization and fall back to a direction-based account. Negative result: <=5 pp above control means the correspondence signal is epiphenomenal and the causal-mechanism claim fails.

Experiment 4 (H1/H3 - generalization scope, dose-response): Tests the hypothesis's scope claim that productive rule application generalizes across held-out pairs and degrades predictably. Data: Exp. 1 items, varying exemplar count k in {1,3,5,10}, regular vs irregular/exceptional items, and lang2vec typological distance between source and target. Decisive metric: Spearman correlation between nonce correspondence-obedience and each of (typological distance, correspondence regularity). Convincing result: |rho| >= 0.4 with a 95% CI excluding 0 in the predicted direction (obedience falls with distance and with irregularity). Indecision band: |rho| 0.2-0.4, or CI touching 0, is reported as suggestive only, not confirmatory. Negative result: rho approximately 0 means no systematic generalization structure, bounding the hypothesis to memorized-like behavior. Ablations (secondary, not hypothesis tests): layer sweep for where the rule is malleable; exemplar order/count; probe transfer across the three models; proto-form reconstruction as an exploratory productive task. Reported metrics throughout: correspondence-obedience, exact-match, edit distance, switch/repair/induction rates, Spearman with distance and regularity, specificity, and generation fluency (perplexity).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Nonce words may still partially overlap memorized substrings, blurring the rule-vs-memorization line; we control by using segments/positions where the correspondence is the only cue and by comparing against a copy baseline. 2. Probe/logit-lens decodability may reflect the readout basis rather than a used representation; the causal patching-switch and steering induction (Exp. 5) are required to establish functional relevance. 3. The correspondence mechanism may be diffuse rather than localized; we report degree of localization and fall back to a direction-based account. 4. Some models may simply copy or transliterate rather than apply correspondences, collapsing the effect; even documenting the near-absence of productive rule use, and its dependence on family/distance, is an informative finding, and three models give statistical power. 5. Tokenization fragments words unevenly across scripts, complicating segment-level attribution; we restrict to clean-tokenizing pairs, work at last-token-of-word where needed, and report tokenization statistics. 6. Ground-truth 'correct' cognate forms for real words can involve irregular changes; we separate regular vs irregular items and rely on nonce items for the cleanest rule test. 7. Steering may trade rule application for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: The core novelty is fairly strong: it asks whether multilingual LLMs productively apply cross-language sound-correspondence rules in-context, rather than only memorizing cognate pairs, and it adds causal mechanistic evidence via patching/steering. Compared with prior cognate-prediction and multilingual probing work, the delta is not just a new benchmark but a new claim about implicit comparative-method computation inside generative LLMs. The main weakness is that the rule-vs-analogy distinction may collapse unless carefully controlled.
