Name: conceptual_metaphor_override
Title: Anger Is Not Always Fire: How Multilingual LLMs Override Culture-Specific Idiom Meanings with Their Dominant Language's Conceptual Metaphors
Short Hypothesis: When interpreting an idiom in a non-dominant language, multilingual LLMs covertly retrieve the figurative meaning implied by their DOMINANT language's conceptual-metaphor system, and this dominant-language figurative reading is co-activated as a latent competitor. For idioms whose source-language conceptual metaphor differs from the dominant language's (culture-specific idioms), this causes systematic misinterpretation, whereas idioms grounded in a shared/universal conceptual metaphor are interpreted correctly. The override is a locatable figurative-retrieval-and-selection failure whose strength scales with the conceptual-metaphor distance between the query language and the dominant language, not with resource level.
Related Work: Monolingual mechanistic work localizes idiom processing to early-layer 'Idiom Heads' and competing figurative/literal pathways (Anatomy of an Idiom 2025; Tug-of-war between figurative and literal 2025; NMT idiom analysis 2022). Cross-lingual work shows figurative-detection knowledge sits in middle layers and transfers across languages (Metaphors in PLMs 2022), that a reusable cross-lingual figurative-GENERATION steering direction exists (Cross-Lingual Steering for Figurative Language Generation 2026), and that cross-lingual lexical overlap and shared idioms boost PIE disambiguation (MultiCoPIE 2025; Meta4XNLI 2024). All of these treat figurativeness as a single transferable feature and study detection/generation of figurativeness, or literal-vs-figurative disambiguation WITHIN a language. None asks whether the SPECIFIC figurative MEANING retrieved for a foreign idiom is contaminated by the dominant language's conceptual-metaphor mapping, nor identifies a cross-lingual conceptual-metaphor OVERRIDE as a co-activation/selection failure. We reframe idiom comprehension as a cross-cultural meaning-SELECTION problem grounded in Conceptual Metaphor Theory, provide causal (patching + steering) evidence for a figurative-retrieval locus that inherits the dominant metaphor, and dissociate conceptual-metaphor distance from resource level.
Abstract: Idioms encode culture-specific conceptual metaphors: 'anger is fire' is near-universal, but many idioms map emotions and concepts through images idiosyncratic to one language's cultural history. A multilingual model reading an idiom in a non-dominant language must retrieve the meaning licensed by THAT language's conceptual system, not its own dominant one. We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs instead default to their dominant language's conceptual-metaphor mapping, covertly co-activating the dominant-language figurative reading and systematically misinterpreting idioms whose source metaphor diverges from it. We test this with a controlled set of idioms drawn from multilingual idiom corpora (MultiCoPIE, IdiomX, Meta4XNLI), each annotated with its underlying conceptual metaphor and labeled shared (same mapping as the dominant language) or culture-specific (divergent mapping), rendered across 10+ languages spanning several scripts and families. Behaviorally, we measure interpretation accuracy and the rate at which the model's paraphrase/entailment judgment matches the dominant-language metaphor rather than the correct source meaning. Mechanistically, we (i) show via logit-lens and probes that the dominant-language figurative meaning is decodable during foreign-idiom processing (co-activation), (ii) locate a mid/early-layer figurative-retrieval stage via activation patching whose swap flips the selected meaning, and (iii) steer along a recovered conceptual-metaphor direction to causally repair culture-specific misinterpretations and to induce override on shared idioms. We predict override strength scales with conceptual-metaphor distance and not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. The work gives the first mechanistic account of cross-cultural conceptual-metaphor interference in multilingual LLMs and a training-free fix.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout; the "dominant language" is operationalized per model as English (its highest-resource pretraining language), verified by measuring monolingual idiom-interpretation accuracy per language. Probes are L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers on cached hidden states (60/20/20 train/validation/test split by idiom, 3 seeds {0,1,2}); behavioral items are scored under greedy decoding. Steering and activation patching modify activations at inference with no weight updates. "pp" = percentage points. Stimuli: from MultiCoPIE, IdiomX, and Meta4XNLI (thousands of idiom entries combined), we curate 250 idioms across 10+ languages (Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari, 4+ families); fewer than the source pools because each idiom needs native-speaker-validated annotation of (a) correct figurative meaning, (b) underlying conceptual metaphor, (c) a SHARED vs CULTURE-SPECIFIC label relative to the dominant-language metaphor, and, for culture-specific idioms, the incorrect meaning the dominant-language metaphor implies. We keep only idioms with >=0.7 inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff alpha) on the label. Per idiom we build multiple-choice paraphrase items and NLI items, and compute a conceptual-metaphor distance to the dominant language.

Experiment 1 (H1 - dominant-language co-activation as a latent competitor): Tests whether, while processing a non-dominant-language idiom, the dominant-language figurative reading is decodable internally before selection. Data: the 250 idioms; hidden states cached at idiom-span tokens (last-token and pooled-span). A linear probe and logit-lens test whether the dominant-language paraphrase's answer tokens are decodable in early/mid layers, contrasting SHARED vs CULTURE-SPECIFIC idioms and a monosemous-phrase control. Systems compared: trained probe vs label-shuffled control vs random-direction baseline. Decisive metric: rank/log-prob of the dominant-language reading's tokens at the peak layer relative to the shuffled control. Convincing result: the dominant-language reading is decodable >=15 pp (or >2 nats in log-prob) above control for culture-specific idioms, and above its own final-layer selection rate (co-activation that is later suppressed). Indecision band: 5-15 pp (or 0.5-2 nats) is inconclusive - reported as weak co-activation, not confirmation. Negative result: within 5 pp of control means no latent dominant-language competitor, and the co-activation claim fails. Decodability alone is not use; Exp. 3 supplies causal evidence.

Experiment 2 (H2 - culture-specific misinterpretation vs shared correctness): Tests whether idioms whose metaphor diverges from the dominant language are systematically misinterpreted while shared-metaphor idioms are not. Data: the 250 idioms as paraphrase-selection and NLI items in each language. Systems compared: (i) native-language query, (ii) query-in-dominant-language upper bound, (iii) translate-to-English-first, (iv) literal-only control. Decisive metric: OVERRIDE RATE = fraction of culture-specific items where the chosen meaning matches the dominant-language conceptual mapping rather than the correct source meaning; secondary: interpretation accuracy for SHARED vs CULTURE-SPECIFIC. Convincing result: override rate on culture-specific idioms exceeds override rate on shared idioms by >=15 pp AND interpretation accuracy is >=15 pp lower on culture-specific than shared, averaged over models. Indecision band: a 5-15 pp gap is inconclusive - reported per language/family rather than as a global override claim. Negative result: <5 pp gap means culture-specificity does not drive misinterpretation and the hypothesis's central behavioral claim fails.

Experiment 3 (H3 - a locatable, causal figurative-retrieval/selection stage): Tests whether a compact early/mid-layer component selects the figurative meaning and can be flipped. Data: culture-specific idioms run twice - under a disambiguating context forcing the CORRECT source meaning vs one forcing the DOMINANT-metaphor meaning, yielding different downstream judgments. Activation patching transfers early/mid-layer components (seeded by known idiom-processing "Idiom Head" locations from prior work) from one run into the other; steering uses a conceptual-metaphor direction (mean activation difference between correct-source and dominant-override runs). Systems compared: patch/steer at candidate components vs random-component and random-direction controls; steering to REPAIR culture-specific errors and to INDUCE override on shared idioms. Decisive metric: meaning-flip rate under patching, and steering repair/induction rate, each minus its control, with idiom-identity preservation reported. Convincing result: flip and repair/induction rates >=15 pp above control with specificity (unrelated items unchanged) and fluency (perplexity) within 10% of baseline. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control indicates a distributed rather than localized stage; we then report degree of localization. Negative result: <=5 pp above control means selection is not causally locatable and the override-as-selection-failure claim fails.

Experiment 4 (H3 - conceptual-metaphor distance, not resource level, sets override strength): Tests the dissociation between conceptual-metaphor distance and resource level. Data: per-idiom and per-language conceptual-metaphor distance vs a resource-level proxy (pretraining share estimate and per-language benchmark accuracy); the key contrast is a low-resource language with SHARED metaphors vs a high-resource language with CULTURE-SPECIFIC ones. Decisive metric: partial Spearman correlation of override rate with conceptual-metaphor distance controlling for resource, and with resource controlling for distance. Convincing result: correlation with distance is >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0) while the partial correlation with resource is not distinguishable from 0 (CI includes 0), and the low-resource-shared language shows lower override than the high-resource-culture-specific one. Indecision band: distance correlation 0.2-0.4, or both partial correlations sharing sign and overlapping CIs, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: override tracks resource (|rho| with resource >=0.4) and not distance, refuting the distance-driven claim. Ablations (secondary): layer sweep; a shared-lexical-overlap subset from MultiCoPIE to separate lexical overlap from conceptual-metaphor sharing; probe transfer across models; whether the competitor is the dominant language or the typologically-nearest high-resource language. Reported metrics throughout: interpretation accuracy, override rate, co-decodability rank/log-prob, causal flip/repair/induction rates, identity preservation, Spearman with distance vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Annotating each idiom's 'underlying conceptual metaphor' and shared-vs-culture-specific labels is subjective; we use Conceptual Metaphor Theory categories, multiple native-speaker annotators, and report inter-annotator agreement, restricting to high-agreement items. 2. Probe co-decodability may reflect the readout basis rather than functional co-activation; the causal patching flip (Exp. 4) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) are required to establish functional relevance. 3. Override could be confounded with lexical overlap rather than conceptual-metaphor sharing; Exp. 7's shared-lexical subset and Exp. 5's dissociation controls address this. 4. Tokenization fragments multi-word idioms unevenly across scripts; we use last-token-of-idiom or full-span pooled representations and report tokenization statistics. 5. Strong models may resolve context so well that override is rare in disambiguating contexts; weak/neutral-context and induction experiments still yield informative causal results, and multiple languages/models give statistical power. 6. Steering may trade interpretation accuracy for fluency; we report both. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) multilingual LLMs misinterpret non-dominant-language idioms when the source idiom's conceptual metaphor differs from the model's dominant-language metaphor; (2) the failure is not just generic figurativeness transfer, but a specific dominant-language conceptual-metaphor override/co-activation problem; (3) the effect scales with conceptual-metaphor distance more than resource level; (4) the claim is measurable behaviorally and mechanistically via override rate, probing, patching, and steering; (5) shared/universal-metaphor idioms should be preserved while culture-specific ones fail. Relative to the cited prior work, the behavioral phenomenon is only partly new: the search summary says a very similar broad claim already exists in work on cultural translation and multicultural proverbs. The novelty therefore lives mainly in the tighter framing via Conceptual Metaphor Theory, the SHARED-vs-CULTURE-SPECIFIC contrast, the proposed distance metric, and the causal mechanistic localization of a figurative-selection stage. That is a meaningful delta, but it is an extension and mechanistic sharpening of an emerging line rather than a cleanly new problem. The closest prior work family is cross-lingual idiom/figurative-language benchmarking plus mechanistic idiom retrieval work and cross-lingual figurative steering. The actual delta is: from 'figurative language is transferable' to 'the wrong culture-specific conceptual mapping is actively selected from the dominant language, and this is causally localizable.'

Define the conceptual-metaphor distance metric operationally enough to show it is not just a post hoc label.
Separate novelty of the behavioral finding from novelty of the mechanistic explanation; claim only the latter if behavior already exists.
Clarify whether the contribution is a new task, new annotation scheme, new metric, or new causal mechanism.

impact.reasoning: The problem under study is whether multilingual LLMs preserve the intended meaning of idioms across languages or instead impose a dominant-language conceptual framework. Who cares: multilingual NLP researchers, cultural-alignment/fairness researchers, figurative-language researchers, and anyone deploying multilingual assistants in culturally diverse settings. If true, downstream work could shift toward explicit cultural-metaphor modeling, better evaluation of figurative language across languages, and mitigation strategies for culturally biased interpretation. The strongest one-line case: it exposes a specific, linguistically meaningful failure mode in multilingual reasoning that matters for cross-cultural reliability. This is not a niche curiosity because idioms and proverbs are common in human communication and are a realistic stress test for multilingual systems. However, the search summary suggests the broad phenomenon is already partly documented, so the upside is less 'new field-opening surprise' and more 'important mechanistic clarification.' So what? If the result holds, serious researchers would likely use the benchmark and mechanism as a diagnostic for multilingual cultural robustness; if it does not, they may conclude dominant-metaphor contamination is not a general explanation and look elsewhere. That is still useful, but not obviously direction-changing at the level of the whole area.

Include an example of how a positive or negative result would change model evaluation or deployment practice.

review.reasoning: The proposal is plausible and testable, but several claims are underspecified. The biggest logical gap is the assumption that each idiom has a single correct underlying conceptual metaphor and that 'dominant-language' metaphor can be cleanly identified and measured across 10+ languages; that is contestable and may blur with translation choices, lexical overlap, or general semantic priors. The hypothesis is directionally clear but not yet fully falsifiable because 'override' could be explained by many correlated factors unless the controls are very strong. Related work is reasonably specific, and the search summary indicates the behavioral idea is not entirely new, so the paper must win on mechanism and measurement rather than broad claim alone. The experiment plan is concrete, but some pieces need tightening: probe decodability alone is not causal; patching/steering helps, but you need stronger controls to show the dominant-language meaning is specifically selected rather than merely more linearly readable. Missing analyses include human validation of metaphor annotations across cultures, robustness to prompt/context variation, comparisons against translation-based and retrieval-based baselines, and tests for whether the effect persists after controlling for token frequency, lexical overlap, and model pretraining exposure. Overall, if executed carefully with strong annotation and causal controls, this could be publishable at a serious ML venue, but as written it reads a bit overclaimed and vulnerable to annotation ambiguity. Minimum viable edits: narrow the claim to a specific benchmarked phenomenon, define the operational metric precisely, add controls for lexical overlap/frequency/translation artifacts, and spell out causal tests that distinguish metaphor override from generic semantic confusion.

Name: language_as_temporal_anchor
Title: What Year Is It in Your Language? Query Language as a Covert Temporal Anchor for Time-Sensitive Facts in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: For facts whose correct answer changes over time (e.g., current heads of state, champions, populations), the language a question is asked in covertly sets the model's default temporal anchor: the model tends to answer with the fact-state that was dominant in that language's training data era, so different languages return answers 'frozen' at different points in time. We hypothesize (a) a shared, language-agnostic temporal-anchor representation exists that determines which fact-version is retrieved; (b) the query language causally sets this anchor, producing systematic per-language recency offsets on time-sensitive facts; and (c) the size of the offset scales with the resource/coverage recency of the language rather than with typological distance, and can be causally corrected by steering the shared temporal-anchor direction without retraining.
Related Work: Parametric Temporal Conflict (Hossain et al. 2026) shows LLMs store both outdated and updated facts and default to the outdated one via a localized upper-layer representational preference, but the study is monolingual (English) and never treats language as a variable. Time Travel Engine (2026) shows a continuous, cross-lingually isomorphic temporal manifold and steers 'zeitgeist', but studies stylistic/era navigation, not factual-recency errors and not the query language's causal role in choosing which factual version is recalled. TiEBe (2025) and LiveCLKTBench (2025) document geographic and language-dependent recall gaps for time-sensitive events, but interpret them as resource/transfer gaps and provide no mechanistic account. EverGreenQA (2025) classifies question mutability but does not study per-language temporal drift. Multilingual knowledge-editing work (MLaKE, XME, LangEdit, LU-LAFNs) treats facts as static and studies edit propagation. None frames the query language as an implicit temporal anchor that selects among stored fact-versions, nor gives causal (patching + steering) evidence for a language-set temporal-anchor variable that produces predictable per-language recency offsets. We contribute this reframing, a quantitative per-language 'temporal offset' metric, and a training-free anchor-steering fix.
Abstract: Many facts have no timeless answer: the head of state, the reigning champion, or a country's population all change over time, and a language model must decide which era's answer to give. We ask whether the language in which a question is posed covertly determines this decision. We hypothesize that the query language acts as an implicit temporal anchor, biasing a multilingual LLM toward the fact-state dominant in that language's training data, so the same question answered in different languages returns answers effectively frozen at different times. We build TIME-DRIFT, a set of time-sensitive facts with dated ground-truth transitions (from Wikidata position-holder changes and dated records), rendered in 12+ languages spanning several scripts and families, and measure a per-language Temporal Offset: how far behind the true current state each language's default answer sits. Mechanistically, we test for a shared, language-agnostic temporal-anchor representation using linear probes and vocabulary projection, then use activation patching to test whether swapping late-layer language-identity signals shifts the retrieved fact-version, and whether steering a recovered temporal-anchor direction moves answers forward or backward in time. We predict systematic per-language offsets that scale with a language's data-recency/coverage rather than typological distance, that the offset is causally set by a language-conditioned anchor separable from fact content, and that anchor-steering recovers the current answer in low-recency languages without harming fluency, outperforming date-prefix prompting and translate-to-English baselines. Experiments span Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2. The work reframes cross-lingual factual disparities as a controllable temporal-anchoring phenomenon.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout. Probes are L2-regularized logistic/linear regressors on cached hidden states (60/20/20 train/validation/test by fact, 3 seeds {0,1,2}); default answers are elicited by greedy decoding with no date cue. Steering and activation patching modify activations at inference with no weight updates. "pp" = percentage points. Dataset (TIME-DRIFT), constructed from Wikidata: facts with dated transitions - position-holders (heads of state, club managers, CEO tenures) and dated records (sports champions, tallest building, world-population brackets) - each with a full timeline of (value, valid-from, valid-to). Wikidata exposes hundreds of thousands of such position statements; we select facts with >=2 transitions inside the models' plausible pretraining window and clean, matchable answer tokens, targeting ~400 facts x 12+ languages (Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari, 4+ families) with matched entity names, plus an evergreen/timeless-fact control set (~100 facts). Fewer than all Wikidata positions because each fact needs a verified transition timeline and cross-language name matching. Per language we compute data-recency/coverage proxies (topic Wikipedia edit recency, article length, pretraining-share estimate) and lang2vec typological/script distance to the dominant language.

Experiment 1 (H-behavior - query language produces per-language recency offsets): Tests whether the same time-sensitive question, asked in different languages, returns answers frozen at different times. Data: the ~400 TIME-DRIFT facts in each language; each default answer is mapped to its validity interval via the timeline. Decisive metric: per-language Temporal Offset = (true current date) minus (midpoint of the answered value's validity interval), in years; secondary: fraction returning the outdated vs current value, and cross-language answer-disagreement rate on identical facts. Systems compared: each language vs the dominant-language offset; evergreen control set (should show near-zero offset). Convincing result: at least half the non-dominant languages show a mean offset differing from the dominant language by >=1.0 year with 95% CI excluding 0, and cross-language disagreement on time-sensitive facts exceeds disagreement on evergreen facts by >=15 pp. Indecision band: per-language offset differences of 0.3-1.0 year, or CIs touching 0, are reported as suggestive only. Negative result: offsets within 0.3 year of the dominant language across languages means the query language does not set a temporal anchor and the behavioral claim fails.

Experiment 2 (H-a - a shared, language-agnostic temporal-anchor representation): Tests whether a single representation encodes the retrieved fact's era across languages. Data: TIME-DRIFT hidden states at answer positions, mid/late layers. A probe decodes the era/date of the retrieved fact; a probe trained on one language is applied to others (transfer). Systems compared: within-language probe, cross-language transfer probe, label-shuffled control. Decisive metric: cross-language transfer accuracy of the era probe minus shuffled control; secondary: agreement between decoded era and the answered value's actual date. Convincing result: transfer accuracy >=15 pp above control and decoded era matches the answered value's date on held-out languages (evidence of one shared anchor). Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control indicates a partially shared representation; reported as such. Negative result: transfer within 5 pp of control means anchors are language-specific, not shared, weakening claim (a). Decodability is not use; Exp. 3 is required.

Experiment 3 (H-b - the query language causally sets the anchor): Tests whether swapping the language-identity signal shifts which fact-version is retrieved. Data: facts where a low-recency language returns the outdated value and the dominant language returns the current value. Activation patching transfers the late-layer language-identity signal from the dominant run into the low-recency run. Systems compared: patch at the language-identity component vs random-component control; also compare against date-prefix prompting ("As of 2024, ...") to confirm the newer value is present but not defaulted-to (distinguishing anchoring from ignorance). Decisive metric: fact-version shift rate (fraction of low-recency runs that flip toward the current value) minus control, with fact identity preserved. Convincing result: shift rate >=15 pp above control AND date-prefix prompting also recovers the current value on the same items (co-present versions, not missing knowledge). Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control is inconclusive - reported as partial causal role. Negative result: <=5 pp above control, or date-prefix failing to recover the current value, means the offset reflects missing knowledge rather than a language-set anchor, and claim (b) fails.

Experiment 4 (H-c - offset scales with data-recency, not typological distance): Tests the dissociation between recency/coverage and typology. Data: per-language Temporal Offset vs (i) recency/coverage proxies and (ii) lang2vec typological/script distance; the key contrast is a typologically distant but well-covered language vs a close but sparsely-covered one. Decisive metric: partial Spearman of offset with recency controlling for typology, and with typology controlling for recency. Convincing result: partial correlation with recency >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0) while partial correlation with typology is indistinguishable from 0 (CI includes 0). Indecision band: recency correlation 0.2-0.4, or both partials overlapping in CI, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: offset tracks typology (|rho| >=0.4) and not recency, refuting claim (c)'s scaling half.

Experiment 5 (H-c - training-free correction by steering the shared anchor): Tests whether steering the temporal-anchor direction moves answers in time without retraining. Data: low-recency-language queries returning outdated values; the evergreen control set for specificity. A temporal-anchor direction = mean activation difference between "as of [recent year]" and "as of [older year]" framings, pooled across languages. Systems compared: anchor steering vs date-prefix prompting vs translate-to-English-first; a reverse-steer control (steer backward) to confirm the direction is temporal, not a generic correctness push. Decisive metric: recency-correction rate (fraction flipped to the current value) minus the outdated-answer baseline; secondary: specificity on evergreen facts (should stay unchanged), output-language fidelity, fluency (perplexity), and a monotone dose-response for reverse steering (older values recalled at larger backward magnitude). Convincing result: forward steering corrects >=15 pp more items than the baseline while changing <=5 pp of evergreen facts, and reverse steering yields a monotone shift to older values. Indecision band: 5-15 pp correction, or evergreen change of 5-10 pp, is reported as a weak/selective effect. Negative result: <5 pp correction or evergreen change exceeding forward correction means the direction is not functionally temporal, refuting the steerability claim. Ablations (secondary): layer sweep; probe transfer across models; fact-type breakdown (positions vs records); model scale. Reported metrics throughout: Temporal Offset, outdated-answer rate, cross-language disagreement, probe/transfer accuracy, patching shift rate, steering correction/induction rate, specificity, fluency, Spearman with recency vs typology.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Ground-truth 'current' value and exact transition dates can be ambiguous or lag reality; we restrict to Wikidata-verified transitions with clear valid-from/valid-to intervals and exclude contested cases. 2. The observed offset could reflect missing recent knowledge rather than a language-set anchor over co-present versions; the patching (Exp. 5) and the demonstration that date-prefix prompting recovers the current value (as in PTC) test whether newer knowledge is present but not defaulted-to, distinguishing anchoring from ignorance. 3. Probe decodability of era may reflect the readout basis, not a used representation; we require the causal patching and steering results to establish functional relevance. 4. Per-language recency proxies are noisy; we use multiple proxies and report robustness, and the typology-vs-recency dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts. 5. Steering may over-shift and harm evergreen facts; the evergreen control set and specificity/fluency metrics test selectivity. 6. Tokenization/entity-name differences across scripts complicate answer matching; we restrict to entities with clean, matchable answer tokens and use last-token-of-answer representations. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) multilingual LLMs exhibit time-sensitive factual disagreement across languages; (2) query language acts as a causal temporal anchor selecting among fact versions; (3) the offset tracks language-specific training-data recency more than typological distance; (4) a latent temporal-anchor direction can be recovered and steered to correct answers without retraining; (5) the work introduces a TIME-DRIFT benchmark/metric. The behavior is interesting, but the closest prior families already cover the two main halves: cross-lingual timeliness gaps are known, and latent temporal drift/steering is already known (even if mostly English). The genuine delta is the unified causal framing around query language as the anchor plus the causal patching test. That is non-trivial, but it is an incremental mechanistic extension rather than a fundamentally new task or theory. Novelty lives mostly in the mechanism claim and the cross-lingual setting, not in the phenomenon itself.

impact.reasoning: Phenomenon under study: multilingual factual freshness / recency reliability, specifically whether asking in different languages yields different temporal versions of the same fact. This matters to anyone using multilingual LLMs for current facts: search, assistants, translation-based QA, RAG, and knowledge editing. Strongest one-line case: if language itself determines which historical snapshot the model uses, then multilingual systems are systematically unreliable in a way that affects real users and may require language-aware mitigation. So what? Even if the method is simple, a demonstrated causal language-to-temporal-bias effect would change how people evaluate, debug, and patch multilingual knowledge freshness. This is important, but likely not direction-shifting at the field level because the general class of cross-lingual timeliness issues is already documented. Uptake could be decent if the benchmark is clean and the causal result is strong, since practitioners care about freshness and fairness across languages.

review.reasoning: The hypothesis is interesting and reasonably falsifiable, but there are several gaps. The main logical leap is from correlation between language and recency to a specific latent 'temporal anchor' mechanism; activation patching and probing can support this, but they do not by themselves establish causality without stronger controls. The proposal risks overclaiming if it frames the effect as a shared language-agnostic anchor rather than one of several plausible explanations (translation artifacts, tokenization, retrieval differences, training-data skew, answer-format priors). The hypothesis is scoped, but some terms are underspecified: 'temporal offset,' 'dominant in that language's training-data era,' and 'shared temporal-anchor representation' need operational definitions. Related work is decent but the positioning should be sharper about what is already known versus what is being newly unified. Experiments are promising and mostly feasible, but need stronger controls: matched translation quality checks, prompt-length and tokenization controls, bilingual paraphrase controls, model-family generalization, and explicit negative controls showing evergreen facts do not shift. The causal steering experiment needs careful reversibility and specificity tests to avoid simply measuring generic recency or answer-confidence shifts. If executed well, this could fit a serious ML venue as a mechanistic/benchmarking paper, but only if it tightens the causal story and pre-registers the exact claims. Minimum viable edits: define the metric rigorously, narrow the causal claim, add confound controls, and specify success/failure criteria for each experiment.

Name: digraphia_script_language_dissociation
Title: Same Language, Two Scripts: Using Digraphia to Causally Dissociate Script Identity from Language Identity in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: What prior work calls a model's 'language-identity' representation is substantially a *script-identity* representation. Using digraphic languages (one spoken language written in two scripts, e.g. Serbian Cyrillic/Latin, Uzbek Latin/Cyrillic, Punjabi Gurmukhi/Shahmukhi, Hindi/Urdu), we hypothesize that (a) script and language are separable, causally-manipulable directions; (b) factual/semantic knowledge stored while reading one script of a digraphic language fails to transfer to the SAME language in its other script far more than the near-identical spoken content warrants, and this failure is a script-binding artifact, not genuine language separation; and (c) a training-free 'latent transliteration' steering (swapping only the script direction) recovers cross-script knowledge without translation.
Related Work: Prior work shows script is linearly encoded and that writing-system identity is what token-embedding geometry captures (Hyperpolyglot LLMs 2023), that LLMs latently romanize non-Roman scripts as an intermediate bridge (RomanLens 2025), that script vectors linearly steer output script in speech models (Linear Script Representations 2026), that script similarity dominates cross-lingual knowledge sharing and cross-lingual editing fails across script families (Beneath the Surface 2024; XME 2024), and that transliteration to a common script improves multilingual modeling (Does Transliteration Help 2023; Aksharantar 2022). All of these treat script and language as entangled, or study script effects across *different* languages, where script and language covary. None uses digraphia—the unique natural experiment where language is held constant and only script varies (and where the same script can be shared across different languages)—to causally *dissociate* a script-identity representation from a language-identity representation, nor tests whether cross-script knowledge-transfer failure within one language is a re-bindable script artifact. We contribute this dissociation, a causal script-vs-language localization, and a training-free latent-transliteration fix.
Abstract: Multilingual language models are said to compute in a shared concept space and carry a 'language-identity' variable that governs decoding. But in almost all prior studies, language and script covary, so it is unknown how much of that 'language' variable is really *script*. Digraphic languages—a single spoken language written in two scripts (Serbian in Cyrillic and Latin, Uzbek in Latin and Cyrillic, Punjabi in Gurmukhi and Shahmukhi, Hindi/Urdu)—provide a clean natural experiment: they hold language constant while varying script, and (via shared scripts across languages) hold script constant while varying language. We use them to dissociate a script-identity representation from a language-identity representation. First, we train linear probes and use activation patching to test whether script and language are separable, causally-manipulable directions, and whether the classic 'language vector' is dominated by its script component. Second, we measure within-language cross-script knowledge transfer: a fact taught or queried in one script of a digraphic language should be recoverable in the other script if knowledge is language-shared, but we predict a large script-bound gap, especially where the two scripts are orthographically dissimilar. Third, we localize where script gates retrieval and test a training-free 'latent transliteration'—steering only the script direction—to recover cross-script knowledge, compared against surface transliteration and translation baselines. Experiments span Serbian, Uzbek, Kazakh, Punjabi, Hindi/Urdu, and Sindhi using Dakshina/Aksharantar transliteration resources and mLAMA facts, on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. The work turns digraphia into a precise instrument for separating what multilingual models know about *languages* from what they know about *scripts*.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout. Probes are L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers on cached hidden states (60/20/20 train/validation/test by utterance, 3 seeds {0,1,2}); factual queries scored under greedy decoding. Steering, activation patching, and locate-and-edit (ROME/MEMIT) modify activations/weights only as each experiment specifies; base weights are otherwise frozen. "pp" = percentage points; "digraphic" = one spoken language written in two scripts. Data: identical utterances/facts rendered in both scripts of each digraphic language - Serbian (Cyrillic/Latin), Uzbek (Latin/Cyrillic), Kazakh (Cyrillic/Latin), Punjabi (Gurmukhi/Shahmukhi), Hindi/Urdu (Devanagari/Perso-Arabic), Sindhi (Perso-Arabic/Devanagari) - using Dakshina (~10k romanization/native pairs per language) and Aksharantar (~26M transliteration pairs across 21 Indic languages) as verified transliteration sources; facts from mLAMA/BMLAMA (tens of thousands of templated facts across 50+ languages). We use ~2,000 parallel utterances and ~1,500 facts per digraphic language (both scripts), fewer than the pools because each item must be verified in both scripts and clean-tokenizing. Cross-language same-script controls (Serbian-Cyrillic vs Russian-Cyrillic; Uzbek-Latin vs Turkish-Latin) hold script constant while varying language. Per script pair we compute an orthographic-dissimilarity index (character-overlap and romanization edit distance).

Experiment 1 (H-a - script and language are separable, and the classic "language vector" is mostly script): Tests whether script identity and language identity are distinct decodable directions, and whether the standard mean-difference language vector projects onto the script direction. Data: hidden states from digraphic parallel items (decorrelating script from language) plus same-script cross-language controls. Per-layer probes decode (i) script identity and (ii) language identity. Systems compared: script probe, language probe, label-shuffled controls; the mean-difference "language vector" projected onto recovered script vs language directions. Decisive metric: cosine angle between the recovered script and language directions at the peak layer, and the fraction of the language-vector norm lying along the script direction; secondary: per-layer probe accuracies above shuffled control. Convincing result: script and language are both decodable >=15 pp above control AND the language vector places >50% of its norm on the script direction (supporting "language-identity is substantially script-identity"). Indecision band: language-vector script-projection of 35-50%, or direction angle near 45 degrees, is reported as partial entanglement. Negative result: language-vector script-projection <35% and a large script/language angle means the two are already well separated, refuting the reframing. Decodability is not use; Exp. 2 supplies causal separability.

Experiment 2 (H-a - script and language are independently, causally controllable): Tests whether each attribute can be flipped by patching without disturbing the other. Data: (i) same Serbian sentence run in Cyrillic vs Latin (swap script signal, language constant); (ii) same-script different-language runs Serbian-Cyrillic vs Russian-Cyrillic (swap language signal, script constant). Activation patching transfers the targeted signal between runs. Systems compared: patch at the targeted (script or language) component vs random-component control. Decisive metric: independent controllability = flip rate for the targeted attribute minus preservation-error of the other attribute; reported as a pair (targeted-flip rate, off-target-change rate). Convincing result: targeted-flip rate >=15 pp above control with off-target change <=5 pp, for both the script swap and the language swap. Indecision band: targeted flip 5-15 pp above control, or off-target change 5-10 pp, indicates entangled control; reported as such. Negative result: targeted flip <=5 pp above control, or off-target change exceeding the flip, means the attributes are not independently manipulable and claim (a) fails.

Experiment 3 (H-b - within-language cross-script knowledge fails beyond what surface differences warrant, and the gap tracks orthographic distance): Tests whether knowledge in one script of a digraphic language transfers to the other script, and whether the gap scales with orthographic dissimilarity rather than typology (language is held constant). Data: for each digraphic language, (a) query-side - the same fact asked in each script; (b) edit-side - a ROME/MEMIT update applied while reading one script, then queried in the other. Systems compared: same-script paraphrase control (upper bound), different-language control (lower bound), and the cross-script condition; gap correlated with the orthographic-dissimilarity index. Decisive metric: cross-script accuracy gap = same-script-paraphrase accuracy minus other-script accuracy (query-side), and edit-propagation rate across scripts (edit-side); dose-response Spearman of the gap with orthographic dissimilarity. Convincing result: cross-script gap exceeds the same-script-paraphrase gap by >=15 pp (a script-bound loss beyond surface variation) AND Spearman of gap with orthographic dissimilarity >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0). Indecision band: a 5-15 pp gap, or Spearman 0.2-0.4, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: cross-script gap within 5 pp of the same-script-paraphrase gap means knowledge transfers across scripts and the script-binding-artifact claim fails. Coverage proxies and same-content controls rule out ignorance as the cause.

Experiment 4 (H-c - training-free latent transliteration recovers cross-script knowledge): Tests whether steering only the script direction (language fixed) recovers knowledge without translation. Data: the low-performing script of each digraphic language; a script direction extracted from digraphic pairs. Systems compared: latent-transliteration steering (script direction toward the model's stronger script) vs surface transliteration-then-query vs translate-to-English vs RomanLens-style romanization; a shared-script cross-language control to check steering script alone never changes language. Decisive metric: cross-script knowledge-recovery rate = accuracy gain over the untouched low-performing script; secondary: output-script fidelity, language-preservation (should not flip language), and fluency (perplexity). Convincing result: latent-transliteration recovers >=15 pp accuracy with output-script fidelity >90%, language unchanged (<5 pp language flips), and fluency within 10% of baseline, matching or beating surface transliteration without a separate translation step. Indecision band: 5-15 pp recovery, or language flips of 5-10 pp, indicates a weak/leaky fix; reported as such. Negative result: <5 pp recovery, or steering that flips language, means the script direction does not carry recoverable knowledge and claim (c) fails. Ablations (secondary): layer sweep for where script is malleable; probe transfer across models; model scale. Reported metrics throughout: probe accuracy, script/language direction angle and language-vector projection, causal flip/preservation rates, cross-script accuracy gap, edit-propagation across scripts, Spearman with orthographic distance, steering recovery rate, output-script fidelity, language-preservation, fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of script vs language may reflect the readout basis; the causal patching (Exp. 3) and steering recovery (Exp. 7) are required to establish functional relevance. 2. For some digraphic pairs the two scripts share many characters (Serbian) while others do not (Hindi/Urdu), so effect sizes vary; this is exactly the orthographic-distance dose-response (Exp. 5) rather than a confound. 3. Low-resource scripts (Shahmukhi, Sindhi-Devanagari) may have thin pretraining coverage, confounding script-binding with ignorance; we control with same-language same-content items and report coverage proxies. 4. Transliteration ground truth can be noisy for context-dependent scripts (Perso-Arabic vowel omission); we use validated Dakshina/Aksharantar pairs and native-speaker spot-checks. 5. Tokenization differs sharply across scripts, complicating representation alignment; we use last-token / pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics. 6. Steering may trade knowledge recovery for fluency or accidentally change language; the shared-script control (Exp. 8) and fidelity/fluency metrics test selectivity. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims are: (1) script and language can be causally separated in multilingual LLMs using digraphic languages; (2) cross-script knowledge failure within one language is mainly a script-binding artifact, not true language separation; (3) a latent-transliteration steering direction can recover cross-script knowledge. The search summary strongly narrows novelty: a 2026 digraphia paper already uses Serbian digraphia to probe script-invariance, another directly argues script dominates language identity, and prior work already covers cross-script transfer failure plus script-direction steering/romanization. So this is not genuinely new at the level of problem or mechanism; it is mostly a new setting and a more causal experimental design. Relative to the proposal’s own related work, the core claim is non-trivial but still an obvious next step given the field’s current direction. Closest prior family: script-invariance / script-dominates-language-identity / cross-script knowledge-transfer / linear script representations. Actual delta: bidirectional causal patching to separate script vs language, and testing edit propagation across scripts within the same language.

Name: evidential_source_binding
Title: How Do You Know? A Causal Study of the Abstract Information-Source Representation and Its Binding to Evidential Grammar in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs build a shared, language-agnostic representation of the SOURCE of a piece of information (first-hand perception vs. hearsay/report vs. inference), stored separately from surface evidential morphology. In languages that grammatically force an evidential marker (Turkish, Bulgarian, Quechua, Tibetan), the model reads this source variable off via a late-layer binding step; and critically the same source variable causally governs the model's EXPRESSED CERTAINTY. We hypothesize (a) an abstract source-of-information direction decodable across languages including evidentiality-free ones like English; (b) that evidential-marking errors in obligatory-evidential languages are a binding failure that lazily inherits the source implied by the input/query language; and (c) that the shared source variable causally modulates downstream confidence, so mis-binding source produces miscalibrated certainty and hallucination-style errors, correctable by steering the shared direction.
Related Work: Linguistics establishes evidentiality as grammaticalized marking of information source, tightly linked to shared conceptual representations of knowledge sources across speakers (Relations Between Language and Cognition 2018; Aikhenvald typology; semantic-map work 2010-2020). Interpretability work shows multilingual models compute in a shared concept space with late-layer language decoding and that consistency failures arise at the transition (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Are Knowledge and Reference Cross-Lingually Consistent 2025), that grammatical concepts share cross-lingual directions (Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025), and that linguistic uncertainty/epistemic cues are progressively encoded in deeper layers (Mapping Clinical Doubt 2025). However, all evidentiality work is descriptive-linguistic or behavioral; interpretability work on uncertainty studies input-side epistemic MODALS in English, and multilingual mechanistic work targets factual content, gender, tense, or register. None (i) isolates an abstract, language-agnostic SOURCE-of-information variable, (ii) studies its late-layer binding onto obligatory evidential grammar, or (iii) causally links this source variable to the model's expressed certainty and calibration. We uniquely use evidential-marking typology as a controlled probe of the shared-vs-specific epistemic representation, give causal (patching + steering) evidence for a source-binding step, and connect it to the safety-critical problem of miscalibrated confidence.
Abstract: Languages differ starkly in how they encode where information comes from. Turkish, Bulgarian, Quechua, and Tibetan grammatically force speakers to mark whether a statement is based on first-hand perception, hearsay, or inference; English leaves this to optional lexical hedges. Any competent multilingual model must nonetheless recover the same abstract information source and, in evidential languages, commit to a grammatical marker. We ask how multilingual LLMs represent this source-of-information variable, how they bind it to evidential grammar, and—crucially—whether the same variable governs the model's expressed certainty. We distinguish an abstract, language-agnostic source variable (perception / report / inference, present regardless of grammatical marking) from surface evidential morphology. Using parallel statements whose information source is fixed by context across evidential and non-evidential languages, we train linear probes and localize where source is encoded and where it is bound to grammar. We predict (1) the abstract source direction is decodable across languages, including English; (2) evidential-marking errors in obligatory-evidential languages stem from a late-layer binding failure that lazily inherits the source implied by the query language; and (3) the shared source variable causally modulates downstream confidence, so mis-binding produces miscalibrated certainty and hallucination-style errors. We test binding via activation patching and repair errors by steering the shared source direction, measuring restored marking correctness and calibration without harming fluency. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across 10+ languages. The work gives the first mechanistic, controllable account of information-source representation in multilingual LLMs and ties it to trustworthiness.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout. Probes are L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers on cached hidden states (60/20/20 train/validation/test by item, 3 seeds {0,1,2}); generations scored under greedy decoding; verbalized-confidence and answer-token log-probs read directly from the frozen model. Steering and activation patching modify activations at inference with no weight updates. "pp" = percentage points; "information source" has three values - direct perception, reportative/hearsay, inference; ECE = expected calibration error. Stimuli (constructed): parallel statements whose information source is fixed by context, in three categories (direct "I saw...", reportative "they say...", inference "judging by X, it must..."), rendered in 10+ languages spanning OBLIGATORY-EVIDENTIAL (Turkish -mIs vs direct, Bulgarian renarrative, Quechua, Tibetan), OPTIONAL/LEXICAL (English, German, Spanish), and mixed types, in bare-context and explicit-context variants. We build ~150 base statements x 3 sources x 10+ languages, native-speaker-validated for the correct marker/source and kept only above 0.7 inter-annotator agreement; a per-language evidential-grammaticalization index orders obligatory verbal marking > particle/auxiliary > lexical-only. Fewer than an exhaustive set because each item needs native validation in every language.

Experiment 1 (H-a - an abstract, language-agnostic source variable, distinct from surface morphology): Tests whether the information source is decodable across languages, including evidentiality-free ones, separately from which marker appears. Data: mid-layer hidden states on held-out items. A probe decodes the source category; a probe trained on one language is applied to others (transfer), including to English/German; a separate surface-morphology probe decodes which marker appears. Systems compared: source probe, surface-marker probe, label-shuffled control. Decisive metric: cross-language source-probe transfer accuracy minus shuffled control; secondary: the abstract-vs-surface dissociation (source decodable in non-evidential languages that carry no marker). Convincing result: transfer accuracy >=15 pp above control AND source is decodable in English/German >=15 pp above control despite no grammatical marking. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control is reported as a partially shared source representation. Negative result: transfer within 5 pp of control means no shared abstract source variable, and claim (a) fails. Decodability is not use; Exps. 3, 4, 5 supply causal evidence.

Experiment 2 (H-b - source-marking errors and lazy inheritance of the input-language source): Tests whether obligatory-evidential languages mis-mark, and whether the error inherits the source implied by the query/framing language. Data: generate continuations/reformulations in each language and score whether the produced evidential marking matches the context-mandated source; then hold the target generation language fixed (e.g. Turkish) while varying the framing/input language (English direct framing vs Turkish reportative context). Systems compared: matched vs mismatched framing language; obligatory vs optional vs lexical language types. Decisive metric: INHERITANCE RATE = fraction where output marking matches the input-language-implied source rather than the context-mandated source; secondary: source-marking error rate by language type and context strength. Convincing result: inheritance rate is >=15 pp higher when generating an obligatory-evidential language from a non-evidential input language than in the matched-framing condition. Indecision band: a 5-15 pp gap is reported per language rather than as a global inheritance claim. Negative result: <5 pp gap means marking does not lazily inherit the input-language source, and the binding-failure account is not supported behaviorally.

Experiment 3 (H-b - a locatable late-layer source-binding step): Tests whether a compact late-layer component binds source to grammatical marking and can be flipped. Data: identical items run under context forcing DIRECT vs REPORTATIVE source in an obligatory-evidential language, producing different markers. Activation patching transfers late-layer components from the direct run into the reportative run. Systems compared: patch at candidate components vs random-component control. Decisive metric: marker-flip rate (fraction where the produced marker switches) minus control, with message content preserved. Convincing result: flip rate >=15 pp above control with content preserved and fluency within 10% of baseline. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control indicates a distributed binding step; reported as such. Negative result: <=5 pp above control means binding is not causally locatable and the binding-step claim fails.

Experiment 4 (H-c - the shared source variable causally modulates expressed certainty and calibration): Tests whether steering the source variable changes the model's confidence and calibration, so that mis-bound source (treating hearsay as direct) inflates confidence. Data: factual-QA and NLI items with a stated source and known ground truth, where hearsay should lower warranted confidence. The source direction = mean activation difference across sources, pooled across languages, extracted at the Exp. 3 binding layer. Systems compared: steer source from "direct" toward "reportative/inference" vs random-direction control; matched items with correct vs mis-bound source. Decisive metric: change in expressed confidence (verbalized probability and answer-token log-prob) under source steering, and change in ECE; secondary: hallucination-style error rate. Convincing result: steering toward reportative/inference lowers expressed confidence by a magnitude whose 95% CI excludes 0 and improves ECE relative to the mis-bound baseline, while random-direction steering does not. Indecision band: a confidence shift with CI touching 0, or ECE change under 1 absolute point, is reported as weak coupling. Negative result: no confidence/calibration change under source steering means source does not drive certainty - itself a safety-relevant calibration-blind-spot finding that bounds claim (c).

Experiment 5 (H-c - steering repairs mis-marking and, per the dose-response, effects track grammaticalization not resource): Tests the training-free repair and the distance dissociation. Data: mis-marked items for repair; bare-context items for induction; per-language grammaticalization index vs a resource-level proxy, with the key contrast non-evidential high-resource English vs evidential lower-resource Quechua/Tibetan (Turkish/Bulgarian as higher-resource evidential anchors). Systems compared: source-direction steering vs explicit source-instruction prompting vs translate-context-first. Decisive metric: marking-repair rate (fraction corrected) minus baseline, and partial Spearman of source-marking error/inheritance with grammaticalization controlling for resource; secondary: induction rate on bare context, content preservation, fluency, specificity. Convincing result: repair rate >=15 pp over baseline with specificity (unrelated items unchanged), AND partial correlation with grammaticalization >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0) while the partial with resource includes 0. Indecision band: repair 5-15 pp, or grammaticalization correlation 0.2-0.4, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: repair <5 pp, or error tracking resource (|rho| >=0.4) not grammaticalization, refutes the repair-and-scaling half of claim (c). Ablations (secondary): layer sweep; probe transfer across models; perception vs report vs inference separability; whether evidential languages recruit extra late components tied to verb-ending tokens; model scale. Reported metrics throughout: source-marking error rate, inheritance rate, probe accuracy and transfer, causal flip/repair/induction rates, source-driven confidence shift, ECE, content preservation, Spearman with grammaticalization vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of abstract source may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used variable; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 4), the source-to-certainty steering (Exp. 7), and the steering repair/induction (Exp. 8) to establish functional relevance. 2. Ground-truth source in bare-context items can be genuinely ambiguous; we restrict to native-speaker-validated items with high inter-annotator agreement. 3. Separating abstract source from surface morphology is hard in obligatory-evidential languages where they nearly coincide; the non-evidential languages and bare-context condition are the crucial dissociating cases. 4. Low-resource evidential languages (Quechua, Tibetan) may have thin pretraining coverage, confounding binding failure with ignorance; we control with same-content items across languages and report coverage proxies, and Turkish/Bulgarian provide higher-resource evidential anchors. 5. The source-to-certainty link may be weak if the model ignores stated source when judging confidence; even documenting this (a calibration blind spot) is a valuable, safety-relevant finding. 6. Tokenization of evidential verb endings varies across languages; we use verb-final/reply-final or pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics; obligatory vs particle vs lexical cases analyzed separately. 7. Steering may trade marking correctness or calibration for fluency; we report all three. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims that would need to be novel: (1) multilingual LLMs encode an abstract, language-agnostic source-of-information variable (perception/report/inference) independent of surface evidential marking; (2) this variable is shared across evidential and non-evidential languages and is decodable cross-lingually, including in English-like languages without obligatory evidentials; (3) evidential errors in obligatory-evidential languages arise from a late-layer binding failure between the abstract source representation and language-specific morphology/syntax, rather than absence of the concept itself; (4) the same source variable causally modulates expressed certainty/calibration, so source mis-binding contributes to hallucination-style overconfidence; (5) steering/patching this source direction can repair both evidential marking and confidence calibration. From the proposal plus search summary, the tri-part combination is genuinely novel. Prior work covers evidentiality behaviorally in Turkish and linguistics descriptively, and separate uncertainty/calibration work in English, but not a mechanistic cross-lingual source representation, late binding account, and source-to-confidence causal link together. Relative to the proposal's own related work, this is more than an obvious extension of multilingual concept directions: evidentiality is typologically specialized, obligatoriness matters, and the confidence coupling is a nontrivial new target. The closest prior family is multilingual representation/interpretability work on shared concept spaces and uncertainty representations, plus Turkish behavioral evidentiality benchmarks. The actual delta is substantial, especially on the mechanistic binding and calibration claims. Main caveat: some individual components (cross-lingual latent concept probing, late binding, causal steering) are established techniques, so novelty lives more in the object of study and the synthesis than in fundamentally new methodology.

impact.reasoning: The problem under study is whether LLMs correctly represent and use information source provenance across languages, and whether failures in that representation/binding distort the model's expressed certainty. Who cares: multilingual NLP researchers building reliable generation/translation systems; mechanistic interpretability researchers studying language-agnostic concepts; computational linguists interested in evidentiality; and trustworthiness/safety researchers concerned with confidence calibration and hallucination. If the claims hold, downstream implications include better diagnosis of multilingual generation errors, new controls for confidence expression, improved handling of source-sensitive reasoning and translation in evidential languages, and a sharper mechanistic account of one class of calibration failure. Strongest one-line case: a single cross-lingual latent 'information source' variable may causally drive both grammatical evidential marking and model confidence, making a typological phenomenon directly relevant to hallucination and AI trustworthiness. This passes the 'so what?' test better than many linguistically motivated interpretability papers because it connects a niche grammatical phenomenon to broad reliability concerns. Still, impact depends heavily on Exp4: if the source-to-confidence link is weak or only visible in contrived prompts, the work becomes a specialized multilingual interpretability study with narrower audience. Real-world reach is meaningful but indirect; it is more likely to shape scientific understanding and evaluation practice than immediate deployment.

review.reasoning: The proposal is ambitious, interesting, and reasonably well structured, but a strict senior ML reviewer would see several threats to identification. The central hypothesis is fairly precise and falsifiable in broad strokes, yet some constructs remain underspecified: what exactly operationalizes 'source' independently of lexical content; how 'expressed certainty' is measured robustly across languages; and what pattern would distinguish a true late-layer binding failure from simple lack of knowledge, translation habits, or prompt-induced register effects. Experiments are specific and mostly feasible on 7B-8B models, but the dataset is small (~150 base statements) relative to the number of languages and source categories, making overfitting, lexical confounds, and weak statistical power plausible. The use of low-resource evidential languages is scientifically valuable but creates a major confound: poor performance may reflect pretraining sparsity rather than an interpretable binding mechanism. The proposal acknowledges this but does not fully solve it. Exp1 probing needs stronger controls for semantic content, genre, lexicalized report verbs, translationese, and language identification artifacts; shuffled controls are not enough. Exp2's 'inheritance rate' is clever but could conflate pragmatics and prompt framing with evidential source. Exp3 patching is an appropriate causal test, but the localization target ('late-layer components') is too vague; heads, MLPs, residual stream directions, and token positions should be prespecified. Exp4 is the highest-risk part: verbalized probability and answer-token log-prob are noisy proxies for certainty, ECE on factual QA/NLI with 'stated source' may not isolate source-conditioned calibration, and the proposed causal chain from source steering to reduced hallucination is not yet tightly designed. Exp5 repair is promising but needs fluency/tradeoff analysis and negative controls to show specificity. Related work is directionally adequate but still too high-level; strong reviewers will expect closer engagement with multilingual concept localization, uncertainty representation, and causal abstraction work. If executed well, this could fit a strong ACL/EMNLP findings-to-main or CoNLL/CL venue, perhaps stronger if the causal confidence result is clean; for a top-tier broad ML audience, the empirical rigor would need to be substantially sharper.
