Name: spatial_frame_of_reference_default
Title: Left of the Tree or North of the Tree? How the Query Language Sets a Default Spatial Frame of Reference in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Human languages default to different spatial frames of reference (FoR) - egocentric-relative (English, Dutch), object-intrinsic, or geocentric-absolute/cardinal (Guugu Yimithirr, Tzeltal, some Tamil/Balinese conventions). We hypothesize that (a) a multilingual LLM builds an abstract, language-agnostic spatial-relation representation, but (b) the query language covertly sets a DEFAULT frame of reference that is applied when a spatial description is ambiguous, so the SAME ambiguous scene ('the ball is left/front of the tree', 'X is beyond Y') is resolved differently depending on the query language; (c) this frame default is carried by a small, causally-manipulable 'frame-register' representation separable from the underspecified spatial content; and (d) the strength with which a language imposes its default (overriding explicit frame cues) scales with how strongly that language grammaticalizes/conventionalizes a single FoR, not with resource level, and can be repaired by steering the recovered frame direction.
Related Work: The Levinson/Pederson semantic-typology program (Semantic Typology and Spatial Conceptualization 1998; 527 cites) established that languages systematically differ in default frame of reference (relative/intrinsic/absolute), and that a community's non-linguistic cognitive frame correlates with its linguistic one - a foundational linguistic-relativity result. A computational Sapir-Whorf study (2016) modeled spatial-relation naming across five languages. On the model side, COMFORT (2024) shows VLMs are behaviorally inconsistent about frames of reference and default to English conventions, but it is a purely behavioral VLM benchmark with no mechanistic account. Interpretability work shows LLMs encode linear spatial world models and space/time directions (Language Models Represent Space and Time 2023; Linear Spatial World Models 2025; More than Correlation 2023), and that multilingual models have orthogonal language-sensitive vs language-neutral axes (Geometry of Multilingual Representations 2022). None of these (i) studies frame of reference (the interpretive coordinate system), as opposed to absolute geolocation or object position; (ii) tests whether the QUERY LANGUAGE sets a default FoR that biases resolution of ambiguous spatial descriptions in a text LLM; or (iii) provides a causal, steerable 'frame-register' representation. We uniquely port the classic FoR typology into multilingual text LLMs and give a causal, controllable mechanistic account.
Abstract: When someone says 'the cat is to the left of the tree', the meaning depends on an unstated coordinate system: is 'left' from the speaker's viewpoint (relative), the tree's intrinsic sides (intrinsic), or a cardinal direction (absolute)? A classic result in cognitive linguistics is that languages default to different frames of reference, and this default shapes how speakers interpret and remember space. We ask whether multilingual LLMs inherit these language-specific spatial defaults. We hypothesize that a model computes an abstract, underspecified spatial relation but resolves its ambiguity using a frame of reference that is covertly set by the query language, so the identical ambiguous scene is interpreted differently across languages. We construct FRAME-SPACE, a controlled set of spatial-description items with (i) frame-ambiguous versions whose truth value flips depending on the assumed frame, and (ii) frame-forcing versions with explicit relative/intrinsic/absolute cues, rendered across 12+ languages spanning relative-default, intrinsic-favoring, and absolute/cardinal-favoring conventions. Behaviorally, we measure per-language frame-choice distributions and how often the query language overrides an explicit frame cue. Mechanistically, we probe for an abstract spatial-relation direction shared across languages, then use activation patching to localize a compact frame-register whose swap flips the interpretation without changing the spatial content, and steer a recovered frame direction to repair or induce frame choices. We predict frame-override strength tracks a language's frame-conventionalization index rather than resource level. Experiments span Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2. The work ports spatial frame-of-reference typology into mechanistic interpretability and yields a controllable account of a linguistic-relativity effect in LLMs.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout. Probes are L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers on cached hidden states (60/20/20 train/validation/test by scene, 3 seeds {0,1,2}); interpretations elicited under greedy decoding via multiple-choice over frame-consistent answers. Steering and activation patching modify activations at inference with no weight updates. "pp" = percentage points; "frame of reference" (FoR) = the coordinate system for projective terms - relative (speaker viewpoint), intrinsic (object's own sides), or absolute (cardinal). Dataset (FRAME-SPACE, constructed): scenes with an observer, a landmark object with clear intrinsic sides (car/person/house), and a target. Each scene yields (a) FRAME-AMBIGUOUS descriptions using projective terms ("left", "in front of", "behind", "beyond") whose truth flips across relative/intrinsic/absolute frames, with a question whose correct answer differs by frame; and (b) FRAME-FORCING variants adding explicit cues ("from where you are standing" -> relative; "the car's own front" -> intrinsic; "to the north of" -> absolute). We build ~200 scenes x these variants x 12+ languages spanning RELATIVE-default (English, Dutch, German, Japanese), INTRINSIC/mixed (Spanish, Mandarin, Hausa), and ABSOLUTE/cardinal-favoring (Tamil, Balinese, constructed Guugu-Yimithirr-style items, a cardinal-heavy register). Native speakers validate each language's canonical default frame (kept above 0.7 agreement) and a per-language frame-conventionalization index (how obligatory/preferred one frame is). Fewer than an exhaustive set because each scene needs frame-controlled construction and native validation.

Experiment 1 (H-b - the query language sets a default frame that resolves ambiguous scenes differently): Tests whether the identical ambiguous scene is interpreted according to the query language's default, and whether that default overrides an explicit conflicting cue. Data: FRAME-AMBIGUOUS items (default test) and FRAME-FORCING items whose explicit cue conflicts with the query language's default (override test). Systems compared: per-language interpretation; query-in-English (relative anchor); translate-to-English-first. Decisive metric: frame-override rate = fraction of conflicting-cue items where the output follows the query-language default rather than the explicit cue; secondary: per-language frame-choice distribution and cross-language disagreement rate on identical ambiguous scenes. Convincing result: cross-language disagreement on identical ambiguous scenes exceeds 15 pp AND override rate differs across language types by >=15 pp (strongly-conventionalized languages override more), averaged over models. Indecision band: disagreement or override differences of 5-15 pp are reported per language rather than as a global claim. Negative result: <5 pp cross-language disagreement means the query language does not set a default frame and claim (b) fails.

Experiment 2 (H-a - an abstract, language-agnostic spatial-relation representation distinct from the resolved frame): Tests whether the underspecified projective relation is shared across languages while the resolved frame is what varies. Data: hidden states on ambiguous items. One probe decodes the underspecified relation (e.g. "left-type"), another decodes the resolved frame; a relation probe trained on one language is applied to others (transfer). Systems compared: relation probe, frame probe, label-shuffled control. Decisive metric: cross-language relation-probe transfer accuracy minus control; secondary: the relation-vs-frame dissociation (relation transfers, resolved frame is language-dependent). Convincing result: relation transfer >=15 pp above control while the resolved-frame probe shows language-dependent structure, supporting a shared relation with a variable frame. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control is reported as partial sharing. Negative result: relation transfer within 5 pp of control means no shared abstract relation, weakening claim (a). Decodability is not use; Exp. 3 supplies causal evidence.

Experiment 3 (H-c - a compact, separable, causally-manipulable frame-register): Tests whether a small component carries the resolved frame and can be flipped without changing the scene/relation. Data: identical ambiguous items run under context forcing RELATIVE vs ABSOLUTE (or intrinsic) interpretation, yielding different answers. Activation patching transfers mid-layer components from one run into the other. Systems compared: patch at candidate components vs random-component control; overlap of the recovered frame direction with language-identity and prior absolute-geolocation directions (separability check). Decisive metric: frame-flip rate (answer switches frame) minus control, with scene/relation content preserved; secondary: cosine overlap of the frame direction with language-identity and geolocation directions (should be low). Convincing result: flip rate >=15 pp above control with content preserved AND frame-direction overlap with language/geolocation directions <0.3 cosine (separable register). Indecision band: 5-15 pp flip, or overlap 0.3-0.5, indicates a diffuse/entangled register; reported as such. Negative result: <=5 pp flip means the frame is not causally locatable and claim (c) fails.

Experiment 4 (H-d - override strength tracks frame-conventionalization, not resource level): Tests the dissociation between conventionalization and resource. Data: per-language frame-override rate and default-strength vs the frame-conventionalization index and a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / benchmark accuracy); key contrast a lower-resource strongly-absolute language vs a higher-resource mixed language. Decisive metric: partial Spearman of override rate with conventionalization controlling for resource, and with resource controlling for conventionalization. Convincing result: partial correlation with conventionalization >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0) while the partial with resource includes 0, and the low-resource-absolute language imposes its frame more than the high-resource-mixed one. Indecision band: conventionalization correlation 0.2-0.4, or overlapping partial CIs, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: override tracks resource (|rho| >=0.4) not conventionalization, refuting claim (d)'s scaling half.

Experiment 5 (H-d - training-free repair/induction by steering the frame direction): Tests whether steering the frame-register repairs mis-framed interpretations and induces non-default frames. Data: mis-framed items (repair); items where a non-default frame was not chosen (induction); a frame-UNambiguous spatial control set (should have no flippable register) and non-spatial items (specificity). Frame direction = mean activation difference between relative-forced and absolute/intrinsic-forced runs, pooled across languages. Systems compared: frame steering vs explicit frame-instruction prompting vs translate-first. Decisive metric: repair rate (fraction correctly re-framed under explicit context) minus baseline, and induction rate on non-default frames; secondary: interpretation accuracy, fluency (perplexity), specificity (non-spatial and frame-unambiguous items unchanged). Convincing result: repair and induction rates >=15 pp over baseline with specificity change <=5 pp and fluency within 10% of baseline. Indecision band: 5-15 pp effects, or specificity change 5-10 pp, indicate a weak/leaky intervention. Negative result: <5 pp effect means the frame direction is not functionally causal, refuting the steerability half of claim (d). Ablations (secondary): layer sweep; probe transfer across models; model scale. Reported metrics throughout: frame-choice distribution, cross-language disagreement, frame-override rate, relation vs frame probe accuracy and transfer, causal flip/repair/induction rates, content preservation, Spearman with conventionalization vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Annotating each language's default frame and building a conventionalization index is subjective and some languages are mixed; we ground labels in the established typology literature, use multiple native-speaker annotators, restrict to high-agreement items, and report robustness to index operationalization. 2. Probe decodability of an abstract relation/frame may reflect the readout basis rather than a used representation; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 4) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) to establish functional relevance. 3. Frame preference could be confounded with translation artifacts of projective terms across languages; the frame-forcing and override conditions and native-speaker validation isolate the default from mere translation. 4. Strong models may collapse to a single (English-relative) frame regardless of query language, weakening cross-language variation; even documenting this near-universal English-relative default and its resistance to explicit cues is a valuable linguistic-relativity finding, and multiple models/languages give power. 5. Constructed items for very-low-resource absolute languages (e.g., Guugu Yimithirr) may have thin coverage, confounding frame-imposition with ignorance; we include higher-resource absolute/cardinal registers (Tamil, cardinal-heavy phrasing) and control with same-scene items. 6. Tokenization of projective/cardinal terms varies across scripts; we use pooled-span or last-token representations and report tokenization statistics. 7. Steering may trade frame correctness for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims that would need to be novel: (1) in multilingual text LLMs, the query language sets a default spatial frame of reference that resolves otherwise ambiguous spatial descriptions differently across languages; (2) the model contains a language-agnostic abstract spatial-relation representation separable from a language-conditioned frame-of-reference variable; (3) this frame variable is implemented as a compact, causally manipulable 'frame-register' whose activation can be patched or steered to flip frame interpretation without changing spatial content; (4) the strength of frame override scales with a language's frame conventionalization/grammaticalization rather than resource level; (5) the recovered frame direction is separable from language-identity and geolocation directions and can be used to repair model behavior. Relative to prior work, the behavioral phenomenon itself is not fully new: COMFORT already studies frame-of-reference ambiguity across languages and finds English-default behavior, though in VLMs; the search summary also suggests a later multilingual text-LLM spatial reasoning diagnostic may partially cover the text-only behavioral extension. So the actual novelty does not lie in 'models show language-conditioned FoR biases' per se. The strongest novel delta is the mechanistic claim: isolating a causal, steerable frame-register distinct from underspecified spatial content, plus the conventionalization-vs-resource dissociation. As a setting transfer, moving from VLMs to text LLMs is somewhat meaningful because textual ambiguity resolution may rely more directly on linguistic priors, but by itself it is not enough for high novelty. Relative to the proposal's own related work, the mechanistic extension is non-trivial rather than an obvious benchmark increment, but the behavioral part risks reading as an expected port of COMFORT/FoREST into text. Closest prior family: multilingual FoR behavioral benchmarks (COMFORT, FoREST) plus spatial representation interpretability (Gurnee & Tegmark-style linear directions). Actual delta: combining multilingual FoR typology with causal representation analysis and steering in text LLMs.
revision_notes: Make the novelty claim narrower: explicitly state that behavioral language-conditioned FoR effects are expected from COMFORT-like results, and that the central new contribution is the causal/mechanistic frame-register account in text LLMs.
Differentiate more concretely from the multilingual text-LLM spatial reasoning diagnostic: specify which tasks, ambiguity structure, and mechanistic analyses are absent there.
Define what would count as a truly new result mechanistically, e.g. frame patching flips answers while preserving non-frame spatial semantics and generalizes across languages/models.
Reduce reliance on constructed low-resource language proxies if those are central to the novelty claim; otherwise reviewers may see the typological component as too synthetic.

impact.reasoning: Problem under study: whether multilingual LLMs resolve ambiguous spatial language using language-specific default frames of reference, and whether that bias is represented in a manipulable internal variable rather than inseparable task heuristics. Who cares: multilingual NLP, interpretability researchers, cognitive science/linguistic relativity communities, and to a lesser extent embodied AI/robotics/VLM researchers interested in spatial grounding and cross-lingual instruction following. If the claims hold, downstream changes could include better multilingual spatial benchmarks, frame-aware prompting or steering methods, more faithful cross-lingual interfaces, and a cleaner conceptual link between linguistic typology and internal model representations. Strongest one-line case: this would show that multilingual LLMs do not just mistranslate spatial ambiguity but internally instantiate language-conditioned coordinate systems that can be causally isolated and corrected. The importance is moderate rather than maximal. Spatial frame-of-reference ambiguity is scientifically interesting and relevant for model reliability, but in text-only LLMs the practical real-world stakes are narrower than for broad reasoning, safety, or high-volume product tasks. Uptake in interpretability and multilingual semantics could be good if the causal evidence is convincing, and the benchmark could become a useful diagnostic. However, direction-shifting impact is limited unless the discovered mechanism generalizes broadly and the repair method materially improves multilingual instruction following. Real-world reach is stronger if connected to navigation, embodied agents, mapping, or multilingual assistants; as written, it is more of a foundational/cognitive-science contribution than a deployment-changing one. So the 'so what?' answer is solid for scientific understanding and diagnostic value, but only moderate for broad applied ML.
revision_notes: Strengthen the practical case by tying FoR errors to concrete downstream failures: navigation instructions, map QA, robotics commands, and multilingual assistant misunderstandings.
Quantify why current systems should care: estimate how often ambiguous spatial language appears or show examples where frame mismatch changes user-visible outputs.
Clarify whether steering is meant as an analysis tool or a deployable correction method; impact rises if it reliably improves multilingual spatial tasks without harming general behavior.
Emphasize the cross-disciplinary significance as a test of whether LLMs internalize typological semantic defaults, not just benchmark performance differences.

review.reasoning: The proposal is ambitious and interesting, but under a strict senior ML review standard there are several logical and methodological vulnerabilities. The hypothesis is reasonably precise in spirit but still underspecified in operational terms: 'abstract underspecified spatial relation', 'frame-register', and 'conventionalization index' need sharper definitions to be falsifiable. The key mechanistic claim is hard to establish cleanly because decodable directions and patch effects can reflect generic answer mediation, language identity, or lexical cue transfer rather than a compact latent frame variable. The proposal does include stronger-than-usual causal tools—activation patching and steering—which is a plus, but the controls must be extremely careful. Related work awareness is decent, though the proposal should be more explicit that the behavioral effect is already substantially established in VLMs and perhaps partly in text LLMs. Experimental plan is fairly specific and feasible at benchmark scale, but several components need tightening: the language set mixes naturally occurring typology with constructed 'Guugu-Yimithirr-style' and cardinal-heavy registers, which weakens claims about real language defaults; annotation of default frame and a scalar conventionalization index is subjective and could become the central source of researcher degrees of freedom; translation artifacts and lexical asymmetries in 'left/right/north of' terms may fully explain some cross-language differences; and the patching/steering setup needs negative controls proving it is not simply biasing toward one answer class. The proposed partial Spearman analysis over ~12 languages is also statistically fragile for a claim about conventionalization vs resource. Missing or underemphasized controls include: bilingual paraphrase consistency, human baselines per language on the exact items, adversarial lexical substitutions, non-spatial patching controls, same-language wording variants to separate syntax from language identity, and transfer to naturally sourced rather than constructed data. The narrative weakness is that it bundles three papers' worth of claims—behavioral benchmark, mechanistic dissociation, and typological scaling law—so any one weak link can sink the whole story. If executed very well, this is likely a strong ACL/EMNLP/ICLR-style paper and potentially high-interest workshop-to-conference trajectory; the mechanistic part is the venue-strength determinant. Minimum viable edits would focus the paper on one primary claim, define variables sharply, and add stronger controls around causality and typology measurement.

Name: negative_concord_polarity_flip
Title: Nobody Didn't Get Sick: How the Query Language's Negation Grammar Covertly Flips the Truth Value of Stacked Negations in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Languages split into Negative Concord (NC: multiple negatives = one negation, e.g. Spanish/Italian/Russian) and Double Negation (DN: two negatives cancel, e.g. formal English/Mandarin). We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a shared, language-agnostic truth-conditional polarity representation but that, when a sentence contains multiple negation cues, the query language covertly sets a DEFAULT resolution rule (NC vs DN) that is applied to interpretation. Consequently the SAME multiply-negated proposition is assigned OPPOSITE truth values depending on the query language; this flip is carried by a small, causally-manipulable 'polarity-resolution' representation separable from the propositional content, its strength scales with how strongly the query language grammaticalizes negative concord (not with resource level), and it is most dangerous—producing safety-critical instruction inversions—when the model must act on multiply-negated commands.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows negation scope is carried by identifiable attention heads (Kim & Linzen-style 2020 BERT negation-scope analysis), that negation/passivization leave removable representational imprints (Controlling the Imprint, INLP 2020), that LMs form 'strong hallucinations' from negation because latent operators don't respect logic (Strong Hallucinations 2024), that NPI licensing and grammatical illusions mirror humans (NPI in BERT 2023; LSTM NPI 2018), and that negation instructions cause ironic rebound via middle-layer heads (White Bear 2025). Linguistic typology firmly establishes the NC-vs-DN macroparameter and its unclear-at-the-margins interpretation (Zeijlstra 2016; de Swart 2010; Mandarin vs Spanish negation 2023; quantifier-negation scope in bilinguals 2024). However: (i) all interpretability negation work is monolingual (mostly English) and studies scope or single-negation logic, never the cross-lingual NC/DN resolution of MULTIPLE negatives; (ii) all NC/DN work is descriptive-linguistic or behavioral, with no mechanistic account inside an LLM; and (iii) none frames the query language as a covert default that flips a truth value, nor tests the safety consequence of inverted multiply-negated instructions. We uniquely port the NC/DN typology into multilingual mechanistic interpretability, give causal (patching + steering) evidence for a polarity-resolution representation, and transfer the phenomenon into a safety-critical instruction-following domain.
Abstract: In many languages two negatives make a negative: Spanish 'no vino nadie' (literally 'not came nobody') simply means 'nobody came'. In formal English and Mandarin, two negatives cancel to an affirmative. These are the classic Negative Concord (NC) and Double Negation (DN) types of the world's languages. A competent multilingual model reading a multiply-negated sentence must recover its actual truth value—but which rule does it apply, and does the language it is asked in decide for it? We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs compute a shared truth-conditional polarity but resolve multiple negatives using a default rule covertly set by the query language, so the identical proposition is judged true in one language and false in another. We build POLARITY-FLIP, controlled minimal pairs with one, two, and three negation cues whose truth value differs under NC vs DN resolution, rendered across 12+ languages spanning strongly-NC, DN, and mixed types, plus a safety-critical subset of multiply-negated instructions (medical/lab/legal) where a flip inverts the required action. Behaviorally we measure per-language truth-value assignment and instruction-inversion rate. Mechanistically we probe for a shared polarity direction, use activation patching to localize a compact polarity-resolution representation whose swap flips the judgment without altering content, and steer a recovered polarity direction to repair or induce flips. We predict flip strength tracks a language's negative-concord grammaticalization index, not its resource level, and that steering repairs safety-critical inversions without harming fluency. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout. Probes are L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers on cached hidden states (60/20/20 train/validation/test by proposition, 3 seeds {0,1,2}); truth-value and NLI judgments elicited under greedy decoding. Steering and activation patching modify activations at inference with no weight updates. "pp" = percentage points; NC = Negative Concord (multiple negatives = one negation), DN = Double Negation (two negatives cancel). Dataset (POLARITY-FLIP, constructed): minimal-pair propositions with 1, 2, and 3 negation cues (sentential negator plus negative indefinites nobody/nothing/never), each paired with a yes/no truth-value question or an NLI hypothesis whose correct answer differs under NC vs DN resolution. Rendered in 12+ languages spanning STRONG-NC (Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Polish, Greek), DN/no-concord (formal English, Mandarin, Japanese, standard German), and MIXED/optional (French, Afrikaans). A SAFETY subset renders multiply-negated instructions in medical/lab/legal register (e.g. "do not fail to withhold the second dose unless...") where NC-vs-DN resolution inverts the required action, each with an unambiguous single-negation control paraphrase. We build ~180 base propositions x cue-count x 12+ languages plus ~120 safety items; native speakers validate the canonical resolution per language (kept above 0.7 agreement) and a per-language negative-concord grammaticalization index (obligatory > optional > absent). Fewer than an exhaustive set because each item needs cue-controlled construction and native validation.

Experiment 1 (H-behavior - the query language flips the truth value of stacked negations): Tests whether the identical multiply-negated proposition is judged true in one language and false in another, with disagreement growing in the number of cues. Data: truth-value/NLI items with 1, 2, 3 cues in each language. Systems compared: single-negation control (should agree across languages), query-in-English, per-language judgments. Decisive metric: cross-language DISAGREEMENT rate on identical propositions; secondary: per-language truth-value distribution and the growth of disagreement from 1 to 2 to 3 cues. Convincing result: disagreement on 2-3-cue items exceeds disagreement on single-negation controls by >=15 pp AND rises monotonically with cue count, averaged over models. Indecision band: a 5-15 pp excess over control is reported per language rather than as a global flip claim. Negative result: disagreement within 5 pp of the single-negation control means the query language does not set a resolution rule and the behavioral claim fails.

Experiment 2 (H-safety - multiply-negated instructions invert disproportionately): Tests whether NC-vs-DN resolution inverts prescribed actions on the safety subset. Data: the ~120 safety instructions vs their single-negation control paraphrases, per language and register. Decisive metric: INSTRUCTION-INVERSION rate = fraction where the model prescribes the opposite of the correct action; compared against the single-negation control's inversion rate. Convincing result: inversion rate on multiply-negated safety items exceeds the single-negation control by >=15 pp and is elevated specifically in languages whose default resolution rule differs from the correct one. Indecision band: a 5-15 pp excess is reported as a bounded risk rather than a strong safety claim. Negative result: inversion within 5 pp of the single-negation control means multiple negation does not create disproportionate instruction risk, bounding the safety claim.

Experiment 3 (H-shared - a shared, language-agnostic polarity representation distinct from cue count): Tests whether resolved truth-value polarity is decodable and transfers across languages while the resolved value varies. Data: hidden states on held-out items. One probe decodes resolved truth-value polarity; a surface-cue-count probe decodes the raw number of negators; the polarity probe trained on one language is applied to others (transfer). Systems compared: polarity probe, cue-count probe, label-shuffled control. Decisive metric: cross-language polarity-probe transfer accuracy minus control; secondary: the abstract-polarity-vs-cue-count dissociation. Convincing result: transfer accuracy >=15 pp above control while the resolved value is what varies with query language, and polarity is decodable beyond mere cue count. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control is reported as partial sharing. Negative result: transfer within 5 pp of control means no shared polarity representation, weakening the hypothesis. Decodability is not use; Exp. 4 supplies causal evidence.

Experiment 4 (H-locate - a compact, separable, causally-manipulable polarity-resolution representation): Tests whether a small component carries the resolution rule and flips the judgment without altering content. Data: identical multiply-negated items run under context/framing forcing NC vs DN resolution, yielding opposite judgments. Activation patching transfers mid/late-layer components from one run into the other. Systems compared: patch at candidate components vs random-component control; overlap of the recovered polarity-resolution direction with prior negation-scope heads (separability check). Decisive metric: truth-value flip rate minus control, with propositional content preserved; secondary: overlap with negation-scope heads (should be partial/low). Convincing result: flip rate >=15 pp above control with content preserved and fluency within 10% of baseline. Indecision band: 5-15 pp flip indicates a distributed representation; reported as such. Negative result: <=5 pp flip means resolution is not causally locatable and that part of the hypothesis fails.

Experiment 5 (H-dose - flip strength tracks negative-concord grammaticalization, not resource): Tests the dissociation between grammaticalization and resource. Data: per-language flip/disagreement rate vs the grammaticalization index and a resource-level proxy; key contrast a lower-resource strong-NC language (e.g. Polish) vs a higher-resource DN language. Decisive metric: partial Spearman of flip/disagreement with grammaticalization controlling for resource, and with resource controlling for grammaticalization. Convincing result: partial correlation with grammaticalization >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0) while the partial with resource includes 0. Indecision band: grammaticalization correlation 0.2-0.4, or overlapping partial CIs, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: flips track resource (|rho| >=0.4) not grammaticalization, refuting the scaling claim.

Experiment 6 (H-steer - steering repairs safety inversions and induces flips): Tests the training-free causal fix and induction. Data: flipped safety instructions (repair); correctly-resolved items (induction); single-negation and non-negated items (specificity). Polarity-resolution direction = mean activation difference between NC-forced and DN-forced runs, pooled across languages, at the Exp. 4 layer. Systems compared: steering vs explicit disambiguation prompting ("interpret two negatives as cancelling") vs translate-to-English-first. Decisive metric: safety-repair rate (fraction of inverted instructions corrected) minus baseline; secondary: induction rate, truth-value/instruction accuracy, specificity (single-negation and non-negated items unchanged), fluency (perplexity). Convincing result: repair rate >=15 pp over baseline with specificity change <=5 pp and fluency within 10% of baseline; induction confirms functional causality. Indecision band: 5-15 pp repair, or specificity change 5-10 pp, indicates a weak/leaky fix. Negative result: <5 pp repair means the direction is not functionally causal, refuting the steerability claim. Ablations (secondary): layer sweep; probe transfer across models; adjacent vs long-distance negators; model scale. Reported metrics throughout: truth-value distribution, cross-language disagreement, instruction-inversion rate, polarity probe accuracy and transfer, causal flip/repair/induction rates, content preservation, Spearman with grammaticalization vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of resolved polarity may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 5) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 7) to establish functional relevance. 2. Even within NC/DN languages, native interpretation of stacked negatives can be prosody/context-dependent and genuinely ambiguous (as the Mandarin-Spanish 2023 study notes); we restrict to native-speaker-validated high-agreement items and treat mixed languages as a separate class rather than forcing a binary. 3. The flip could be confounded with translation artifacts of negative indefinites across languages; single-negation controls and the cross-language agreement they should show isolate the concord effect from mere translation noise. 4. Strong models may collapse to one default rule (likely DN/English) regardless of query language, weakening cross-language variation; even documenting a near-universal English-DN default that resists explicit NC instructions, and its safety consequences, is a valuable finding, and multiple models/languages give statistical power. 5. Tokenization of negators/negative indefinites varies across scripts; we use pooled-span or clause-final token representations and report tokenization statistics. 6. The grammaticalization-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report robustness to index operationalization and alternative language choices. 7. Steering may trade polarity correctness for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims that need to be novel: (1) multilingual LLMs maintain a shared, language-agnostic propositional polarity representation while stacked-negation resolution is applied separately; (2) the query language acts as a covert default rule selecting NC-like vs DN-like interpretation, causing opposite truth values for the same multiply-negated proposition; (3) this resolution rule is localized in a compact, causally manipulable representation separable from propositional content and can be swapped/steered to flip judgments; (4) flip strength scales with negative-concord grammaticalization rather than training-resource level; (5) this mechanism yields safety-relevant inversions on multiply-negated instructions. From the proposal plus search summary, the broad behavioral phenomenon is not fully new: prior survey/behavioral work already flags multilingual negative-concord failures and cross-lingual negation disparities. So the strongest novelty is not 'models differ across languages on negation' but the mechanistic account, the query-language-default framing, and the grammaticalization-vs-resource test. Relative to the proposal's own related work, the jump from monolingual negation mechanism work to cross-lingual NC/DN multiple-negation resolution is non-trivial. Still, some parts risk reading as an expected extension: once multilingual disparities and monolingual negation heads are known, looking for a causal representation in multilingual multiple negation is a natural next step. Closest prior family: multilingual negation-understanding evaluations plus monolingual mechanistic negation studies. Actual delta: causal/mechanistic localization of cross-lingual stacked-negation resolution, plus safety framing, not the existence of behavioral failures itself.

impact.reasoning: Problem under study: whether multilingual LLMs invert the meaning of stacked negations across languages, including in action-oriented instructions. Who cares: multilingual NLP, semantics/linguistics, interpretability, evaluation, and reliability/safety teams deploying LLMs in multilingual settings. If the claim holds, downstream changes could include multilingual safety eval suites with stacked-negation stress tests, language-conditional instruction filters, training interventions for negation handling, and mechanistic diagnostics/steering tools. Strongest one-line case: the same multilingual model may take opposite actions on the same instruction solely because the query language changes how stacked negation is resolved. This is more than a niche linguistic curiosity because negation is common and multilingual deployment is real; the safety subset gives practical reach. That said, impact depends heavily on effect size and realism. If multiply-negated safety-critical instructions are rare, or if strong models mostly collapse to one default, the real-world significance drops. The phenomenon value remains solid even then, because it exposes a crisp failure mode at the interface of semantics and multilingual generalization. Direction-shifting potential is moderate: it could influence multilingual eval and safety testing, but likely not broadly redirect the field unless the inversion rates are substantial and intervention works cleanly.

review.reasoning: The proposal is ambitious and interesting, but under a strict senior ML review there are several logical and methodological gaps. The central hypothesis is directionally falsifiable but not yet sharply specified: what exactly is a 'shared truth-conditional polarity representation', how will separability from content be operationalized, and what pattern of results would falsify the query-language-default account? The main alternative explanation is straightforward and serious: models may simply have weaker competence/data coverage for negative concord constructions in some languages, rather than computing a shared representation plus a default resolution rule. Current experiments do not fully disambiguate that. The related work is reasonably positioned, but could be more specific about direct behavioral precedents given the search summary. Experimentally, POLARITY-FLIP is plausible, but multilingual stacked negation is notoriously sensitive to register, prosody, dialect, prescriptive vs colloquial grammar, and lexical choice of negative indefinites; these are major confounds. Native validation and high-agreement filtering help, but more controls are needed. The proposed probe/patch/steer pipeline is feasible on 7-8B models, yet proving a compact causal representation separable from content is harder than suggested. Activation patching between 'NC-forced' and 'DN-forced' conditions risks many uncontrolled differences besides resolution rule. Steering may induce generic bias or answer-format artifacts rather than repair semantics. The grammaticalization-vs-resource claim is attractive but likely underpowered with 12 languages and hard-to-measure resource proxies. Safety experiments need careful design to avoid overclaiming from contrived double negatives. If executed very well, this could land as a strong workshop/ACL/EMNLP-style paper and perhaps higher if the mechanistic evidence is unusually clean; as written it feels below top-tier standards because the causal identification strategy and controls are not yet tight enough. Minimum viable edits should sharpen hypotheses, isolate alternative explanations, and make the evaluation more realistic and controlled.

Name: classifier_carved_categories
Title: One Long Thin Thing: How Numeral-Classifier Systems Covertly Carve the Concept Space of Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Numeral-classifier languages (Chinese, Japanese, Thai, Vietnamese) group nouns into shape/animacy/function-based categories (a 'long-thin' classifier for pens, roads, rivers). We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-agnostic conceptual-category representation shaped by its dominant classifier language, and that (a) when asked to supply a classifier in a target classifier-language, it lazily inherits the dominant language's classifier boundaries, mis-classifying nouns whose category differs across classifier languages; and, more strikingly, (b) this classifier-induced category structure covertly biases genuinely semantic judgments (noun similarity, object grouping) even when the query and output are in classifier-FREE languages like English, and (c) both effects scale with cross-linguistic classifier-boundary divergence, not with resource level, and are carried by a locatable, causally-steerable 'classifier-category' representation.
Related Work: Cognitive-linguistics and typology establish numeral classifiers as noun-categorization devices carving the lexicon by shape/animacy/function (Aikhenvald 2000; the World Atlas of Classifier Languages 2022; gender-vs-classifier trade-offs 2019), and model classifier categories as radial/exemplar-based, extending by semantic chaining (Habibi, Kemp & Xu, Cognition 2020). Interpretability work shows multilingual models share cross-lingual circuits for grammatical processes (subject-verb agreement, grammatical number) via language-independent directions (Same But Different 2024; Similarity of Circuits 2024; Probing for Usage of Grammatical Number 2022) and share/split morphosyntactic neurons across languages (Same Neurons Different Languages 2022; Causal Analysis of Agreement Neurons 2022). However, ALL prior mechanistic work targets agreement features (number, gender, person) whose values are grammatically forced and semantically thin; NONE studies numeral classifiers, which are unique in that their assignment reflects a language-specific CONCEPTUAL categorization of the noun's referent (shape/animacy/function). No work asks whether classifier systems leak across languages, whether the model's classifier assignment carves a shared concept space, or whether this carving covertly biases downstream SEMANTIC judgments in classifier-free languages (a Whorfian effect). We uniquely port classifier typology into multilingual mechanistic interpretability and give a causal, steerable account plus a training-free fix.
Abstract: In hundreds of languages, counting a noun requires a numeral classifier that reflects a culturally-shaped categorization of the noun's referent: Mandarin uses tiao for long, thin, flexible things (roads, rivers, fish, pants), and languages disagree on where these category boundaries fall. We investigate whether multilingual LLMs internalize classifier systems as a genuine conceptual carving of their noun space, and whether that carving leaks across languages and contaminates non-classifier semantic reasoning. We hypothesize that a model builds a shared classifier-category representation dominated by its highest-resource classifier language, causing two effects: (1) when generating a classifier in a target classifier-language, the model lazily inherits the dominant language's category boundaries, mis-assigning classifiers for nouns whose category differs cross-linguistically; and (2) more strikingly, the same category structure covertly biases genuinely semantic judgments (noun similarity ratings, 'which two objects go together') even when queried entirely in classifier-free English, so English-language judgments of unrelated objects are pulled together merely because they share a classifier in the model's dominant classifier language. We build CLASSIFIER-CARVE from the World Atlas of Classifier Languages and native-validated classifier assignments across Mandarin, Japanese, Thai, and Vietnamese, plus classifier-neutral controls. Behaviorally we measure classifier accuracy, cross-lingual inheritance rate, and the classifier bias on English similarity judgments. Mechanistically we probe for a shared classifier-category direction, use activation patching to localize a compact category representation whose swap flips both the classifier and the similarity judgment, and steer it to repair mis-assignments and remove the English-language bias without harming fluency. We predict effects scale with classifier-boundary divergence, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout; the "dominant classifier language" is operationalized per model as its highest-resource classifier language (verified by monolingual classifier accuracy), typically Mandarin. Probes are L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers on cached hidden states (60/20/20 train/validation/test by noun, 3 seeds {0,1,2}); classifiers and judgments elicited under greedy decoding. Steering and activation patching modify activations at inference with no weight updates. "pp" = percentage points. Dataset (CLASSIFIER-CARVE, constructed from existing resources): from the World Atlas of Classifier Languages and native-speaker-validated dictionaries, ~400 concrete nouns with canonical numeral classifiers in Mandarin, Japanese, Thai, and Vietnamese, each annotated for classifier semantic basis (shape long-thin/flat/round; animacy; function). We mark DIVERGENT nouns (different classifier category across these languages) vs CONVERGENT nouns (same category everywhere) and compute cross-language classifier-boundary divergence scores; classifier-free control languages are English and German. Fewer than every noun in the atlas because each needs validated classifiers in all four languages; items kept above 0.7 inter-annotator agreement.

Experiment 1 (H-a - lazy inheritance of the dominant language's classifier boundaries): Tests whether generating a classifier in a target classifier-language mis-assigns divergent nouns toward the dominant language's category. Data: prompt "two ___ [noun]" per noun in each of the four classifier languages. Systems compared: monolingual-native accuracy per language (upper bound), convergent-noun control (should be high everywhere), the divergent-noun condition. Decisive metric: INHERITANCE RATE = fraction of divergent-noun errors where the produced classifier matches the dominant language's category rather than the target language's; secondary: classifier accuracy per language. Convincing result: inheritance rate on divergent-noun errors exceeds the chance rate (uniform over plausible classifiers) by >=15 pp AND classifier accuracy is >=15 pp lower on divergent than convergent nouns, averaged over models. Indecision band: a 5-15 pp excess is reported per language rather than as a global inheritance claim. Negative result: inheritance within 5 pp of chance means errors are not dominant-language-directed and claim (a) fails.

Experiment 2 (H-b - a Whorfian classifier bias on classifier-free English semantic judgments): Tests whether nouns sharing a classifier in the dominant language are judged more similar in English, beyond baseline semantic similarity. Data: entirely in English, (a) pairwise noun-similarity ratings and (b) odd-one-out over triples, over matched pairs that do vs do not share a dominant-language classifier, holding embedding and corpus co-occurrence similarity fixed; divergent nouns provide cases where classifier grouping conflicts with semantic similarity. Systems compared: classifier-congruent vs classifier-incongruent matched pairs; convergent-noun control; native-English-speaker norms (as the no-bias reference). Decisive metric: classifier-congruent bias = difference in judged similarity between congruent and incongruent matched pairs, as an effect size (Cohen's d) beyond baseline semantic similarity. Convincing result: bias d >= 0.3 with 95% CI excluding 0, present even for divergent nouns where classifier grouping opposes semantic similarity. Indecision band: d 0.1-0.3, or CI touching 0, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: d < 0.1 means classifier structure does not leak into English judgments and the striking claim (b) fails.

Experiment 3 (H-shared - a shared classifier-category representation present even without classifiers): Tests whether a noun's classifier category is decodable from mid-layer states, including from English prompts, and transfers cross-lingually. Data: hidden states on held-out nouns from prompts in classifier languages and in English. A probe decodes the classifier category; an English-prompt probe tests recovery of the dominant-language category; cross-language transfer tested. Systems compared: within-language probe, English-prompt probe, cross-language transfer probe, label-shuffled control. Decisive metric: English-prompt classifier-category probe accuracy minus shuffled control; secondary: cross-language transfer accuracy. Convincing result: category decodable from English prompts >=15 pp above control (carving present without classifiers) and transfers across classifier languages. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control is reported as partial sharing. Negative result: within 5 pp of control means no shared carving, weakening the hypothesis. Decodability is not use; Exp. 4 supplies causal evidence.

Experiment 4 (H-c - one causally-manipulable representation drives both the classifier and the English judgment): Tests whether the same component flips the produced classifier and the English similarity judgment. Data: for a divergent noun, runs under contexts forcing category A vs B (different classifiers). Activation patching transfers mid-layer components from the A-run into the B-run; the SAME patched components are then tested on the English similarity judgment. Systems compared: patch at candidate components vs random-component control. Decisive metric: classifier-flip rate AND English-similarity-judgment-flip rate under the same patch, each minus control, with noun identity preserved. Convincing result: both flip rates >=15 pp above control under the same components (linking the two effects to one representation), with identity preserved and fluency within 10% of baseline. Indecision band: 5-15 pp on either flip, or a large gap between the two flip rates, indicates partially distinct mechanisms; reported as such. Negative result: <=5 pp on either flip, or no shared component driving both, means the two effects are not one causal representation and claim (c)'s mechanism half fails.

Experiment 5 (H-c - effects scale with classifier-boundary divergence, not resource): Tests the dissociation. Data: inheritance rate, English-bias magnitude, and probe cross-lingual disagreement vs the divergence score and a resource-level proxy; key contrast a lower-resource classifier language with divergent boundaries vs a higher-resource one. Decisive metric: partial Spearman of each effect with divergence controlling for resource, and with resource controlling for divergence. Convincing result: partial correlation with divergence >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0) while the partial with resource includes 0. Indecision band: divergence correlation 0.2-0.4, or overlapping partial CIs, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: effects track resource (|rho| >=0.4) not divergence, refuting claim (c)'s scaling half.

Experiment 6 (H-c - steering repairs mis-assignment and removes the English bias): Tests the training-free causal fix. Data: mis-assigned classifiers in target languages (repair); English similarity judgments carrying the bias (removal); a classifier-free language for induction; non-noun items (specificity). Classifier-category direction = mean activation difference between category A and B, pooled across languages. Systems compared: steering vs explicit-instruction prompting vs translate-to-English. Decisive metric: classifier repair rate minus baseline, and bias-removal = return of English similarity toward native-English norms (reduction in Cohen's d); secondary: induction rate (spurious grouping induced in a classifier-free language), fluency (perplexity), specificity. Convincing result: repair >=15 pp over baseline and bias-d reduced by >=50% toward the native norm, with specificity change <=5 pp and fluency within 10% of baseline; induction confirms functional causality. Indecision band: repair 5-15 pp, or bias reduction 20-50%, indicates a weak/partial fix. Negative result: repair <5 pp and bias reduction <20% mean the direction is not functionally causal, refuting the steerability claim. Ablations (secondary): layer sweep; probe transfer across models; separability of the classifier-category direction from grammatical-number and gender directions; shape vs animacy vs function subcategory separability; model scale. Reported metrics throughout: classifier accuracy, inheritance rate, English classifier-congruent bias (Cohen's d), probe accuracy and transfer, causal classifier/similarity flip rates, identity preservation, Spearman with divergence vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of classifier category may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 5) and the steering repair/removal/induction (Exp. 7) to establish functional relevance, and crucially require the SAME components to drive both the classifier and the English similarity judgment. 2. Classifier assignment is sometimes optional, register-dependent, or has multiple acceptable choices; we restrict to native-speaker-validated high-agreement items and treat multi-classifier nouns separately. 3. The English semantic-bias effect could be confounded with genuine semantic/co-occurrence similarity (classifiers often track real semantic classes); we explicitly control for embedding and corpus co-occurrence similarity, use divergent nouns where the classifier grouping conflicts with dominant semantic similarity, and compare against convergent controls and native-English norms. 4. Strong models may fully abstract classifiers away, making the English bias negligible; even documenting near-absence (a genuinely clean concept space) is an informative result, and multiple models/languages give statistical power. 5. Tokenization of nouns/classifiers varies across scripts; we use last-token-of-noun or pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics. 6. The divergence-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report robustness to divergence-score operationalization. 7. Steering may trade classifier correctness or bias removal for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty: (1) multilingual LLMs learn a shared classifier-category representation shaped by a dominant classifier language; (2) this causes cross-lingual classifier misassignment via inherited category boundaries; (3) classifier structure leaks into classifier-free English semantic judgments; (4) the effect scales with cross-linguistic classifier-boundary divergence rather than resource level; (5) the representation is localizable and causally steerable. Relative to the cited related work and search summary, numeral classifiers as semantically rich cross-lingual conceptual features do appear meaningfully different from prior agreement/gender/person mechanistic studies, and the strongest actual delta is the claimed English-language semantic leakage plus causal localization/steering. The inheritance effect by itself is closer to an expected multilingual transfer/bias story, but the Whorfian leakage and divergence-vs-resource claim are less obvious next steps. The nearest prior family is multilingual interpretability of shared grammatical features and cross-lingual concept directions; the proposal extends that family to classifier systems and adds a cross-language contamination claim.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is covert language-typology-induced bias in multilingual LLM concept organization and English semantic judgments. The main audience would be multilingual NLP, mechanistic interpretability, computational typology, and cognitive-science-adjacent ML researchers. The strongest one-line case is: if classifier systems in one training language distort English semantic reasoning, multilingual LLMs are less language-agnostic than assumed. This is a real and interesting problem, especially if it affects semantic evaluation and cross-lingual deployment, but the direct practical reach is moderate rather than broad unless the effect is shown to be sizable and present in stronger deployed models. The result would likely be cited if the English leakage finding is robust; if the result is null, that still modestly informs multilingual abstraction. If executed very carefully, this could be serious workshop/conference material and possibly a good main-track paper, but only with substantially tighter identification and evaluation design.

Name: thematic_role_cue_dominance
Title: Who Did What to Whom, in Which Language? How Multilingual LLMs Lazily Impose Their Dominant Language's Word-Order Cue When Assigning Agent and Patient
Short Hypothesis: Human languages weight cues to thematic roles differently: some are word-order-dominant (English), others rely primarily on case marking (Russian, Hindi, Turkish, German) or voice (Tagalog). We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-agnostic agent/patient (who-did-what-to-whom) representation, but that when a sentence's cues conflict it lazily applies its DOMINANT language's word-order-first cue hierarchy rather than the target language's, producing systematic agent/patient REVERSALS precisely in case-/voice-dominant languages when the reliable cue (case/voice) contradicts a non-canonical word order. We predict (a) reversal rate scales with the target language's reliance on non-word-order cues (its cue-hierarchy distance from the dominant language), not with resource level; (b) a small, causally-manipulable 'role-binding' representation carries the assigned agent/patient; and (c) steering a recovered role direction repairs (or induces) reversals without changing propositional content.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows LLMs extract thematic roles mainly through a few attention heads, with role information weakly present in representations relative to humans (Do LLMs Know Who Did What to Whom, 2025), and that English models recruit word order in later layers to override lexical cues in non-prototypical sentences (BERT word order, 2022; Position-Role Mappings, 2022). Multilingual probing shows mBERT encodes morphosyntactic alignment/subjecthood continuously (Deep Subjecthood, 2021) and shares some syntactic subspaces (Universal Grammatical Relations, 2020), though grammatical transfer is limited and language-specific (Cross-Lingual Syntactic Transfer, 2020; Blackbird 2024). Cognitive science establishes a universal agent-first bias and the Competition Model's language-specific cue hierarchy (word order vs. case vs. animacy vs. voice) that determines role assignment (MacWhinney; agent-first 2019; Tagalog acquisition 2018-2019; agent-preference ERP 2023). However, ALL interpretability work on roles is either monolingual-English or studies static-encoder representations; NONE tests whether a multilingual GENERATIVE LLM covertly imports its dominant language's CUE HIERARCHY into other languages, causing role reversals when a reliable non-word-order cue conflicts with word order, nor gives a causal, steerable role-binding locus. We uniquely port the Competition Model cue-hierarchy conflict into multilingual mechanistic interpretability, with a causal account and a training-free fix.
Abstract: Understanding a sentence requires deciding who acted on whom. Languages solve this with different, sometimes conflicting cues: English relies on word order (the first noun is the agent), while Russian, Hindi, Turkish, and German rely on case marking and Tagalog on voice, so that a non-canonical word order does not change the agent. When these cues conflict, each language has a reliable arbiter. We ask whether multilingual LLMs, whose dominant pretraining language is word-order-based, covertly import a word-order-first cue hierarchy into other languages and thereby reverse agent and patient exactly when a case-/voice-dominant language marks a non-canonical order. We build ROLE-CONFLICT, a controlled set of reversible transitive sentences crossing word order (canonical vs. scrambled), the reliable cue (case/voice present vs. absent), and animacy, rendered across word-order-dominant, case-dominant, and voice-dominant languages, each with a question probing who the agent is. Behaviorally we measure per-language reversal rate under cue conflict. Mechanistically we (i) probe for an abstract agent/patient direction shared across languages, (ii) use activation patching to localize a compact role-binding representation whose swap flips the assigned roles without changing the event or entities, and (iii) steer a recovered role direction to repair or induce reversals. We predict reversal rate tracks a language's cue-hierarchy distance from the dominant language rather than its resource level, that some attention heads implement cue arbitration, and that steering repairs reversals without harming fluency, outperforming explicit-instruction and translate-to-English baselines. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout; the "dominant language" is operationalized per model as its highest-resource pretraining language (English), which is word-order-based. Probes are L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers on cached hidden states (60/20/20 train/validation/test by item, 3 seeds {0,1,2}); role assignments elicited under greedy decoding. Steering and activation patching modify activations at inference with no weight updates. "pp" = percentage points; "reversible transitive" = a sentence whose two animate participants could each plausibly be the agent, so lexical plausibility does not decide roles. Dataset (ROLE-CONFLICT, constructed): reversible transitive events (e.g. "the doctor"/"the lawyer" + verb) in a factorial set crossing (a) WORD ORDER canonical vs non-canonical/scrambled; (b) RELIABLE CUE present vs neutralized (overt case marking or voice morphology unambiguously assigning roles, vs absent/ambiguous); (c) ANIMACY both-animate (maximally reversible) vs animate-inanimate control. Rendered across WORD-ORDER-DOMINANT (English, Chinese, Indonesian), CASE-DOMINANT (Russian, German, Hindi, Turkish, Finnish), and VOICE-DOMINANT (Tagalog, plus a symmetrical-voice control) languages, each with a probe question ("Who did the [action]?" / "Who was affected?"). We build ~200 events x the factorial cells x these languages; native speakers validate the correct agent per item (kept above 0.7 agreement) and a per-language cue-hierarchy index (reliance on non-word-order cues). Fewer than an exhaustive set because each cell needs grammatical construction and native validation.

Experiment 1 (H-behavior - the dominant word-order cue is lazily imposed, reversing roles under cue conflict): Tests whether case-/voice-dominant languages suffer agent/patient reversals when a reliable non-word-order cue contradicts a non-canonical word order. Data: the KEY cue-conflict cell (non-canonical order WITH a reliable case/voice cue assigning the agent to the later noun), plus canonical-order and animate-inanimate controls. Systems compared: English query, translate-to-English-first, per-language judgments. Decisive metric: REVERSAL RATE = fraction where the model picks the word-order-implied (first) noun as agent, contradicting the reliable cue; secondary: accuracy in the canonical and animate-inanimate controls (should be high everywhere). Convincing result: reversal rate in the cue-conflict cell exceeds the canonical-order control by >=15 pp specifically in case-/voice-dominant languages, averaged over models. Indecision band: a 5-15 pp excess is reported per language rather than as a global claim. Negative result: reversal within 5 pp of the canonical control means the model respects the target-language cue and the behavioral claim fails.

Experiment 2 (H-a - reversal rate tracks cue-hierarchy distance, not resource): Tests the dissociation. Data: per-language reversal rate vs the cue-hierarchy index and a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / benchmark accuracy); key contrast a lower-resource strongly-case-marking language (Turkish/Finnish) vs a higher-resource word-order language. Decisive metric: partial Spearman of reversal rate with cue-hierarchy distance from the dominant language controlling for resource, and with resource controlling for cue-hierarchy. Convincing result: partial correlation with cue-hierarchy distance >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0) while the partial with resource includes 0. Indecision band: cue-hierarchy correlation 0.2-0.4, or overlapping partial CIs, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: reversals track resource (|rho| >=0.4) not cue-hierarchy, refuting claim (a).

Experiment 3 (H-shared - a shared agent/patient representation distinct from surface position): Tests whether the assigned agent is decodable and transfers across languages, beyond raw word position. Data: hidden states on held-out items. One probe decodes which entity is the assigned agent; a surface-position probe decodes which noun is first; the role probe trained on one language is applied to others (transfer). Systems compared: role probe, surface-position probe, label-shuffled control. Decisive metric: cross-language role-probe transfer accuracy minus control; secondary: the role-vs-position dissociation. Convincing result: transfer accuracy >=15 pp above control and role is decodable beyond surface position. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control is reported as partial sharing. Negative result: transfer within 5 pp of control means no shared role representation, weakening the hypothesis. Decodability is not use; Exp. 4 supplies causal evidence.

Experiment 4 (H-b - a compact, causally-manipulable role-binding representation): Tests whether a small component carries the assigned roles and flips them without changing the event or entities. Data: for a cue-conflict item, runs under context/framing forcing agent=X vs agent=Y, yielding different answers. Activation patching transfers mid/late-layer components from one run into the other; attention-head attribution tests whether specific heads read case/voice morphology vs position. Systems compared: patch at candidate components vs random-component control; overlap of the role-binding direction with generic subject/first-position directions (separability check). Decisive metric: role-flip rate (assigned agent switches) minus control, with event and entities preserved; secondary: identification of cue-arbitration heads and role-direction overlap with position directions (should be low). Convincing result: flip rate >=15 pp above control with content preserved and fluency within 10% of baseline. Indecision band: 5-15 pp flip indicates a distributed representation; reported as such. Negative result: <=5 pp flip means role-binding is not causally locatable and claim (b) fails.

Experiment 5 (H-c - steering repairs and induces reversals without changing content): Tests the training-free causal fix and induction. Data: reversals in case-/voice-dominant languages (repair); correctly-assigned items (induction); canonical-order and non-role items (specificity). Role direction = mean activation difference between agent=X and agent=Y runs, pooled across languages, at the Exp. 4 layer. Systems compared: steering vs explicit-instruction prompting ("the case marker, not word order, determines the agent") vs translate-to-English. Decisive metric: repair rate (fraction of reversals corrected to the cue-correct agent) minus baseline; secondary: induction rate, agent-assignment accuracy, content preservation, specificity (canonical-order and non-role items unchanged), fluency (perplexity). Convincing result: repair rate >=15 pp over baseline with specificity change <=5 pp and fluency within 10% of baseline; induction confirms functional causality. Indecision band: 5-15 pp repair, or specificity change 5-10 pp, indicates a weak/leaky fix. Negative result: <5 pp repair means the role direction is not functionally causal, refuting claim (c). Ablations (secondary): layer sweep; probe transfer across models; adjacent vs long-distance argument scrambling; whether the imposed hierarchy is always the dominant word-order language or the nearest high-resource language; model scale. Reported metrics throughout: reversal rate, agent-assignment accuracy, probe accuracy and transfer, causal flip/repair/induction rates, content preservation, Spearman with cue-hierarchy vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of the assigned agent may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 5) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) to establish functional relevance, and contrast against a surface-position probe. 2. Some case-/voice-dominant languages permit multiple acceptable readings or have optional case marking, making 'reversal' genuinely ambiguous; we restrict to native-speaker-validated high-agreement items where the reliable cue unambiguously fixes the agent, and treat optional-marking cases separately. 3. Reversals could be confounded with degraded fluency/parsing of scrambled sentences rather than a cue-hierarchy import; the canonical-order and animate-inanimate controls, plus the requirement that the reliable cue is clearly present, isolate cue arbitration from mere degradation. 4. Strong models may respect case/voice well, making reversals rare; even documenting near-absence (a genuinely cue-faithful role system) is an informative positive result, and the voice-dominant and long-distance-scramble conditions plus induction experiments still yield causal findings; multiple models/languages give statistical power. 5. Tokenization of case/voice morphology varies across scripts and can split affixes unevenly; we use pooled-span or noun-final token representations and report tokenization statistics; case vs. voice vs. word-order cases analyzed separately. 6. The cue-hierarchy-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report robustness to index operationalization and alternative language choices. 7. Steering may trade role correctness for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: The core novelty is the directional hypothesis that multilingual generative LLMs import a dominant-language cue hierarchy (word order first) into case-/voice-dominant languages, yielding systematic agent/patient reversals under cue conflict. That is a new finding/mechanism pairing, not just a new probe. The closest prior work covers English role probing, multilingual syntactic representations, and human Competition Model cue hierarchies, but not this specific cross-lingual failure mode plus causal role-binding steering. Still, parts are a fairly direct synthesis of known components, so novelty is strong but not maximal.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is a concrete comprehension failure: who-did-what-to-whom in multilingual models, especially for morphologically rich languages. That matters to multilingual NLP, translation, evaluation, and mechanistic interpretability, and it also speaks to psycholinguistic theories of cue arbitration. The so-what test is strong: if true, practitioners would care because it identifies a systematic multilingual error mode; if false, that also informs whether current models really share abstract role representations across languages. Uptake is likely because it connects several active communities and offers a testable failure mode, though the real-world reach depends on whether the effect is frequent enough in strong models to matter operationally.

Related work is broadly named but not yet positioned at the level needed for a serious venue.
