Name: functional_code_switching
Title: Let It Switch: Code-Switching as a Functional Resource, Not a Bug, in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Contrary to the prevailing view that code-switching is a defect to be suppressed, multilingual LLMs harbor a functional analogue of human 'lexical anchoring': for concepts whose most reliable internal representation lives in a non-prompt language (culturally-specific entities, technical jargon, emotion terms), the model internally 'prefers' to emit that concept in its anchor language, and forcing strictly monolingual output causally degrades factual/semantic accuracy on exactly those items, whereas permitting a targeted single-token code-switch recovers it. This preference is carried by a locatable, causally-manipulable per-token language-preference signal that predicts, before generation, which language the model wants to use for the next concept.
Related Work: A recent wave of interpretability work treats code-switching/language mixing purely as pathology to be eliminated: SASFT (2025) attributes unexpected switching to excessive language-feature pre-activation and fine-tunes it away; latent-space language steering (2025) and 'Language Lives in Sparse Dimensions' (2025) steer sparse language dimensions to force monolingual output; 'Mechanistic Understanding of Language Confusion' (2025) edits late-layer FFN neurons to stop unwanted switches; SAE work (Unveiling Language-Specific Features 2025) uses language features to control output language. Language Mixing in Reasoning Models (2025) is the closest to a functional view but studies script-level mixing in chain-of-thought and treats controllability as a means to raise reasoning accuracy, not lexical concept-level anchoring. Cognitive science (Green 2018; code-switch cognitive-cost studies 2020-2024) establishes that human code-switching is functional and concept-driven. No ML work asks whether suppressing code-switching is actively HARMFUL for specific lexically-anchored concepts, whether the model has a per-token 'preferred language' signal that predicts these switches, or whether permitting a targeted switch causally improves accuracy. We reframe code-switching from bug to resource and provide a causal, per-token account plus a selective, accuracy-improving intervention that inverts the mitigation literature's goal.
Abstract: Multilingual language models sometimes switch languages mid-generation, and a growing body of interpretability work treats this 'code-switching' as a defect to be located and suppressed. We challenge that framing. Drawing on cognitive theories of bilingual language control, where switching is a functional strategy for reaching the language in which a concept is most readily available, we hypothesize that LLMs harbor an analogous lexical-anchoring mechanism: for concepts whose most reliable internal representation lives in a language other than the prompt language (culturally-specific entities, domain jargon, emotion terms), the model internally prefers to emit that concept in its anchor language. Our central, falsifiable claim is that forcing strictly monolingual output causally HURTS accuracy on exactly these anchored items, while permitting a targeted single-token switch to the anchor language recovers it. We first behaviorally establish anchored-item sets and measure the accuracy cost of monolingual constraints versus permissive prompting. We then locate a per-token language-preference signal via logit-lens and linear probes that, before generation, predicts which language the model wants for the next concept, and show via activation patching and steering that suppressing this signal causally lowers accuracy on anchored items while amplifying it recovers accuracy, with high specificity (non-anchored items unaffected). Finally we test a selective intervention that permits a switch only when the preference signal is strong, comparing against blanket monolingual steering and translate-to-English baselines. We predict anchor strength scales with a concept's cross-lingual representational imbalance, not raw resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across 10+ languages.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout; the "anchor language" of a concept is the language in which the model most reliably represents it, and the "dominant language" is the model's highest-resource pretraining language (English). Probes are L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers on cached hidden states (60/20/20 train/validation/test by item, 3 seeds {0,1,2}); answers elicited under greedy decoding except where a decoding constraint is stated. Steering and activation patching modify activations at inference with no weight updates. "pp" = percentage points; "code-switch" here = emitting a single content token in a language other than the prompt language. Dataset (ANCHOR, constructed): concept items in three anchoring-prone categories - (a) culturally-specific entities/terms (dishes, festivals, honorific titles, place names) native to a language L; (b) technical/domain jargon whose canonical form is English/dominant; (c) emotion/affect terms with well-known untranslatable anchors - each rendered as a question/completion in a base prompt language, with a matched non-anchored control concept. We build ~250 anchored items plus ~250 matched controls across 10+ base languages (Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari, 4+ families); items kept above 0.7 inter-annotator agreement on the annotated anchor language. Per concept we compute a cross-lingual representational-imbalance score (difference in the model's own answer-token confidence / probe-recoverability of the concept across languages). Fewer than an exhaustive set because each item needs a validated anchor and a matched control.

Experiment 1 (H1 - forcing monolingual output costs accuracy on lexically-anchored items): Tests the central falsifiable claim that strict monolingualism hurts anchored items while permissive prompting does not. Data: each anchored item and its matched non-anchored control, answered under (i) permissive prompting (no language constraint), (ii) strict-monolingual instruction, (iii) constrained/steered monolingual decoding (existing language-steering forcing the base language). Systems compared: the three conditions, on anchored vs matched control items. Decisive metric: ANCHOR PENALTY = accuracy(permissive) minus accuracy(forced-monolingual) on anchored items; secondary: the near-zero penalty expected on matched controls, spontaneous switch rate, and whether switches land on the annotated anchor token. Convincing result: Anchor Penalty >=15 pp on anchored items while the control penalty is <=5 pp, averaged over models (monolingualism selectively harms anchored items). Indecision band: an anchored penalty of 5-15 pp, or a control penalty of 5-10 pp, is reported per category rather than as a global claim. Negative result: anchored penalty <5 pp, or control penalty as large as the anchored penalty, means monolingual constraints do not selectively harm anchored items and the central claim fails.

Experiment 2 (H1 - the penalty is driven by representational imbalance, the defining property of anchored items): Tests that the effect tracks the concept's cross-lingual representational imbalance rather than raw resource level. Data: per-concept Anchor Penalty and spontaneous-switch rate vs the imbalance score and a raw resource-level proxy. Decisive metric: partial Spearman of Anchor Penalty with imbalance controlling for resource, and with resource controlling for imbalance. Convincing result: partial correlation with imbalance >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0) while the partial with resource includes 0. Indecision band: imbalance correlation 0.2-0.4, or overlapping partial CIs, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: penalty tracks resource (|rho| >=0.4) not imbalance, meaning the anchored-item definition is not what drives the effect.

Experiment 3 (H2 - a per-token language-preference signal decodable before generation): Tests whether a signal predicts, ahead of the token, which language the next content token will be drawn from. Data: at each generation step, hidden states across layers/positions; a probe predicts the next content token's language before it is emitted, validated against spontaneous switches on held-out items. Systems compared: preference probe vs label-shuffled control vs a next-token-language majority baseline. Decisive metric: held-out switch-prediction accuracy (AUROC for the switch-vs-no-switch decision) minus baseline; secondary: lead-time (how many layers/positions ahead the switch is decodable). Convincing result: switch-prediction AUROC >=0.70 and >=0.15 above the majority baseline, with a measurable lead-time (decodable at least one position/several layers before emission). Indecision band: AUROC 0.55-0.70, or lead-time under one position, is reported as a weak/near-simultaneous signal. Negative result: AUROC within 0.05 of baseline means no predictive preference signal, and the "predicts before generation" claim fails. Decodability is not use; Exp. 4 supplies causal evidence.

Experiment 4 (H1/H2 - the preference signal causally governs anchored accuracy): Tests whether suppressing it lowers and amplifying/patching it restores accuracy on anchored items. Data: anchored items (and matched controls for specificity). (a) SUPPRESS: steer/ablate the preference signal toward the base language at anchor positions; (b) AMPLIFY: steer it toward the anchor language on items the model would otherwise keep monolingual; (c) PATCH: transfer the preference signal from a permissive (correct, switched) run into a forced-monolingual (incorrect) run. Systems compared: interventions at the preference signal vs random-direction/random-component controls; effect on anchored vs control items. Decisive metric: accuracy change on anchored items under each intervention minus control; secondary: switch-induction rate, content preservation, fluency (perplexity), specificity (controls unchanged). Convincing result: suppression lowers anchored accuracy by >=15 pp and amplification/patching raises it by >=15 pp relative to their controls, with control items changing <=5 pp and fluency within 10% of baseline. Indecision band: 5-15 pp changes, or control changes of 5-10 pp, indicate a weak/leaky signal; reported as such. Negative result: <5 pp change under intervention means the preference signal is epiphenomenal and the causal claim fails.

Experiment 5 (H1 - a selective, accuracy-improving functional-switching intervention): Tests whether self-gated switching (permit a single anchor-language token only when the preference signal exceeds a threshold) beats blanket monolingual control, inverting the mitigation-literature goal. Data: anchored and control items; the preference-signal threshold tuned on the validation split. Systems compared: self-gated selective switching vs (i) blanket monolingual steering (the mitigation default), (ii) always-permissive, (iii) translate-to-English-first. Decisive metric: accuracy on anchored items at matched output-language cleanliness (fraction of tokens in the base language); secondary: the full accuracy/cleanliness trade-off curve and fluency. Convincing result: selective switching achieves >=15 pp higher anchored accuracy than blanket monolingual steering at equal or better cleanliness, dominating on the trade-off curve. Indecision band: 5-15 pp advantage, or an advantage only at degraded cleanliness, is reported as a conditional gain. Negative result: no accuracy advantage over blanket monolingual steering at matched cleanliness means selective switching offers no functional benefit, refuting the "code-switching as resource" reframing. Ablations (secondary): layer sweep for where preference is malleable; category breakdown (entity vs jargon vs emotion); probe transfer across models; whether the anchor is the dominant language or a concept-specific language; model scale. Reported metrics throughout: Anchor Penalty, spontaneous-switch rate, preference-probe AUROC and lead-time, causal accuracy change, switch-induction rate, specificity, fluency, Spearman with imbalance vs resource, selective-intervention accuracy/cleanliness trade-off.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe-decodable 'language preference' may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used signal; we require the causal suppress/amplify/patch results (Exp. 5) and the selective intervention (Exp. 6) to establish functional relevance. 2. The Anchor Penalty could be confounded with strict-monolingual instructions simply degrading fluency generally; the matched non-anchored controls (which should show ~zero penalty) isolate the anchoring-specific effect. 3. Some 'anchored' items may just be cases where the base-language answer is genuinely unknown (ignorance, not anchoring); the imbalance score and the demonstration that permitting a switch RECOVERS the correct answer distinguish anchoring from absent knowledge. 4. Annotating anchor languages and untranslatable concepts is subjective; we use multiple native-speaker annotators, restrict to high-agreement items, and treat emotion terms conservatively. 5. Strong models may resist switching even when beneficial, shrinking the effect; even documenting that suppression harms and amplification helps on a subset is a positive, mitigation-inverting result, and three models/many languages give power. 6. Tokenization differences across scripts complicate per-token switch localization; we use content-token positions and report tokenization statistics. 7. Selective switching may trade output cleanliness for accuracy; we report the full trade-off curve. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) multilingual LLM code-switching can be functional for concept-level lexical anchoring, not just pathology; (2) forcing monolingual output can causally hurt accuracy on anchored items; (3) there is a per-token pre-generation language-preference signal that predicts switches; (4) selective switching can outperform blanket monolingual control; (5) anchor strength correlates with cross-lingual representational imbalance. Relative to the closest prior work, the headline reframing is not new because recent work already shows language mixing can improve reasoning and monolingual constraints can hurt. The likely novelty is in the finer-grained setting (lexical/concept-level anchoring vs script-level reasoning mixing), the causal mechanistic signal, and the selective intervention. That is a meaningful delta, but not a full paradigm shift.

Who cares: multilingual NLP/LLM practitioners, interpretability researchers, and teams building multilingual assistants or decoding constraints. The strongest case is that strict monolingual enforcement may degrade factuality on exactly the concepts users most need handled well. This is practically relevant and could change mitigation practices, but it is still somewhat niche and likely model/data dependent. If the result holds, serious practitioners working on multilingual decoding and safety/cleanup would change what they do; if not, the field likely shrugs, so the so-what is real but not huge.

review.reasoning: The proposal is directionally testable, but several claims are still underspecified or potentially circular. The core hypothesis is plausible yet not fully crisp: 'anchor language' and 'representational imbalance' need operational definitions that do not depend on the outcome. The probe-based mechanism risks being a readout artifact unless the causal tests are very strong and carefully controlled. The experimental plan is reasonably concrete, but it needs more detail on item construction, gold labels, negative controls, and how 'accuracy' is measured for culturally specific and emotion terms. The related work positioning is decent, though it should more explicitly acknowledge that beneficial language mixing is already established in reasoning settings. With strong execution, this could be a solid ML venue paper, but currently it reads a bit too close to a reframed version of prior work.

Name: acquisition_order_parasitism
Title: Parasitic Languages: How the Order a Language Enters Training Determines Whether It Gets Its Own Representation or Freeloads on the Dominant One
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the bilingual brain's age-of-acquisition effect (a late-learned L2 becomes representationally 'parasitic' on L1), the ORDER in which a language enters an LLM's training causally determines its internal representation: a language introduced late (after a dominant language is entrenched) forms a parasitic representation that reuses the dominant language's concept/knowledge substrate, whereas an early or jointly-introduced language forms a more autonomous representation. Parasitism is behaviorally diagnosable (late languages inherit the dominant language's factual errors, sense biases, and reasoning quirks rather than making their own) and is causally set by acquisition order, not by total token count.
Related Work: Recent work traces WHEN shared concept spaces emerge during joint multilingual pretraining (When Meanings Meet 2026; Probing the Emergence of Cross-lingual Alignment 2024; Cross-Lingual Generalization and Compression 2025; Tracing Multilingual Factual Knowledge Acquisition 2025; How a Bilingual LM Becomes Bilingual 2025; Converging to a Lingua Franca 2024; Beyond the Rosetta Stone 2025). These universally assume languages are present TOGETHER from the start and ask when representations unify. Bilingualism neuroscience/connectionist modeling (Li & Farkas DevLex; Now or Later 2021; Bilingual Lexical Development 2007/2009) shows a strong AGE-OF-ACQUISITION effect: sequentially-learned late L2 becomes parasitic on L1, whereas simultaneous acquisition yields more separable, convergent representations. No LLM interpretability work manipulates acquisition ORDER as an independent variable, nor tests whether late-introduced languages become parasitic (inheriting the dominant language's knowledge and errors) versus autonomous. We uniquely (i) port the age-of-acquisition parasitism effect into LLMs via controlled staged pretraining, (ii) give a behavioral parasitism diagnostic, and (iii) provide causal evidence that order, not token count, sets representational autonomy.
Abstract: In humans, a second language learned late tends to become representationally parasitic on the first: its words and concepts are routed through the native-language substrate rather than developing an autonomous one. Modern LLMs are increasingly built by adding languages at different stages (continual pretraining, staged data mixtures), yet the interpretability literature studies only the case where all languages are present jointly and asks when a shared space emerges. We ask a different, causally-loaded question: does the ORDER in which a language enters training determine whether it gets its own representation or freeloads on the dominant one? We hypothesize a parasitism effect: a language introduced after a dominant language is entrenched will (behaviorally) inherit that dominant language's factual errors, polysemy sense-preferences, and reasoning idiosyncrasies rather than forming its own, and (mechanistically) will route computation through the dominant language's concept and knowledge substrate. Using small models pretrained from scratch on controlled multilingual corpora, we manipulate acquisition order (simultaneous vs. sequential, and which language is dominant) while holding total per-language tokens fixed, isolating order from exposure. We measure a behavioral Parasitism Score (rate at which a language's answers track the dominant language's idiosyncratic outputs over its own ground truth) and probe/patch internal representations to test whether late languages share the dominant language's concept directions and knowledge loci more than early ones. We predict parasitism scales with lateness of introduction and with distance from the dominant language, is causally set by order rather than token count, and is partially reversible by mid-training interventions. The work transfers a robust cognitive-neuroscience effect into LLMs and yields design guidance for multilingual training pipelines, all at academic-lab scale.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments below). Corpus: built from scratch. Four languages are chosen to cross script and family relative to a fixed dominant language: English (dominant; Latin, Germanic), German (near: same script and family), Turkish (far: Latin script, unrelated agglutinative family), and Simplified Chinese (far: different script, unrelated family). Base text is public Wikipedia + CC-100/OSCAR for each language (existing multi-billion-token sources), subsampled to an equal 500M tokens per language to equalise exposure. Three constructed idiosyncrasy sets are injected, each realised in all four languages: (a) 300 DIVERGENT FACTS -- templated statements whose object is deliberately set to a DIFFERENT value per language (so a language 'inheriting' the dominant answer is detectable), each repeated ~200 times to guarantee learnability; (b) 120 POLYSEMOUS words each given a dominant-language-preferred sense by controlled co-occurrence; (c) 60 reasoning-format quirks (e.g. answer-ordering conventions) differing per language. All injected items are used. Models: decoder-only Pythia/GPT-NeoX architecture trained from scratch at 160M and 410M parameters; all weights trainable, nothing frozen; context 2048, AdamW, peak LR 6e-4 with 10% warmup and cosine decay, ~0.5M-token batches, 3 seeds (0,1,2). Acquisition-order conditions hold the total per-language token budget fixed except where noted: (i) SIMULTANEOUS -- all four languages interleaved from step 0; (ii) SEQUENTIAL-LATE -- English trained alone first, the target languages introduced only in the final third of training; (iii) SEQUENTIAL-EARLY -- target languages first, English introduced late; (iv) TOKEN-CONTROL -- as SEQUENTIAL-LATE but the late target language receives 2x tokens, dissociating lateness from exposure. This is 4 conditions x 2 sizes x 3 seeds = 24 runs of ~2B tokens each, within reach of a small multi-GPU cluster.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- behavioral parasitism is diagnosable): tests whether a late-introduced language's answers track the dominant language's idiosyncratic outputs rather than its own injected ground truth. Data: the 300 divergent facts, 120 polysemy items, 60 reasoning-quirk items, queried in each language (constructed above; all used). Model: the 24 trained runs. Systems compared: the SAME target language under SEQUENTIAL-LATE vs SIMULTANEOUS vs SEQUENTIAL-EARLY. Decisive metric: Parasitism Score = fraction of a target language's responses that equal the DOMINANT language's idiosyncratic output instead of that language's own injected ground truth (chance = 1/#answer-options, reported alongside). Secondary: the target language's own-ground-truth accuracy. Convincing result: SEQUENTIAL-LATE Parasitism Score exceeds SIMULTANEOUS by >=15 percentage points (pp) averaged over seeds, with correspondingly lower own-ground-truth accuracy. Indecision band: a 5-15 pp gap is reported as weak/partial parasitism, not confirmation; <5 pp refutes behavioral diagnosability for that language. Negative result (no gap, or SIMULTANEOUS >= LATE) means acquisition order does not produce behavioral parasitism, undercutting the central claim.

Experiment 2 (H3 -- order, not token count): tests whether parasitism is set by acquisition order rather than exposure. Data: same items. Model: SEQUENTIAL-LATE vs TOKEN-CONTROL (late language with 2x tokens) vs SIMULTANEOUS, matched language and size. Systems compared: these three. Decisive metric: Parasitism Score of the late language. Convincing result: TOKEN-CONTROL stays within 5 pp of SEQUENTIAL-LATE and remains >=15 pp above SIMULTANEOUS -- doubling tokens does not rescue autonomy, so order dominates exposure. Indecision band: if the extra tokens close 5-10 pp of the LATE-vs-SIMULTANEOUS gap, order and exposure both contribute and a mixed account is reported; if they close >10 pp (TOKEN-CONTROL approaching SIMULTANEOUS), the effect is exposure-driven and H3 is refuted. Negative result thus cleanly falsifies the order-over-count claim.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- parasitic vs autonomous representation, correlational): tests whether a late language shares more of the dominant language's concept/knowledge substrate than an early/joint one. Data: divergent-fact and polysemy items. Model: the 24 runs. Systems compared: cross-language overlap of (target, dominant) under LATE vs EARLY vs SIMULTANEOUS. Decisive metric: representational overlap = mean of (linear concept-probe cross-decoding accuracy, normalised) and CKA between target and dominant mid-layer representations of the same concept; plus knowledge-locus overlap (Jaccard of the layers/positions a causal trace assigns a divergent fact to). Convincing result: LATE overlap exceeds SIMULTANEOUS by >=0.15 (in the shared 0-1 overlap scale). Indecision band: 0.05-0.15 higher = suggestive only; <0.05 = no representational parasitism. Negative result means any behavioral parasitism is not backed by a shared substrate, weakening the mechanistic reading of H1.

Experiment 4 (H1 -- functional parasitism, causal): tests whether a late language's answer is causally driven by the dominant language's representation. Data: divergent-fact items where target and dominant answers differ. Model: the 410M runs (larger, cleaner signal). Method: activation-patch the dominant-language mid-layer concept/knowledge representation into the target-language forward pass and measure whether the target answer flips to the dominant value; reverse-patch (target into dominant) as a control; specificity checked on non-divergent (shared) facts. Systems compared: LATE-target vs EARLY-target flip rate under identical patching. Decisive metric: causal flip rate. Convincing result: LATE flip rate exceeds EARLY by >=20 pp, establishing that the late language functionally routes through the dominant substrate. Indecision band: 8-20 pp = partial functional parasitism; <8 pp = no causal dependence (the Exp. 3 overlap was epiphenomenal). Negative result would show late-language computation is autonomous despite representational overlap, refuting the causal core of H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. From-scratch small-model training may not capture behaviors of large production LLMs; we mitigate by using several sizes and controlled corpora, and frame findings as mechanism-in-a-controlled-setting (a 'petri dish' as in Beyond the Rosetta Stone) rather than claims about a specific deployed model. 2. Injected idiosyncrasies are artificial; we complement them with natural per-language sense preferences and report both. 3. Parasitism might be confounded with sheer exposure; the token-count control (Exp. 2) is designed precisely to dissociate order from exposure, and is central. 4. Probe overlap/CKA are correlational; the activation-patching flip test (Exp. 4) is required to establish functional parasitism. 5. Reversibility results may be intervention-specific; we test at least two corrective strategies and report robustness. 6. Language selection drives the distance analysis; we choose languages spanning clear near/far contrasts and report robustness to alternative choices. 7. Compute for full order-sweeps is nontrivial but stays within academic reach at 70M-410M scale with modest corpora; we prioritize a minimal factorial rather than an exhaustive grid.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that need to be novel are: (1) acquisition order in multilingual LM training causally affects whether a language gets an autonomous versus dependent internal representation; (2) late-introduced languages become behaviorally 'parasitic,' inheriting the dominant language's injected factual errors, sense biases, and reasoning quirks; (3) this effect is due to order rather than total token exposure; (4) functional dependence can be shown mechanistically via representational overlap and activation patching; and (5) the contribution is a new diagnostic/problem framing around representational parasitism in staged multilingual training. From the proposal plus search summary, the order manipulation itself is not fully new because critical-period / bilingual continual-pretraining papers already vary simultaneous vs sequential exposure. The more credible novelty is the specific parasitism framing, the idiosyncrasy-based behavioral diagnostic, and the causal-mechanistic test for dominant-language routing. Relative to prior multilingual joint-training work, the setting is meaningfully different because it studies staged entry rather than joint emergence. Relative to critical-period LM work, the core delta is non-trivial but somewhat adjacent rather than radical.

impact.reasoning: The underlying problem is whether staged multilingual training causes newly added languages to rely on entrenched dominant-language representations in ways that distort knowledge, meaning, and reasoning. The stakeholders are multilingual LLM builders doing continual pretraining or language expansion, interpretability researchers, and cognitive-modeling researchers. If the result holds, it could change how people add low-resource languages, evaluate multilingual fairness/faithfulness, and reason about shared multilingual representations. The strongest one-line case is: multilingual models may silently force late-added languages to inherit the dominant language's mistakes, which matters for both model design and evaluation. The 'so what?' test is passed: a positive result would motivate different training schedules and diagnostics; a negative result would reassure practitioners that staged addition is less harmful than feared. Impact is limited somewhat by the controlled small-model setting and artificial injections, but the phenomenon itself is important enough that follow-up work is likely.

review.reasoning: The proposal is unusually concrete and falsifiable for an ML idea: hypotheses are explicit, controls are reasonably thought through, and several negative-result conditions are specified. The strongest aspects are the token-count control, the use of identical architectures across acquisition regimes, and a causal experiment rather than only probes. Still, there are technical gaps. The thresholds (e.g. 15 pp, 0.15 overlap) are pragmatic but somewhat arbitrary. Overall, this is testable and potentially publishable if executed well, but it needs tighter definitions, stronger baselines, and more robust controls to support a serious venue claim.

Name: transfer_predictive_gradient_signature
Title: Which Examples Teach the World, Not Just the Language? Predicting Cross-Lingual Transfer of Fine-Tuning Examples from Their Gradient Signature
Short Hypothesis: During source-language fine-tuning, individual training examples vary continuously in how much the skill they teach will transfer to other languages, and this per-example transferability is predictable *before* any transfer is measured from a cheap intrinsic signature: how much the example's gradient update lands on language-shared middle-layer components versus language-specific top/bottom-layer components. Consequently, curating a source-language training set toward high-shared-recruitment examples yields larger cross-lingual gains than random or size-matched training, at no extra data cost.
Related Work: Prior work shows reasoning/skill transfers cross-lingually far better than knowledge (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024), that skill vs. language capabilities occupy separable, largely non-overlapping parameters (Layer Swapping 2024; Unreasonable Effectiveness of Model Merging 2025), that middle-layer representation alignment aids transfer (Middle-Layer Alignment 2025), that language distance predicts transfer gaps (Language Distance & Transfer 2023), and that circuit-targeted fine-tuning of task heads improves low-resource adaptation (CT-SFT 2026). All of these operate at the granularity of whole tasks, whole layers, or whole models, and treat transferability as a property of a *task* or a *language pair*. None treats transferability as a *per-example* property of the source-language training data, none provides an intrinsic pre-transfer predictor computable from the fine-tuning gradient itself, and none uses such a predictor to *curate* the source-language set for maximal transfer. We uniquely reframe cross-lingual transfer as a data-attribution problem at example granularity and deliver a cheap, actionable transfer-predictive signature.
Abstract: It is well established that skills fine-tuned in one language often transfer to others, while knowledge does not, and that skill and language capabilities live in separable parts of a language model. But transfer is measured coarsely, at the level of whole tasks. We ask a finer, actionable question: within a single fine-tuning task, do individual training examples differ in how much they transfer cross-lingually, and can we predict which ones will before running any transfer? We hypothesize that an example's transferability is governed by *where its gradient update lands*: examples whose learning signal is carried predominantly by language-shared middle-layer components transfer broadly, whereas examples whose signal recruits language-specific top/bottom-layer components stay language-locked. We define a per-example Shared-Recruitment Signature, the fraction of the example's fine-tuning gradient norm (or update magnitude) falling on empirically-identified language-agnostic middle layers versus language-anchored peripheral layers, computable in a single source-language pass. We validate on multilingual reasoning (MGSM-style math, XCOPA, logical/arithmetic templates) by fine-tuning Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B on a source language and measuring per-example contribution to target-language gains via influence-style ablations. We predict (1) the signature correlates strongly with realized cross-lingual transfer per example, (2) the correlation strengthens for typologically distant targets where language-specific recruitment matters most, and (3) curating the source set toward high-signature examples beats random and size-matched baselines on target-language accuracy. The result turns cross-lingual transfer into a predictable, curatable property of training data.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across experiments). Tasks: multilingual math word problems (MGSM, existing; 250 parallel problems each in the target languages) with an English GSM8K training pool (existing; 8.5k problems) subsampled to 2,000 for tractable per-example influence estimation. Targets: 10 languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B; fine-tuned on English (source) with LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32, LR 2e-4, 3 epochs) -- base weights frozen, adapters trainable -- plus a full-fine-tuning replicate (LR 1e-5) as a robustness check; 3 seeds (0,1,2), temperature 0 at eval.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- examples vary in cross-lingual transferability): tests whether per-example transferability is a real, continuous, non-degenerate quantity rather than uniform across examples. Data/model as Setup. Method: estimate each training example's contribution to target-language accuracy via TracIn-style gradient influence, verified on a 100-example subset by leave-one-group-out retraining. Decisive metric: the Spearman correlation between TracIn influence and retraining-verified influence on the subset, together with the ratio of top-quartile to bottom-quartile realized per-example transfer. Convincing result: verified-vs-TracIn Spearman >=0.5 AND top-quartile examples carry >=2x the mean per-example transfer of the bottom quartile. Indecision band: Spearman 0.3-0.5 = influence usable but noisy (downstream claims reported with that caveat); <0.3 = ground truth unreliable, blocking the causal and curation claims. Negative result (flat influence distribution, top approximately equal to bottom quartile) means transferability is not an example-level property, refuting the premise.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the Shared-Recruitment Signature predicts transfer): the core predictive test. Prerequisite within this experiment: identify each model's language-shared vs language-specific layers by (a) layer-wise cross-lingual representation-retrieval alignment and (b) language-ID linear probes, assigning each layer a sharedness weight (middle layers expected shared, top/bottom language-specific). Then compute, for each English training example, the Shared-Recruitment Signature = (gradient/update magnitude on shared middle layers) / (total gradient magnitude), from a single fine-tuning pass; also a sharedness-weighted variant. Data/model as Exp. 1. Systems compared: signature vs realized per-example cross-lingual transfer (Exp. 1 ground truth), and -- critically -- signature vs realized in-language (English) gain, to show it predicts cross-lingual transfer specifically, not generic usefulness. Decisive metric: Spearman(signature, cross-lingual transfer). Convincing result: Spearman >=0.4 for cross-lingual transfer AND at least 0.15 higher than Spearman(signature, in-language gain). Indecision band: 0.2-0.4 = weak predictor (reported as partial); <0.2 = the signature does not predict transfer, refuting H2. If it predicts in-language gain as strongly as cross-lingual transfer (difference <0.15), it is a generic-usefulness proxy, a partial refutation. Negative result refutes the predictability claim.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- causal dependence on the shared components): tests that high-signature examples transfer BECAUSE of their shared middle-layer update, not incidentally. Data: high- vs low-signature examples matched on in-language (English) gain (from Exps. 1-2). Model as Setup. Method: ablate (zero/freeze) the middle-layer portion of each example's update and re-measure its cross-lingual transfer. Decisive metric: transfer drop under middle-layer ablation, contrasted across the matched groups. Convincing result: high-signature examples lose >=50% of their cross-lingual transfer under ablation while matched low-signature examples lose <=20% (the interaction is the evidence). Indecision band: high-signature drop 25-50% = partial mechanistic support; <25% = the middle-layer components are not causally responsible, demoting the signature to a correlate. Negative result refutes the mechanistic reading of H2 while leaving the predictive claim (Exp. 2) intact.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- curation beats baselines at fixed data cost): tests that curating toward high-signature examples improves transfer without extra data. Data: rank the 2,000-example English pool by signature. Model: fine-tune (same config, 3 seeds) on the top-k high-signature subset, a random size-matched subset, the bottom-k, and the full pool. Systems compared: these four. Decisive metric: target-language accuracy averaged over the 10 languages (source-language retention reported for specificity), plotted as a full k-vs-accuracy curve. Convincing result: top-k beats random size-matched by >=2 accuracy points and beats bottom-k by >=4 points at the same k, with source-language accuracy dropping <=1 point. Indecision band: 0.5-2 point gain over random = marginal (report the whole curve); <0.5 point = no practical benefit, refuting H3. Negative result (random >= top-k) refutes the actionable claim even if the predictor correlates.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Ground-truth per-example transferability is expensive; retraining ablations may be noisy, so we rely on validated gradient-influence approximations (TracIn) and confirm on a small retraining-verified subset. 2. Gradient magnitude on a layer may not equal functional contribution to transfer; Exp. 3 (causal middle-layer ablation) is required to promote correlation to a functional claim. 3. The shared/specific layer split may not be crisp for all models; we validate it per model before computing signatures and report robustness. 4. The signature may merely track example difficulty or generic usefulness rather than cross-lingual transfer specifically; controlling against in-language gain (Exp. 2) and matched-difficulty ablations (Exp. 3) isolates the cross-lingual component. 5. Effects may be small for very close languages where almost everything transfers; the inclusion of typologically distant target languages addresses power. 6. Curation gains could be modest if high-signature examples are rare; we report the full ranking curve. 7. Findings may be model- or task-specific; three model families and four task types (spanning knowledge-free to knowledge-heavy) address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) per-example cross-lingual transfer varies within a source-language fine-tuning set; (2) that transfer is predictable from an intrinsic gradient-based layer-landing signature; (3) high-shared-middle-layer examples can be used to curate data for better transfer. The closest prior work family is Blevins et al. 2023 on TracIn-based multilingual data influence, plus language-pair gradient similarity and middle-layer alignment work. The real delta is moving from post hoc example influence / task-level transfer to a pre-transfer, example-level predictor and a curation rule. That is a meaningful reframing, but it is still close to existing gradient-attribution and layer-localization ideas, so the novelty is moderate rather than strong.
revision_notes: State explicitly that the contribution is not just TracIn attribution, but a new layer-aware predictor computed before target-language evaluation, and separate this from the curation result.
Add a sharper novelty claim about what is newly discovered: e.g., that example-level transferability is structured by shared-vs-specific layer recruitment, not merely that influential examples exist.
Position against Blevins 2023 more precisely: specify why their retrieval/analysis cannot already recover the proposed signature and what information your signature adds.
If possible, add a new dataset or benchmark protocol for per-example cross-lingual transfer prediction to strengthen novelty beyond a recombination of known tools.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether source-language examples differ in how much they teach transferable skill to other languages, and whether we can select training data that improves multilingual transfer without extra data. This matters to multilingual LLM builders and data-curation researchers, and if true it could change dataset selection practice. The 'so what?' is real: better cross-lingual transfer at fixed budget. But it is still fairly niche, tied to multilingual fine-tuning and probably strongest for low-resource adaptation. It is more likely to be cited as a useful empirical result than to shift the field broadly unless the effect is large and robust across tasks/models.
revision_notes: Broaden the stated downstream relevance beyond multilingual LLMs: explain how the result informs data selection for any transfer setting with shared vs task-specific features.
Add an explicit practitioner-facing use case: reduce annotation cost for low-resource language adaptation, or improve target-language performance under fixed compute/data budgets.
Quantify the expected magnitude of benefit in a realistic deployment scenario, not just accuracy points, to make the practical payoff legible.
Include an argument for why the result would change data curation policy, not just add an interesting analysis.

review.reasoning: The proposal is testable and has a reasonably clear hypothesis, but there are logical and methodological gaps. The main issue is that the proposed signature may collapse to generic example usefulness, gradient norm, or difficulty rather than cross-lingual transfer specifically; the controls help, but the causal story is still not fully pinned down. Related work is decent but not yet specific enough to prove the gap over prior per-example TracIn multilingual influence work. The experiments are concrete and mostly feasible, though per-example retraining/influence across multiple models and languages may be noisy and expensive. Stronger controls are needed to justify that the signature is truly pre-transfer, layer-specific, and causally linked to transfer rather than a correlated proxy. If executed well, this could be a solid workshop/conference paper, but it needs tighter scope and cleaner identification.

Name: language_refusal_threshold
Title: The Cheapest Jailbreak Is a Translation: A Causal Account of the Query-Language Refusal Threshold in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Aligned multilingual LLMs carry a single, largely content-agnostic 'refusal threshold' scalar whose default value is covertly set by the query language: for borderline-harmful requests, the model refuses in high-alignment-coverage languages but complies with the identical request in low-coverage languages. We hypothesize (a) a shared, language-agnostic harm/permissibility representation exists that is separable from a language-set threshold that gates refusal; (b) cross-lingual refusal inconsistency is driven by a per-language threshold shift, NOT by the model computing a genuinely different harm assessment; and (c) the threshold shift scales with the language's safety-alignment coverage (a resource/RLHF-coverage proxy) rather than with typological distance, and can be causally moved by steering a single recovered 'refusal-threshold direction'.
Related Work: Multilingual moral-reasoning work shows judgments differ across languages (One Model Many Morals 2025; Untangling Input from Reasoning Language 2026; Do Moral Judgment Capabilities Change with Language 2024) but is purely behavioral and treats disagreement as genuine cultural variation. Value/culture-neuron work localizes value or cultural representations (ValueExploration 2025; Culturescope 2025; Isolating Culture Neurons 2025) but studies value alignment, not a scalar refusal gate, and does not connect to safety/jailbreaks. Low-resource-language jailbreak work (e.g. translation-based attacks on GPT-4) demonstrates the vulnerability behaviorally but offers NO mechanistic account of why it happens. Refusal-direction interpretability (Arditi et al. 2024, 'refusal is mediated by a single direction') is monolingual/English and never asks whether the refusal direction's activation baseline is language-conditioned. Our contribution is to (i) reframe cross-lingual moral inconsistency and low-resource jailbreaks as a SINGLE phenomenon—a language-set refusal threshold—rather than genuine moral difference; (ii) causally dissociate a shared harm-assessment representation from a language-conditioned threshold; and (iii) show the threshold, not the harm computation, drives the safety gap, dissociating it from typological distance and providing a steering fix.
Abstract: Aligned language models refuse harmful requests, but the same model asked the identical borderline-harmful question in a low-resource language often complies. This is usually attributed either to genuine cross-cultural moral difference or, in the jailbreak literature, treated as an unexplained behavioral vulnerability. We propose a unifying mechanistic account: multilingual LLMs compute a largely shared, language-agnostic assessment of a request's harmfulness, but gate refusal through a scalar threshold whose default value is covertly set by the query language. Under this view, cross-lingual refusal inconsistency arises not because the model judges the request as less harmful in another language, but because the language shifts the refusal threshold, so a fixed harm level crosses the gate in one language and not another. We build BORDERLINE-MULTI, a set of graded borderline-harmful requests (spanning safety-relevant domains such as cyber, chemical/biological info-hazards, and self-harm advice) rendered across 15+ languages spanning several scripts, families, and safety-alignment-coverage levels. Behaviorally we measure per-language refusal rates and dose-response over a harm-severity gradient. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared harm-assessment direction that is decodable and cross-lingually transferable even in languages where the model complies; (ii) use activation patching to test whether the harm assessment is the same across languages while a separable threshold differs; and (iii) recover a single refusal-threshold direction and steer it to raise refusal in leaky languages and lower it in strict ones. We predict the threshold shift tracks safety-alignment coverage, not typological distance, and that steering closes the cross-lingual safety gap without harming benign-request compliance. Experiments span Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Dataset BORDERLINE-MULTI (constructed from existing public red-team resources): 150 base harmful intents drawn from AdvBench/HarmBench (existing), each templated at 4 severity levels (clearly benign -> mildly sensitive -> clearly disallowed) = 600 graded items, plus 250 matched clearly-benign controls from XSTest (existing). Rendered in 15 languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari, 4+ families, and a spread of safety-alignment-coverage levels (machine translation + native-speaker validation). Per-language safety-alignment-coverage proxy = benign-refusal false-positive rate on the XSTest controls, pretraining resource share, and an alignment-data-availability estimate. Models: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B-Instruct, frozen, temperature 0, 3 paraphrase seeds. Refusal vs compliance scored by a validated multilingual refusal classifier with human spot-checks on 5% of outputs. Dual-use note: only borderline items already in public benchmarks are used, completions are kept coarse (refuse-vs-comply plus short text), and no novel operational harmful content is released.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- the cross-lingual refusal gap and its crossover shift exist): tests that identical borderline items receive different refusal decisions by language, quantified as a threshold-like crossover shift. Data/model as Setup. Decisive metric: cross-language refusal-rate gap on identical disallowed items, and each language's crossover severity (the severity level at which the model flips to refusing). Convincing result: max cross-language refusal gap on identical disallowed items >=20 pp AND a crossover shift of >=1 severity level between the highest- and lowest-coverage languages, while benign controls agree across languages (gap <=5 pp). Indecision band: an 8-20 pp gap = weak effect (reported as such); <8 pp = no exploitable gap, undercutting the whole account. Negative result (uniform refusal across languages) refutes the phenomenon.

Experiment 2 (H3 -- the shift tracks coverage, not typology): tests whether the per-language threshold shift is explained by safety-alignment coverage rather than typological distance. Data/model as Setup. Predictors: the safety-alignment-coverage proxy vs lang2vec typological+script distance to the dominant language. Decisive metric: Spearman(crossover-shift, coverage) vs Spearman(crossover-shift, typological distance), with bootstrap CIs; key contrast = a typologically distant but well-aligned language vs a close but poorly-aligned one. Convincing result: |Spearman with coverage| >=0.5 and exceeds |Spearman with typology| by >=0.2, with the key-contrast pair ordered by coverage not distance. Indecision band: the two correlations within 0.05-0.2 of each other = mixed account; coverage not stronger, or gap <0.05 = H3's coverage claim refuted. Negative result reassigns the effect to typology.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- a shared harm-assessment representation, separable from the gate): tests that harm/permissibility is decodable and cross-lingually transferable even where the model complies. Data: the 600 graded items across languages. Model: hidden states at each layer, weights frozen. Method: train a linear probe / logit-lens to decode graded harm severity from hidden states on held-out dominant-language items; test transfer to low-coverage languages, INCLUDING items the model complies with; compare decoded harm level to true severity regardless of the refusal outcome. Decisive metric: cross-lingual harm-probe transfer accuracy (dominant -> low-coverage). Convincing result: transfer accuracy within 10 pp of in-language probe accuracy AND decoded harm on complied-with low-coverage items still correlates with true severity at Spearman >=0.6 -- the model represents the harm even when it does not refuse. Indecision band: transfer 10-25 pp below in-language = partially shared; >25 pp below = harm is not shared, favoring genuine reassessment and refuting H1. Negative result means harm is recomputed per language.

Experiment 4 (H2 -- harm same, threshold differs, causal): tests that the refusal difference is a threshold shift, not a different harm computation. Data: identical borderline items refused in language A and complied-with in language B. Model: activation patching. Method: (a) patch A's mid-layer harm-assessment representation into the B run and test whether refusal is restored; (b) separately patch A's late-layer language-identity signal into B and test whether that alone flips B to refuse. Decisive metric: causal flip rate (comply -> refuse) under each patch. Convincing result: patching the harm assessment flips <=15% of cases (harm already present in B) while injecting the language/threshold signal flips >=50% -- localizing the gap to the threshold. Indecision band: language-signal flip rate 25-50% = partial localization; harm-patch flip rate 15-30% indicates the assessment also differs somewhat (mixed). If harm-patching flips more than the language signal, H2 is refuted. Negative result discriminates the two accounts directly.

Experiment 5 (H3 -- a single steerable refusal-threshold direction): tests that one recovered direction moves the gate both ways. Data: genuinely harmful items (to raise refusal in leaky languages) and benign controls (to measure over-refusal). Model: recover a refusal-threshold direction as the mean activation difference between refuse and comply runs pooled across languages; steer to (a) RAISE refusal in leaky low-coverage languages and (b) LOWER refusal in strict languages. Systems compared: steering vs translate-to-English-first vs an explicit safety-prompt baseline. Decisive metrics (in order): cross-lingual refusal-gap reduction on held-out harmful items; benign over-refusal rate (specificity); generation fluency (perplexity); generalization to domains held out from direction extraction. Convincing result: steering closes >=50% of the refusal gap on held-out harmful items while adding <=5 pp benign over-refusal and <5% perplexity increase, and generalizes to held-out domains. Indecision band: 25-50% gap closure = partial; <25%, or benign over-refusal >10 pp = the direction is not a clean single gate, refuting the single-direction claim. Negative result (steering fails or destroys benign compliance/fluency) refutes H3's steerability. Attack-success-rate reduction by language on truly-disallowed items is reported as the applied safety framing.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Dual-use hazard: the dataset touches harmful topics; we use only borderline/graded items already present in public red-team benchmarks, keep completions coarse (refuse-vs-comply and short), do not release novel operational harmful content, and follow responsible-disclosure norms since findings expose a jailbreak surface. 2. Probe decodability of harm-assessment may reflect the readout basis, not a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 4) and steering (Exp. 5) are required to promote correlation to mechanism. 3. Some cross-lingual refusal differences may be GENUINE cultural/legal variation rather than a threshold artifact; the shared-harm-probe transfer and the harm-same/threshold-differs patching test are designed precisely to separate genuine reassessment from a pure gate shift, and we restrict to items with cross-culturally stable harm status where possible. 4. The coverage proxy is noisy and coverage may correlate with resource level and typology; the dissociation (Exp. 2) hinges on carefully chosen contrasting languages, and we report multiple proxies and robustness. 5. Strong models may refuse near-uniformly, shrinking the gap; even a small measurable gap on the severity gradient plus the induction (lowering refusal) experiment yields causal evidence, and low-coverage languages plus multiple models give power. 6. Judging refusal vs compliance across languages is nontrivial; we use a validated multilingual refusal classifier plus human spot-checks. 7. Steering may trade safety-gap closure for benign over-refusal; we report the full trade-off curve. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims are: (1) multilingual refusal inconsistency is due to a language-conditioned refusal threshold rather than different harm judgments; (2) that threshold tracks safety-alignment coverage more than typological distance; (3) a single refusal-threshold direction can causally steer behavior; (4) a graded multilingual borderline-harm dataset enables the test. But the provided search summary says very close prior work already shows shared harm representations, late language-specific gating, and causal steering, so the main mechanism is largely preempted. The remaining novelty is mostly in the specific scalar framing, the BORDERLINE-MULTI dataset, and the coverage-vs-typology dissociation, which looks incremental rather than foundational.

Name: metacognition_transfer_gap
Title: Knowing What You Know, In Which Language? A Shared Metacognition Direction Decoupled From Knowledge in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: A multilingual LLM's *metacognition* (its internal, latent estimate of whether its own answer is correct) is carried by a largely language-agnostic direction that is computationally SEPARATE from the underlying factual knowledge, but its READ-OUT is language-specific. Consequently, for a fact the model actually knows, it can nonetheless fail to 'know that it knows' when queried in a low-resource language, and this metacognition-readout failure—not the knowledge itself—drives poor cross-lingual calibration and abstention. Because the metacognition direction is shared, it can be extracted in a high-resource language and transplanted to repair calibration/abstention in a low-resource language WITHOUT transferring the knowledge.
Related Work: Multilingual calibration work shows non-English languages are systematically worse-calibrated and that late-intermediate layers give a better confidence signal (Beyond the Final Layer 2025; MlingConf 2024; Contrastive Cross-Lingual Calibration 2025; On the Calibration of MMLMs 2022; Humans Overrely on Overconfident LMs 2025). Abstention work teaches models to decline via multilingual feedback (Feng et al. 2024) and cross-lingual self-alignment (CALM 2025). Knowledge-consistency work localizes cross-lingual factual inconsistency to a language-transition failure in final layers, distinct from a language-agnostic concept space (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Are Knowledge and Reference Cross-Lingually Consistent 2025), and knowledge-boundary work shows LLMs encode a pre-generation correctness signal in English (C3 2025). ALL of these either (i) measure/repair calibration behaviorally or by ensembling layer read-outs, or (ii) study whether KNOWLEDGE transfers/aligns across languages. NONE dissociates metacognition (the self-correctness estimate) from knowledge as separate representations, tests whether the self-correctness latent is SHARED across languages while its read-out is language-specific, or shows that a metacognition direction extracted in one language causally repairs another language's calibration WITHOUT transferring the fact. We uniquely reframe multilingual reliability failure as a metacognition-readout transfer problem and provide causal (probe-transfer + patching + steering) evidence plus a training-free fix.
Abstract: A trustworthy model must not only know facts but know when it knows them. In multilingual settings the second ability is far less understood than the first. We ask a sharp question: when a multilingual LLM is unreliable in a low-resource language, is it because it lacks the knowledge, or because it has the knowledge but fails to know that it has it? We hypothesize that models carry a largely language-agnostic *metacognition* direction—an internal estimate of whether their own answer is correct—that is computationally separate from the factual knowledge it evaluates, but whose read-out into calibrated confidence and abstention is language-specific. This predicts a striking dissociation: for facts the model demonstrably knows (correct under greedy decoding), it can still fail to internally 'flag' that it knows them when queried in a distant, low-resource language, producing miscalibration and wrong abstention. We test three claims: (1) a linear metacognition probe predicting per-item correctness transfers across languages far better than an accuracy-matched knowledge probe, evidencing a shared self-correctness representation; (2) via activation patching, the metacognition signal and the answer content are separable, and low-resource calibration failures localize to a language-specific read-out step rather than to a missing self-correctness signal; and (3) extracting the metacognition direction in a high-resource language and steering it into a low-resource forward pass repairs calibration and abstention on known facts WITHOUT changing which facts are known, outperforming translate-to-English and layer-ensemble baselines. We predict the read-out gap scales with typological/script distance and resource level. Experiments span mLAMA/BMLAMA factual QA and MMLU-style multiple-choice across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Data: multilingual factual QA (mLAMA + BMLAMA, existing; tens of thousands of (fact, language) cloze items) subsampled to 2,000 facts x 15 languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels, plus a translated multiple-choice knowledge subset (Belebele, existing; 900 items/language, and a translated MMLU subset). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen. For each (fact, language) record greedy correctness and a behavioral confidence (answer-token probability / verbalized confidence). Items are partitioned into KNOWN (greedy-correct) vs UNKNOWN per language. A fixed high-resource language (English) is the anchor.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- the metacognition gap on known facts): tests whether, restricted to facts the model demonstrably knows, calibration/abstention degrades in low-resource languages. Data/model as Setup. Decisive metric: Metacognition Gap = AUROC(confidence vs correctness) in the anchor minus AUROC in the target language, computed on KNOWN facts only (ECE and appropriate-abstention rate also reported). Convincing result: a positive Metacognition Gap >=0.10 AUROC for low-resource/distant languages while greedy accuracy on the shared known-set is held comparable -- the failure is in knowing-that-it-knows, not in knowing. Indecision band: gap 0.03-0.10 AUROC = weak; <0.03 = no metacognition-specific gap, undercutting H2. Negative result (no gap once restricted to known facts) means cross-lingual reliability failures are knowledge failures, refuting the framing.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- metacognition is more shared across languages than knowledge): tests that a self-correctness latent transfers cross-lingually better than a knowledge latent. Data/model as Setup. Method: at each layer train (a) a metacognition probe -- a linear classifier predicting whether THIS item is correct -- and (b) a knowledge probe -- a linear classifier predicting the correct answer content; train each in one language, test cross-lingually. Decisive metric: cross-lingual transfer accuracy of the metacognition probe minus that of the (in-language-accuracy-matched) knowledge probe, at the best layer. Convincing result: metacognition-probe transfer exceeds knowledge-probe transfer by >=10 pp, with cross-language cosine alignment of metacognition directions >=0.6. Indecision band: 3-10 pp = suggestive; <3 pp = metacognition is no more shared than knowledge, refuting H1's language-agnostic-direction claim. Negative result (knowledge transfers as well or better) refutes the separateness/sharedness claim.

Experiment 3 (H1/H2 -- separability and read-out localization, causal): tests that the metacognition signal is separable from answer content and that low-resource calibration fails at a late read-out, not for lack of a mid-layer signal. Data: KNOWN facts well-flagged in an anchor run but poorly-flagged in a low-resource run. Model: activation patching. Method: (a) patch the mid-layer metacognition-carrying representation from the anchor run into the low-resource run and test whether calibrated confidence/abstention improves while the emitted answer is unchanged; (b) compare patching the late-layer language-identity signal vs the mid-layer metacognition direction for which restores calibration. Decisive metrics: low-resource AUROC/ECE improvement; and answer-unchanged rate (specificity). Convincing result: injecting the mid-layer metacognition direction improves low-resource AUROC by >=0.08 while leaving the emitted answer unchanged in >=95% of items -- the self-correctness signal was present but not read out. Indecision band: AUROC gain 0.03-0.08 = partial; <0.03 = not separable/localizable, refuting the read-out account; if patching also changes the emitted answer (>5%), metacognition is entangled with knowledge, weakening H1. Negative result favors a signal-genuinely-absent account.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- training-free repair without transferring knowledge): tests that a metacognition direction extracted in the anchor repairs low-resource calibration/abstention on known facts while leaving which facts are known unchanged. Data: a mixed KNOWN/UNKNOWN low-resource set (so overconfidence on unknowns is penalized). Model: extract the metacognition direction (mean activation difference between correct and incorrect items pooled in the anchor); at inference on low-resource items, steer along it and read confidence from the steered state. Systems compared: steering vs translate-to-English-first vs temperature scaling vs a late-intermediate-layer ensemble confidence read-out. Decisive metrics (in order): abstention F1 on the mixed set; ECE and AUROC improvement; and a specificity check that greedy accuracy (which facts are known) is unchanged (within 1 pp). Convincing result: steering improves abstention F1 by >=0.05 and AUROC by >=0.05 over the best baseline, greedy accuracy unchanged, and false-confidence rate on UNKNOWN items not increased by >3 pp. Indecision band: F1 gain 0.02-0.05 = marginal; <0.02, or greedy accuracy shift >1 pp (knowledge changed) = repair not achieved cleanly, refuting H3. Negative result (no calibration gain, or gain only by altering answers) refutes the transplant claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of a 'metacognition' signal may reflect the read-out basis rather than a functionally used self-estimate; we require the causal patching (Exp. 3) and steering repair (Exp. 4) to promote correlation to mechanism, and the specificity check that emitted answers are unchanged. 2. The metacognition probe could be partly capturing knowledge (harder items are both unknown and low-confidence); we restrict the key transfer and repair analyses to KNOWN facts to isolate self-knowledge from knowledge, and compare against an accuracy-matched knowledge probe. 3. Ground-truth correctness across low-resource languages may be noisy due to translation/answer-matching; we use human-verified benchmark subsets and last-token/answer-span matching, reporting tokenization statistics. 4. Some models may genuinely lack the metacognition signal in low-resource languages (i.e., it is recomputed, not shared), which would refute the transfer hypothesis—this is itself an informative outcome, and the probe-transfer contrast is designed to decide it. 5. The distance-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report multiple resource proxies and robustness. 6. Steering may over-boost confidence and increase overconfidence on truly UNKNOWN items; we evaluate on mixed known/unknown sets and report abstention F1 and false-confidence rate, not just calibration on known facts. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty: (1) multilingual reliability failures can arise from a metacognition-readout failure rather than missing knowledge; (2) the self-correctness/metacognition signal is more language-shared than factual knowledge representations; (3) metacognition and answer content are separable and the failure localizes to a language-specific late read-out; (4) a metacognition direction extracted in a high-resource language can be transplanted/steered to improve low-resource calibration and abstention without changing knowledge; (5) the gap scales with language distance/resource. From the search summary, the broad shared cross-lingual confidence-direction claim is substantially anticipated by Shared Doubt, and monolingual internal-correctness/steering work also reduces novelty of the basic mechanism. The remaining real delta is the explicit dissociation from knowledge, the restriction to known facts, the causal localization of failure to read-out, and the no-knowledge-transfer repair framing. That is non-trivial relative to cited work, but narrower than the proposal presents.
revision_notes: Reframe the main novelty away from 'shared metacognition direction' and toward the stronger residual claim: dissociating metacognition from knowledge on known facts plus causal localization of language-specific read-out failure.
Explicitly discuss Shared Doubt and monolingual confidence-manifold work, stating exactly what they already establish and what this paper newly tests.
Tighten the contribution statement to one or two crisp deltas: read-out failure vs knowledge failure, and repair without fact transfer.
Add a stronger negative-control baseline showing that any transferable intermediate-layer confidence probe is not enough to explain the effect unless it is separable from answer-content knowledge.

impact.reasoning: The problem under study is multilingual unreliability: models may know a fact yet still miscalibrate confidence or abstain poorly in low-resource languages. People who care include trustworthy-ML, multilingual NLP, deployment teams serving non-English users, and hallucination/calibration researchers. If true, the work would shift practice from 'improve multilingual knowledge' toward 'repair confidence read-out,' and offers a training-free intervention path. Strongest case: poor low-resource reliability may stem from a fixable confidence-readout failure rather than missing knowledge. This is an important problem with likely citations and follow-up. The so-what test is passed: either outcome matters—if the effect exists, practitioners can target calibration without retraining knowledge; if not, the field learns that knowledge deficits dominate and confidence-transfer methods are limited.
