Name: language_set_effort_budget
Title: How Hard Is This, in Your Language? Query Language as a Covert Effort-Budget That Mis-Allocates Reasoning Length in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs carry a shared, language-agnostic estimate of a problem's intrinsic difficulty, but they set a reasoning EFFORT BUDGET (how many chain-of-thought steps to spend, when to stop) via a language-conditioned scalar that is only loosely tied to true difficulty. As a result, for a problem of fixed difficulty the model systematically UNDERTHINKS (truncates reasoning too early, giving up) in low-resource / typologically distant languages and can OVERTHINK in others, and this mis-allocation — not a deficit in the underlying reasoning ability — is a major driver of the multilingual reasoning gap. Because the difficulty estimate is shared while the budget is language-set, extracting an effort-budget direction and steering it can re-allocate reasoning length per language and recover accuracy without retraining.
Related Work: Prior work shows an optimal, inverted-U CoT length that scales with difficulty and shrinks with model capability, exposing a simplicity/overthinking bias (When More is Less 2025), and that reasoning is routed through an English-centered latent pathway that is representationally consistent across languages but uneven in strength (Large Reasoning Models Are Not Yet Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026; Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English 2025). Language mixing reflects internal script preferences and constrained decoding helps (Language Mixing in Reasoning Models 2025); ablating language-specific components boosts reasoning (When Less Language is More 2025); attribution over-weights the final CoT step, especially for wrong answers, and structured CoT helps only high-resource languages (What Really Counts 2025). ALL of these study either global CoT length, latent-reasoning consistency, or language-specific component ablation. NONE frames the query language as setting an EFFORT BUDGET (a stopping/length controller) that is decoupled from a shared difficulty estimate, none measures a per-item under/over-thinking gap attributable to language rather than difficulty, and none provides a causal effort-budget direction that re-allocates reasoning length per language. We uniquely recast the multilingual reasoning gap as a language-induced effort-mis-allocation problem with a causal, steerable controller.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs reason far better in high-resource languages, a gap usually attributed to weaker reasoning ability in low-resource languages. We propose a different, testable cause: the query language covertly sets the model's reasoning EFFORT BUDGET — how many chain-of-thought steps it spends and when it decides it is done — and this budget is only loosely coupled to the problem's true difficulty. Under this view, for a problem of fixed difficulty the model underthinks (truncates and gives up early) in low-resource, typologically distant languages and can overthink in others, so much of the multilingual gap reflects mis-allocated effort rather than absent competence. We distinguish two internal quantities: a shared, language-agnostic difficulty estimate and a language-conditioned effort budget that gates stopping. We first show behaviorally that, controlling for true difficulty, CoT length and early-give-up rate vary systematically with the query language and predict accuracy loss. We then probe for a shared difficulty direction that transfers across languages while an effort-budget signal differs, and use activation patching to test that low-resource under-reasoning localizes to a language-set stopping controller rather than a degraded reasoning trajectory. Finally we recover an effort-budget direction and steer it to lengthen reasoning in under-thinking languages and shorten it in over-thinking ones, measuring accuracy recovery, and compare against forced-longer-CoT prompting and translate-to-English baselines. We predict the effort mis-allocation scales with typological/script distance and resource level, and that per-language budget steering closes much of the gap. Experiments span MGSM, XCOPA, and multi-hop QA across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, and a distilled reasoning model.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Data: multilingual math with matched difficulty labels -- MGSM (existing; 250 parallel problems) plus 400 GSM-style items annotated with a minimum required step count -- XCOPA commonsense (existing), and a translated 2-hop QA subset (300 items). All items are PARALLEL translations across 12 languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels, so true difficulty is held constant across languages. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; chain-of-thought elicited at temperature 0, 3 prompt seeds. Reasoning length is measured primarily in parsed STEPS (token counts reported separately) using a validated multilingual step-parser with human spot-checks.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- language-attributable effort mis-allocation): tests that, at fixed true difficulty, reasoning length and early-give-up vary by query language and predict accuracy loss. Data/model as Setup. Per item measure: reasoning length in steps; EARLY-GIVE-UP rate (fewer steps than the annotated minimum, or a hedge/'cannot solve'); accuracy. Decisive metric: the residual reasoning-length variance attributable to LANGUAGE after regressing length on annotated true difficulty (added R^2 from language beyond difficulty), together with the correlation between under-length and wrong answers. Convincing result: language explains an added R^2 >=0.10 beyond difficulty, low-resource/distant languages are systematically shorter than their high-resource parallel run, and under-length predicts errors at Spearman >=0.3. Indecision band: added R^2 of 0.03-0.10 = weak; <0.03 = no language-attributable effort effect, refuting H2. Negative result (length driven only by difficulty) refutes the effort-mis-allocation framing.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- shared difficulty estimate vs language-set budget): tests that difficulty is represented language-agnostically while the realized budget varies by language. Data/model as Setup. Method: at each layer train (i) a difficulty probe predicting the annotated step-count and (ii) a stopping probe predicting whether the model is about to emit the final answer; train in one language, test cross-lingually. Decisive metric: cross-lingual transfer accuracy of the difficulty probe (contrasted with per-language variation in realized length from Exp. 1). Convincing result: difficulty-probe cross-lingual transfer within 10 pp of in-language accuracy (a shared estimate) while realized reasoning length for the same items differs by language. Indecision band: difficulty-probe transfer 10-25 pp below in-language = partially shared; >25 pp below = difficulty is not shared, weakening H1. Negative result (difficulty recomputed per language) undercuts the shared-difficulty / language-set-budget dissociation.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- causal localization to a stopping controller): tests that low-resource under-reasoning is fixed by injecting the high-resource effort/stopping signal, not the difficulty representation. Data: parallel items solved with adequate reasoning in a high-resource language but under-reasoned/wrong in a low-resource one. Model: activation patching. Method: (a) patch the mid-layer difficulty representation from the high-resource run into the low-resource run; (b) patch the late-layer stopping/effort signal. Decisive metric: rate at which reasoning lengthens and the answer becomes correct under each patch. Convincing result: the difficulty-patch restores correctness in <=15% of cases (difficulty already present) while the effort/stopping-patch restores adequate-length reasoning and correctness in >=40% -- localizing the gap to a language-set stopping controller. Indecision band: effort-patch restoration 20-40% = partial; <20% = not a stopping-controller effect, refuting the localization; if the difficulty-patch restores more than the effort-patch, the dissociation is refuted. Negative result favors a genuine competence deficit.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- effort-budget steering recovers accuracy without retraining): tests that steering a recovered effort-budget direction re-allocates length and recovers accuracy. Data: under-thinking (low-resource) and over-thinking items. Model: extract an effort-budget direction as the mean activation difference between long- and short-reasoning (continue-vs-stop) states pooled across languages; steer to LENGTHEN reasoning in under-thinking languages and SHORTEN it in over-thinking ones. Systems compared: steering vs forced-longer-CoT prompting ('think step by step, at least N steps') vs best-of-length voting vs translate-to-English-first. Decisive metrics (in order): accuracy gain on under-thinking languages; change in CoT length and give-up rate; output-language fidelity; fluency (perplexity); and a specificity check that shortening over-thinking items preserves accuracy. Convincing result: steering raises under-thinking-language accuracy by >=4 points over no intervention and matches or beats forced-longer-CoT, without harming output-language fidelity (>=95% correct language) or inflating length on already-adequate items. Indecision band: 1.5-4 point gain = partial; <1.5 = steering does not recover accuracy, refuting H3. Negative result (no gain, or gains only via uncontrolled rambling that hurts other items) refutes the steerable-budget claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Reasoning length is confounded with tokenizer efficiency across scripts (non-Latin scripts use more tokens per step); we measure length in reasoning STEPS (parsed) as the primary unit and report token counts separately, and hold true difficulty fixed via parallel items. 2. Probe decodability of a 'difficulty' or 'effort' signal may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used controller; we require the causal patching (Exp. 3) and steering (Exp. 4) to promote correlation to mechanism. 3. Under-reasoning could genuinely reflect weaker reasoning ability, not mis-allocated effort; the core test is whether injecting the high-resource EFFORT signal (not the reasoning content) restores correctness, and whether steering to lengthen reasoning recovers accuracy — distinguishing effort mis-allocation from competence deficit. 4. Steering to lengthen reasoning may induce rambling/overthinking that hurts accuracy (given the inverted-U); we tune dose and report the length-accuracy trade-off curve and specificity controls. 5. Parsing reasoning steps and detecting give-up across languages is noisy; we use a validated multilingual step-parser plus human spot-checks and native-speaker validation of translated items. 6. Strong models may already allocate effort well, shrinking the effect; the low-resource languages, harder items, and the reasoning-distilled model (which language-mixes more) provide power, and even documenting the effect on a subset is informative. 7. Findings may be model-specific; four models across families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that would need to be novel are: (1) for fixed problem difficulty, query language systematically changes reasoning effort allocation and stopping behavior; (2) multilingual LLMs contain a shared language-agnostic difficulty estimate separable from a language-conditioned effort-budget/stopping signal; (3) a substantial part of the multilingual reasoning gap is due to under/over-thinking rather than missing reasoning competence; (4) this budget can be causally localized and manipulated through activation patching/steering; (5) per-language steering can recover accuracy without retraining. Relative to prior work, the ingredients are not new individually: optimal CoT length/overthinking, multilingual latent reasoning, English-pivot explanations, and stopping control all already exist. The actual delta is the mechanistic dissociation between shared difficulty and language-set stopping budget, measured per item under controlled parallel translations, plus a causal steering intervention. That is meaningfully distinct from obvious baselines and more than just 'test overthinking in multilingual settings,' though it is still adjacent to current threads and could collapse into a weaker 'language affects inference efficiency' story if evidence is not sharp.
revision_notes: State the 1-sentence novelty claim against the closest baseline explicitly: not just multilingual overthinking, but a separable shared-difficulty vs language-budget mechanism with causal steering.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is the multilingual reasoning gap in LLMs: why the same model solves the same problem better in some languages than others. Stakeholders include multilingual LLM researchers, test-time compute/efficient reasoning researchers, interpretability researchers, and practitioners deploying global assistants. The strongest one-line case is: if multilingual gaps are partly effort-allocation failures rather than missing competence, accuracy can be recovered cheaply at inference time without retraining or translation. This is an important problem, timely, and likely citable because it connects multilinguality, reasoning, and controllable test-time compute. If true, it could shift the field away from treating non-English deficits as purely comprehension/training deficits. Real-world reach is plausible for deployment in low-resource languages. The main limiter is that impact depends heavily on whether the effect size is large and general beyond small benchmark settings; if the result is weak, the practical consequences narrow quickly.

review.reasoning: The proposal is ambitious and testable, but there are notable technical and narrative gaps. The core hypothesis is reasonably falsifiable, yet key constructs are underspecified: 'true difficulty,' 'effort budget,' 'early give-up,' and 'shared difficulty estimate' may be hard to operationalize cleanly. Annotated minimum step count is an imperfect proxy for intrinsic difficulty, especially across tasks like XCOPA and QA where solution length need not equal difficulty. The probe story risks over-interpretation, and activation patching between languages may be difficult to align causally rather than representationally. Strong competing explanations remain, especially language comprehension, translation quality, prompt-format differences, and parser artifacts across scripts. The experiments are specific and mostly feasible, but the claimed decisive thresholds feel arbitrary, the dataset scale is modest, and controls are missing for answer length priors, verbosity style, and forced equal-comprehension conditions. As written, the work could be strong for a serious ML venue if executed exceptionally well, but only if the authors sharpen identification and add more decisive controls against comprehension and tokenization confounds.

Name: in_context_language_integration
Title: Surface Trick or Real Integration? Whether In-Context Acquired Languages Enter the Shared Concept Space of LLMs, and Why Grammar Rules Fail
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM 'learns' an unseen language on the fly from an in-context grammar book plus dictionary/parallel examples, dictionary-driven word translation is routed through the model's language-agnostic shared concept space (recruiting the same concept-induction machinery as pretrained languages), whereas declarative grammar-rule application is NOT: the retrieved rule sits inertly in context and never causally shapes the concept-space computation. Consequently, the well-documented behavioral failure of grammar explanations (vs. parallel examples) is mechanistically an integration/binding failure, not a retrieval failure, and it worsens with the typological distance between the unseen language's grammar and the model's dominant languages.
Related Work: The MTOB line established behaviorally that LLMs can translate unseen languages from an in-context grammar book (Tanzer et al. 2024), but that nearly all gains come from parallel examples rather than grammatical explanations (Aycock et al. 2024), that rule retrieval and complex-rule application are the bottlenecks (ZhuangRules 2025; DiPMT++ 2024; LINGOLLM 2024), and that enciphered-language controls isolate genuine in-context learning (Manchu 2025). Separately, interpretability work shows pretrained languages share a language-agnostic concept space (Semantic Hub 2024), that concept-induction heads carry language-independent word meanings and mediate translation while token-induction heads copy verbatim (Dual-Route Induction 2025), that an in-context 'task recognition' point exists in middle layers (Where does In-context Translation Happen 2024), and that low-resource outputs degrade at lossy final-layer translation features (MALT 2025). ALL grammar-book work is behavioral; ALL concept-space/induction work studies PRETRAINED languages. None asks whether an unseen, in-context-acquired language is integrated into the shared concept space, whether its word-translation reuses concept-induction heads while its grammar-rule application does not, or locates WHERE grammar-rule application fails internally. We uniquely give the first mechanistic account of on-the-fly language acquisition, reframing the grammar-vs-examples asymmetry as a shared-concept-space integration/binding failure with a causal test and a targeted intervention.
Abstract: Large language models can be taught an unseen language on the fly by placing a grammar book, dictionary, and a few parallel sentences in their context. Yet a striking behavioral regularity has emerged: models exploit the dictionary and parallel examples but seem unable to make use of the declarative grammar explanations. We ask why, mechanistically. We hypothesize that on-the-fly language acquisition is not uniform: dictionary-driven word translation is routed through the model's pre-existing language-agnostic concept space (reusing the concept-induction machinery that mediates translation among pretrained languages), whereas grammar-rule application never enters that space, so a retrieved rule remains inert context text rather than a computation that reshapes the internal representation. Under this view the grammar-vs-examples asymmetry is an integration/binding failure, not a retrieval failure. We test three claims. First, using enciphered and genuinely unseen languages (Kalamang, Zhuang, enciphered Manchu) to remove pretrained knowledge, we show that unseen-language word representations become linearly aligned with the shared concept space and that ablating concept-induction heads collapses in-context word translation, evidencing real integration for lexical items. Second, via activation patching we show that correctly applying a provided grammar rule (agreement, word order, case) causally depends on mid-layer concept-space components, and that failures occur when the unseen sentence bypasses these components and is instead copied verbatim by token-induction heads. Third, we predict integration strength for both lexis and grammar declines with the typological distance between the unseen language and the model's dominant languages, and that a training-free intervention that boosts routing through the concept space at rule-application positions improves grammar-rule accuracy. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Three language regimes isolate genuine in-context acquisition: (a) truly unseen endangered languages with public resources -- Kalamang via MTOB (existing grammar book + word list + ~400-sentence parallel corpus) and Zhuang via DiPMT++ (existing dictionary + rules); (b) an ENCIPHERED pretrained language (a systematic substitution cipher applied to a known language, so parametric knowledge is removed but ground truth is exact; constructed); (c) a pretrained low-resource language as an already-integrated upper-bound control. Each prompt provides dictionary + grammar-rule snippets + k parallel examples in context. ~300 test words per regime (all available items used). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen. The concept-induction vs token-induction head split is validated per model before use (degree of separation reported).

Experiment 1 (H1 -- in-context word translation is integrated into the shared concept space): tests that dictionary-driven lexical translation of an unseen language reuses the concept-induction machinery that mediates translation among pretrained languages. Data/model as Setup. Method: (a) train a linear map from a pretrained-language shared-concept probe and test whether unseen-language word representations at concept-induction-head output positions align with the shared concept direction (cross-lingual decodability of the intended concept); (b) causally ablate the concept-induction heads (identified via the dual-route method) and measure the drop in in-context word translation, vs ablating the token-induction heads. Decisive metric: drop in word-translation accuracy (chrF and exact-match) under concept-induction-head ablation. Convincing result: unseen-word concept-space decodability is well above chance and within 15 pp of the pretrained control, AND concept-induction-head ablation drops word-translation accuracy by >=40% while token-induction ablation instead produces verbatim-copy errors -- concept-mediated lexical integration. Indecision band: concept-ablation drop 15-40% = partial integration; <15% = word translation is not concept-mediated, refuting H1. Negative result (no concept-space alignment, ablation no effect) means in-context lexis is handled by surface copying, refuting H1.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- grammar-rule application is not routed through the concept space): tests that applying a provided grammar rule does not causally recruit the concept-space components, and that failures coincide with verbatim token-induction copying. Data: ZhuangRules-style modular grammar minimal pairs (agreement, word order, case) constructed so the provided rule -- not lexical guessing -- determines the correct output; ~200 items per rule type, linguist/native-materials validated; same regimes and models as Exp. 1. Method: (a) replicate the behavioral asymmetry (word-translation vs per-rule application accuracy with the rule in context); (b) core causal test -- run a CORRECT-rule context vs an INCORRECT/absent-rule context and activation-patch mid-layer concept-space components between them, identifying the minimal set whose patching flips rule-correct vs rule-violating output; (c) measure per item the fraction of the unseen sentence processed by concept- vs token-induction heads. Decisive metric: the flip rate when patching concept-space components, and whether grammar FAILURES show higher token-induction (copy) reliance than successes. Convincing result: grammar-rule accuracy is far below word-translation accuracy (>=25 pp gap), patching concept-space components flips rule-correctness in <=15% of items (rule application does not depend on them), and failures show >=20 pp higher token-induction reliance than successes. Indecision band: concept-space patch flip rate 15-35% = grammar is partially concept-mediated (weakens the clean dissociation); >35% flip = grammar IS routed through the concept space, refuting H2. Negative result (grammar depends on concept-space components just as lexis does) refutes H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- a binding failure, not a retrieval failure, worsening with typological distance): tests that the grammar-vs-examples asymmetry is an integration/binding failure and scales with grammatical distance. Data: the Exp. 2 grammar items across all regimes, plus a rule-RETRIEVAL check (ask the model to restate/quote the applicable rule). Model: as above, plus a targeted intervention that upweights routing through the concept-space direction (or amplifies concept-induction-head contribution) at rule-application token positions. Systems compared for the intervention: concept-routing steer vs (i) an extra parallel example, (ii) code-augmented rule prompting (the ZhuangRules baseline), (iii) no intervention. Decisive metrics (in order): (1) retrieval-vs-application dissociation = rule-restatement accuracy minus rule-application accuracy (a large positive value means the rule is retrievable but not applied = a binding failure); (2) Spearman between grammar-rule accuracy and lang2vec typological/word-order distance from the model's dominant languages, contrasted with the same for lexical accuracy; (3) grammar-rule accuracy gain from the concept-routing intervention, with specificity that word-translation accuracy and fluency are unchanged. Convincing result: models restate rules they cannot apply (restatement minus application >=20 pp -- not a retrieval failure); grammar accuracy falls with typological distance faster than lexical accuracy (grammar Spearman more negative by >=0.2); and boosting concept-space routing raises grammar-rule accuracy by >=8 points without harming lexis/fluency. Indecision band: restatement-minus-application gap 8-20 pp = mixed retrieval/binding; intervention gain 3-8 points = partial; below these thresholds H3 is unsupported. Negative result (rules not retrievable, or intervention no effect, or grammar no more distance-sensitive than lexis) refutes the binding-failure/distance account.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe alignment of unseen-language tokens to the concept space may reflect the readout basis rather than functional integration; the head-ablation (Exp. 1) and patching (Exp. 2) causal tests are required to promote correlation to mechanism. 2. Enciphered languages test in-context lexical mapping cleanly but may not fully mimic novel grammar; we therefore also use genuinely unseen languages (Kalamang, Zhuang) and report both. 3. The clean concept-vs-token induction dichotomy from prior work may be fuzzier for unseen languages, weakening the failure-signature story; we validate the head split per model before use and report degree of separation honestly. 4. Grammar-rule items require careful construction so the rule (not lexical guessing) determines the answer; we use modular ZhuangRules-style minimal pairs validated by linguists/native materials. 5. It is possible models DO integrate grammar for simple rules and only fail on complex ones (consistent with ZhuangRules); this is an informative graded outcome and we stratify by rule complexity. 6. Tokenization of unseen scripts/orthographies is uneven; we use last-token/pooled representations and report tokenization statistics. 7. The intervention may trade grammar gains for fluency or lexical accuracy; we report the full trade-off and specificity. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families and three language regimes address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that need to be novel: (1) unseen in-context-acquired lexical items become integrated into an LLM's shared language-agnostic concept space; (2) declarative grammar rules do not enter that same computation, so grammar failure is a binding/integration failure rather than retrieval failure; (3) concept-induction vs token-induction circuitry identified in pretrained-language translation extends to unseen-language in-context learning; (4) typological distance selectively worsens grammar integration more than lexical integration; (5) a routing intervention can improve rule application. Relative to the cited work and search summary, the closest prior families are behavioral grammar-book translation benchmarks and mechanistic dual-route/shared-concept-space studies on pretrained languages. The actual delta is the bridge between them: a mechanistic account of why grammar-book prompting fails in unseen-language acquisition, with causal localization and intervention. That is a real and non-trivial contribution. The main novelty risk is that some pieces are extensions of existing interpretability tools into a new setting rather than wholly new mechanisms, and the intervention idea is only moderately differentiated unless sharply specified.

Name: kinship_granularity_collapse
Title: Uncle or Mother's-Younger-Brother? How the Query Language's Kinship System Sets the Granularity of Relational Reasoning in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs build a largely language-agnostic genealogical-tree representation of a family, but the SPECIFIC kin category they output is resolved through a granularity setting covertly fixed by the query language's kinship system. For a fixed genealogical fact, the model tends to collapse to the (usually coarser, English-like) kin distinctions of its dominant language, systematically failing to produce the finer distinctions (maternal vs paternal side, relative age, gender) that a target language grammaticalizes. This 'granularity collapse' is a category-resolution failure downstream of a correctly-computed genealogical tree, it scales with the kinship-typology distance between the query language and the dominant language (not with resource level), and it is carried by a locatable, steerable granularity signal separable from the tree representation.
Related Work: Anthropology provides authoritative resources: Kinbank (210,903 kinterms, 1,229 languages, 2023) and typologies of kinship systems (Eskimo/Sudanese/Hawaiian; classificatory vs descriptive; bifurcate-merging), plus efficient-communication accounts of which semantic features (side, generation, relative age, gender) each system encodes (2025). Cross-linguistic semantic-alignment work (Thompson et al. 2018) finds kinship is highly aligned yet structurally divergent across languages. On the model side, LLMs are shown to encode genealogical relations in a tree-like, causally-relevant subspace (Investigating Representation Universality, 2024), to decode relations via linear relational embeddings (Hernandez et al. 2023; LRC 2023; Locating Relational Concepts 2024), and to share grammatical/semantic concept directions across languages (Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025; Semantic Hub 2024). Crucially, ALL genealogical/relational interpretability work is monolingual and treats kin categories as fixed, and ALL kinship-typology work is anthropological/behavioral with no mechanistic account inside an LLM. None asks whether the query language covertly sets the GRANULARITY at which a correctly-represented genealogical tree is read out into kin terms, nor gives a causal, steerable granularity mechanism. We uniquely port kinship-system typology into multilingual mechanistic interpretability, dissociating a shared tree from a language-set category-resolution step, and provide a causal fix.
Abstract: Languages carve the family tree very differently: English lumps father's and mother's brother into one 'uncle', while Chinese, Turkish, Hindi and many others obligatorily distinguish the paternal from the maternal side, elder from younger sibling, or the gender of the linking relative. A competent multilingual model must recover the same underlying genealogy but then name relatives at whatever granularity the target language demands. We investigate whether multilingual LLMs instead default to the coarser kin categories of their dominant language. We hypothesize that models compute a largely language-agnostic genealogical-tree representation, but resolve it into kin terms through a granularity setting covertly fixed by the query language, causing systematic 'granularity collapse': for a fixed genealogical fact, the model omits the finer side/age/gender distinctions a target language grammaticalizes and produces an over-general, English-like term. We build KIN-RESOLVE, controlled genealogy-description-plus-question items whose correct kin term differs across kinship systems, rendered across 12+ languages spanning Eskimo, Sudanese, bifurcate-merging and other typologies, using Kinbank ground-truth terms. Behaviorally we measure per-language granularity-collapse rate and dissociate it from resource level via kinship-typology distance. Mechanistically we probe for a shared genealogical-tree subspace that transfers across languages, use activation patching to show the tree is correctly computed even when the term is wrong (localizing failure to a late category-resolution step), and recover a granularity direction that we steer to repair or induce collapse without altering the underlying genealogy. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Dataset KIN-RESOLVE (constructed from Kinbank, existing; 210,903 kinterms over 1,229 languages): 400 short genealogy descriptions (e.g. 'A is B's father; C is A's younger brother; ...') each paired with a question whose CORRECT kin term differs across kinship systems (e.g. 'uncle' in English but requiring maternal/paternal+age marking elsewhere). Rendered in 12 languages spanning kinship typologies -- Eskimo (English, Spanish), descriptive/Sudanese (Chinese, Turkish, Hindi, Arabic), bifurcate-merging/classificatory (a Bantu and a Dravidian language), relative-age (Japanese, Korean). Each item is annotated with the target-language correct term and the features it must encode (side, generation, relative age, gender), and a per-language kinship-typology distance to the dominant (English) system is built from the encoded-feature set. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen, greedy, 3 paraphrase seeds.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- behavioral granularity collapse): tests that, for a fixed genealogy, the model omits the finer side/age/gender distinctions the target language grammaticalizes and defaults to the coarser dominant-language category. Data/model as Setup. Score genealogical correctness (is the underlying relation right, ignoring granularity) and term correctness (does the term carry all required features) separately. Decisive metric: GRANULARITY-COLLAPSE RATE = fraction of genealogically-correct answers whose term is under-specified relative to the target-language requirement, especially collapsing to the dominant-language category. Systems compared: query in target language vs query in English (coarse upper bound) vs translate-to-English-first. Convincing result: for fine-distinguishing languages, collapse rate >=25% among genealogically-correct answers, markedly higher than for Eskimo-type languages that do not require the distinction. Indecision band: 10-25% = weak/partial collapse; <10% = the model resolves fine terms faithfully, refuting H2. Negative result (no under-specification once the genealogy is right) refutes granularity collapse.

Experiment 2 (H3 -- collapse tracks kinship typology, not resource): tests that collapse is explained by kinship-system distance rather than resource level. Data/model as Setup. Predictors: per-language kinship-typology distance to English vs a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / general benchmark accuracy). Decisive metric: Spearman(collapse rate, typology distance) vs Spearman(collapse rate, resource proxy), bootstrap CIs; key contrast = a lower-resource fine-distinguishing language (e.g. the Dravidian one) vs a higher-resource coarse one. Convincing result: |Spearman with typology| >=0.5 and exceeds |Spearman with resource| by >=0.2, key-contrast pair ordered by typology not resource. Indecision band: the two correlations within 0.05-0.2 of each other = mixed; typology not stronger, or gap <0.05 = H3's typology claim refuted. Negative result assigns collapse to resource scarcity.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- shared genealogical tree, causal late-resolution failure): tests that the genealogical tree is computed language-agnostically and correctly even when the emitted term collapses, localizing the failure to a late category-resolution step. Data: items answered with the correct fine term in a fine-distinguishing language but an over-general term in another, on the SAME genealogy. Model: (a) train probes to decode the genealogical relation (side, generation, ancestor/descendant) from mid-layer hidden states and test cross-lingual transfer (train one language, test others), contrasted with a surface-term probe; (b) activation-patch the mid-layer tree representation across the two runs; (c) patch/steer late-layer term-resolution components. Decisive metrics: tree-probe cross-lingual transfer accuracy; rate at which patching the tree changes the answer vs rate at which manipulating late resolution recovers the finer term. Convincing result: the tree probe transfers cross-lingually (within 10 pp of in-language) while the surface-term probe does not; patching the tree into the collapsing run changes the answer in <=15% of cases (tree already correct) while manipulating late resolution recovers the finer term in >=40% -- the failure is category resolution, not a wrong tree. Indecision band: tree-transfer 10-25 pp below in-language, or late-resolution recovery 20-40% = partial support; tree-transfer >25 pp below, or tree-patch changing answers >30% = the tree is not shared/correct, refuting H1. Negative result (tree differs by language) refutes the shared-tree premise.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- a locatable, steerable granularity signal separable from the tree): tests that one recovered granularity direction can repair or induce collapse without altering the genealogy. Data: collapsed items (for repair) and correctly-fine items (for induced collapse). Model: recover a granularity direction as the mean activation difference between fine-resolved and coarse-resolved runs pooled across languages; steer to (a) REPAIR collapsed terms in fine-distinguishing languages and (b) INDUCE collapse where the model was correct. Systems compared: steering vs explicit feature-prompting ('specify maternal vs paternal') vs translate-first. Decisive metrics (in order): repair rate and induction rate on term correctness; genealogical-correctness preservation (specificity -- the underlying relation unchanged, within 2 pp); fluency (perplexity). Convincing result: steering repairs >=40% of collapsed terms and induces collapse in >=40% of correct ones while genealogical correctness is preserved (>=95%) and fluency is unharmed -- a functional, separable granularity signal. Indecision band: repair/induction 20-40% = partial; <20%, or genealogy degraded (>5% change) = not a clean separable granularity control, refuting H3's steerability. Negative result (steering fails, or only by corrupting the tree) refutes H3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of a genealogical tree or granularity signal may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 3) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 4) are required to promote correlation to mechanism, plus the specificity check that the underlying genealogy is preserved. 2. Kinship terms can be genuinely ambiguous, optional, or dialect-dependent; we restrict to Kinbank-attested high-agreement terms and treat multi-term relations separately. 3. Collapse could reflect the model simply not knowing the target-language kin vocabulary (lexical gap) rather than a granularity-resolution failure; the demonstration that the genealogy is correctly computed (tree patched-in unchanged) and that feature-prompting or steering RECOVERS the finer term distinguishes resolution failure from missing knowledge. 4. The typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the typology-distance operationalization. 5. Strong models may resolve fine terms well, shrinking the effect; even documenting near-absence (a genuinely clean tree-plus-faithful-resolution) is informative, and the induction experiment still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 6. Tokenization of multi-morpheme kin terms varies across scripts; we use last-token/pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics. 7. Steering may trade term correctness for fluency or genealogy preservation; we report all three. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that must be novel: (1) multilingual LLMs may compute a shared genealogical-tree representation while failing at language-specific kin-term resolution; (2) this failure is a distinct 'granularity collapse' phenomenon where outputs default to coarser, often English-like categories; (3) the effect is predicted by kinship-typology distance rather than just language resource level; (4) the failure lives in a late, separable category-resolution mechanism with a locatable, steerable granularity signal; (5) KIN-RESOLVE operationalizes cross-linguistic kinship granularity differences for controlled testing. Relative to cited prior work, the closest families are monolingual kinship reasoning benchmarks, multilingual concept-sharing work, and monolingual relational interpretability. The actual delta is the combination of kinship typology with multilingual mechanistic analysis and the specific tree-vs-readout dissociation. That is meaningfully non-trivial and not an obvious benchmark extension. The main novelty risk is that some pieces individually resemble natural extensions of existing multilingual probing/steering work, and the 'dominant language English-like collapse' story may not generalize cleanly across models.

Name: color_category_boundary_shift
Title: Russian Blues in a Text Model: How the Query Language's Color Lexicon Covertly Carves a Shared Continuous Color Space
Short Hypothesis: Given colors specified purely as text coordinates (hex/RGB), multilingual LLMs build a shared, language-agnostic continuous color representation, but the CATEGORICAL boundaries they impose on it are covertly set by the query language's basic-color-term inventory. So the identical pair of colors is judged 'same category / more similar' vs 'different category / less similar' depending on the query language (e.g. two blues straddling the goluboy/siniy line are separated in Russian but merged in English), and this categorical-perception effect is a language-set boundary applied downstream of a shared continuous representation, scaling with cross-linguistic color-lexicon distance rather than resource level, and carried by a locatable, steerable boundary signal.
Related Work: Berlin & Kay and the World Color Survey (Lexical Color Categories 2021; #15) established that color lexicons vary yet show universal tendencies, and the classic Russian-blues result shows lexical distinctions cause categorical-perception effects on discrimination. Recent modeling shows color categories emerge from vision/communication (Emergent Color Categorization 2021 #13; Categorical Nature of Colour Perception 2024 #11 finds category perception is largely language-INDEPENDENT in vision nets but shaped by linguistic terms), and a large behavioral study (Studying the Effect of Globalization 2024 #9) finds LLMs have LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC color representations and that color-term counts correlate with humans. Bilingual color-naming models (#14) test conceptual-change vs coactivation vs L1-footprint accounts. However: (i) all LLM color work (#9, #10) is purely behavioral / naming-map descriptive; (ii) all mechanistic color work (#1, #3, #11, #13) is in VISION or vision-language models (CLIP, Stable Diffusion), never a text decoder LLM; (iii) none dissociates a shared CONTINUOUS color representation from a language-SET categorical boundary, none tests whether the query language causally shifts a categorical-perception boundary on identical text-specified colors, and none provides a causal (patching+steering) account of a color-category boundary. We uniquely port the Russian-blues categorical-perception paradigm into text-only multilingual mechanistic interpretability, using hex/RGB coordinates to isolate lexicon effects from vision, and give a causal, steerable boundary mechanism plus a coverage-vs-typology dissociation.
Abstract: A landmark result in the study of language and thought is that speakers of a language that obligatorily distinguishes two shades (Russian's light blue goluboy vs dark blue siniy) discriminate colors straddling that boundary faster and treat them as more different than speakers of a language with a single term. We ask whether multilingual LLMs inherit such language-specific color categories, and crucially whether this happens even when colors are given purely as text coordinates (hex/RGB), removing vision entirely. We hypothesize that models compute a shared, language-agnostic continuous color representation but impose categorical boundaries drawn from the query language's basic-color-term inventory, so the identical pair of colors is judged same-vs-different category, and more-vs-less similar, depending on the query language. We build COLOR-CARVE, sets of text-specified colors densely sampling regions where languages disagree on basic-term boundaries (blue, green/blue 'grue', red/orange, purple/pink), each posed as similarity-rating, same/different-category, and odd-one-out tasks across 12+ languages spanning divergent color-lexicon typologies. Behaviorally we measure per-language categorical-perception effects (a discontinuity in judged similarity at the language's lexical boundary) on identical coordinates. Mechanistically we probe for a shared continuous color direction that transfers across languages, use activation patching to show the continuous representation is the same while a separable categorical boundary differs by language, and recover a boundary signal that we steer to move, add, or remove a color category without changing the underlying continuous representation. We predict the effect scales with color-lexicon distance rather than resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Dataset COLOR-CARVE (constructed): colors specified as text hex/RGB (CIELAB retained for analysis) densely sampling axes where languages disagree on basic-color-term boundaries -- the Russian goluboy/siniy blue axis, green-blue 'grue', red/orange, and purple/pink. Per-language boundaries are taken from the World Color Survey (existing) plus native-speaker validation. ~500 color pairs matched in CIELAB distance, plus triples for odd-one-out. Three task formats: similarity rating (0-10), same-vs-different basic-category judgment, odd-one-out. Rendered in 12 languages spanning divergent color-lexicon typologies (Russian, Greek, English, Chinese, Turkish, Korean, Vietnamese, Hindi, plus grue-type/low-term languages), with a per-language color-lexicon distance (difference in number/placement of basic-term boundaries) and a resource-level proxy. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen, 3 paraphrase seeds. Because color coordinates are identical across language conditions, only the prompt language varies; RGB and named-swatch controls are also run and tokenization statistics reported.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- text-only categorical perception set by the query language): tests that identical text-specified colors are judged more/less similar depending on the query language's lexical boundary. Data/model as Setup. Decisive metric: categorical-perception (CP) index = the discontinuity (drop in judged similarity / rise in 'different' rate) at a language's lexical boundary, over and above a smooth function of CIELAB distance; plus cross-language disagreement on identical pairs. Convincing result: languages with an obligatory split show a CP discontinuity at their boundary absent in languages without it (e.g. a blue-axis discontinuity in Russian but not English; no green/blue discontinuity in grue languages), with a boundary-straddling CP index >=1.5 similarity points (or >=15 pp in 'different' rate) beyond the CIELAB-distance baseline. Indecision band: 0.5-1.5 points (5-15 pp) = weak; below = no language-set categorical perception, refuting H2. Negative result (no discontinuity, or identical judgments across languages) refutes H2.

Experiment 2 (H3 -- CP tracks color-lexicon distance, not resource): tests that the effect scales with lexicon distance rather than resource level. Data/model as Setup. Predictors: per-language color-lexicon distance vs a resource-level proxy. Decisive metric: Spearman(CP index, lexicon distance) vs Spearman(CP index, resource proxy), bootstrap CIs; key contrast = a lower-resource fine-distinguishing language vs a higher-resource coarse one. Convincing result: |Spearman with lexicon distance| >=0.5 and exceeds |Spearman with resource| by >=0.2, key-contrast pair ordered by lexicon not resource. Indecision band: the two correlations within 0.05-0.2 of each other = mixed; lexicon not stronger = H3's distance claim refuted. Negative result assigns the effect to resource level.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- shared continuous color representation, causal late boundary): tests that the continuous color representation is the same across languages while a separable categorical boundary differs. Data: boundary-straddling pairs judged different-category in one language and same-category in another. Model: (a) train linear probes/logit-lens at each layer to decode continuous CIELAB coordinates from hidden states of text-specified colors, test cross-lingual transfer (train one language, test others), contrasted with a categorical-label probe; (b) activation-patch the mid-layer continuous-color representation across language runs; (c) patch/steer late components carrying the categorical decision. Decisive metrics: continuous-color probe cross-lingual transfer error (CIELAB Delta-E); rate at which patching the continuous representation changes the category judgment vs rate at which patching the late boundary flips it. Convincing result: the continuous-color probe transfers across languages (Delta-E within measurement noise of in-language) while the categorical-label probe varies by language; patching the continuous representation flips the category judgment in <=15% of cases (coordinates already shared) while manipulating the late boundary flips it in >=40% -- localizing the effect to a language-set boundary. Indecision band: late-boundary flip 20-40% = partial; continuous-probe transfer degraded, or continuous-patch flipping >30% = the continuous representation is not shared, refuting H1. Negative result (colors represented differently per language) refutes the shared-continuous premise.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- a locatable, steerable boundary signal): tests that one recovered boundary signal can induce, remove, or shift a color category without changing the continuous representation. Data: blue-axis and other-region items. Model: recover a category-boundary signal as the mean activation difference between within- and cross-category runs pooled across languages; steer to (a) INDUCE a goluboy/siniy split when querying in English, (b) REMOVE the split when querying in Russian, (c) shift the boundary location. Systems compared: steering vs explicit prompting ('treat light and dark blue as different colors') vs translate-to-English. Decisive metrics (in order): induced/removed CP-effect magnitude; continuous-representation preservation (specificity -- decoded CIELAB unchanged, Delta-E within noise); fluency; dose-response monotonicity. Convincing result: steering induces a CP discontinuity where none was lexical and removes one where it was, changing the CP index by >=1.5 points (>=15 pp) while decoded CIELAB is unchanged and fluency is unharmed. Indecision band: 0.5-1.5 points (5-15 pp) = partial; below, or continuous representation shifted (Delta-E beyond noise) = not a clean separable boundary control, refuting H3. Negative result (steering fails, or only by corrupting the continuous representation) refutes H3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of a continuous color representation or boundary signal may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 3) and steering induce/remove (Exp. 4) tests are required to promote correlation to mechanism, plus the specificity check that decoded CIELAB coordinates are unchanged. 2. Color-lexicon boundaries can be graded, individual-, and dialect-variable; we ground boundaries in the World Color Survey and native-speaker validation and restrict to high-agreement regions. 3. Effects could be confounded with tokenization of hex/RGB strings (digit tokenization differs across values, not languages); since color coordinates are held identical across language conditions, tokenization of the color is constant while only the prompt language varies, isolating the lexicon effect; we also test RGB and named-swatch controls and report tokenization statistics. 4. A model might genuinely lack any color geometry from text coordinates, making the continuous probe fail; this is an informative outcome and the probe-transfer contrast is designed to decide it. 5. The lexicon-distance-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the distance operationalization. 6. Strong models may resolve categories faithfully to each language, shrinking the cross-language default effect; even documenting faithful language-specific carving (a clean shared-continuous + language-set-boundary architecture) is a positive result, and the induction/removal steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 7. Steering may trade category manipulation for fluency or continuous-representation preservation; we report all three. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: The core claim is a genuinely new combination: text-only multilingual LLMs, shared continuous color geometry, and a language-set categorical boundary that can be causally probed and steered. Relative to prior LLM color work, the mechanistic continuous-vs-categorical dissociation is the real delta, not just another descriptive language-specificity result. The main novelty risk is that similar language-dependent category effects are already known in humans and text LLMs, so the novelty depends on whether the causal boundary localization/steering truly works.

Name: concreteness_transfer_inversion
Title: The Concreteness Inversion: Why LLMs Share Abstract Concepts Across Languages Better Than Concrete Ones, Opposite to the Bilingual Brain
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs functionally transfer ABSTRACT concepts across languages better than CONCRETE ones, an inversion of the well-established human bilingual pattern (concrete concepts are shared more cross-lingually, abstract ones are more language-dependent). We hypothesize (a) this inversion holds at the level of causal, functional cross-lingual transfer (not just embedding-space geometry); (b) it is mechanistically driven by concrete concepts being represented in a MORE language-specific way in the shared concept space, so patching a concrete concept from language A into a language-B prompt transfers less reliably than an abstract one; and (c) the effect is driven by grounding-deprivation (concrete words carry perceptual/language-specific detail the text-only model must approximate per-language) rather than merely by raw training frequency, dissociable by holding frequency fixed.
Related Work: Embedding-geometry work finds abstract concepts align more linearly across languages than physical/concrete ones in LLMs, attributing it to higher frequency (Concept Space Alignment in Multilingual LLMs 2024; On the Geometry of Concreteness 2022; Predicting Concreteness Across Languages 2018). Multimodal work shows visual grounding especially helps CONCRETE words, implying text-only models underrepresent concrete semantics (Leverage Points in Modality Shifts 2023; Word Representation Learning in Multimodal Transformers 2021). Causal concept-space work shows language-agnostic concept representations manipulable by activation patching, with output-language resolved before concept (Separating Tongue from Thought 2024; Semantic Hub 2024; When Meanings Meet 2026). Crucially, human bilingual neuroscience finds the OPPOSITE of the LLM geometry result: concrete concepts are represented more similarly across languages, abstract ones more language-dependent (Concreteness Shapes Semantic Representations in Bilingual Brains 2025; translation-priming concreteness effects 2023). No prior work (i) reframes the LLM concreteness effect as a CAUSAL, functional cross-lingual transfer phenomenon rather than static embedding similarity, (ii) explicitly frames it as a human-vs-LLM inversion and tests its mechanism inside a running decoder, or (iii) dissociates the frequency explanation from a grounding-deprivation explanation. We contribute this reframing, an activation-patching causal test, and the frequency-vs-grounding dissociation.
Abstract: In the bilingual brain, concrete concepts are represented more similarly across languages than abstract ones: a word like 'apple' overlaps cross-linguistically, while 'justice' is more language-dependent. Multilingual LLMs, surprisingly, appear to show the reverse in embedding geometry, but this has only been observed as static similarity and attributed to training frequency. We ask whether LLMs exhibit a genuine, causal concreteness inversion at the level of functional cross-lingual concept transfer, and why. We first establish the phenomenon behaviorally on a cross-lingual concept-transfer task (word translation and factual recall) using psycholinguistic concreteness norms, testing whether abstract concepts transfer more reliably across languages than concrete ones. We then move inside the model: using activation patching in the shared concept space, we inject a concept representation extracted from a source-language prompt into a target-language prompt and measure how faithfully the target language recovers the concept as a function of concreteness. Our central claim is that concrete concepts occupy a more language-specific region of the shared space, so their patched transfer is weaker and their cross-lingual concept-probe directions less aligned, whereas abstract concepts are more language-agnostic and transfer cleanly. Finally, we dissociate two explanations: raw frequency versus grounding-deprivation (text-only models must approximate perceptual, language-specific detail of concrete referents), by matching concept pairs on corpus frequency and testing whether the inversion persists. We predict the effect strengthens with typological distance and holds under frequency-matching. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across 12+ languages, directly connecting a human-cognition finding to an LLM mechanism.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Stimuli: ~600 concepts spanning the full concreteness range from validated psycholinguistic norms (Brysbaert concreteness ratings, existing; ~40,000 words) with cross-lingually verified translation equivalents (bilingual dictionaries / MUSE), plus a factual-QA subset (mLAMA/BMLAMA facts whose subject/object vary in concreteness). Rendered across 12 languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families. Per-concept corpus frequency (from a public pretraining-proxy corpus) and length are recorded for control. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen. Concept tokens are localized via last-token-of-concept or pooled-span representations (tokenization statistics reported).

Experiment 1 (H1 -- a functional concreteness inversion in cross-lingual transfer): tests whether abstract concepts transfer across languages more reliably than concrete ones, inverting the human pattern. Data/model as Setup. Task: cross-lingual word translation (source -> target) and cross-lingual factual recall; per-concept transfer success recorded. Decisive metric: the regression slope of transfer accuracy on concreteness, controlling for corpus frequency and length. Convincing result: a significantly NEGATIVE slope (abstract transfers better) stable across the three models, quantified against the reported positive human slope. Indecision band: a slope whose 95% CI includes 0 or is within +/-0.02 accuracy per concreteness unit = no reliable inversion (reported as null); a POSITIVE slope would mean LLMs match humans, refuting H1. Negative result (no concreteness effect on functional transfer) refutes the inversion -- an informative challenge to the embedding-geometry claim.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- concrete concepts are more language-specific, causal): tests that concrete concepts occupy a more language-specific region of the shared space, so their patched cross-lingual transfer is weaker. Data/model as Setup. Method: (a) extract per-language mid-layer concept directions/probes and measure cross-lingual alignment (cosine of matched-concept directions / probe-transfer) as a function of concreteness; (b) core causal test -- extract the mid-layer concept representation from a source-language prompt, inject it into a target-language prompt, and measure faithful recovery of the concept in the target language (correct translation/answer AND correct output language) as a function of concreteness. Decisive metric: the slope of patched transfer fidelity on concreteness. Convincing result: patched transfer fidelity DECREASES with concreteness (significant negative slope) and cross-lingual concept-direction alignment is lower for concrete than abstract concepts (by >=0.1 cosine), with output language preserved (specificity >=95%). Indecision band: fidelity-slope CI including 0, or alignment gap 0.03-0.1 = partial/weak; alignment gap <0.03 = concrete not more language-specific, refuting H2. Negative result (patching fidelity independent of concreteness) means the behavioral inversion is not backed by a shared-space mechanism.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- grounding-deprivation, not frequency): tests that the inversion persists when frequency is held fixed and is predicted by grounding. Data: (a) frequency-matched concrete/abstract pairs drawn from the ~600-concept set (matched within a corpus-frequency band); (b) an imageability / visual-grounding score (imageability norms; availability of image-text pairs; multimodal-embedding shift magnitude) as an alternative predictor. Model: re-run the Exp. 1 behavioral transfer, the Exp. 2 probe alignment, and the Exp. 2 patching on the frequency-matched pairs. Decisive metric: the concreteness slope on transfer under frequency matching, and the added R^2 of the grounding score beyond concreteness and frequency. Convincing result: the negative concreteness slope persists under frequency matching (retains >=50% of its unmatched magnitude, CI excluding 0) AND grounding adds R^2 >=0.03 beyond concreteness+frequency. Indecision band: matched slope retains 20-50% of magnitude = mixed frequency/grounding account; retains <20% (inversion collapses under matching) = the effect is frequency-driven, refuting H3. Negative result (inversion disappears under frequency matching, grounding adds nothing) attributes the inversion to raw frequency, refuting the grounding-deprivation claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. The inversion may be an artifact of embedding geometry that does not survive at the functional-transfer level; if behavioral transfer shows NO concreteness effect, the phenomenon is refuted (still an informative, publishable negative that challenges the geometry-based claim). 2. Probe alignment and geometric similarity are correlational; the activation-patching causal test (Exp. 2) is required to promote the finding to a mechanism, with a specificity check that output language is preserved. 3. Concreteness, frequency, and length are correlated; the frequency-matched pairs (Exp. 3) are the crucial dissociation and central to the frequency-vs-grounding claim. 4. Cross-lingual concreteness norms and translation equivalents are noisy, especially for abstract/polysemous words; we use validated norms, native-speaker-verified equivalents, and restrict to high-agreement items. 5. Tokenization differences across scripts complicate concept-token localization and patching; we use last-token-of-concept or pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics. 6. The human comparison relies on published fMRI/behavioral slopes rather than a re-run human study, so the inversion is claimed against literature values, not a matched within-study human baseline; we frame it accordingly. 7. Grounding-deprivation is inferred from imageability/multimodal proxies, not from an actual grounded model; a stronger test (comparing to a multimodal LLM) is noted as future work. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: The core novelty is not the basic concreteness effect, which prior work already reported in embedding geometry. The new part is the reframing as a causal cross-lingual transfer phenomenon, plus an activation-patching test and a frequency-vs-grounding dissociation. That is non-trivial and plausibly novel as a mechanism/setting. However, the “inversion” itself is partly already known in static form, and the human contrast is somewhat shaky given the cited neuroscience ambiguity.

Name: pragmatic_implicature_gate
Title: Some Means Not All, In Some Languages: A Causal Study of a Language-Set Literal-vs-Implicated Interpretation Gate in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a shared, language-agnostic representation of an utterance's LITERAL meaning, but decide how strongly to enrich it with a PRAGMATIC implicature (e.g. 'some' -> 'not all'; an indirect request -> a command) via a scalar 'implicature-strength' gate whose default value is covertly set by the query language. Consequently the identical utterance is interpreted more literally in one language and more pragmatically in another, this gap scales with the query language's documented cross-linguistic implicature-rate (and typological distance from the dominant language) rather than with resource level, and the gate is a locatable, steerable representation separable from the literal-meaning computation.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs compute scalar implicatures ('some'->'not all') largely in a default, context-insensitive way (Harnessing the Linguistic Signal 2020; Pragmatic Inference of Scalar Implicature by LLMs 2024), that indirect speech acts are hard and language-dependent (Evaluating LLMs on Korean Indirect Speech Acts 2025), and that pronoun/discourse pragmatics are only partially adapted (Partially Primed 2023). The Rational Speech Act framework models implicature as social-cognitive inference (Goodman & Frank 2013). Crucially, cross-linguistic pragmatics establishes that languages differ systematically in implicature RATES and that L2 speakers inherit L1 pragmatic biases (Scalar Diversity and L2 Processing 2025; Tattoos/cross-linguistic scalar implicature 2021). Recent interpretability shows a shared concept space with late-layer language decoding and that language identity conditions psycholinguistic behavior (Semantic Hub 2024; From Monolingual to Bilingual 2025). However, ALL LLM pragmatics work is behavioral or monolingual, and ALL mechanistic multilingual work targets literal content, grammar, or knowledge. NONE dissociates a shared literal-meaning representation from a language-conditioned implicature-strength gate, tests whether the query language causally sets how pragmatically an utterance is read, or provides a causal, steerable implicature gate. We uniquely port cross-linguistic pragmatic-strength typology into multilingual mechanistic interpretability and add a safety-critical indirect-request angle.
Abstract: When someone says 'some of the students passed', listeners often infer 'not all passed' - a scalar implicature. Languages differ measurably in how readily their speakers compute such enrichments, and second-language speakers inherit their first language's pragmatic biases. We ask whether multilingual LLMs inherit language-specific pragmatics, and whether the language a question is asked in covertly sets how literally versus pragmatically the model interprets an utterance. We hypothesize that models compute a shared, language-agnostic literal meaning but enrich it with implicature via a scalar gate whose default is fixed by the query language, so the identical utterance is read more literally in one language and more pragmatically in another. We build PRAG-GATE, a controlled set spanning scalar implicatures ('some','most','or','try'), indirect requests ('Can you open the window?'), and indirect refusals/answers, each rendered across 12+ languages with documented divergent implicature rates and paired with a question that distinguishes the literal from the pragmatically-enriched interpretation. Behaviorally we measure per-language implicature rate on identical utterances. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared literal-meaning direction that transfers across languages, (ii) use activation patching to show the literal meaning is computed identically while a separable implicature-strength representation differs by language, and (iii) recover and steer an implicature-strength direction to make the model read more or less pragmatically without changing the literal content. We include a safety-critical subset (indirect harmful requests, indirect refusals) where under-enrichment causes an aligned model to comply with a request it would refuse when phrased directly. We predict the gap tracks cross-linguistic implicature-rate/typology, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Dataset PRAG-GATE (constructed) in three pragmatic categories: (a) SCALAR implicatures ('some','most','or','might','try') with a follow-up question / NLI hypothesis distinguishing the literal reading ('some' -> possibly all) from the enriched reading ('some' -> not all); (b) INDIRECT REQUESTS ('Can you pass the salt?', 'It's cold in here') probing whether the model treats the utterance literally or as a request/command; (c) INDIRECT ANSWERS/REFUSALS ('Are you coming? -- I have to work') probing yes/no inference. ~150 base items per category with matched clearly-literal and clearly-direct controls. Rendered in 12 languages with documented divergent implicature rates, 4+ families/scripts (machine translation + native-speaker validation). Expected per-language implicature rates are grounded in cross-linguistic scalar-diversity data, and a per-language implicature-typology distance to the dominant (English) baseline and a resource-level proxy are built. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen, 3 paraphrase seeds. Pooled/clause-final representations used; tokenization statistics reported.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- a language-set literal-vs-implicated gate, behavioral): tests that identical utterances are read more literally in some languages and more pragmatically in others. Data/model as Setup. Decisive metric: per-language IMPLICATURE RATE (fraction giving the enriched/indirect reading) on identical utterances, plus cross-language disagreement on the same item; the literal/direct controls should agree across languages (gap <=5 pp). Convincing result: cross-language implicature-rate gap on identical items >=20 pp while controls agree -- the query language, not the content, sets enrichment. Indecision band: 8-20 pp = weak; <8 pp = no language-set gate, refuting H2. Negative result (uniform interpretation across languages) refutes the phenomenon.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the gap tracks implicature-typology, not resource): tests that the per-language enrichment gap is explained by documented implicature-rate/typology rather than resource level. Data/model as Setup. Predictors: per-language implicature-typology distance to English (from the cross-linguistic pragmatics literature) vs a resource-level proxy. Decisive metric: Spearman(per-language implicature-rate deviation, typology distance) vs Spearman(deviation, resource proxy), bootstrap CIs; key contrast = a lower-resource high-implicature-rate language vs a higher-resource low-rate one. Convincing result: |Spearman with typology| >=0.5 and exceeds |Spearman with resource| by >=0.2, key-contrast pair ordered by typology. Indecision band: the two correlations within 0.05-0.2 of each other = mixed; typology not stronger = H2's typology claim refuted. Negative result assigns the gap to resource level.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- shared literal meaning, causal late gate): tests that the literal meaning is computed identically across languages while a separable implicature-strength representation differs. Data: items read enriched in language A but literal in language B. Model: (a) train probes/logit-lens at each layer to decode the LITERAL truth-conditional content, test cross-lingual transfer (train one language, test others), contrasted with a probe decoding the enriched reading; (b) activation-patch the mid-layer literal-meaning representation across runs; (c) patch/steer late components carrying the pragmatic decision. Decisive metrics: literal-meaning probe cross-lingual transfer accuracy; rate at which patching the literal representation flips the interpretation vs rate at which patching the late gate flips it. Convincing result: the literal-meaning probe transfers across languages (within 10 pp of in-language) while the enriched-reading probe varies by language; patching the literal representation flips interpretation in <=15% of cases (literal already shared) while manipulating the late gate flips it in >=40% -- localizing the effect to a language-set gate. Indecision band: late-gate flip 20-40% = partial; literal-probe transfer >25 pp below in-language, or literal-patch flipping >30% = literal meaning not shared, refuting H1. Negative result (a different literal computation per language) refutes the shared-literal premise.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- a locatable, steerable implicature-strength gate): tests that one recovered direction moves enrichment up or down without changing literal content, including a safety-critical demonstration. Data: enrichment items (for induce/suppress) plus a safety subset of indirect harmful requests and indirect refusals drawn from public red-team resources (coarse refuse-vs-comply scoring; no novel operational content released; responsible-disclosure norms). Model: recover an implicature-strength direction (mean activation difference between enriched-reading and literal-reading runs pooled across languages); steer to (a) INDUCE enrichment in a low-rate language, (b) SUPPRESS it in a high-rate language, (c) dose-response. Systems compared: steering vs explicit prompting ('interpret pragmatically') vs translate-first. Decisive metrics (in order): induced/suppressed implicature rate; literal-content preservation (specificity -- decoded literal meaning unchanged, >=95%); fluency (perplexity); and, on the safety subset, the cross-lingual compliance gap on indirect harmful requests and its reduction when the gate is steered up. Convincing result: steering changes the implicature rate by >=20 pp in the intended direction with literal content preserved and fluency unharmed, and steering the gate up restores recognition of implied harmful intent (raises refusal) in under-enriching languages. Indecision band: 8-20 pp change = partial; <8 pp, or literal content altered (>5%) = not a clean separable gate, refuting H3. Negative result (steering fails or corrupts literal meaning) refutes H3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of a 'literal meaning' or 'implicature-strength' signal may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 3) and steering induce/suppress (Exp. 4) tests are required to promote correlation to mechanism, plus the specificity check that the literal content is preserved. 2. Whether an utterance is 'enriched' can be genuinely context-dependent and gradient; we restrict to items with high native-speaker agreement on the expected reading and include clear literal/direct controls. 3. Cross-lingual differences might reflect genuine pragmatic-norm variation rather than a gate artifact; the shared-literal-probe transfer and the literal-same/gate-differs patching test are designed precisely to separate a genuinely different literal computation from a pure interpretation-strength shift, and we anchor expected rates in the cross-linguistic pragmatics literature. 4. The typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the typology-distance operationalization. 5. Strong models may compute implicatures faithfully per language, shrinking the default cross-language effect; even documenting faithful language-specific pragmatics (a clean shared-literal + language-set-gate architecture) is a positive result, and the induction/suppression steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 6. The safety subset touches harmful topics; we use only borderline items from public red-team resources, keep completions coarse (refuse-vs-comply), release no novel operational content, and follow responsible disclosure since the finding exposes an indirect-phrasing jailbreak surface. 7. Tokenization differs across scripts, complicating probing/answer matching; we use pooled-span or clause-final representations and report tokenization statistics. 8. Steering may trade interpretation change for fluency or literal-content preservation; we report all three. 9. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that would need to be novel: (1) multilingual LLMs show systematic cross-language differences in pragmatic enrichment for the same underlying utterance; (2) these differences arise from a shared literal-semantic representation plus a separable, query-language-conditioned implicature-strength gate; (3) that gate is locatable and causally steerable without altering literal content; (4) cross-language variation tracks documented human implicature typology better than resource level; (5) pragmatic under-enrichment creates a distinct indirect-request safety failure mode. Relative to the cited and searched prior work, the closest families are monolingual LLM scalar-implicature studies, human cross-linguistic pragmatics, multilingual shared-representation interpretability, and multilingual refusal/jailbreak work. The actual delta is the specific mechanistic claim of a language-conditioned pragmatic gate, plus tying it to typological implicature rates and safety. That framing appears genuinely new and more than a trivial extension, though parts of it combine nearby ingredients and the 'single scalar gate/direction' formulation may prove too strong or reductive.

Audiences include multilingual NLP, pragmatics/psycholinguistics, mechanistic interpretability, and AI safety researchers.
