Name: functional_interference_tree
Title: The Tree the Model Actually Uses: Cross-Lingual Functional Interference Recapitulates Script and Co-occurrence, Not Linguistic Phylogeny
Short Hypothesis: The pattern of how a behavioral change induced in one language (via a targeted fine-tune, knowledge edit, or in-context skill) leaks into other languages forms a coherent 'functional interference tree' over languages. We hypothesize this causal/functional tree is systematically DIFFERENT from the linguistic phylogenetic tree that prior work recovers from static representation geometry: it is dominated by shared script and training-corpus co-occurrence rather than genealogical relatedness. Where the two trees disagree (e.g. Hindi-Urdu: same genealogy, different script; Turkish-Uzbek: shared Latin script, different family branch), functional interference follows the script/co-occurrence structure, not phylogeny, and this divergence predicts which cross-lingual edits/transfers unexpectedly help or harm.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work shows that STATIC representation geometry of multilingual encoders recapitulates the linguistic phylogenetic tree: mBERT distances recover family trees (Probing mBERT for Genetic/Typological Signals 2020), joint matrix factorization of representations yields phylogenetic clustering (Joint Matrix Factorization 2023), and morphosyntactic neuron overlap is higher for same-genus languages (Same Neurons Different Languages 2022; What Language Does Aya-23 Think In 2025). Separately, cross-lingual editing/transfer work reports that script similarity dominates knowledge sharing and that edits fail across script families (Beneath the Surface of Consistency 2024; XME 2024). No prior work (i) builds a language tree from CAUSAL, functional interference (how a targeted intervention in language A perturbs behavior in language B) rather than from static similarity, (ii) directly CONTRASTS this functional tree against both the linguistic phylogenetic tree and a script/co-occurrence tree as competing explanations, or (iii) uses the phylogeny-vs-script divergence to predict per-pair transfer/interference. We reframe cross-lingual relatedness as a functional, causal quantity and show the model's operative tree is not the linguists' tree.
Abstract: A striking result in multilingual interpretability is that the geometry of a model's internal representations recapitulates the linguistic family tree: distances between language representations reconstruct phylogenies close to those drawn by linguists. But representation similarity is correlational. We ask a causal, behavioral question: if we change a model's behavior in one language, which other languages change with it, and does that pattern of functional interference form the same tree? We hypothesize it does not. We define a functional interference tree by measuring, for every ordered language pair, how much a targeted intervention in a source language (a small knowledge edit, a short skill fine-tune, or an in-context skill demonstration) shifts behavior in a target language, then clustering languages by this causal leakage. We predict this tree is dominated by shared script and training-corpus co-occurrence rather than genealogy, so it diverges sharply from the phylogenetic tree recovered from static representations of the SAME model. We test the divergence on diagnostic minimal pairs where genealogy and script disagree (Hindi/Urdu, Serbian Cyrillic/Latin, Turkish/Uzbek, Persian/Tajik) across 20+ languages and Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2. We further show the phylogeny-minus-script residual predicts, per language pair, where cross-lingual edits and skill transfer unexpectedly succeed or backfire. The result challenges the tidy 'models rediscover the family tree' narrative: the tree the model computes with is a script- and corpus-shaped one, not the linguists' phylogeny, with direct consequences for multilingual editing and transfer.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Languages: 20 languages chosen to span 4+ families (Indo-European, Turkic, Sino-Tibetan, Afro-Asiatic, Dravidian) and 5 scripts (Latin, Cyrillic, Perso-Arabic, Devanagari, CJK), and to include the diagnostic minimal pairs where genealogy and script dissociate: Hindi/Urdu (same genealogy, Devanagari vs Perso-Arabic), Serbian written in Cyrillic vs Latin (same language, two scripts), Turkish/Uzbek (Turkic, both Latin), Persian/Tajik (same branch, Perso-Arabic vs Cyrillic). Models (all decoder-only, 7-8B, one A100-80GB each for inference/LoRA; MEMIT edits fit on one GPU): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. Reference resources (all existing, off-the-shelf): Glottolog/URIEL genealogical distances via lang2vec; URIEL typological distance; a binary same-script matrix; two training-corpus co-occurrence proxies (per-language corpus-size similarity from the CC-100 language sizes, and a script-sharing indicator), reported separately because true co-occurrence is unobservable. Three intervention families are used throughout: (a) KNOWLEDGE EDIT via MEMIT applied to 100 source-language facts, all base weights frozen except the MEMIT-targeted MLP down-projection rows at its located layers; (b) SKILL FINE-TUNE via LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, AdamW) on 1,000 source-language items of a from-scratch templated task set (arithmetic + fixed-format extraction, 2,000 items built by template and rendered per language, 1,000 train / 1,000 held-out test), base frozen, adapters trainable; (c) IN-CONTEXT SKILL, base frozen, 8 demonstrations. Facts are 1,000 parallel triples taken from the intersection of mLAMA (multilingual LAMA; ~tens of thousands of templated triples across 53 languages) that exist in all 20 languages, so items are matched across languages. Three seeds vary the edited-fact sample, LoRA init, and demonstration order.

Experiment 1 (H1 - coherent functional interference tree). Tests whether a targeted behavioral change in a source language leaks into other languages in a pattern coherent enough to define a single tree. For every ordered pair (source, target) and each intervention family, apply the intervention in the source and measure the behavior shift in the target on held-out parallel probes (the 1,000 matched facts for edits; the 1,000 held-out task items for fine-tune/in-context), giving a directed interference matrix M[source, target] = mean absolute change in target accuracy (percentage points). Symmetrize and build a tree by neighbor-joining. Data as in the shared setup. Model as above; the interference matrix uses inference only after each intervention. Systems compared: the three intervention families' trees against one another, per model. Decisive metric: mean bootstrap edge support of the functional tree - the fraction of internal edges reproduced across 1,000 item-resampled bootstraps - averaged over the three families; secondary, the normalized quartet distance between the three families' trees (0 = identical, 1 = maximally different). Convincing: mean edge support >= 0.70 AND the three families mutually agree at quartet distance <= 0.25. Indecision band: edge support 0.50-0.70 or quartet distance 0.25-0.40; landing here means we do not assert a single tree and instead carry the interference MATRIX (not a tree) into Experiments 2-5, testing the same structure without the tree claim. Negative result: edge support < 0.50 or families disagreeing at quartet distance > 0.40 refutes H1 - leakage is idiosyncratic, not tree-structured.

Experiment 2 (H2 - functional tree differs from static representation phylogeny). Tests whether the causal functional tree diverges from the model's own static representation tree. Build the representation tree from mean per-language hidden states over 500 held-out parallel sentences drawn from FLORES-200 devtest (1,012 parallel sentences across 200+ languages; 500 used to bound compute), pairwise cosine distance at the best layer, neighbor-joining. Baseline anchor: quartet distance of this representation tree to the Glottolog reference, replicating prior "representations recover phylogeny" claims. Model: same three, inference only, all weights frozen. Systems compared: functional tree (Exp. 1) vs representation tree. Decisive metric: normalized quartet distance between functional and representation trees. Convincing: functional-vs-representation quartet distance >= 0.40 (substantial divergence) WHILE representation-vs-Glottolog quartet distance <= 0.30 (the representation tree genuinely tracks phylogeny, so the divergence is meaningful). Indecision band: functional-vs-representation quartet 0.25-0.40; reported as partial divergence, supporting only the weak "not identical" reading, not "systematically different". Negative result: quartet < 0.25 means the trees coincide, refuting H2. Guard: if representation-vs-Glottolog quartet > 0.30 (representations do not recover phylogeny in these decoder LLMs), the contrast is uninformative for "differs from phylogeny"; we then compare the functional tree to the Glottolog reference directly and report that substitution explicitly.

Experiment 3 (H3 - dominated by script/co-occurrence, not genealogy). Tests what structure the functional tree encodes. Reference matrices from the shared setup: genealogy (Glottolog/URIEL), script identity, and the two co-occurrence proxies. Decisive metric: partial Mantel/Spearman correlation of the functional distance matrix with each reference, each controlling for the others; the contrast is (script + co-occurrence) partial correlation minus genealogy partial correlation. Model/data as Exp. 1-2. Systems compared: functional matrix vs representation matrix against the same references. Convincing: the functional matrix's partial correlation with script/co-occurrence exceeds its partial correlation with genealogy by >= 0.20 in Spearman rho (with the genealogy partial not significantly > 0), AND the representation matrix shows the reverse ordering. Indecision band: difference 0.05-0.20; script/co-occurrence leads but not decisively, reported as suggestive rather than "dominated by". Negative result: genealogy partial rho >= script/co-occurrence partial rho refutes H3.

Experiment 4 (H4 - diagnostic minimal pairs follow script, not genealogy). Tests, on pairs where genealogy and script disagree, whether interference tracks script. Data: the four minimal pairs (Hindi/Urdu, Serbian-Cyrillic/Serbian-Latin, Turkish/Uzbek, Persian/Tajik) plus, as a same-family same-script anchor per region, a control pair (e.g. Hindi/Nepali, both Devanagari). Facts and interventions as shared. Model as above. Decisive metric: within-pair directed interference magnitude (accuracy-point shift on held-out parallel probes), compared against the same-family same-script anchor. Convincing: for the genealogically close but script-different pairs (Hindi/Urdu, Persian/Tajik) interference is < 50% of the same-family same-script anchor's interference, and Serbian-Cyrillic->Serbian-Latin interference (identical language, differing only in script) is likewise suppressed relative to Serbian-Cyrillic->Serbian-Cyrillic self-consistency. Indecision band: cross-script interference 50-75% of the anchor; treated as script partially but not decisively gating, reported per pair. Negative result: cross-script interference within genealogically close pairs at or above the anchor refutes H4 (genealogy, not script, governs leakage).

Experiment 5 (H5 - divergence predicts transfer help/harm). Tests whether the phylogeny-vs-script divergence predicts, per pair, where cross-lingual edits/skill transfer unexpectedly help or backfire. Outcome per ordered pair: sign and magnitude of transfer (edit propagation to matched facts; skill-transfer accuracy change on held-out task items), labeled positive/neutral/backfire relative to no-intervention baseline. Predictors: phylogenetic distance, script identity, co-occurrence proxy, and the phylogeny-minus-script residual. Fit on a random 70% of the ~380 ordered pairs, evaluate on the held-out 30%, 3 seeds. Decisive metric: held-out AUC for classifying backfire vs non-backfire pairs from the residual; secondary, standardized regression coefficients. Convincing: script/co-occurrence terms carry the largest significant standardized coefficients AND the residual predicts backfire pairs at held-out AUC >= 0.70. Indecision band: AUC 0.60-0.70; reported as weak predictive signal, not actionable. Negative result: AUC < 0.60 or genealogy dominating the coefficients refutes H5 - the tree divergence has no predictive payoff for transfer.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. The functional tree from edits/fine-tunes could be dominated by which languages the model is simply BETTER at (resource level) rather than pairwise structure; we control by measuring interference relative to each target's baseline competence and by including resource-matched pairs. 2. Different intervention types (edit vs fine-tune vs in-context) may yield different trees, undercutting a single 'functional tree'; this is itself an informative result and we report agreement across the three rather than assuming one. 3. Script and co-occurrence are correlated (same-script languages co-occur more), making them hard to separate; the diagnostic minimal pairs (same genealogy, different script; same script, different family) are designed precisely to dissociate them, and the transliteration ablation further isolates script. 4. Tree-inference is sensitive to distance-metric choice and noise; we report multiple metrics and bootstrap confidence over trees. 5. Knowledge edits can fail entirely in low-resource languages, confounding interference with edit failure; we condition on successful source edits and report edit success separately. 6. The representation-tree replication may be weaker in decoder-only LLMs than in mBERT; even a partial phylogenetic signal suffices to test divergence, and finding NO phylogenetic signal in representations would also be a notable result. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: counterfactual_override_gate
Title: In Which Language Can You Pretend? A Causal Study of the Query-Language-Set Counterfactual-Override Gate in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Counterfactual reasoning requires a model to suppress its stored real-world knowledge and instead follow an in-context stipulation ('suppose water boils at 50 degrees; a pot heated to 60 is...'). We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs compute a largely language-agnostic representation of BOTH the stipulated counterfactual premise and the stored real-world fact, but gate which one wins via a scalar 'counterfactual-override' strength whose default is covertly set by the query language. Consequently, for a fixed hypothetical, the model correctly overrides real knowledge in high-resource languages but lazily leaks the true-world answer in low-resource / typologically distant languages; this leakage scales with the query language's distance from the dominant language, not with the difficulty of the counterfactual itself, and is carried by a locatable, steerable override representation separable from the premise and fact content.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs can override real-world knowledge in counterfactual conditionals but often via lexical cues, and struggle with formal counterfactual inference (Counterfactual Reasoning 2022/2023; CRASS 2021; CounterBench 2025; multi-modal C-VQA 2023). Multilingual counterfactual work is purely about counterfactual EXAMPLE GENERATION and its cross-lingual edit patterns (Parallel Universes 2026), not about reasoning-time override. Cross-lingual factual-consistency interpretability shows a language-independent concept space with a late-layer language-transition bottleneck and entity-alignment failures (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; On the Entity-Level Alignment 2025; Are Knowledge and Reference Cross-Lingually Consistent 2025), and BICAUSE (Under the Shadow of Babel 2025) shows language shapes CAUSAL reasoning attention. Larger models drift into language-specific subspaces hurting consistency (Language-Specific Latent Process 2025). NONE of these studies COUNTERFACTUAL override across languages, nor asks whether the query language sets how strongly a model suppresses its stored fact in favor of an in-context stipulation, nor provides a causal, steerable override gate. We uniquely reframe multilingual reasoning failure on hypotheticals as a language-set knowledge-override gating problem and give a causal (probe + patching + steering) account plus a training-free fix, adopting the triangulation acceptance standard (Triangulation 2025) of necessity+sufficiency+cross-lingual invariance.
Abstract: Reasoning about hypotheticals ('suppose water boiled at 50 degrees Celsius') requires a model to hold a stipulated premise that contradicts what it knows and follow the premise, not reality. We investigate whether multilingual LLMs can do this equally well in every language, and whether the query language covertly decides how strongly the model overrides its stored knowledge. We hypothesize that models compute a largely language-agnostic representation of both the stipulated counterfactual premise and the true real-world fact, but resolve the conflict through a scalar counterfactual-override gate whose default value is set by the query language. Under this view, the same hypothetical is followed faithfully in high-resource languages but leaks the true-world answer in low-resource, typologically distant languages, because the override gate is weaker there. We build CF-OVERRIDE, controlled counterfactual conditionals whose correct answer under the stipulation differs from the real-world answer, rendered across 15+ languages spanning several scripts and families, with matched real-world (non-counterfactual) controls. Behaviorally we measure a per-language real-world-leakage rate on identical hypotheticals. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared premise representation and a shared real-world-fact representation that transfer across languages; (ii) use activation patching to show both are computed similarly across languages while a separable override signal differs, localizing leakage to a language-set gate rather than a failure to encode the premise; and (iii) recover an override direction and steer it to strengthen override in leaky languages and weaken it in strict ones without harming fluency, validated with a triangulation standard (necessity, sufficiency, cross-lingual invariance). We predict leakage tracks typological/script distance, not counterfactual difficulty. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Dataset CF-OVERRIDE (built from scratch): 300 counterfactual-conditional items in which a stipulated premise contradicts a well-known real-world fact and a yes/no follow-up has DIFFERENT correct answers under the stipulation vs reality (physics, geography, biology, social-rule stipulations), spanning a difficulty gradient (150 one-step, 150 two-step inference from the premise). Each item carries two matched controls: (a) a REAL-WORLD variant with no counterfactual premise (correct answer = the real fact, to verify the model knows the fact in each language) and (b) a neutral-premise variant. All 900 base strings are rendered into 15 languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Perso-Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels (13,500 rendered items), each translation checked by two native speakers plus back-translation; items failing agreement are dropped and reported. Per language we compute lang2vec typological/script distance to the model's dominant language (English) and a resource proxy (CC-100 corpus share). Models (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference + light steering only): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B; all weights frozen except where a steering vector is added at inference. Analyses use 3 seeds (prompt-template variant and few-shot order).

Experiment 1 (H3 - real-world leakage varies by query language). Tests whether, for a fixed hypothetical, the model overrides real knowledge in high-resource languages but leaks the true-world answer in low-resource/distant ones. Restrict to items where the model demonstrably knows the fact (control (a) answered correctly in that language) and can do the inference (the item is answered correctly in the English anchor), so leakage is not ignorance. Decisive metric: REAL-WORLD-LEAKAGE RATE = fraction of counterfactual items answered with the true-world answer instead of the stipulation-consistent answer, per language. Systems compared: each language against the English upper bound and a translate-to-English-first baseline. Convincing: leakage rate in the low-resource/distant language group exceeds the high-resource group by >= 15 percentage points in all three models. Indecision band: 5-15 pp gap; reported as a weak language effect, insufficient to claim a query-language-set default. Negative result: gap < 5 pp (models override or leak equally across languages) refutes H3.

Experiment 2 (H4 - leakage tracks language distance, not counterfactual difficulty). Tests whether leakage scales with the query language's distance rather than with inference difficulty. Regress per-item leakage on (typological/script distance to English, resource proxy) and on counterfactual difficulty (1- vs 2-step). Key designed contrast: a typologically DISTANT but well-covered language vs a CLOSE but sparsely-covered one, to separate distance from resource. Data/model as shared. Decisive metric: standardized regression coefficient on distance vs the coefficient on difficulty (and Spearman of leakage with each, 95% CIs). Convincing: the distance coefficient is significant and larger in magnitude than the difficulty coefficient, and difficulty alone does not order leakage. Indecision band: the two coefficients within 0.05 (standardized) of each other, or overlapping CIs; reported as "distance and difficulty comparable", not supporting the distance-dominates claim. Negative result: difficulty coefficient significantly larger than distance refutes H4.

Experiment 3 (H1 - shared, language-agnostic premise and fact representations). Tests whether both the stipulated premise and the stored real-world fact are represented similarly across languages (so leaky languages still ENCODE the premise). Train linear probes and read the logit lens at each layer to decode (i) the stipulated premise content and (ii) the true real-world fact from mid-layer hidden states; evaluate cross-lingual transfer (train on one language, test on the others). Contrast with a probe decoding the RESOLVED answer, which should vary by language. Data: held-out CF-OVERRIDE items; probes are the only trainable parameters (logistic regression on frozen activations), base model frozen; 3 seeds for the probe split. Decisive metric: cross-lingual transfer accuracy of the premise and fact probes (accuracy on unseen languages) relative to in-language accuracy. Systems compared: premise/fact probes (expected to transfer) vs resolved-answer probe (expected not to). Convincing: premise and fact probes transfer with <= 10-point accuracy drop off in-language accuracy and both stay well above chance, while the resolved-answer probe's cross-lingual transfer collapses toward chance. Indecision band: transfer drop 10-20 points; reported as partial sharing, weakly supporting H1. Negative result: premise/fact probes fail to transfer (drop > 20 points, near chance) refutes H1 - representations are language-specific, not shared.

Experiment 4 (H2 - a language-set override gate, causally localized). Tests whether leakage is a gating failure (premise present but not followed) rather than a missing premise, and whether the deciding signal is language-set. Take items overridden correctly in a high-resource language but leaked in a low-resource one. (a) Activation-patch the mid-layer premise representation from the correct run into the leaked run and confirm the premise is already present in the leaked run (patching it changes the answer little). (b) Patch/steer the components carrying the override decision and test whether the answer flips to premise-consistent. Apply a triangulation standard: NECESSITY (ablating the gate reintroduces leakage where the model was correct), SUFFICIENCY (injecting it repairs leakage), and CROSS-LINGUAL INVARIANCE (the same component works across languages). Model frozen; patching at inference; specificity control = patching a matched non-gate site. Decisive metric: premise-consistent flip rate from gate patching (repair) with a matched-site flip rate as specificity floor. Convincing: gate patching repairs >= 50% of leaked items, premise patching alone repairs < 15% (premise already present), the matched non-gate site repairs < 15%, and necessity + sufficiency + invariance all hold. Indecision band: gate-patch repair 25-50%, or premise-patch repair 15-30% (premise partly missing); reported as mixed evidence - gating contributes but a representational deficit is also present. Negative result: gate-patch repair < 25%, or premise patching itself repairs the answer (premise was absent), refutes the language-set-gate account.

Experiment 5 (H5 - a locatable, steerable override direction separable from content). Tests whether a single override direction repairs leaky languages and induces leakage in strict ones without harming content. Recover an override direction as the mean activation difference between premise-following and real-world-leaking runs, pooled across languages. Steer to (a) STRENGTHEN override in leaky languages and (b) WEAKEN it to INDUCE leakage where the model was correct, with a dose-response over steering coefficient. Model frozen; only the added vector varies; compare against explicit prompting ("ignore real-world facts; follow only the supposition") and translate-first. Decisive metric: leakage reduction (repair) in leaky languages, reported first; then induced-leakage rate in strict languages; alongside specificity (premise and fact probe content preserved), fluency (perplexity change), and output-language fidelity. Convincing: steering reduces leakage by >= 15 percentage points in leaky languages AND induces >= 15 points of leakage in strict ones, with a monotone dose-response, < 5% perplexity increase, and preserved premise/fact content; the direction generalizes across the three models better than prompting. Indecision band: 5-15 point repair/induction, or dose-response non-monotone; reported as a real but weak causal handle. Negative result: < 5 point effect, or effect only at doses that break fluency/content, refutes H5 - no separable steerable override representation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Leakage could be confounded with the model simply not KNOWING the real fact or being unable to do the inference in a low-resource language rather than a gating failure; the real-world control (knows the fact) and high-resource-anchor inference check restrict the analysis to items where both prerequisites hold, and the patching test (premise present but not followed) is the crucial disambiguator. 2. Probe decodability of premise/fact/override may reflect the readout basis, not a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering induce/repair (Exp. 6), held to the triangulation standard, are required to promote correlation to mechanism, plus specificity checks that premise and fact content are preserved. 3. Some counterfactual items may leak via lexical cues (as prior monolingual work found) rather than genuine reasoning; we construct items where lexical overlap does not decide the answer and report a lexical-cue control subset. 4. The distance-vs-difficulty dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts and a clean difficulty axis; we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the distance operationalization. 5. Strong models may override faithfully in all languages, shrinking the effect; even documenting faithful language-invariant override (a clean shared-premise + strong-gate architecture) is informative, and the induction steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 6. Translations may inadvertently soften or strengthen the counterfactual framing across languages; native-speaker validation and matched neutral-premise controls mitigate this. 7. Tokenization differs across scripts, complicating probing/answer matching; we use pooled-span or answer-token representations and report tokenization statistics. 8. Steering may trade override strength for fluency or content preservation; we report all three. 9. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) multilingual LLMs exhibit a query-language-dependent counterfactual override failure; (2) the model can represent the stipulated premise and real-world fact in a shared space, but a separable override gate determines which wins; (3) leakage tracks language distance more than counterfactual difficulty; (4) this gate is causally steerable and localizable. The closest prior family is counterfactual-knowledge conflict work plus multilingual knowledge-conflict studies and monolingual override/steering work. The actual delta is not the existence of override failure or steerable conflict resolution per se, but the specific multilingual claim that query language covertly sets override strength and that this effect is dissociable from premise/fact representations. That is a plausible and non-obvious extension, though it is adjacent to established monolingual findings and therefore not a wholly new mechanism in the broad sense. Novelty lives mainly in the finding + multilingual setting + causal decomposition.

Who cares: multilingual reasoning researchers, interpretability folks, and safety/reliability teams using LLMs across languages. review.reasoning: The hypothesis is interesting but somewhat over-specified and at risk of being underidentified. Main gaps: 'override strength' is not yet a precise latent variable; shared representations plus a separable gate are plausible but not uniquely identifiable from probes and patching alone; distance vs difficulty may be confounded by script, tokenization, frequency, and translation artifacts; and the claim that leakage is 'covertly set by query language' is stronger than the proposed evidence can cleanly establish without stronger causal controls. The experimental plan is decent and testable, with matched controls, multiple languages, and causal steering, but it needs sharper falsifiable predictions and stronger controls for translation quality, fact familiarity, item difficulty, and model-specific decoding artifacts. Related work is enough to position the paper, though it should cite more directly the multilingual query-language memory work and mechanistic conflict-resolution literature. If executed well, this could be a solid ML venue paper because it combines behavior, mechanism, and intervention; however, the current narrative risks sounding like it already knows the mechanism before the evidence is in.

Name: crosslingual_capacity_contention
Title: The Polyglot Bottleneck: Inference-Time Capacity Contention and Active Arbitration Among Languages in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: A small set of shared 'polyglot' components in a multilingual LLM forms a fixed-capacity bottleneck that multiple languages must contend for at inference time. We hypothesize (a) cross-lingual interference is a dynamic, dose-dependent CAPACITY-CONTENTION effect, not a static property: forcing the model to hold a second language active (via a preceding multilingual context) causally degrades competence in the target language in proportion to how much shared-bottleneck capacity the intruder language consumes; (b) this contention is concentrated in an identifiable set of shared middle-layer components (an inference-time analogue of a 'shared region'), and its degradation is causally removable by protecting/steering those components; and (c) the model performs weak ACTIVE ARBITRATION (interference suppression) over this bottleneck, so contention cost scales with how strongly the intruder competes (its similarity/co-activation to the target), mirroring the bilingual brain's language-conflict-and-control dynamics.
Related Work: Static-region work shows a ~1% shared 'core linguistic region' and language-specific regions whose removal destroys competence (Unveiling Linguistic Regions 2024), and that entanglement with a dominant variety can HURT related varieties, fixable by subspace decoupling (When Alignment Hurts 2025); training-side work shows language-general vs language-specific FFN neurons and reduces training interference by selective/sparse fine-tuning (Neuron Specialization 2024; LANDeRMT 2024; Sparse Subnetwork Enhancement 2025). The Stem Cell Hypothesis (2021) shows shared attention heads cause TRAINING-time multi-task interference in encoders. Bilingualism neuroscience shows non-target languages are automatically co-activated and require active interference suppression via cognitive-control circuits whose engagement adapts to interactional context (Language Conflict in the Bilingual Brain 2008; Adaptive Control Hypothesis 2013). ALL region/neuron work is about STATIC parameter partitions or TRAINING-time interference and their editing fixes; NONE studies INFERENCE-TIME, dose-dependent CAPACITY CONTENTION where dynamically loading one language degrades another, treats interference as a limited-shared-resource being arbitrated on the fly, or tests active-arbitration (suppression) over a shared bottleneck in a decoder LLM. We uniquely reframe cross-lingual interference as dynamic capacity contention with active arbitration, give causal (patching + steering + capacity-protection) evidence, and connect it to the bilingual-control literature.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs are often described via static partitions: a shared 'core' region plus language-specific regions. We propose a complementary, dynamic account. Drawing on bilingual-brain findings that non-target languages are automatically co-activated and must be actively suppressed, we hypothesize that a small set of shared middle-layer 'polyglot' components forms a fixed-capacity bottleneck that languages contend for at inference time, and that the model weakly arbitrates this contention on the fly. This yields a sharp, testable prediction absent from static-partition work: forcing the model to hold a second (intruder) language active while answering in a target language should causally degrade target-language competence in a dose-dependent way, with cost scaling by how much shared-bottleneck capacity the intruder consumes and how strongly it competes with the target. We test this with a controlled contention paradigm: identical target-language questions are answered either alone or after a preceding context that loads an intruder language, varying intruder amount (dose) and intruder-target relatedness. We measure a per-pair Contention Cost and locate the shared components whose activation is co-claimed by both languages. Causally, we (i) activation-patch the shared-component state from the alone-run into the contention-run to test whether protecting the bottleneck removes the degradation, (ii) steer to suppress intruder co-activation and measure target recovery (active-arbitration proxy), and (iii) show a matched non-contending control (a task-irrelevant intruder) produces little cost. We predict contention cost is highest for typologically near, high-co-activation intruders and that steering the shared bottleneck recovers performance without retraining. Experiments span mLAMA/BMLAMA factual QA and MGSM reasoning across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Tasks/data (existing, used as is): multilingual factual QA from BMLAMA-53 (parallel cloze/QA facts across 53 languages; sample 1,000 facts that exist in all chosen languages) and multilingual grade-school math from MGSM (250 problems; MGSM ships 11 languages, so the reasoning arm uses its 10-11 languages, and the factual arm supplies the 15+ language breadth). Chosen languages span Latin/Cyrillic/Perso-Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels. Models (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference + steering only, all weights frozen): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. Per-pair typological distance from lang2vec; resource proxy from CC-100 shares. 3 seeds (intruder-item sampling and order). "Intruder" = a non-target language the model must process before answering; "target" = the language the question is answered in.

Experiment 1 (H-contention - dose-dependent capacity contention). Tests whether forcing the model to hold a second language active degrades target-language competence in proportion to intruder load. For each target-language item, two matched conditions: ALONE (target question only) and CONTENTION (an intruder-language preceding context the model must attend to before the identical target question). Vary INTRUDER DOSE (number of intruder-language items / context tokens: 1, 3, 6 items) and intruder identity. Decisive metric: CONTENTION COST = accuracy(ALONE) - accuracy(CONTENTION) on the same target item (percentage points), and the slope of cost vs dose. Systems compared: dose levels against ALONE, per model and per task. Convincing: mean Contention Cost > 0 with a monotone, significant positive dose-response (cost at dose 6 exceeds cost at dose 1 by >= 5 pp) in all three models. Indecision band: cost present (> 0) but dose-slope flat or cost 2-5 pp at max dose; reported as static interference, not the dynamic dose-dependent effect the hypothesis claims. Negative result: Contention Cost <= 2 pp and no dose-response refutes the capacity-contention claim.

Experiment 2 (H-contention - specificity to competing other-language load). Tests that the cost is cross-lingual contention, not generic context-length degradation. Replace the intruder-language context with (i) a same-language (target) distractor context of equal token length and (ii) a non-linguistic filler (digits/symbols) of equal token length; matching is by token count, reported alongside item count. Decisive metric: the gap between Contention Cost under an other-language intruder and the cost under each equal-length control. Convincing: the other-language cost exceeds both controls by >= 5 pp. Indecision band: 2-5 pp above controls; reported as weak specificity - contention and length-degradation are entangled. Negative result: other-language cost <= 2 pp above controls means the effect is generic context degradation, refuting the cross-lingual reading.

Experiment 3 (H-arbitration - cost scales with intruder competition, dissociated from resource). Tests that cost is highest for intruders that compete most strongly (near, high co-activation), not merely for low-resource intruders. Correlate Contention Cost with (i) lang2vec typological/script distance between intruder and target and (ii) an internal CO-ACTIVATION score (overlap of the shared components each language activates, from Exp. 4). Designed contrast: a near-but-low-resource intruder vs a far-but-high-resource intruder. Decisive metric: Spearman of cost with typological proximity and with co-activation (95% CIs), and the partial correlation controlling for the resource proxy. Convincing: cost correlates positively with proximity/co-activation (Spearman >= 0.4) and this survives partialling out resource. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.4 or correlation vanishing after resource control; reported as resource-confounded, not competition-driven. Negative result: no correlation (< 0.2) or resource dominating refutes the competition-scaling claim.

Experiment 4 (H-bottleneck - locate the shared middle-layer bottleneck). Tests whether a small, identifiable set of shared components is co-claimed by multiple languages. From ALONE runs, score middle-layer FFN neurons / attention heads / activation directions by cross-language activation overlap (LAPE-style activation entropy over languages) and by probing; define a shared-bottleneck set and per-language capacity-consumption profiles, contrasted with language-specific components. Model frozen; this is measurement, promoted to causal only in Exp. 5-6. Decisive metric: the fraction of components that are high-overlap (shared) and the concentration of shared activation in them (e.g., top-k components carrying the majority of cross-language overlap). Convincing: a small set (e.g., <= 5% of middle-layer components) accounts for the majority of cross-language activation overlap and its per-language consumption profile predicts Exp. 3's co-activation ordering. Indecision band: the shared set is diffuse (needs 5-20% of components to reach majority overlap); reported as weakly localized. Negative result: no concentration (overlap spread evenly across components) means there is no identifiable bottleneck to protect, undercutting H-bottleneck and Exp. 5.

Experiment 5 (H-bottleneck - protecting the bottleneck causally removes contention). Tests whether the located bottleneck is the causal locus of the degradation. Activation-patch the shared-bottleneck state from the ALONE target run into the CONTENTION run; specificity control = patching a matched non-bottleneck set of equal size. Model frozen; patching at inference. Decisive metric: target-accuracy restoration under bottleneck patching (recovered fraction of the Contention Cost), reported first, with the non-bottleneck patch as the specificity floor. Convincing: bottleneck patching restores >= 50% of the Contention Cost while the matched non-bottleneck patch restores < 15%. Indecision band: bottleneck restoration 25-50%, or non-bottleneck restoration 15-30%; reported as partial/non-specific localization. Negative result: bottleneck restoration < 25% or indistinguishable from the non-bottleneck patch refutes the located-bottleneck causal claim.

Experiment 6 (H-arbitration - active suppression over the bottleneck). Tests whether the model arbitrates contention and whether suppressing intruder co-activation recovers the target (and amplifying it worsens the cost). Recover an intruder-co-activation direction and steer to SUPPRESS the intruder's presence in the shared components during the contention run; conversely AMPLIFY it, over a dose-response. Also test the Adaptive-Control-Hypothesis analogue: a "single-language framing" vs an "explicit dual-language framing" prompt. Model frozen; only the steering vector / framing varies. Decisive metric: target-accuracy recovery under suppression (reported first), then added cost under amplification, with output-language fidelity and fluency (perplexity) reported alongside. Convincing: suppression recovers >= 10 pp of the Contention Cost with a monotone dose-response and < 5% perplexity change, amplification worsens cost monotonically, and dual-language framing raises the cost/arbitration demand relative to single-language framing. Indecision band: 5-10 pp recovery or non-monotone dose; reported as a weak arbitration handle, and we frame arbitration as a functional effect rather than a dedicated circuit. Negative result: < 5 pp recovery from suppression, or recovery only at fluency-breaking doses, refutes the active-arbitration claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Contention Cost could be confounded with generic context-length degradation or attention dilution rather than cross-lingual capacity contention; the equal-length same-language and non-linguistic-filler controls (Exp. 3) are the crucial dissociators, and the effect must exceed them to support the claim. 2. Probe/overlap-based bottleneck localization is correlational; the activation-patching restoration (Exp. 6) and suppression/amplification steering (Exp. 7) are required to promote 'located' to 'causal', with matched non-bottleneck controls for specificity. 3. Co-activation and typological distance may correlate, and both may track resource level; the near-low-resource vs far-high-resource contrast (Exp. 4) is designed to dissociate them, and we report multiple proxies. 4. 'Active arbitration' is a strong claim; suppression-helps evidence is consistent with, but not proof of, a dedicated control mechanism, so we frame arbitration as a functional (steering-testable) effect rather than a named circuit unless localization is clean. 5. Strong models may show little contention on easy items, shrinking the effect; harder items, higher intruder doses, and low-resource targets provide power, and even a bounded effect is informative. 6. Tokenization/length differ across scripts, complicating equal-length matching; we match by token count and report both token and item counts. 7. Steering may trade recovery for fluency or output-language fidelity; we report all three. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families across two task types address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) cross-lingual interference in multilingual LLMs is not just static shared-parameter overlap but a dynamic inference-time capacity-contention effect triggered by keeping a second language active; (2) the contention is concentrated in shared middle-layer components that can be causally protected/steered; (3) there is weak active arbitration/suppression analogous to bilingual cognitive control; (4) the effect is dose-dependent and scales with intruder strength/relatedness. Relative to prior work, the shared-bottleneck idea is partly anticipated by shared/specific neuron and curse-of-multilinguality work, but the proposed setting—forcing an intruding language context and measuring dose-response at inference time—could be genuinely new. The closest prior family is static region/neuron/subspace analyses and training-time interference work; the delta is moving from static attribution to a causal, temporally ordered, language-contingent inference-time paradigm plus intervention tests. Novelty is therefore more in the finding/setting/mechanism than in the existence of shared components themselves.
revision_notes: State explicitly which part is new versus inherited from shared-neuron / curse-of-multilinguality work: dynamic inference-time contention and arbitration, not shared bottlenecks per se.
Tighten the novelty claim around one primary hypothesis to avoid looking like a bundle of adjacent interpretability ideas.
Define the exact operational criterion for 'active arbitration' so it is clearly distinct from generic robustness or prompt sensitivity.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether multilingual LLMs suffer target-language degradation when a competing language is kept active, and whether this reveals a shared, limited-capacity polyglot bottleneck with suppression-like control. People who would care: multilingual NLP, model interpretability, and cognitively inspired ML; possibly practitioners building multilingual assistants or routing/steering methods. If true, it could change how researchers think about multilingual interference from a static representational trade-off to a dynamic competition/control process, and it may motivate targeted interventions on shared components. The strongest one-line case: it explains when and why adding or maintaining multilingual context hurts downstream competence, and suggests causal fixes. That said, real-world reach is moderate: this is likely more of a research-interpretability result than a deployment-changing discovery, and the practical value depends on effect size and model generality. So what? If the result holds, serious researchers would likely cite it and explore control/steering; if it fails, the field would probably still keep working on static shared-representation accounts, so the practical decision impact is limited.

review.reasoning: The proposal is testable and reasonably grounded, but some claims are currently broader than the evidence plan can support. Main gaps: 'active arbitration' is a strong mechanistic claim that could be confounded by generic recency, context length, tokenization, or language-ID effects; the causal story from patching/steering to a limited shared bottleneck is plausible but not yet airtight; and the related work positioning is good but still somewhat broad-brush. Experiments are mostly feasible and better than average: controls, dose variation, typological proximity, patching, and steering are all appropriate. Missing pieces include stronger length/tokenization controls, permutation/randomization baselines, layer-by-layer ablations, model- and task-generalization tests, and negative controls for steering side effects. As written, this could become a solid ML paper if the effects are robust and the interventions cleanly causal; the minimum viable edits are to narrow the claim, pre-register the key causal contrasts, and add stronger confound controls.

Name: lexical_gap_substitution
Title: No Word for That: How Cross-Lingual Lexical Gaps Force Multilingual LLMs to Silently Substitute the Nearest Colexified Sense
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a shared, fine-grained conceptual representation, but when they must express a concept in a target language that has NO single-word lexeme for it (a lexical gap / colexification split), they resolve the gap through a locatable 'lexicalization gate' set by the output language: rather than paraphrasing, they often silently substitute the concept's nearest COLEXIFIED sense in that language (e.g. rendering a distinction the language lumps as a single coarser word), producing meaning-shifting errors. This substitution rate scales with how strongly the target language's lexicon colexifies the two senses (from CLICS), not with resource level, and is carried by a causally-manipulable representation separable from the concept content.
Related Work: Prior work shows multilingual LLMs form shared, linearly-alignable concept spaces where abstract concepts align better than concrete ones (Concept Space Alignment 2024; Semantic Hub 2024; When Meanings Meet 2026), and cross-lingual concept patching can flip polysemy sense selection and homograph translation. Cognitive-typology work quantifies cross-linguistic semantic (mis)alignment and colexification structure (Universal Structure of Lexical Semantics 2016; Semantic Alignment 2018; CLICS colexification database; lexical-gap/lacunae resources 2019/2024). However, ALL LLM concept-space work studies static alignment geometry or word-translation sense selection, and ALL lexical-gap work is descriptive-linguistic. NONE asks the sharp generation-time question: when the output language has NO lexeme for a needed concept, does the model paraphrase (preserving meaning) or silently collapse the concept onto the nearest colexified sense the language DOES lexicalize (an error), and is this a locatable, steerable lexicalization-gate failure driven by the target language's colexification structure? We uniquely turn cross-lingual lexical gaps and CLICS colexification into a controlled causal probe of the shared-vs-language-specific concept boundary, with an activation-patching + steering mechanism and a colexification-vs-resource dissociation.
Abstract: Languages do not carve meaning identically: some pack two senses into one word (colexification), and many concepts simply lack a single-word equivalent in a given language (a lexical gap). A model asked to express such a concept in a language that lacks a word for it faces a choice: paraphrase to preserve the distinction, or fall back on the nearest word the language does have. We investigate which multilingual LLMs do and why. We hypothesize that models compute a shared, fine-grained conceptual representation but resolve lexical gaps through a lexicalization gate set by the output language, and that when a concept is colexified in the target language the model tends to silently substitute the nearest colexified sense, shifting meaning. We build GAP-PROBE from CLICS colexification data and lexical-gap resources: for concept pairs that one language lexicalizes distinctly but another colexifies (e.g. hand/arm, tree/wood, blue/green splits, kin distinctions), we pose translation, paraphrase, and disambiguation tasks across 12+ languages and measure a per-language SILENT-SUBSTITUTION rate on identical concepts. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared fine-grained concept representation that transfers across languages even where the output collapses it; (ii) use activation patching to show the fine distinction is present internally while a separable lexicalization gate discards it; and (iii) recover a gate direction and steer it to make the model paraphrase (repair) or collapse (induce) without changing the underlying concept. We predict substitution tracks CLICS colexification strength, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Dataset GAP-PROBE (built from existing resources): from the CLICS colexification database (CLICS3; thousands of attested colexifications across ~3,000 varieties) and published lexical-gap/lacunae lists, assemble 40 concept pairs (A,B) that some languages lexicalize DISTINCTLY but others COLEXIFY into one word or leave GAPPED - classic cases (hand/arm, finger/toe, tree/wood, blue/green "grue", foot/leg, brother/older-brother, ice/snow) plus culture-specific gaps. For each of 12+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Perso-Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels, annotate each pair as distinctly-lexicalized / colexified / gapped and attach a CLICS-derived colexification-strength score. Three tasks per (pair, language): (a) TRANSLATION of a source sentence unambiguously about sense A; (b) PARAPHRASE/definition of the concept; (c) DISAMBIGUATION NLI ("the sentence is about A, not B - true/false?"). Distinctly-lexicalized items serve as controls (substitution should be near zero). All items native-speaker-validated (two per language); low-agreement items dropped and reported. Resource proxy = CC-100 share. Models (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference + steering, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 3 seeds (template and few-shot order).

Experiment 1 (H3 - silent substitution on lexical gaps). Tests whether, on concepts a language colexifies or lacks a word for, the model silently substitutes the nearest colexified sense rather than paraphrasing. Score each target output as (i) meaning-preserving (paraphrase/circumlocution that keeps the A/B distinction), (ii) SILENT SUBSTITUTION (uses the colexified coarser word, dropping the distinction, without flagging it), or (iii) wrong-sense (picks B), by native-speaker-validated rubric plus an automatic check of whether the emitted word colexifies B. Decisive metric: SILENT-SUBSTITUTION RATE on colexified/gapped items, contrasted with the rate on distinctly-lexicalized control items. Systems compared: against a translate-via-English baseline and an explicit "preserve the distinction" prompt. Convincing: substitution rate on colexified/gapped items exceeds the control rate by >= 20 percentage points in all three models, with inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa) >= 0.6 on the scoring. Indecision band: 8-20 pp gap; reported as a weak tendency, not the claimed silent-substitution regime. Negative result: gap < 8 pp (models paraphrase or flag the gap) refutes H3.

Experiment 2 (H4 - substitution tracks colexification strength, not resource). Tests whether substitution scales with the target language's CLICS colexification strength rather than its resource level. Regress per-item substitution rate on colexification strength and on the resource proxy. Designed contrast: a lower-resource language that lexicalizes the distinction vs a higher-resource language that colexifies it. Decisive metric: Spearman of substitution with colexification strength vs with the resource proxy (95% CIs), and the partial correlation with colexification controlling for resource. Convincing: substitution correlates with colexification strength (Spearman >= 0.4) and this survives partialling out resource, while the resource correlation is weaker. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.4 or the colexification correlation vanishing after resource control; reported as resource-confounded. Negative result: resource dominates and colexification adds nothing refutes H4.

Experiment 3 (H1 - shared fine-grained concept representation). Tests whether the A vs B distinction is represented internally even in languages whose OUTPUT collapses it. Train linear probes and read the logit lens at each layer to decode which sense (A vs B) the input is about, from mid-layer hidden states; evaluate cross-lingual transfer (train one language, test the rest). Contrast with a probe decoding the emitted coarse word. Probes are the only trainable parameters; base frozen; 3 probe-split seeds. Decisive metric: cross-lingual transfer accuracy of the fine-sense probe on languages whose surface output colexifies. Convincing: the fine-sense probe transfers with <= 10-point drop off in-language accuracy and stays well above chance on colexifying languages, while the emitted-word probe does not carry the fine distinction there. Indecision band: transfer drop 10-20 points; partial sharing, weak support for H1. Negative result: probe near chance on colexifying languages (drop > 20 points) refutes the shared-fine-concept claim.

Experiment 4 (H2 - a locatable, output-language-set lexicalization gate). Tests whether substitution is a gating step that discards a present distinction rather than a lost concept. For an item where the source preserves A/B but a target run silently substitutes: (a) activation-patch the mid-layer fine-grained concept representation across runs and confirm the distinction is present in the substituting run (patching changes the output little); (b) patch/steer the late components carrying the lexicalization decision and test whether the output switches to a distinction-preserving paraphrase. Specificity control = patching a matched non-gate site. Model frozen; patching at inference. Decisive metric: paraphrase-repair flip rate from late-gate patching (reported first), with concept-patch flip rate (should be low) and matched-site flip rate as controls. Convincing: late-gate patching produces a distinction-preserving output in >= 50% of substituting items, concept patching alone flips < 15% (distinction already present), and the matched site flips < 15%. Indecision band: gate-patch repair 25-50% or concept-patch repair 15-30% (distinction partly missing); mixed evidence, gating plus representational deficit. Negative result: gate-patch repair < 25% or concept patching itself repairs (distinction was absent) refutes the located-gate account.

Experiment 5 (H5 - a causally-manipulable gate separable from concept content). Tests whether a recovered gate direction repairs collapses and induces them, without changing the underlying concept. Recover a gate direction as the mean activation difference between paraphrase-preserving and collapse runs, pooled across languages; steer to (a) REPAIR collapses in colexifying languages (force paraphrase) and (b) INDUCE collapse in a distinctly-lexicalizing language, over a dose-response. Model frozen; only the vector varies; compare against explicit-instruction prompting and translate-via-English. Decisive metric: repair rate in colexifying languages (reported first), then induction rate in distinctly-lexicalizing ones, with concept-content specificity (the fine-sense probe's A vs B unchanged), fluency (perplexity), and output-language fidelity alongside. Convincing: steering raises meaning-preservation by >= 15 pp in colexifying languages AND induces >= 15 pp of collapse where the model was faithful, with monotone dose-response, preserved A/B content, and < 5% perplexity increase. Indecision band: 5-15 pp repair/induction or non-monotone dose; a weak causal handle. Negative result: < 5 pp effect or only at content/fluency-breaking doses refutes H5.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Distinguishing legitimate paraphrase from silent substitution across languages is nontrivial; we use native-speaker-validated rubrics, high-agreement items, and automatic checks (does the output word colexify B?), reporting inter-annotator agreement. 2. Probe decodability of the fine-grained distinction may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) are required to promote correlation to mechanism, plus the specificity check that the underlying concept (A vs B) is preserved. 3. Substitution could reflect the model genuinely lacking target-language circumlocution vocabulary (a capability gap) rather than a gate defect; the demonstration that the distinction is internally present (probe/patching) and that steering RECOVERS a paraphrase distinguishes gating from missing knowledge. 4. Colexification is graded and CLICS coverage is uneven for low-resource languages; we restrict to well-attested pairs, use multiple colexification-strength operationalizations, and report robustness. 5. The colexification-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report multiple resource proxies. 6. Strong models may paraphrase faithfully everywhere, shrinking the effect; even documenting faithful gap-handling (a clean shared-concept + paraphrase architecture) is informative, and the induction steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 7. Tokenization differs across scripts, complicating probing/output scoring; we use pooled-span or answer-token representations and report tokenization statistics. 8. Steering may trade meaning-preservation for fluency; we report both. 9. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) a generation-time lexical-gap phenomenon in multilingual LLMs where the model silently substitutes the nearest colexified sense instead of paraphrasing; (2) this effect scales with target-language colexification structure/strength rather than resource level; (3) there is a separable, steerable 'lexicalization gate' distinct from the underlying concept representation; (4) the effect can be measured across a curated multilingual lexical-gap dataset; (5) causal intervention can induce/repair the behavior. The closest prior family is lexical-gap detection from embeddings plus shared-concept-space / cross-lingual sense-selection work. The actual delta is meaningful: prior work is mostly representational or descriptive, while this proposal targets output behavior and causal control. That said, the shared-concept-space and steerability ingredients are already known, so novelty is concentrated in the specific behavioral finding and its typological scaling, not in the general mechanism shape. The claim is non-trivial but somewhat vulnerable to being a reframing of known polysemy/translation phenomena in a lexical-gap setting.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether multilingual LLMs preserve meaning when a target language lacks a one-word lexicalization, or instead collapse onto a colexified sense and thereby change meaning. That matters to MT, multilingual generation, evaluation, and semantic typology. If true, it would affect how people assess translation faithfulness, design decoding/revision strategies, and interpret multilingual representations. The strongest one-line case: it reveals a systematic meaning-shift failure mode at the interface between shared conceptual space and language-specific lexicalization, which is directly relevant to multilingual model reliability. So what? If the result is null, practitioners may treat lexical-gap cases as ordinary paraphrase limitations; if positive, serious researchers would likely add targeted tests and controls for lexicalized gaps and colexification effects. Uptake seems plausible because the issue is concrete, cross-lingual, and actionable. Real-world reach is moderate-to-strong via MT, assistants, and multilingual QA, though the task itself is somewhat specialized. The phenomenon value is high even if the proposed mechanism is simple.

If executed well, this is strong enough for a serious ML venue, but only if the behavioral definitions are tightened and the causal story is not overstated.
