Name: numeral_inversion_operand_binding
Title: Five-and-Twenty Plus Three: How Number-Word Inversion in the Query Language Reorders Operand Binding in Multilingual LLM Arithmetic
Short Hypothesis: Languages differ in whether spoken numerals are inverted (German 'fünfundzwanzig' = five-and-twenty for 25; Arabic) or non-inverted (English, Hebrew). We hypothesize that when a multilingual LLM reads a number written as words, the query language's inversion structure covertly sets the internal ORDER in which digit/operand magnitudes are bound before arithmetic, so that in inverted languages the model tends to bind the units-before-tens order it hears rather than the place-value order it must compute over. This produces systematic, direction-consistent arithmetic errors (e.g. transposition/carry errors) on word-form multi-digit and multi-operand problems that are ABSENT in the same problems posed in digits or in non-inverted languages, and the error rate scales with the language's degree of numeral inversion, not its resource level. The binding order is carried by a locatable, causally-manipulable representation separable from the magnitude content.
Related Work: Bilingualism research establishes that number-word inversion causally shapes arithmetic: inverted-language speakers are faster/more accurate when problems match their language's numeral order, and bilinguals flexibly adapt to L1 vs L2 order (Number word structure in first and second language, 2015; operand-order effects reflecting learning history in Chinese-educated adults, 2025; linguistic-arithmetic interaction in word problems, 2020). On the model side, arithmetic-interpretability work shows LLMs rely on positional information and pattern-matching rather than robust rule induction (Positional Description Matters 2023; Do LLMs Truly Grasp Addition 2025; Unraveling Arithmetic 2024), and that math word problems decompose into an abstract-then-compute mechanism (Can LLMs Reason Abstractly 2025). Cross-lingual reasoning work shows knowledge-free reasoning transfers well across languages (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024). However, ALL LLM arithmetic-interpretability work is monolingual (English digits) and studies digit positional encoding, and ALL number-word-inversion work is human cognitive-linguistics with no model-internal account. My own prior proposal on numeral morphology studied MAGNITUDE distortion from vigesimal words, a different axis. NONE tests whether the QUERY LANGUAGE'S INVERSION STRUCTURE reorders internal OPERAND/DIGIT BINDING during multi-digit/multi-operand arithmetic, nor gives a causal, steerable binding-order mechanism. We uniquely port the number-word-inversion arithmetic effect into multilingual mechanistic interpretability.
Abstract: Human languages disagree on the order of spoken numerals: German and Arabic say the units before the tens ('five-and-twenty' for 25), while English and Hebrew do not. A landmark bilingual finding is that this inversion causally shapes arithmetic performance, with speakers faster and more accurate when a problem's presentation matches their language's numeral order. We ask whether multilingual LLMs inherit this effect, and whether the query language's inversion structure covertly reorders how the model internally binds operands during arithmetic. We hypothesize that when numbers are given as words, an inverted query language biases the model toward a units-before-tens binding order that conflicts with the place-value order arithmetic requires, producing systematic transposition and carry errors that vanish when the identical problem is posed in digits or in a non-inverted language. We build INVERT-MATH: multi-digit addition and multi-operand word problems whose numbers are spelled out across inverted (German, Dutch, Danish, Arabic) and non-inverted (English, Hebrew, Chinese, Turkish) numeral languages, with matched digit-form controls. Behaviorally we measure a per-language inversion-error rate and its dose-response with numeral-inversion degree. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared magnitude representation and a separable binding-order signal that inherits the query language's inversion; (ii) use activation patching to show magnitude is correctly recovered while a binding-order representation is mis-set, localizing errors to an order-binding step; and (iii) recover a binding-order direction and steer it to repair inversion errors (or induce them in non-inverted languages) without changing the magnitudes. We predict errors track inversion degree, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Dataset INVERT-MATH (built from scratch): 500 multi-digit ADDITION items requiring carries (two- and three-digit operands where tens/units order matters, e.g. "twenty-seven plus forty-eight") and 200 short multi-operand WORD problems, numbers spelled out as WORDS. Each item is rendered in INVERTED numeral languages (German, Dutch, Danish, Arabic - units before tens) and NON-INVERTED ones (English, Hebrew, Chinese, Turkish), each with a matched DIGIT-form control (same numbers in Arabic numerals, same carrier sentence). Number-word rendering is native-speaker-validated; items with ambiguous morpheme segmentation are dropped and reported. Per language: a numeral-inversion-degree index (fully inverted / teens-only partially inverted / non-inverted) and a resource proxy (CC-100 share). Models (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference + steering, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 3 seeds (operand sampling and template).

Experiment 1 (H2 - inversion-specific arithmetic errors on word forms). Tests whether word-form arithmetic incurs transposition/carry errors in inverted languages that are absent in digit form and in non-inverted languages. Decisive metric: INVERSION-ERROR GAP = accuracy(digit control) - accuracy(word form), per language, and the rate of TRANSPOSITION errors (answer consistent with swapping an operand's tens and units) reported alongside carry errors. Systems compared: inverted vs non-inverted languages, word vs digit, plus a translate-numerals-to-digits prompt and an English word-form baseline. Convincing: the inversion-error gap in inverted languages exceeds that in non-inverted languages by >= 10 percentage points, the transposition-error rate is elevated specifically in inverted word forms, and digit controls are comparable across languages (gap < 3 pp). Indecision band: inverted-vs-non-inverted gap difference 3-10 pp, or transposition errors not preferentially in the inversion-predicted direction; reported as generic word-parsing difficulty, not an inversion effect. Negative result: no excess gap in inverted languages (< 3 pp) refutes H2.

Experiment 2 (H3 - error rate tracks inversion degree, not resource). Tests whether the error gap scales with numeral-inversion degree rather than resource. Regress the inversion-error gap and transposition rate on the inversion-degree index and on the resource proxy. Designed contrasts: a lower-resource inverted language (Danish) vs a higher-resource non-inverted one (Chinese); German (inverted, high-resource) vs Turkish (non-inverted, mid-resource). Decisive metric: Spearman of the error gap with inversion degree vs with the resource proxy (95% CIs) and the partial correlation with inversion controlling for resource. Convincing: the gap correlates with inversion degree (Spearman >= 0.4), surviving resource control, while resource alone does not order it. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.4 or inversion correlation vanishing after resource control; resource-confounded. Negative result: resource dominates and inversion adds nothing refutes H3.

Experiment 3 (H1 - shared magnitude vs query-language binding-order signal). Tests whether operand magnitudes are represented consistently across languages while a binding-order signal inherits the query language's inversion. Train linear probes and read the logit lens at each layer at the operand-final token to decode (i) each operand's true magnitude (anchored to digit-form runs) and (ii) the operand's tens-vs-units digit assignment / binding order; evaluate cross-lingual transfer. Probes are the only trainable parameters; base frozen; 3 probe-split seeds. Decisive metric: magnitude-probe cross-lingual transfer accuracy (should be high and language-consistent) and whether the binding-order probe predicts the MIS-ordered assignment specifically in inverted languages. Convincing: magnitude transfers with <= 10-point drop and is language-consistent, AND the binding-order probe recovers the inverted (units-before-tens) assignment in inverted languages at well above chance while recovering place-value order in non-inverted ones. Indecision band: magnitude transfer drop 10-20 points, or binding-order probe weakly language-dependent; partial support. Negative result: magnitude probe fails to transfer, or binding-order probe shows no language dependence, refutes H1.

Experiment 4 (H4 - errors localized to a binding-order step, magnitude preserved). Tests whether inversion errors are a wrong binding order over correct magnitudes. For an addition item solved correctly in digit/non-inverted form but erred in an inverted word form: (a) activation-patch the mid-layer magnitude representation across runs and confirm magnitudes are correctly present in the erring run (patching changes the answer little); (b) patch/steer the components carrying digit-position binding and test whether the answer corrects. Specificity control = patching a matched non-binding site. Model frozen; patching at inference. Decisive metric: correction rate from binding-order patching (reported first), with magnitude-patch correction (should be low) and matched-site correction as controls. Convincing: binding-order patching corrects >= 50% of erred items, magnitude patching alone corrects < 15% (magnitudes already present), and the matched site corrects < 15%. Indecision band: binding-patch correction 25-50% or magnitude-patch correction 15-30% (magnitude partly wrong); mixed evidence. Negative result: binding-patch correction < 25% or magnitude patching itself corrects (magnitude was wrong) refutes the binding-order localization.

Experiment 5 (H4 - a steerable binding-order representation separable from magnitude). Tests whether a recovered binding-order direction repairs inversion errors and induces them, without changing magnitudes. Recover a binding-order direction as the mean activation difference between correctly place-value-ordered and inverted-ordered runs, pooled across languages; steer to (a) REPAIR inversion errors in inverted-language word problems and (b) INDUCE transposition errors in non-inverted languages, over a dose-response. Model frozen; only the vector varies; compare against an explicit "read the number in place-value order" prompt and translate-to-digits. Decisive metric: arithmetic-accuracy repair in inverted languages (reported first), then induced-transposition rate in non-inverted ones, with magnitude-preservation specificity (operand-value probe unchanged), fluency (perplexity), reported alongside. Convincing: steering raises accuracy by >= 15 pp in inverted-language word problems AND induces >= 15 pp of transposition errors in non-inverted ones, monotone dose-response, magnitudes preserved, < 5% perplexity increase. Indecision band: 5-15 pp repair/induction or non-monotone dose; weak causal handle. Negative result: < 5 pp effect or only at fluency-breaking doses refutes H4.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Word-form arithmetic errors could stem from generic difficulty of parsing number words rather than an inversion-specific binding-order effect; the matched DIGIT controls (comparable across languages) and the transposition-error signature (tens/units specifically swapped, in the direction the language's inversion predicts) are the crucial dissociators, and non-inverted word-form languages serve as a further control. 2. Probe decodability of magnitude or binding order may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) are required to promote correlation to mechanism, plus the specificity check that operand magnitudes are preserved. 3. Tokenization of number words is uneven across languages and scripts and may itself split tens/units unevenly, confounding the effect; we curate items with clean morpheme boundaries, use operand-final/pooled representations, report tokenization statistics, and analyze partially-inverted teens separately. 4. The inversion-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts (German vs Chinese, Danish vs Turkish); we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the inversion-degree operationalization. 5. Strong models may resolve place value robustly regardless of spoken order, shrinking the effect; even documenting robust place-value binding (a clean shared-magnitude + order-invariant architecture) is an informative positive result, and the induction steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 6. Some 'errors' may reflect the model answering a different (mis-parsed) problem; we manually classify error types and restrict the causal analysis to clear transposition/carry cases. 7. Steering may trade arithmetic correctness for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families across two task families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims that would need to be novel: (1) numeral inversion in the query language causes multilingual LLMs to bind tens/units or operands in the spoken order rather than the place-value order during arithmetic over number words; (2) this produces direction-consistent arithmetic errors, especially transposition/carry-like errors, specifically for word-form inputs and not for digit-form controls; (3) the size of the effect scales with a language's inversion degree rather than mainly with language resource level; (4) the effect is mediated by a separable internal binding-order representation distinct from magnitude content; (5) that representation is causally manipulable via patching/steering to repair or induce errors. Relative to prior work, the closest family is LLM arithmetic interpretability showing digit-wise/base-10 internal structure and positional sensitivity, plus human cognitive studies on numeral inversion. The actual delta is substantial: moving from English digit arithmetic to multilingual number-word arithmetic conditioned by language-specific numeral syntax, and proposing a causal mechanistic account centered on operand-binding order. From the proposal text and search summary, this does appear to be a genuinely new finding/mechanism/setting combination rather than a simple benchmark extension. The setting is meaningfully different because number-word inversion is a linguistic structural feature absent from standard digit arithmetic studies, and the prediction of direction-specific transposition signatures is non-obvious. The strongest novelty is not merely the dataset, but the explanatory claim that query-language structure sets internal binding order and that this representation can be isolated and manipulated. Main caveat: some parts of the mechanism claim risk being an ambitious extension of known token-order/position effects, so the behavioral effect feels more clearly novel than the full causal internal story.

impact.reasoning: The underlying problem is whether multilingual LLMs perform arithmetic and quantitative reasoning robustly across languages, or whether superficial linguistic form distorts internal computation. Who cares: multilingual reasoning researchers, interpretability researchers, benchmark designers, model developers deploying systems in non-English settings, and cognitive-science-inspired ML audiences. The strongest one-line case is: if language-specific numeral syntax systematically changes arithmetic behavior in LLMs, then current claims of language-agnostic reasoning are overstated and multilingual evaluation/design must account for numeral structure. This is a real problem, not just a curiosity, because arithmetic and quantity understanding are foundational capabilities and multilingual deployment is widespread. On the 'so what?' test, if the result holds, serious researchers would likely change multilingual arithmetic evaluation protocols and perhaps training/data normalization practices; if it fails, that too is informative because it would suggest strong normalization across numeral languages. So the result is worth knowing either way.

review.reasoning: The proposal is interesting and unusually falsifiable, but as a strict ML reviewer I see several technical gaps. The core hypothesis is reasonably precise at the behavioral level: inverted numeral languages should show larger word-vs-digit gaps and direction-specific transposition errors. The mechanistic hypothesis is more slippery: 'binding-order representation' is evocative but underdefined, and the proposal does not yet specify enough to distinguish it from ordinary token-position features, parsing states, or attention routing. Related work positioning is decent, and the search summary supports the claimed gap, but the proposal should cite closest multilingual and numeral-representation baselines more concretely. The regression on inversion degree versus resource level is directionally good, yet with only a handful of languages the inference may be underpowered and confounded by script, tokenization, morphology, and training data quality. Digit controls are necessary but not sufficient: you also need non-arithmetic number-word controls, paraphrases with normalized order, transliterations, and tokenization-matched manipulations to isolate inversion from generic number-word difficulty. The mechanistic experiments need stronger controls: if patching a site changes output, that may reflect broad causal importance rather than a specific 'binding-order' variable. The proposal should predefine what counts as preserving magnitude while changing order, and should test whether the same sites matter in non-number word-order tasks. Narrative-wise, the story currently overreaches from a plausible behavioral phenomenon to a strong internal causal interpretation. If executed extremely well, this could be workshop-to-main-conference quality in multilingual reasoning or interpretability, but as written it needs tighter operationalization and stronger controls before it looks submission-ready for a serious ML venue.

Name: abstract_vs_surface_priming_channels
Title: Priming Across the Word-Order Divide: Two Competing Structural Channels Behind Cross-Lingual Structural Priming in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Cross-lingual structural priming in multilingual LLMs is carried by TWO coexisting, dissociable channels: an abstract, word-order-invariant structure representation and a surface token/order-copying channel. For typologically aligned language pairs both channels agree, but for word-order-divergent pairs (e.g. verb-final vs. verb-medial) they conflict, and the model's realized priming reflects whichever channel dominates. We predict (a) genuine abstract, order-inverting priming (a structure primed in one language raises the analogous structure in another even when the surface word orders differ), (b) that a locatable abstract-structure representation is causally responsible for this order-invariant transfer while a separate surface-copy channel drives order-matched priming, and (c) that the abstract channel's dominance scales with typological/word-order distance being bridged, and can be causally amplified to repair failed cross-lingual priming across divergent word orders.
Related Work: A rich line shows LLMs exhibit structural priming that behaviorally indexes abstract grammar (Sinclair et al. 2022; Prasad et al. 2019; Finding Structure in Language Models 2024) and cross-lingual priming that causally influences generation across languages (Structural Priming Demonstrates Abstract Grammatical Representations in Multilingual LMs 2023; Michaelov et al. 2023; RNN/Transformer Chinese-English priming 2024; acquisition dynamics 2023/2025). Human/connectionist work debates whether identical word order is required for cross-language priming (error-driven learning account, Kaan et al. 2021) and finds it is not. Mechanistic multilingual work shows shared syntactic subspaces (Universal Grammatical Relations in mBERT 2020), shared circuits for shared processes (The Same But Different 2024), and shared agreement neurons (Causal Analysis of Agreement Neurons 2022). ALL existing LLM priming work is BEHAVIORAL and treats priming as a single effect indexing 'abstract structure'; none dissociates an abstract order-invariant channel from a surface order-copying channel, none uses word-order-divergent pairs as a controlled instrument to separate them, and none provides a causal (patching + steering) account of which internal representation carries order-inverting cross-lingual priming. We uniquely turn cross-lingual priming into a two-channel diagnostic with a causal, steerable abstract-structure locus.
Abstract: Structural priming—where encountering a syntactic structure makes its reuse more likely—has become a key behavioral probe showing that multilingual LLMs share abstract grammatical representations across languages. But behavior alone cannot tell whether cross-lingual priming rides on a genuinely abstract, order-invariant representation of structure or on a shallower channel that copies surface token order. We propose that both channels coexist and can be dissociated by pitting them against each other: in language pairs with divergent word order (e.g. a verb-final prime language and a verb-medial target), abstract structural priming predicts the analogous construction should be primed despite different surface orders, whereas a surface-copy channel predicts priming only when orders match. We build a controlled cross-lingual priming suite over alternating constructions (dative, active/passive, genitive) across language pairs spanning aligned and divergent word orders, and measure order-invariant versus order-matched priming. Mechanistically, we (i) probe for an abstract construction representation that is shared and decodable across languages independent of surface order, (ii) use activation patching to test whether this abstract representation is causally sufficient to prime the analogous target structure across a word-order divide, while a separate surface-form representation drives order-matched priming, and (iii) recover an abstract-structure direction and steer it to repair cross-lingual priming that fails across divergent orders. We predict the abstract channel's contribution scales with the word-order distance being bridged and that steering it induces order-invariant priming without harming fluency. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Priming suite (adapted from the Prime-LM cross-lingual priming framework plus new templates): parallel prime-target items over three alternating constructions with clear structural variants - dative (double-object vs prepositional-object), voice (active vs passive), genitive (of- vs 's-type or cross-linguistic analogues) - 200 item templates per construction (600 total), each with a congruent, an incongruent, and a neutral prime. A prime is presented in a SOURCE language and a target continuation describing a NEW event is elicited in a TARGET language, forcing a construction choice. Language directions cover WORD-ORDER-ALIGNED pairs (English<->Spanish, both SVO) and WORD-ORDER-DIVERGENT pairs (Japanese/Korean/Hindi/Turkish verb-final <-> English/Spanish verb-medial), plus within-language priming as an upper-bound calibration. Lexical overlap and semantic similarity are controlled following Prime-LM factors, with no-overlap conditions. Templates native-speaker-validated for grammaticality; low-agreement items dropped and reported. Per-pair word-order/typological distance from lang2vec; resource proxy from CC-100. Models (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference + steering, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 3 seeds (item sampling and prime order).

Experiment 1 (H1/prediction-a - order-invariant vs order-matched priming coexist). Tests whether cross-lingual priming shows an abstract order-invariant component (present across divergent word orders) and a surface order-matched component (present only when orders match). Decisive metric: priming strength = log-odds increase of the target construction after a congruent prime vs an incongruent/neutral prime, decomposed into an ORDER-INVARIANT component (priming that persists across word-order-divergent pairs) and an ORDER-MATCHED component (priming that appears only for aligned pairs), per construction. Systems compared: divergent vs aligned pairs; within-language priming as the upper bound. Convincing: a significant positive order-invariant component across divergent pairs (log-odds shift with 95% CI excluding 0) AND a distinct order-matched component larger for aligned than divergent pairs, in all three models. Indecision band: order-invariant component present but small (log-odds shift 0-0.1) or CI touching 0; reported as weak abstract priming, not a clean two-channel picture. Negative result: no order-invariant component across divergent pairs (shift indistinguishable from 0) refutes the abstract channel; no order-matched excess for aligned pairs refutes the surface channel.

Experiment 2 (prediction-c - abstract-channel share scales with word-order distance). Tests whether the abstract channel's relative contribution rises (or surface-copy fails) as the word-order gap grows. Correlate the order-invariant priming magnitude and the abstract:surface ratio with lang2vec word-order distance between prime and target. Dissociate from resource via matched contrasts (a divergent low-resource pair vs an aligned high-resource pair). Decisive metric: Spearman of abstract-channel share with word-order distance (95% CIs), partialled for resource. Convincing: abstract-channel share rises with word-order distance (Spearman >= 0.4) and survives resource control. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.4 or vanishing after resource control; reported as suggestive. Negative result: no relationship (< 0.2) refutes prediction (c)'s scaling claim.

Experiment 3 (H1 - a shared, order-invariant abstract construction representation). Tests whether an abstract construction identity is decodable across languages independent of surface order. Train linear probes and read the logit lens at each layer to decode abstract construction identity (e.g. dative-DO vs dative-PO) from post-prime hidden states; evaluate cross-lingual transfer (train one language's primes, decode another's) and invariance to surface order. Contrast with a surface-order probe (which token order appeared). Probes are the only trainable parameters; base frozen; 3 probe-split seeds. Decisive metric: cross-lingual, order-invariant transfer accuracy of the abstract-construction probe. Convincing: the abstract probe transfers across languages and across word orders with <= 10-point drop off in-language accuracy and well above chance, while the surface-order probe does not carry construction identity across divergent orders. Indecision band: transfer drop 10-20 points; partial sharing. Negative result: abstract probe near chance across orders (drop > 20 points) refutes a shared order-invariant representation.

Experiment 4 (prediction-b - causal channel dissociation). Tests whether the abstract representation is causally sufficient to prime across a word-order divide while the surface representation drives only order-matched priming. (a) Abstract-channel sufficiency: extract the mid-layer abstract construction representation from a divergent-order source prime and patch it into a neutral target-language run; test whether it primes the analogous target construction WITHOUT forcing the source's surface order. (b) Surface-channel test: patch the surface-order representation and test whether it drives order-matched priming but misfires across divergent orders. Model frozen; patching at inference; specificity = matched non-construction site. Decisive metric: construction-choice shift induced by the abstract patch across the divide (log-odds), reported first, with output order-fidelity and the matched-site shift as controls. Convincing: the abstract patch induces the analogous construction across divergent orders (log-odds shift with CI excluding 0) without copying source order, the surface patch induces order-matched priming that fails across divergence, and the matched site does neither. Indecision band: abstract-patch shift positive but small (0-0.1 log-odds) or CI touching 0; weak causal support. Negative result: abstract patch produces no cross-divide priming refutes prediction (b).

Experiment 5 (prediction-c - steering the abstract channel repairs failed cross-lingual priming). Tests whether amplifying a recovered abstract-structure direction repairs priming that fails across divergent orders (and can induce a construction unprompted). Recover an abstract construction direction as the mean activation difference between the two construction variants, pooled across languages and orders; steer during target generation, over a dose-response. Model frozen; only the vector varies; compare against explicit-instruction prompting and within-language priming. Decisive metric: increase in order-invariant priming (log-odds) for previously-failing divergent pairs (reported first), then unprompted induction rate, with grammaticality/fluency (perplexity) and specificity (non-target constructions unchanged) alongside. Convincing: steering raises order-invariant priming by >= 0.2 log-odds on failing divergent pairs with a monotone dose-response, preserves grammaticality, and < 5% perplexity increase. Indecision band: 0.05-0.2 log-odds gain or non-monotone dose; weak handle. Negative result: < 0.05 log-odds gain or repair only at grammaticality-breaking doses refutes the abstract-channel steering claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Cross-lingual priming may be dominated by lexical/semantic overlap rather than structure; we control lexical overlap and semantic similarity (Prime-LM style) and include no-overlap conditions to isolate abstract structure. 2. Probe decodability of an 'abstract construction' representation may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used channel; the activation-patching sufficiency test (Exp. 5) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) are required to promote correlation to mechanism, with order-fidelity and specificity checks. 3. The two-channel dissociation may be fuzzy—real behavior could be a graded mixture rather than clean channels; we present the abstract vs. surface contribution as a continuous decomposition and report effect sizes rather than forcing a binary. 4. Eliciting a clean construction choice in the target language across divergent-order languages is nontrivial; we use native-speaker-validated templates, constrained elicitation, and grammaticality checks, and analyze order-aligned vs. divergent pairs separately. 5. Strong models may show robust order-invariant priming everywhere (only an abstract channel), which would simplify the picture—still an informative positive result establishing genuine abstract structural sharing, and the steering/patching still localizes it. 6. Priming magnitudes can be small and noisy; we aggregate over many items/constructions and report confidence intervals, and use within-language priming as a calibration upper bound. 7. Tokenization and length differ across scripts/orders, confounding probability comparisons; we use log-odds between minimally-different construction variants (length-matched where possible) and report tokenization statistics. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families across multiple constructions and language pairs address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims that would need to be novel: (1) cross-lingual structural priming in multilingual LLMs is not a unitary effect but the sum of two dissociable channels: an abstract, word-order-invariant structural channel and a surface token/order-copying channel; (2) word-order-divergent language pairs can be used as an instrument to behaviorally separate these channels because the two channels make conflicting predictions there; (3) there exists a locatable internal representation/circuit causally responsible for order-invariant cross-lingual transfer, distinct from a surface-form/order representation driving order-matched priming; (4) the relative contribution of the abstract channel scales with typological/word-order distance; (5) steering the abstract channel can repair weak priming across divergent pairs. The proposal does not appear novel on the basic finding that abstract cross-lingual priming can survive different word orders: the search summary says this is already shown behaviorally in prior multilingual LLM priming work, and human literature also supports it. The genuine novelty therefore lives mainly in the decomposition/mechanism claim, the use of divergent word-order pairs as a diagnostic setting, and the causal mechanistic account with patching/steering. That is a meaningful delta, but it is also narrower than the proposal's framing suggests. Relative to its own related work, the core two-channel dissociation is non-trivial and not just an obvious benchmark extension, though it is adjacent to existing behavioral priming plus multilingual syntax-circuit interpretability. Closest prior family: multilingual structural priming papers showing abstract cross-lingual priming behaviorally, plus mechanistic multilingual syntax papers showing shared syntactic subspaces/units. Actual delta: not discovering order-invariant priming per se, but attempting to separate abstract vs surface channels and causally assign them to different internal representations.

Narrative-wise, the story currently bundles behavioral replication, decomposition, mechanistic localization, causal sufficiency, and steering repair into one proposal; that breadth makes each piece less defensible. If executed extremely well, the contribution could be serious-venue worthy, but as written it reads as high-risk/high-variance and would need tighter claims and stronger identification to be submission-ready.

Name: paraphrase_controlled_inconsistency
Title: Is Cross-Lingual Inconsistency Special? Using Within-Language Paraphrase Variation to Isolate the Language-Transition Component of Multilingual Factual Instability
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual factual inconsistency has two additive components: a language-agnostic instability that also causes a model to answer differently across paraphrases of the SAME language, and a genuinely language-specific instability introduced at the late-layer language-transition stage. We hypothesize (a) that a large, previously-unmeasured fraction of what is reported as 'cross-lingual inconsistency' is actually this baseline paraphrase instability rather than anything language-specific; (b) that the residual, language-specific component is causally localized to a distinct late-layer transition locus separable from the mid-layer concept computation; and (c) the size of the residual (not the total) is what scales with script/typological distance, while the paraphrase-baseline component does not.
Related Work: A wave of recent work attributes cross-lingual factual inconsistency to a late-layer 'language transition' failure over a shared concept space (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Paths Not Taken 2025; On the Entity-Level Alignment 2025; Are Knowledge and Reference Cross-Lingually Consistent 2025; Language-Specific Latent Process 2025), and proposes fixes (linear shortcut, translation-difference vectors, SubSub/SubInj, steering to a shared space). Separately, LLMs are known to be highly unstable to meaning-preserving surface changes WITHIN a language (Prompt-Format Sensitivity 2023; RoParQ 2025). Crucially, ALL cross-lingual consistency work compares one prompt per language and implicitly treats every observed disagreement as language-caused, never subtracting the model's baseline within-language paraphrase instability. No prior work measures the paraphrase-controlled residual, tests whether the celebrated 'language-transition' locus explains the residual specifically (rather than total inconsistency), or checks whether existing fixes reduce the residual or merely the paraphrase-baseline. We contribute this decomposition, a causal locus test on the residual, and a re-evaluation of prior interventions against the correct baseline.
Abstract: Multilingual language models give different factual answers to the same question asked in different languages, and a growing literature explains this via a late-layer 'language transition' over a shared, language-agnostic concept space. But these studies compare a single prompt per language and treat every disagreement as language-caused, ignoring that the same models also answer inconsistently across meaning-preserving paraphrases within a single language. We ask a sharp question: once we subtract this baseline paraphrase instability, how much cross-lingual inconsistency is genuinely language-specific, and is the language-transition mechanism responsible for that residual rather than for the total? We introduce a paraphrase-controlled decomposition: for each fact we measure within-language answer variability across multiple paraphrases in each language, and define the language-specific residual as cross-lingual disagreement in excess of the pooled within-language baseline. Behaviorally, we predict a large fraction of reported cross-lingual inconsistency is baseline paraphrase noise, and that only the residual scales with script/typological distance. Mechanistically, we test whether the late-layer transition locus (via logit-lens and activation patching) causally explains the residual specifically: patching mid-layer concept representations should fix paraphrase-baseline errors in any language, whereas the residual should require correcting the late-layer transition. Finally we re-evaluate published fixes (linear shortcut, translation-difference vectors, SubInj) against the correct baseline, testing whether they reduce the language-specific residual or merely the paraphrase-agnostic component. Experiments span mLAMA/BMLAMA across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B, sharpening what is and is not special about cross-lingual factual instability.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Data (existing, adapted): factual QA from mLAMA/BMLAMA (parallel templated facts; BMLAMA-53 supplies parallel items across 53 languages). Use 1,000 facts that exist in all chosen 15+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Perso-Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels. For each fact in each language, generate K=5 meaning-preserving paraphrase templates, validated by back-translation and native-speaker spot checks; low-agreement paraphrases dropped and reported. This yields both within-language (across the 5 paraphrases) and cross-language variants for every fact. Per-language typological/script distance to the dominant language (English) from lang2vec; resource proxy from CC-100. Models (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference + light patching, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. Answer matching is alias-aware with answer-span normalization. 3 seeds (paraphrase sampling).

Experiment 1 (claim-a - how much cross-lingual inconsistency is really paraphrase baseline). Tests whether a large fraction of reported cross-lingual inconsistency is baseline within-language paraphrase instability. For each fact compute: (a) WITHIN-LANGUAGE instability = answer-disagreement rate across the 5 paraphrases within each language, averaged over languages; (b) TOTAL cross-lingual inconsistency = disagreement across languages using one canonical prompt each (matching prior single-prompt protocols); (c) LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC RESIDUAL = cross-lingual disagreement across paraphrase-matched prompts minus the pooled within-language baseline. Decisive metric: the fraction of total inconsistency attributable to the paraphrase baseline vs the residual, per model. Convincing: the paraphrase baseline accounts for >= 30% of what the single-prompt protocol reports as cross-lingual inconsistency, in all three models, establishing that a substantial share is not language-specific. Indecision band: 15-30%; reported as a non-trivial but modest overcount. Negative result: baseline < 15% of total (cross-lingual inconsistency is overwhelmingly language-specific) refutes claim (a) - itself a clean, publishable vindication of the language-transition narrative on the correct baseline.

Experiment 2 (claim-c - only the residual scales with distance). Tests whether the language-specific residual, not the paraphrase baseline, tracks script/typological distance. Correlate each of (i) total inconsistency, (ii) paraphrase baseline, and (iii) residual with lang2vec typological/script distance to English. Decisive metric: Spearman of the residual with distance vs Spearman of the paraphrase baseline with distance (95% CIs). Convincing: the residual correlates with distance (Spearman >= 0.4) while the paraphrase baseline does not (|Spearman| < 0.2), and the total's apparent distance-dependence is driven by the residual. Indecision band: residual Spearman 0.2-0.4, or the baseline also correlating (0.2-0.4); reported as partial separation. Negative result: the paraphrase baseline correlating with distance as strongly as the residual, or the residual not correlating at all, refutes claim (c).

Experiment 3 (claim-b - concept vs late-layer transition locus by error type). Tests whether paraphrase-baseline errors are fixable at the mid-layer concept stage (any language) while the language-specific residual specifically requires correcting the late-layer transition. Replicate the mid-layer-concept / late-layer-transition split via logit lens per model first. For PARAPHRASE-BASELINE errors (a fact correct under one paraphrase, wrong under another, same language), patch the mid-layer concept representation from the correct run into the wrong run and measure recovery. For RESIDUAL (language-specific) errors, test whether mid-layer concept patching alone recovers the answer or whether correcting the late-layer transition (a translation-difference / language-transition vector) is additionally required. Model frozen; patching at inference. Decisive metric: recovery rate by error type and patch type. Convincing: paraphrase-baseline errors recover >= 50% from mid-layer concept patching regardless of language, while residual errors recover < 20% from concept patching alone but >= 50% once the late-layer transition is corrected. Indecision band: residual concept-patch recovery 20-40%; reported as a partially-shared locus. Negative result: residual errors recovering from mid-layer concept patching as well as baseline errors refutes the distinct-late-locus claim (b).

Experiment 4 (claim-b - locus separability). Tests that the components fixing paraphrase-baseline errors and those fixing residual errors are distinct. Quantify overlap (Jaccard) over the identified layers/heads/directions whose patching fixes each error type. Model frozen. Decisive metric: Jaccard overlap between the baseline-fixing and residual-fixing component sets. Convincing: Jaccard <= 0.3 (largely disjoint), with the residual-fixing set concentrated in later layers than the baseline-fixing set. Indecision band: Jaccard 0.3-0.5; reported as partial separability. Negative result: Jaccard > 0.5 (the same components fix both) refutes the separability claim.

Experiment 5 (claim-b - prior fixes act on the residual, corroborating the transition locus). Tests whether published cross-lingual-consistency fixes reduce the language-specific residual (as a language-transition intervention should) rather than merely the paraphrase baseline. Apply, faithfully re-implemented, the linear-shortcut (bypassing final layers), the translation-difference vector, and the English-subject-injection (SubInj) fixes; measure each fix's effect separately on the paraphrase baseline and on the residual. Model frozen except as each fix prescribes. Decisive metric: per-fix reduction of the residual vs reduction of the paraphrase baseline (percentage points). Convincing: at least one late-layer-targeted fix reduces the residual by >= 10 pp while leaving the paraphrase baseline largely unchanged (< 5 pp), showing the residual is the genuinely language-transition-addressable component. Indecision band: residual reduction 5-10 pp or comparable reduction of both components; reported as a general-robustness rather than transition-specific effect. Negative result: fixes reducing only the paraphrase baseline and not the residual would indicate they do not address a language-specific transition, qualifying claim (b).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Paraphrase quality across languages is uneven; low-quality paraphrases could inflate the within-language baseline and understate the residual. We validate paraphrases via back-translation and native-speaker checks and report sensitivity to K and to paraphrase-quality filtering. 2. Answer matching across languages/scripts is noisy (aliases, transliterations); we use alias-aware matching and last-token/answer-span normalization and report robustness. 3. It is possible the paraphrase baseline is small and cross-lingual inconsistency IS mostly language-specific; this would refute claim (a) but is itself a valuable, publishable clarification that legitimizes the language-transition narrative on the correct baseline. 4. Logit-lens/patching localization may be diffuse; we report degree of localization honestly and require the recovery-by-error-type contrast (Exp. 4) rather than mere layer identification. 5. The concept-vs-transition split may not be crisp in all models; we validate it per model before the locus test. 6. Prior fixes may interact with our paraphrase set differently than their original setups; we replicate them faithfully and report both baseline and residual effects. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims that would need to be novel: (1) the observed cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual LLMs decomposes into a within-language paraphrase instability component plus a language-transition-specific residual; (2) prior evaluations over-attribute total disagreement to language because they use one prompt per language and do not subtract a within-language paraphrase baseline; (3) the late-layer language-transition mechanism established in prior work explains the residual specifically, not necessarily the total inconsistency; (4) only the residual, not the paraphrase-baseline component, should scale with script/typological distance; (5) previously proposed interventions should be re-evaluated by their effect on residual vs baseline. From the proposal plus search summary, the closest prior family is the recent multilingual factual consistency / language-transition literature (e.g., Lost in Multilinguality and follow-ons), with separate prior work on within-language prompt/paraphrase sensitivity. The actual delta is not a brand-new mechanism from scratch, but a new decomposition and measurement protocol that connects two previously separate literatures and potentially corrects a confound in how the effect has been measured. That is a real methodological and conceptual novelty. Relative to the proposal's own related work, the central claim is non-trivial: 'subtract the paraphrase baseline' sounds simple in retrospect, but the search summary indicates this exact control has not been done, and the downstream mechanistic reinterpretation is meaningful. The mechanistic part is less novel than the decomposition itself because it largely re-tests an existing late-layer transition hypothesis under a corrected label partition. So the novelty mainly lives in the finding/problem framing, evaluation methodology, and reinterpretation of an existing mechanism, rather than in inventing a wholly new model or theory.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is factual inconsistency across languages in multilingual LLMs, specifically whether reported cross-lingual disagreement is truly caused by language transfer failures or partly by ordinary prompt/paraphrase instability that would occur even within a single language. Who cares: multilingual LLM evaluation researchers, factuality and reliability researchers, interpretability researchers studying multilingual representations, and teams building multilingual assistants or QA systems. If the result holds, downstream work would likely change evaluation protocols, reinterpret prior cross-lingual inconsistency numbers, and target interventions more precisely at residual language-specific failures rather than all disagreement. Strongest one-line case: this could separate a genuine multilingual failure mode from generic prompt instability, thereby correcting what the field thinks is broken and how it measures progress. On the 'so what?' test: yes, if a large share of reported cross-lingual inconsistency disappears after paraphrase control, serious researchers would change both their claims and benchmarks; if instead the residual remains large, that cleanly strengthens the current language-transition narrative. Either outcome is informative. The problem is important rather than niche because multilingual factual reliability is central to globally deployed LLMs, though this is still more likely to shift research methodology than directly transform end-user products. Uptake/citation potential is solid because benchmark and evaluation corrections are widely cited when they expose confounds. Direction-shifting potential is moderate-to-high: it could recalibrate an active subfield's causal story. Real-world reach is indirect but real through evaluation practice and model debugging. Even if the method is simple, the phenomenon value is high because it tests whether a widely discussed effect is partially artifact.

review.reasoning: This is a strong idea but currently has several technical and inferential vulnerabilities. The biggest logical gap is the decomposition itself: the proposal assumes a pooled within-language paraphrase baseline can be subtracted from cross-lingual disagreement to yield a language-specific residual, but it does not justify identifiability. Cross-lingual prompting may interact with paraphrase sensitivity non-additively, so the 'residual' may not cleanly isolate a causal language-transition component. The hypothesis is reasonably falsifiable, with thresholds and directional predictions, but some thresholds look arbitrary (>=30%, Spearman >=0.4, patch recovery >=50%, overlap <=0.3) and are not statistically motivated. Related work is fairly specific and well positioned. Experimental design is mostly feasible, but paraphrase generation/quality control is a major source of noise, especially across 15+ languages; native-speaker spot checks may be too weak for a paper whose central claim depends on meaning preservation. Another concern is answer matching and alias normalization across scripts, which can easily dominate measured disagreement. The mechanistic experiments are the weakest part: activation patching and logit lens can suggest loci, but the proposal overstates causal separability between 'concept computation' and 'late language transition.' Recovery thresholds by error type are unlikely to map cleanly onto those categories, and patching across paraphrase conditions may reflect generic robustness rather than concept-vs-transition modularity. Re-evaluating prior fixes is useful, but fair implementation details matter a lot. Missing controls include: English-only canonical-vs-paraphrase controls matched for prompt length/format; translationese controls to distinguish paraphrase quality from language effects; interaction analysis testing whether paraphrase instability differs systematically by language rather than being 'language-agnostic'; confidence intervals and hierarchical variance decomposition over fact/language/model/prompt; and human validation of a subset of residual cases. Narrative-wise, the story is compelling but slightly overclaimed where it says the residual is 'causally localized' to a distinct late-layer transition locus; the proposal as written is more likely to provide evidence consistent with differential localization than a crisp causal separation. If executed well, the contribution could be strong enough for a serious ML venue, especially as an evaluation/methodology paper with mechanistic analysis, but only if the decomposition is formalized and validated carefully. Minimum viable edits: tighten the estimand, reduce overclaiming on causality, add stronger paraphrase validation and statistical analysis, and make the controls sufficient to rule out paraphrase-generation artifacts.

Name: depth_budget_truncation
Title: Running Out of Layers: Cross-Lingual Errors as Truncated Concept Computation Under a Fixed Depth Budget
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs allocate the same fixed number of layers to every language, but low-resource and typologically distant languages require MORE layers to finish computing a concept; consequently their concept computation is frequently TRUNCATED by the fixed depth budget before it converges, and this truncation — not missing knowledge — causes a large fraction of cross-lingual errors. The required-depth deficit scales with typological/script distance and resource level, and errors are causally recoverable by granting extra late-layer compute (looping late layers) without any retraining.
Related Work: Probing work shows concepts become decodable at different depths depending on complexity ('Concept Depth' 2024) and that low-resource languages exhibit flatter, shallower layer-wise probing trends than high-resource ones (Cross-Language Probing 2024), and that difficulty is encoded language-agnostically early then language-specifically late ('Shared Geometry of Difficulty' 2026). Cross-Layer Transcoder and latent-language work localize a shared middle-layer space with lossy late-layer decoding (Tracing Multilingual Representations 2025; MALT 2025), and DAMA (2026) reports a U-shaped adaptability pattern in speech ASR. ALL of these are correlational (where a concept is decodable, how well probes align by layer) or propose fine-tuning/adaptation fixes. NONE reframes the layer-wise gap as a CAUSAL compute-deadline problem: that the fixed layer budget TRUNCATES an in-progress concept computation for languages that need more depth, that this truncation (not absent knowledge) is what produces the error, or that granting extra inference-time depth to just those items causally recovers the answer. We contribute this compute-budget-truncation reframing, a per-item 'required depth' measurement, a causal early-exit/late-layer-looping test, and a training-free depth-budget intervention.
Abstract: Multilingual language models answer questions far more reliably in high-resource, typologically close languages, and interpretability work has shown that concepts become decodable at different layer depths across languages. But this has been treated as a correlational fact about representation geometry. We propose a causal, resource-based reframing: transformers apply a fixed number of layers to every input, yet distant, low-resource languages need MORE layers to finish computing a concept, so their computation is often truncated by the depth budget before it converges — the model 'runs out of layers.' Under this view, many cross-lingual errors are not missing knowledge but unfinished computation. We measure, per item and per language, the 'required depth' at which the correct answer first stabilizes via logit-lens/early-exit trajectories, and define a Truncation Gap as the fraction of items whose answer converges only in layers deeper than the model has, or would if given more. We test three claims: (1) required depth is systematically greater for distant/low-resource languages on identical facts, and the excess predicts errors; (2) errors on truncated items are causally distinguished from knowledge failures — early-exiting a high-resource run at the low-resource run's shallower effective depth reproduces the error, and, crucially, granting extra late-layer compute (looping the final transformer layers) at inference recovers correct answers specifically on high-required-depth items; and (3) the required-depth deficit and recovery scale with typological/script distance and resource level. Experiments span mLAMA/BMLAMA factual QA and MGSM reasoning across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. The work recasts the multilingual gap as a depth-budget truncation phenomenon with a cheap, training-free inference-time fix.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Data (existing, used as is): parallel factual QA from mLAMA/BMLAMA-53 (1,000 facts present in all chosen languages) and multilingual grade-school math from MGSM (250 problems; its 10-11 languages for the reasoning arm), so the SAME item is posed in every language. Languages span Latin/Cyrillic/Perso-Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels. Models of differing depth (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference only, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B (32 layers), Aya-23-8B (32 layers), Qwen2-7B (28 layers). Layer-wise readout by logit lens and a tuned lens (the lens's affine map is the only trained parameter, per layer). Per-language typological/script distance from lang2vec; resource proxy from CC-100. Answer matching alias-aware, last-token/answer-span. 3 seeds (item sampling).

Experiment 1 (H1 - distant/low-resource languages need more layers for the same concept). Tests whether required depth is systematically greater for distant/low-resource languages on IDENTICAL facts. For each (item, language) record the CONVERGENCE DEPTH: the shallowest layer after which the top-ranked answer token becomes and stays correct through the final layer (stability judged over the last several layers). Decisive metric: mean convergence depth per language on the shared item set, compared across the resource/distance groups. Convincing: distant/low-resource languages have mean convergence depth deeper than close/high-resource ones by >= 3 layers on the same facts, consistently across models. Indecision band: 1-3 layers deeper; reported as a weak depth shift. Negative result: convergence depth not deeper for distant languages (< 1 layer) refutes H1.

Experiment 2 (H3 - required-depth deficit scales with distance and resource). Tests whether the depth deficit tracks typological/script distance and resource level. Define per-language mean required depth and the TRUNCATION GAP = fraction of items whose answer converges only in the last few layers or is still rising/unconverged at the final layer (right-censored). Correlate both with lang2vec distance and the resource proxy; designed contrast: a distant-but-well-covered language vs a close-but-sparse one to partly separate the axes. Decisive metric: Spearman of required depth / Truncation Gap with distance and with resource (95% CIs). Convincing: both correlate (Spearman >= 0.4) with distance and with resource. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.4; reported as suggestive. Negative result: no correlation (< 0.2) refutes H3.

Experiment 3 (H2 - shallow budget causally reproduces the low-resource error). Tests whether truncation, not missing knowledge, causes the error. Take facts answered CORRECTLY in a high-resource language with convergence depth d_hi; force EARLY EXIT of the high-resource run at the shallower effective depth d_lo observed for a low-resource language and test whether the high-resource answer degrades to the low-resource-style error. Specificity: early-exiting at d_hi should not degrade. Model frozen; early exit via the tuned lens at inference. Decisive metric: degradation rate induced by early exit at d_lo (reported first), with the d_hi early-exit degradation as the specificity floor. Convincing: early exit at d_lo degrades >= 50% of previously-correct high-resource answers while early exit at d_hi degrades < 10%. Indecision band: 25-50% degradation at d_lo; reported as partial support for the budget account. Negative result: < 25% degradation (shallow budget alone does not reproduce the error) refutes the truncation-causes-error claim.

Experiment 4 (H2 - truncation-type vs knowledge-type errors dissociate). Tests the crucial separation between unfinished computation and absent knowledge. Partition low-resource errors into TRUNCATION-type (the fact is answered correctly in the high-resource language, so the knowledge exists; the low-resource error co-occurs with a late/unconverged trajectory) vs KNOWLEDGE-type (wrong in the high-resource language too). Model frozen. Decisive metric: the difference in late-layer-looping recovery (from Exp. 5) between truncation-type and knowledge-type errors; here we first establish the partition sizes and that trajectory lateness predicts truncation-type membership. Convincing: truncation-type errors are a substantial share (>= 30% of low-resource errors) and are marked by significantly later/unconverged trajectories than knowledge-type errors. Indecision band: truncation-type 15-30%; reported as a smaller-than-claimed contribution. Negative result: truncation-type < 15% or trajectory lateness not distinguishing the two types refutes the truncation-vs-knowledge dissociation central to H2.

Experiment 5 (H4 - extra late-layer compute recovers truncated answers, training-free). Tests whether granting extra depth by LOOPING the final k transformer layers at inference recovers correct answers specifically on high-required-depth (truncation-type) items. Feed the last block's residual stream back through the last k blocks one or more times on the low-resource/distant run; dose-response over loop iterations and over k (last-1 vs last-k). Model frozen; no weights changed. Compare against a naive "add CoT tokens" baseline, translate-to-English, and a control that loops RANDOM blocks. Decisive metric: accuracy gain on high-Truncation-Gap items (reported first), split by error type, with output-language fidelity, fluency (perplexity), and specificity (already-converged items unchanged) alongside. Convincing: late-layer looping recovers >= 15 pp on truncation-type items, near-zero (< 5 pp) on knowledge-type items and on already-converged items, exceeds the random-block control, with a coherent dose-response and < 5% perplexity change. Indecision band: 5-15 pp recovery on truncation-type items, or recovery not concentrated on them; reported as a weak/ambiguous fix, while Exp. 1-4 (correlational required-depth + causal early-exit) still stand. Negative result: < 5 pp recovery or looping helping knowledge-type/converged items equally (i.e., generic corruption/help) refutes H4.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Logit-lens convergence depth can reflect the readout basis rather than genuine computation state; we validate with a tuned lens and require the causal early-exit (Exp. 5) and late-layer-looping (Exp. 6) results to promote the depth measurement to a functional claim. 2. Late-layer looping is an untied-weights hack the model was not trained for and may simply corrupt representations rather than 'continue' computation; we mitigate by reporting dose-response, specificity (already-converged items must be unharmed), and by comparing looping the last block vs random blocks; if looping helps only on high-required-depth truncation-type items and not on knowledge-type or converged items, that pattern is strong evidence regardless of the hack's crudeness. A negative looping result still leaves the correlational required-depth + causal early-exit findings intact. 3. Truncation and knowledge failure are entangled; the high-resource-language knowledge control (Exp. 7) is the crucial dissociator and central to the claim. 4. Distance and resource level are correlated; the dissociating language contrasts (Exp. 4) only partly separate them, and we report multiple resource proxies. 5. Right-censored (unconverged) trajectories are hard to distinguish from noise; we use stability criteria over the last several layers and report robustness to the convergence definition. 6. Answer matching across scripts is noisy; we use alias-aware, last-token/answer-span matching and report tokenization statistics. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families of differing depth address but do not exhaust generality, and the model-depth ablation directly tests the budget interpretation.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims are: (1) multilingual cross-lingual errors are caused by truncated concept computation under a fixed depth budget; (2) the required depth is systematically higher for low-resource/typologically distant languages on the same items; (3) errors can be causally reproduced by early exit and recovered by extra late-layer compute; (4) this deficit scales with distance/resource level. Relative to prior probing/representation work, the main delta is a causal compute-deadline framing plus a training-free intervention, not just layerwise correlation. The setting is new enough to make the claim non-obvious, though the ingredients are adjacent to existing depth-probing and looped-inference work.

Define 'required depth' more rigorously for non-monotonic trajectories and ambiguous cases; current stability criterion is vulnerable to noise.
Add an analysis of whether extra layers recover answers because of deeper computation or because of better answer-token re-scoring.

Name: implicit_prosody_attachment_gate
Title: The Inner Voice of the Machine: A Language-Set Implicit-Prosody Gate That Covertly Resolves Syntactic Ambiguity in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs, like silent human readers, compute an implicit prosodic phrasing over text (a default prosodic-boundary / metric structure) and use it to resolve prosody-sensitive syntactic ambiguities. Crucially the default phrasing is covertly set by the query language, so for the classic relative-clause (RC) attachment ambiguity the model resolves high (N1) vs low (N2) attachment differently across languages, mirroring the cross-linguistic prosodic split (e.g. English low-attaching vs Spanish/Croatian high-attaching). This implicit-prosody preference is carried by a locatable, causally-manipulable phrasing-boundary representation separable from the propositional content: steering a recovered prosodic-boundary direction flips attachment without changing the events or entities, and the effect scales with the query language's prosodic-boundary-length typology, not its resource level.
Related Work: The Implicit Prosody Hypothesis (IPH; Fodor 2002; Hirose 2003 [#10]; Breen 2014 [#15]) holds that silent readers impose a default, language-specific prosodic contour that biases syntactic attachment, and that this default differs cross-linguistically (English low-attaches, Spanish/Croatian high-attach)—the strongest known counterevidence to universal parsing. ERP and eye-tracking studies confirm implicit metric/prosodic structure during silent reading (Breen ERP 2019 [#13]; Croatian eye-tracking 2025 [#9]) and that it is prosodic, not mere character-length (deaf-reader controls 2006 [#11]). On the model side, BERT encodes prosodic prominence in middle layers from syntactic/semantic cues (What does BERT learn about prosody 2023 [#1]), transformers encode subphonemic/phonological features (Probing Subphonemes 2025 [#2]; character-embedding perceptual probes 2022 [#4]), and LLMs encode output-length as a disentangled, steerable attention signal (Length Representations 2025 [#3]). Multilingual RC-attachment behavior of LLMs has been noted only behaviorally in scattered work. However, NO prior work (i) tests the Implicit Prosody Hypothesis inside a text-only multilingual LLM, (ii) asks whether the query language covertly sets a default implicit prosodic phrasing that resolves syntactic ambiguity, or (iii) provides a causal, steerable implicit-prosody-boundary representation. Prior LLM prosody work probes prominence descriptively; prior IPH work is human psycholinguistics. We uniquely port the IPH cross-linguistic attachment paradigm into multilingual mechanistic interpretability, giving a causal (patching + steering) account and a prosody-typology-vs-resource dissociation.
Abstract: When silently reading 'Someone shot the servant of the actress who was on the balcony', readers must decide whether the relative clause modifies the servant (high attachment) or the actress (low attachment). A landmark psycholinguistic finding is that this decision differs across languages and is governed by an implicit prosody—a default, language-specific 'inner voice' phrasing imposed during silent reading. English readers prefer low attachment; Spanish and Croatian readers prefer high attachment. We ask whether multilingual LLMs, trained only on text, inherit this implicit-prosody mechanism and whether the query language covertly sets the default phrasing that resolves such ambiguities. We hypothesize that models compute an implicit prosodic-boundary structure over the input and use it to gate attachment, with the default boundary placement set by the query language, so the identical ambiguous sentence is attached high versus low depending on the language, tracking the documented cross-linguistic prosodic split. We build IMPLICIT-PROSODY, a controlled set of RC-attachment and other prosody-sensitive ambiguities (coordination scope, adverbial attachment) rendered across 12+ languages spanning long- vs short-prosodic-boundary typologies, with prosodic-length manipulations and character-length-matched controls that dissociate prosody from surface length. Behaviorally we measure per-language attachment distributions and their sensitivity to prosodic-length (not character-length) manipulation, mirroring human deaf-reader controls. Mechanistically we probe for an implicit prosodic-boundary representation, use activation patching to show it is causally responsible for attachment while the propositional content is unchanged, and steer a recovered boundary direction to flip attachment. We predict the effect scales with prosodic-boundary typology, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Dataset IMPLICIT-PROSODY (built from scratch, grounded in the psycholinguistic RC-attachment literature): prosody-sensitive ambiguities in three families - (a) RC-ATTACHMENT "N1 of N2 who/that RC" (150 items) where high (N1) vs low (N2) attachment is the classic case; (b) COORDINATION scope (100 items); (c) ADVERBIAL/PP attachment (100 items). For each item: a base ambiguous version, PROSODIC-LENGTH manipulations that lengthen N1 vs N2 in ways known to shift the implicit prosodic boundary, and CHARACTER-LENGTH-MATCHED controls that add characters without changing prosodic phrasing (a text analogue of the deaf-reader control). Each item pairs with an attachment diagnostic (gender/number agreement on the RC verb forcing N1 vs N2, or a comprehension question). Rendered across 12+ languages spanning LONG-boundary/high-attaching (Spanish, Croatian, German, Greek, Russian) and SHORT-boundary/low-attaching (English, Romanian, Norwegian, Arabic, Chinese) typologies, native-speaker-validated; low-agreement items dropped and reported. Per-language prosodic-boundary-typology index and a resource proxy (CC-100 share). Models (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference + steering, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 3 seeds (template and diagnostic order).

Experiment 1 (H2 - cross-linguistic attachment split set by query language). Tests whether the identical ambiguous structure is attached high vs low differently across languages, mirroring the human split. Decisive metric: per-language HIGH-ATTACHMENT RATE on the same RC structures, plus cross-language disagreement. Systems compared: high-attaching-typology vs low-attaching-typology languages; baselines query-in-English and translate-to-English-first. Convincing: high-attaching-typology languages attach high more often than low-attaching ones by >= 15 percentage points on identical items, in all three models. Indecision band: 5-15 pp; reported as a weak split, insufficient for a query-language-set default. Negative result: gap < 5 pp (uniform attachment, e.g. always English-like low) refutes H2 - though a documented uniform pattern is itself informative about whether LLMs inherit human implicit prosody.

Experiment 2 (H1 - the effect is prosodic, not surface length). Tests whether attachment shifts under PROSODIC-length manipulation but NOT under matched CHARACTER-length manipulation (establishing an implicit prosody is what resolves the ambiguity). Decisive metric: attachment-rate shift under prosodic-length manipulation vs under character-length-matched manipulation. Convincing: prosodic-length manipulation shifts attachment by >= 15 pp while the character-length-matched control shifts it by < 5 pp, holding tokenized length constant where possible. Indecision band: prosodic-vs-character shift difference 5-15 pp; reported as weak - prosody and length partly entangled. Negative result: character-length manipulation shifts attachment as much as prosodic-length manipulation refutes the prosodic reading (the effect is length/working-memory), undercutting H1.

Experiment 3 (H4 - attachment tracks prosodic typology, not resource). Tests whether the high-attachment rate (and its sensitivity to prosodic-length manipulation) scales with the prosodic-boundary-typology index rather than resource. Correlate both with the typology index and with the resource proxy; designed contrast: a lower-resource high-attaching language (Croatian) vs a higher-resource low-attaching one (English/Chinese). Decisive metric: Spearman of high-attachment rate with the typology index vs with resource (95% CIs), partialled for resource. Convincing: high-attachment rate correlates with the typology index (Spearman >= 0.4), surviving resource control. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.4 or vanishing after resource control; suggestive. Negative result: resource dominates and typology adds nothing refutes H4.

Experiment 4 (H1/H3 - a shared implicit prosodic-boundary representation whose placement varies by language). Tests whether the model represents a prosodic boundary whose placement differs by language. Train linear probes and read the logit lens at each layer to decode where the major boundary falls (e.g. before vs after N2) from mid-layer hidden states at the ambiguity region, using items where prosodic-length manipulation gives a known boundary; evaluate cross-lingual transfer. Contrast with a surface-position/character-count probe. Probes the only trainable parameters; base frozen; 3 probe-split seeds. Decisive metric: cross-lingual transfer accuracy of the boundary probe and whether its decoded placement matches each language's attachment preference. Convincing: the boundary probe transfers across languages with <= 10-point drop, its decoded placement predicts the language's attachment preference, and it outperforms the surface-length probe. Indecision band: transfer drop 10-20 points; partial support. Negative result: boundary probe near chance across languages (drop > 20 points) or not beating the surface-length probe refutes a shared abstract boundary representation.

Experiment 5 (H3 - causal, content-separable boundary representation). Tests whether patching/steering the boundary representation flips attachment while leaving entities/events unchanged. For an item attached high in a high-attaching language and low in a low-attaching one on the SAME structure: (a) activation-patch the mid-layer prosodic-boundary representation across runs and test whether attachment flips; specificity control = patching a content-region site (should not flip). (b) Recover a boundary direction (mean activation difference between high-boundary and low-boundary runs, pooled across languages/conditions) and steer to INDUCE high attachment in a low-attaching language and low attachment in a high-attaching one, over a dose-response. Model frozen; patching/steering at inference; compare against explicit "read with a pause after N2" prompting and translate-first. Decisive metric: attachment-flip rate from boundary patching/steering (reported first), with content-preservation specificity (entities/events unchanged), fluency (perplexity), and the content-region control alongside. Convincing: boundary patching/steering flips attachment in >= 50% of items with a monotone steering dose-response, the content-region patch flips < 15%, content is preserved, and < 5% perplexity increase. Indecision band: flip rate 25-50% or non-monotone dose; weak causal handle. Negative result: flip rate < 25%, or content-region patching flips attachment as much (non-specific), refutes H3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. The behavioral cross-linguistic split might not replicate in LLMs at all (models may attach uniformly, e.g. always low/English-like); this would refute the query-language-default claim but is itself an informative, publishable result about whether LLMs inherit human implicit prosody. 2. Attachment could be driven by frequency/semantic plausibility rather than implicit prosody; we use semantically balanced (either-attachment-plausible) items and the prosodic-vs-character-length dissociation (Exp. 3) is the crucial control isolating prosody from length/memory, directly mirroring the human deaf-reader control. 3. Probe decodability of a 'prosodic boundary' may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 6) and steering induction (Exp. 7) with content-preservation specificity are required to promote correlation to mechanism, and the boundary probe is contrasted against a surface-length probe. 4. Diagnosing intended attachment across languages is nontrivial; we use agreement-forced or comprehension-question diagnostics validated by native speakers and restrict to high-agreement items. 5. The prosodic-typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts (Croatian vs English/Chinese); we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the typology-index operationalization. 6. Tokenization differs across scripts and may itself alter effective 'length', confounding the length control; we hold tokenized length constant where possible in the character-matched condition and report tokenization statistics. 7. Steering may trade attachment change for fluency or content preservation; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families across multiple ambiguity types address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty is in testing the Implicit Prosody Hypothesis inside multilingual text-only LLMs and claiming a causal, steerable prosodic-boundary representation that is set by query language. The setting/mechanism is plausibly new, but the underlying phenomenon (cross-linguistic RC attachment + prosody) is established, and the closest prior LM work already suggests English-like attachment only. The main delta is mechanistic and cross-linguistic, not a wholly new task or theory.
