Name: aspectual_completion_gate
Title: Did It Finish, or Was It Just Happening? How the Query Language's Aspect System Covertly Sets a Default Completion Interpretation in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Languages differ in how obligatorily they mark whether an event is completed vs ongoing (perfective/imperfective, presence vs absence of a grammaticalized perfect). We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs compute a shared, language-agnostic representation of an event's abstract completion state, but resolve whether an underspecified event counts as COMPLETED (endpoint reached, result achieved) through a scalar 'completion-inference' gate whose default is covertly set by the query language's aspect system. Consequently the identical event description yields opposite completed-vs-ongoing inferences across languages, this gap scales with the query language's aspectual-grammaticalization distance from the dominant language (not resource level), and it is carried by a locatable, steerable representation separable from the propositional content.
Related Work: Probing work shows transformers encode telicity/duration/aspect, mostly in final layers, and are biased by tense/word order (About Time 2022; Probing Verbal Aspect in Russian 2024; Do pretrained transformers infer telicity like humans 2021), that tense/aspect are orthogonal, steerable directions (Steering Tense and Aspect 2025), that tense is easy in morphologically-marked languages but hard in Chinese (Multilingual Probe for Tense 2021), and that LLMs fail cross-linguistic perfect-aspect NLI in Chinese/Japanese (LLMs Struggle with NLI for Perfect Aspect 2025). Complement-coercion work studies event recovery (Norwegian 2025). Psycholinguistics shows telicity is encoded differently across languages yet event tracking is similar (Do Cross-Linguistic Differences Influence Event Perception 2024). Crucially, ALL LLM aspect work either (i) probes/steers the surface aspect FEATURE within one language, or (ii) measures behavioral NLI failure, and treats the surface aspect as the target. NONE dissociates a shared abstract COMPLETION-STATE representation from a language-conditioned completion-INFERENCE gate, tests whether the query language causally sets whether an underspecified event is read as finished vs ongoing (biasing downstream semantic/entailment judgments), or provides a causal, steerable completion gate with an aspectual-typology-vs-resource dissociation. My prior tense proposal targeted reference-TIME (past/present/future); this targets a distinct axis: COMPLETION/boundedness. We uniquely port grammatical-aspect typology into multilingual mechanistic interpretability, and add a safety-critical task-completion instantiation.
Abstract: Whether an event is finished ('she was building a house' vs 'she built a house') is marked very differently across languages: Slavic and Romance grammars obligatorily encode perfective vs imperfective, English grammaticalizes the perfect, while Chinese, Indonesian and others leave completion largely to inference. A competent multilingual model must nonetheless recover the same abstract completion state and, when a description is underspecified, decide whether the event counts as completed. We ask whether the language a question is asked in covertly makes that decision. We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs compute a shared, language-agnostic completion-state representation but resolve underspecification through a completion-inference gate whose default is set by the query language's aspect system, so the identical event yields opposite completed-vs-ongoing readings across languages. We build ASPECT-GATE, controlled event descriptions whose completion is underspecified, paired with entailment questions that distinguish a completed from an ongoing reading (e.g., 'Is the house finished?'), rendered across 12+ languages spanning perfective/imperfective, perfect-marking, and aspect-lax typologies, with completion-forcing and completion-neutral controls. Behaviorally we measure per-language completion-inference rate on identical events. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared completion-state direction that transfers across languages including aspect-lax ones; (ii) use activation patching to show the completion state is computed similarly while a separable gate differs by language; and (iii) recover and steer a completion-inference direction to flip readings without changing the events. We include a safety-relevant subset (inferring whether an instruction/action was actually carried out) where under- or over-inference of completion causes an agent to falsely report task success. We predict the gap tracks aspectual-typology distance, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Dataset ASPECT-GATE (built from scratch): 300 event descriptions whose COMPLETION is underspecified (no overt endpoint marker), each paired with a yes/no entailment question distinguishing a completed reading (endpoint reached, result state holds) from an ongoing one (event in progress) - accomplishment verbs (build/write/cross/paint) with quantized vs bare objects, plus resultative and durative variants - across a difficulty gradient, with clearly-completed and clearly-ongoing controls that should agree across languages. Rendered in 12+ languages spanning three aspectual types: PERFECTIVE/IMPERFECTIVE-grammaticalized (Russian, Polish, Spanish, French, Greek), PERFECT-marking (English, German), and ASPECT-LAX/inference-based (Chinese, Indonesian, Thai, Vietnamese). Native-speaker-validated (two per language), translations checked not to insert completion cues; low-agreement items dropped and reported. Per-language aspectual-grammaticalization index (obligatory perfective/imperfective > perfect auxiliary > lexical/pragmatic only) and a resource proxy (CC-100 share). Models (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference + steering, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 3 seeds (template and question order).

Experiment 1 (H3 - cross-language completion-inference gap on identical events). Tests whether the identical underspecified event yields opposite completed-vs-ongoing readings across languages. Decisive metric: per-language COMPLETION-INFERENCE RATE (fraction read as completed) on identical items, plus cross-language disagreement; controls (clearly completed/ongoing) must agree across languages. Systems compared: across the three aspectual types; baselines query-in-English and translate-to-English-first. Convincing: completion-inference rate differs across aspectual-type groups by >= 15 percentage points on identical items while controls agree within 5 pp, in all three models. Indecision band: 5-15 pp difference; reported as a weak language effect. Negative result: gap < 5 pp (language-invariant completion inference) refutes H3 - though documenting faithful language-invariant handling is itself informative.

Experiment 2 (H4 - gap tracks aspectual typology, not resource). Tests whether the gap scales with aspectual-grammaticalization distance rather than resource. Regress per-language completion-inference rate (deviation from the English baseline) on the grammaticalization index and on the resource proxy; designed contrast: a lower-resource strongly-aspectual language (Polish) vs a higher-resource aspect-lax one (Chinese). Decisive metric: Spearman with the grammaticalization index vs with resource (95% CIs), partialled for resource. Convincing: the rate correlates with the grammaticalization index (Spearman >= 0.4), surviving resource control. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.4 or vanishing after resource control; suggestive. Negative result: resource dominates and typology adds nothing refutes H4.

Experiment 3 (H1 - shared, language-agnostic completion-state representation). Tests whether the abstract completion state is represented consistently across languages, including aspect-lax ones. Train linear probes and read the logit lens at each layer to decode the completion state (completed vs ongoing) from mid-layer hidden states on held-out items; evaluate cross-lingual transfer. Contrast with a surface-aspect-morphology probe. Probes the only trainable parameters; base frozen; 3 probe-split seeds. Decisive metric: cross-lingual transfer accuracy of the completion-state probe, including onto aspect-lax languages. Convincing: the probe transfers with <= 10-point drop off in-language accuracy and stays well above chance on aspect-lax languages, dissociating from the surface-aspect probe (which does not carry the state there). Indecision band: transfer drop 10-20 points; partial support. Negative result: probe near chance across languages (drop > 20 points) refutes the shared-state claim (H1).

Experiment 4 (H2 - a language-set completion gate over a shared state). Tests whether the cross-language difference is a gating step over an equally-present state rather than a different completion computation. For an item read completed in language A but ongoing in language B on the SAME event: (a) activation-patch the mid-layer completion-state representation across runs and confirm it is present in both (patching changes the answer little); (b) patch/steer the late components carrying the completion decision and test whether the interpretation flips. Specificity control = a matched non-gate site. Model frozen; patching at inference. Decisive metric: interpretation-flip rate from late-gate patching (reported first), with state-patch flip (should be low) and matched-site flip as controls. Convincing: late-gate patching flips >= 50% of items, state patching alone flips < 15% (state already present in both), and the matched site flips < 15%. Indecision band: gate-patch flip 25-50% or state-patch flip 15-30% (state partly different); mixed evidence. Negative result: gate-patch flip < 25% or state patching itself flips (a different state computation) refutes the language-set-gate account (H2).

Experiment 5 (H5 - a steerable completion-inference direction separable from content). Tests whether a recovered completion-inference direction induces/suppresses completed readings without changing the event. Recover the direction as the mean activation difference between completed-reading and ongoing-reading runs, pooled across languages; steer to (a) INDUCE a completed reading in an aspect-lax/imperfective-defaulting language and (b) SUPPRESS it (force ongoing) in a perfective-defaulting one, over a dose-response. Model frozen; only the vector varies; compare against explicit "assume the action is finished/still ongoing" prompting and translate-first. Decisive metric: induced/suppressed completion rate (reported first), with propositional-content specificity (the event/entities unchanged), fluency (perplexity), and output-language fidelity alongside. Convincing: steering shifts the completion rate by >= 15 pp in each direction with a monotone dose-response, preserved content, and < 5% perplexity increase. Indecision band: 5-15 pp shift or non-monotone dose; weak handle. Negative result: < 5 pp shift or only at content/fluency-breaking doses refutes H5.

Experiment 6 (H3 - safety-critical instantiation: multilingual task-completion inference). Tests the same completion-inference gap in an agentic setting where under- or over-inference makes a model falsely report task success. Build a 100-item subset (from scratch, same schema) describing whether an action was carried out ("The system was applying the patch" vs "applied the patch"), rendered across the same 12+ languages. Measure per-language whether the model reports the task DONE vs IN-PROGRESS, and whether steering the gate (Exp. 5) repairs mis-inferences. Model frozen. Decisive metric: cross-lingual FALSE-COMPLETION gap (falsely reporting success) on identical descriptions, and its reduction under gate steering. Convincing: the false-completion gap across aspectual types is >= 15 pp on identical items and gate steering reduces it by >= 10 pp without harming fluency, confirming the gap is a reliability hazard driven by the same gate. Indecision band: 5-15 pp gap or 5-10 pp repair; reported as a minor reliability effect. Negative result: gap < 5 pp (agentic completion reporting is language-invariant) means the phenomenon does not surface in this safety-relevant setting, bounding H3's practical reach.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of a 'completion state' or 'completion gate' may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering induce/suppress (Exp. 6) tests with content-preservation specificity are required to promote correlation to mechanism. 2. Whether an underspecified event is 'completed' can be genuinely ambiguous and gradient; we restrict to native-speaker-validated high-agreement items and include clear completed/ongoing controls. 3. Cross-lingual differences might reflect genuine aspectual-norm variation rather than a gate artifact; the shared-completion-state probe transfer and the state-same/gate-differs patching test are designed to separate a different completion computation from a pure interpretation-strength shift, and translations are validated to avoid inadvertently inserting completion cues. 4. The typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts (Polish vs Chinese); we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the grammaticalization-index operationalization. 5. Strong models may infer completion faithfully per language, shrinking the default cross-language effect; even documenting faithful language-specific aspect handling (a clean shared-state + language-set-gate architecture) is a positive result, and the induction/suppression steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 6. The surface-aspect feature and abstract completion state nearly coincide in strongly-aspectual languages; the aspect-lax languages and the underspecified/neutral conditions are the crucial dissociating cases. 7. Tokenization of aspect morphology varies across scripts; we use verb-final/clause-final or pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics; perfective/imperfective vs perfect vs lexical cases analyzed separately. 8. Steering may trade interpretation change for fluency or content preservation; we report both. 9. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) multilingual LLMs encode a shared abstract completion state; (2) query language sets a covert completion-inference gate for underspecified events; (3) the effect tracks aspectual typology more than resource level; (4) the gate/state can be causally dissociated by patching/steering; (5) a safety-relevant task-completion failure follows. The first two are not just surface aspect probing; the mechanistic state-vs-gate split and language-conditioned default reading are the main novelty. Closest prior family is cross-lingual perfect-aspect NLI, telicity probes, and aspect steering; the actual delta is moving from behavioral failure or surface-feature decoding to a causal latent-variable hypothesis with cross-lingual dissociation. This is non-trivial, though some behavioral territory is adjacent and the model could still collapse into a dressed-up cross-lingual NLI study.

impact.reasoning: Problem under study: how multilingual LLMs resolve underspecified event completion across languages, and whether they falsely infer task success. Who cares: multilingual NLP, interpretability, and agentic reliability/safety. Strongest one-line case: if query language can silently flip completion judgments, multilingual assistants may report 'done' when work is only in progress. Important and usable, with clear downstream relevance for cross-lingual evaluation and safety-critical agents. The 'so what?' test is moderately positive: if true, researchers would likely care because it exposes a real cross-lingual reliability failure and a mechanistic handle; if false, it still informs what multilingual models do not encode. Impact is limited somewhat by the niche nature of aspectual semantics and by the possibility that effects are mostly annotation/linguistic ambiguity rather than broadly generalizable model behavior.

review.reasoning: The proposal is promising but currently over-ambitious and under-specified in the key causal claims. Main gaps: 'completion-inference gate' is metaphorical unless operationalized precisely; patching a 'late gate component' may be hard to localize; shared-state vs gate separation may be confounded with readout artifacts; and the dataset is described at a high level without enough detail on ambiguity control, annotation protocol, or item construction. The hypothesis is falsifiable in principle, but the experiments need stronger controls: same-item translation quality checks, human agreement thresholds, counterfactual minimal pairs, calibration for tokenization and prompt effects, and explicit baselines against simple language-ID or surface morphology predictors. The related work is decent but should be more specific about what each prior paper tested and why it is insufficient. With careful execution this could reach a serious ML venue, but as written it reads more like a compelling program than a submission-ready study.
